As already stated hereinbefore, three suits, namely: Title Suit Nos.51 of 2004, 176 of 2004 and 81 of 2006, were disposed of by separate judgments and decrees by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka, although there was only one set of evidence in each suit. And we propose to proceed serially according to the number of the suit. 

 27. Title Suit No. 51 of 2004: 

 The trial Court dismissed the suit. One of the findings on which the trial Court dismissed the suit, was that the suit plot was allotted to Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, a BSc Engineer of 157, Bara Moghbazar and not to Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur and that at the time of allotment, he was the Executive Engineer of C&B, Dhaka and he joined the Department in 1952. In coming to the said finding, the trial Court relied upon exhibit-‘ড’, the letter dated 29-10-1966, issued by the then DIT to Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar giving permission to carry on with the proposed construction on the suit plot. The trial Court also relied upon the testimony of PW 2 Shammima Zaman, daughter of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar and PW5-Dr Md Arifur Rahman, her husband who was the principal of National Medical College (they were examined in Title Suit No.81 of 2006 and their depositions were adopted in Title Suit No.51 of 2004) and DW 1 who was examined in Title Suit No.176 of 2004 on behalf of RAJUK. The trial Court came to the further finding that the plaintiff could not file any document to show that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur was a BSc Engineer and Executive Engineer in C&B. From the plaint, it was clear that the address of defendant No.1, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza was given at House No.31, Lane No.6, Section 6/ A, Mirpur, Dhaka. Plaintiff, MA Hashem, in his deposition as PW 1, admitted that as defendant No 1 was not registering the sale deed in respect of the suit plot, he through his lawyer issued a legal notice to him on 20-12-2003 who duly received the same. The trial Court observed that question could not arise that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, a BSc Engineer, who joined Bengal Development Company as Director after leaving the job of C&B and subsequently, became a Director of Uttara Bank Limited, would construct a house atMirpur and reside there. The trial Court came to the further specific finding that the plaintiff on 29-12-2002 entered into the agreement for purchasing the suit plot with Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur, who was not the allottee of the suit plot. Plaintiff, MA Hashem, in the written statement filed in Title Suit No.81 of 2006 (he was defendant No.1 in the suit) clearly asserted that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar was the original allottee, but he as a witness deposed that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur was the allottee of the suit plot and the Court observed that “তাহা হইলে বাদী এম এ হাশেম সাহেব নিজেই সম্পত্তির মূল বরাদ্ধ গ্রহীতার বিষয়ে দুই রকম বক্তব্য প্রদান করিতেছে”।  The two other witnesses examined by the plaintiff were none, but his employees. The trial Court further noticed that DWI (Abu Bakkar Siddique examined on behalf of RAJUK in Title Suit No.176 of 2004) stated in his evidence that the suit plot was a residential plot and an application was filed to convert the same as an industrial plot. The DW further stated that letter was issued to Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza on 14-8-2001 to deposit a sum of Taka 38,28,125 as a conversion fee and pursuant to the said letter, he deposited a sum of Taka 38,28,125 on 25-9-2001. Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza filed an application to RAJUK on 26-9-2001 to accept the said transfer fees. The application for conversion of the suit plot and the letter written by Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza were proved by DWI as exhibits ‘ণ’ and ‘থ’. The trial Court further found that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza gave power of attorney to Eastern Housing Limited to do all acts in respect of the suit plot (in Bangla it has been written নলিশি সম্পত্তির যাবতীয় কার্য পরিচালনার জন্য) and to accept the said power of attorney, he filed an application to RAJUK on 24-12-2003 and RAJUK approved the power of attorney on 5-1-2004 and the said letter was filed and proved and marked as exhibit ‘ন’. There was no paper with RAJUK to show that application was filed to it for permission to sell the suit plot by Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur. The trial Court concluded that the plaintiff did not enter into the agreement on 29-12-2002 with the original allottee to purchase the suit plot, so his suit for specific performance of contract was not maintainable. 

 28. Title Suit No.176 of 2004: 

 The trial Court dismissed the suit on the findings, inter alia, that plaintiff, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, was not the original allottee, therefore, RAJUK could not give permission to him to sell the suit plot and that RAJUK recognized Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar as the allottee of the suit plot and also approved Eastern Housing Limited as his attorney; the plaintiff's suit was not maintainable. In coming to the said findings, the trial Court held that the suit plot was allotted to Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, who was the Executive Engineer of C&B and that RS khatian No.1174 in respect of the suit plot was recorded in the name of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar; plaintiff, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza as PW 1 in his cross-examination clearly stated that he never resided at 157, Bara Moghbazar and while he deposed, he was residing at 911/1 Shewrapara as a tenant of one Monowara; the suit plot was allotted to Executive Engineer, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza and admittedly the plaintiff was Diploma Engineer and therefore, it was not believable that he could join a big Department like C&B as Assistant Engineer in 1950/1952 and was promoted as the Executive Engineer in 1956/57 and therefore, it could not be accepted that the plaintiff got the allotment of the suit plot as Executive Engineer. The trial Court further noticed that PW 1 (Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza) admitted in his cross- examination that in 1965, he was a voter at Ishwardi and after liberation of Bangladesh, he participated in an election at Fulbaria under the district of Dinajpur, which was not believable, asit was not natural that a person, who served as an Executive Engineer, would go to an Upazila and participate in the election. The trial Court further observed that it was not natural that a person, who became the Executive Engineer, would live at Pabna, then at Dinajpur and then in Dhaka. The trial Court further observed that it was also not believable that a person, who got a plot from RAJUK at Gulshan, would reside at Ishwardi in the district of Pabna and then at Fulbaria in the district of Dinajpur. Although the plaintiff claimed that he accepted domicile certificate but that was not with him. The trial Court further observed that the plaintiff in his cross-examination admitted that though he served as an Executive Engineer in C&B, he did not open any bank account, which also proved that he was not an Executive Engineer, because the salary of a first class employee is given through cheque and in the absence of bank account, he could not draw his salary. The trial Court further noticed that the plaintiff admitted in his cross-examination that he had gone to India in 1958 and married his cousin (খালাতো বোন) at 'Arai' in India. The trial Court noticed that a person, who migrated to this country, in 1947 and was a high official in C&B, could not go to India without the permission of his office or the Government for marrying there. PW2, a guard of Sonali Bank, Motijheel Branch, was disbelieved by the trial Court on the ground that when the plaintiff admitted that he had no bank account, it was not believable that he would be acquainted with a guard of Sonali Bank. The trial Court also observed that it was not natural that the plaintiff, who claimed to be an Executive Engineer, would develop a relationship with a guard of a bank. The trial Court disbelieved PW 3 on the ground that he deposed that he got himself acquainted with the plaintiff through one of the relative, namely, Shamim; when PWI in his cross-examination admitted that he had no relative in this country. (PWs 2 and 3 were examined to prove plaintiff's possession in the suit plot.) The trial Court relied on the evidence of DW1, an official of RAJUK that no application was filed by the plaintiff, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, to RAJUK for permission to sell the suit plot to MNH Bulu and that no application was filed by the plaintiff to RAJUK on 18-2-2004 to sell the suit plot. The trial Court further held that RAJUK did not recognize the plaintiff of the instant suit as the allottee of the suit plot, rather RAJUK admitted Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar as the allottee and approved the power of attorney given by him to Eastern Housing Limited. 

 29. Title Suit No.81 of 2006: 

 The trial Court decreed the suit on the findings, inter alia, that the plaintiffs proved conclusively that the suit plot was allotted to Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar; Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Bara Moghbazar after obtaining permission from RAJUK vide letter dated 29-10-1996, exhibit-16(ka) (the letter was also proved by DW1 in Title Suit No.176 of 2004 as exhibit-V) constructed building on the suit plot by mortgaging the same with the House Building Finance Corporation as apparent from exhibit-'17', the loan sanction letter dated 2-3-1967 issued by the House Building Finance Corporation and had been in possession of the building by letting out the same to various tenants vide exhibit-'18 series. The trial Court further observed that the first tenancy agreement was entered into in 1967 wherein the address of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza was written as 157, Bara Moghbazar and in all the subsequent tenancy agreements his address was also written as 157, Bara Moghbazar. The trial Court further found that the plaintiff of Title Suit No.176 of 2004, who was impleaded in the instant suit (Title Suit No.81 of 2006) as defendant No.3, stated in his examination-in-chief as PW1 that he was residing at 911/1 East Sheurapara, Thana Kafrul and in cross-examination, he stated that he never resided at 157, Bara Moghbazar. The trial Court came to further finding that as per own admission, defendant No.3 (plaintiff of Title suit No.176 of 2004) neither resided at Bara Moghbazar nor at the suit plot, but he claimed to have prayed for permission to sell the suit plot. The trial Court further noticed that PW1 (Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza examined in Title Suit No.176 of 2004) stated in his examination-in-chief that he had no issue and that though he got the domicile certificate, but he would not be able to file the same as the same was not with him. The trial Court concluded by saying that defendant No.3, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza was not the owner of the suit plot and that the plaintiffs' father Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza was the owner thereof and had the right, title and possession therein and after his death, the plaintiffs became its owners. The trial Court further noticed that defendant No.1 in his written statement admitted that the plaintiffs father was the owner of the suit plot and thus admitted the plaint case. The trial Court further noticed that in the agreement for sale between defendant No.1 and Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, his address was mentioned at the suit plot and at present Mirpur, whereas the owner of the suit plot was Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence of MA Hashem examined in Title Suit No.51 of 2004 further held that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur neither being the allottee of the suit plot nor being in possession thereof, the agreement, even if, entered into by him with defendant No.1 was not "Executable". The trial Court also found that DW 1 (examined in Title Suit No.176 of 2004 on behalf of RAJUK) clearly admitted in his deposition that in the Nathi of RAJUK, only the names of the plaintiffs were mutated. The trial Court further held that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit plot and after the death of their father, Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar, became its owner. The trial Court came to further finding that RS record of the suit plot was recorded in the name of the plaintiffs predecessor, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, wherein his address has been clearly mentioned as 157, Bara Moghbazar which fact also confirmed that he was the allottee of the suit plot and since defendant No.1 entered into a contract with fake Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur without permission of RAJUK and claimed possession in the suit plot and thus also posed threat to the plaintiffs' possession therein as well as their title, their suit as framed was maintainable and they were entitled to get the relief prayed for in the suit. 

 This leave petition has been filed against the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No.357 of 2009, which was preferred against the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No.51 of 2004. The suit was dismissed by the trial Court. The learned presiding Judge formulated two points for decision: (a) whether the plaintiff entered into the agreement "with false person in the name of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza" and (b) whether the plaintiff proved the necessary ingredients to get the decree for specific performance of contract. The learned Judge on consideration of the evidence on record and the order sheets of the suit, particularly, from 8-2-2004 to 15-7-2004, came to the specific findings that the plaintiff entered into agreement with Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur and he filed the suit for specific performance of contract against him. Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur was not the actual allottee of the suit plot and it was Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar who was the actual allottee and he died on 2-2-2004, i.e. six days before filing of the suit (the suit was filed on 8-2-2004). The learned Judge noticed that on 18-3-2004, the plaintiff filed an application for temporary injunction for restraining defendant No.1 (Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza) and defendant No.2 (Akhtaruzzaman, Director, Eastern Housing Ltd.) from changing the nature and character of the suit plot, in any manner, (although Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar died on 2-2-2004) and the Court by order dated 25-3-2004 issued notices upon the defendants to show cause as to why an order of temporary injunction should not be granted. Considering the order sheets from 8-2-2004 up to 15-7-2004, the learned Judge observed that the plaintiff did not take any step in the suit either for substituting or adding the heirs of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar which indicated that the plaintiff entered into the agreement with Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur and filed the suit against him. And had the plaintiff-MA Hashem, accepted defendant Nos. l(a) to l(c) as the heirs of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar than he would not have moved the High Court Division against the order passed by the learned Additional District Judge, T" Court, Dhaka in Civil Revision No.358 of 2004 adding them as the heirs of late Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza. The learned Judge further noticed that on an application filed by defendant No.2 (name has been mentioned hereinbefore) for the personal appearance of defendant No.1, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur, the learned Joint District Judge by order dated 27-5-2004 directed the plaintiff to produce defendant No.1, but he failed to produce him in Court and till that time (27-5-2004), the plaintiff did not accept Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar as his vendor. The learned Judge further observed "As I find his presence in the suit after six months of filing of the suit and thereafter he disappeared and the plaintiff could not or did not satisfy the Court by producing any documents that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, defendant No.1 resides at Bara Moghbazar at any point of time." The plaintiff made prayer for specific performance of contract from defendant No.1 and also for a direction upon him to obtain necessary sale permission from RAJUK in his favour and had he disowned defendant No.1 than after substitution or addition of defendant Nos.1(a)-1(e), the prayer and other incidental statements of the plaint ought to have been amended, but the plaintiff did not amend the plaint which showed that till hearing, he claimed original defendant No.1, i.e. Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur as his vendor. The learned Judge held that "Thereby it can safely be concluded that so called bainapatra or agreement for sale was entered into by plaintiff with the per- son whom the plaintiff by his own act sometime did and sometime did not recognize as his vendor as plaintiff allowed defendant Nos. 1 (a) to 1(e) to substitute in place of defendant No.1 who did not recognize defendant No.1 as their father as defendant Nos. 1 (a) to 1(e) did not step aside from their original position that they are not substituted heirs of defendant No.1 of Mirpur but they are the heirs of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Magbazar against whom the suit has not been filed and no agreement or bainapatra was arrived at by plaintiff." 

 32. The learned Judge further held that from the conduct of the plaintiff, it was clear that he, in order to grab the suit plot at a meager price of Taka 1,65,00,000, sometime accepted Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur as his vendor and sometime Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Bara Magbazar as his vendor and having dilemma lastly "gulped" Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Sara Moghbazar as his vendor by accepting the heirs added/substituted in place of defendant No.1, but without amending the material statements or prayer of the plaint. The learned Judge further observed that the agreement was entered into on 29-12-2001 in between MA Hashem (the plaintiff) and Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur and in the plaint, the address of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza was given at House No.31, Lane 6, Section 6/1, Mirpur, Dhaka, although from the protest notice published in the daily Janakantha and the corrigendum thereto, it appeared that before filing the suit, the plaintiff could know that the address of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza was 157, Bara Moghbazar, Dhaka. The learned Judge considering the agreement, the evidence of the PWs and the letter allegedly written by the plaintiff to defendant No.1, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur and the legal notices issued by his lawyer on his behalf (exhibits 8/1, 8/2, 9/1, 10/1,10/2,11/1, 11/2) held that the execution of bainapatra was suspicious and that no money was transacted and when there was doubt as to the payment of earnest money, decree for specific performance of contract could not be passed. In this regard, the learned Judge referred to the evidence of PW1, MA Hashem that he would not produce supporting documents "in the matter of passing of earnest money." The learned Judge further observed that on the question of possession, the plaintiff did not "state a single word in his plaint as to whether he was inducted into possession or not, although exhibit-2 was entered on 29-12-2002." The learned presiding Judge further observed that in the plaint, the plaintiff stated that he went to the suit property on 22-12-2003 and found that some people were taking step for construction upon removal of the old structure, but there was no explanation "as to the fact that old structure belonged to whom". The plaintiff did not also inform the matter to defendant No.1 with whom he allegedly entered into the contract or to RAJUK, the lessor, either any GD entry was made or any legal proceeding was taken about the matter and he kept mum till filing the suit on 8-2-2004, i.e. about 8( eight) months from the said date. The learned Judge further observed that in the bainapatra and also in the deposition of PWI, it has been mentioned that all the original papers and documents, i.e. allotment letter of DIT (exhibit-I), standard lease agreement of DIT (exhibit-2), payment of installment receipts from National Bank (exhibit-3) were handed over to the plaintiff; defendant Nos. 1 (a) to 1(e) produced before the Court 28 original deeds documents of them exhibits 1 to 5 "in original copies produced, proved and exhibited in the suit. Plaintiff after finding that original deeds were produced from the side of defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(e) did not challenge as to genuinity of them at least, exhibits 1 to 5 of the defendants documents ought to be challenged but he did not." In the concluding paragraph, the learned Judge gave the finding that the "plaintiff's case for specific performance of contract is totally a hopeless case." 

 33. The learned second Judge, while dismissing the appeal, gave clear finding that it was manifest that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur and Engineer Md Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Gulshan was not the same person and that the dispute regarding the title of the suit plot was started before "expiry of the Engineer Md Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza who died on 2-2-2004", whereas the plaintiff filed the suit on 8-2-2004 impleading defendant No.2, Akhtaruzzaman, a Director of Eastern Housing Limited, as the attorney of late Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza showing defendant No.1 as his vendor. The learned second Judge noticed that on 20-3-2004, 3rd party, i.e. the heirs of late Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, filed an application in the suit under Order I, rule 10 of the Code of the Civil Procedure for adding them as defendants in the suit as his heirs and not to substitute them in place of defendant No.1 stating that they got the information that the suit was filed by the plaintiff on the basis of false bainapatra created by him with fictitious person having no title and interest and possession in the suit plot, but the learned Joint District Judge by his order dated 15-7-2004 allowed the application for addition of party, not as the third party, but as the heirs of defendant No.1. The learned Judge also considered the fact that on 23-3-2004, the plaintiff by filing a fresh vokalatnama prayed for hearing the application for temporary injunction filed on 18- 3-2004 and the Court on hearing the application issued notices upon defendant Nos.1 and 2 to show cause as to why an order of temporary injunction should not be granted and on 27-5- 2004 defendant Nos.1 and 2 filed hajira and then again concluded that "So, from the record and conduct of the plaintiff it was crystal clear that defendant No.1, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur and Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157 Bara Maghbazar is not the same and one person." Considering the evidence of PW1 (the plaintiff) the learned Judge came to the findings that "it is further manifest" that the plaintiff at the time of filing the suit and sometime after, did not admit rather denied the existence, right, title and possession of Engineer Md Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Bara Moghbazar, later on only to escape and justify his earlier false activities admitted "with a device that defendant Nos.1(a) to 1(e) are the legal heirs of defendant No.1, i.e. Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur" by substituting them. The plaintiff neither made a contract for purchasing the suit plot with a genuine person nor the documents submitted in Court were genuine and on the basis of those documents, he could not get decree for specific performance of contract and that the total case of the plaintiff was nothing but a got-up story only to grab the suit plot on the basis of forged deed and papers with the help of a fake person. The plaintiff failed to prove his alleged bainapatra and part payment of consideration money. The learned Judge disbelieved PWs 2 and 3 on the finding that they being employees of the plaintiff could not but oblige their master. The learned Judge also took adverse presumption against the plaintiff for non-examination of a vital and important witness, namely, Shawkat Ali, who figured as a witness in the bainapatra and lived in the same holding with defendant No.1, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza at Mirpur. In this regard, the learned Judge further opined that the identity of defendant No.1 could only be clarified by Shawkat Ali, who is also a relative of the plaintiff. The learned Judge concluded that "plaintiff not only failed to prove his own case but produced some forged and fabricated deeds and papers because from the facts and circumstances it (sic) clear that plaintiff PW.1 produced the exhibit 1,2, 3, 4 and 5 in the court showing his vendor as custodian of those exhibit's who failed to appear before the court and from the materials on record it is proved that he is none but a fake person. So, exhibit "6" (the agreement) is nothing but obviously the creation of forgery only to grab the suit property. Furthermore, the defence story and facts as set forth are quite believable not only by' oral evidences, however, facts and circumstances with possession and documentary evidences, as find support from the testimony of PWs of title suit No.81 of 2006 which has been adopted in this case with the consent of all the parties." 

 This petition has been filed by the plaintiff, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Title Suit No.176 of 2004 against the judgment and decree passed in First Appeal No.327 of 2009 which was filed against the judgment and decree passed in the said suit. In this appeal, the learned presiding Judge formulated only one point for determination namely, "whether there was any application pending before the defendants to be considered by RAJUK." It may be stated that in the suit 4(four) persons, namely: the Chairman, RAJUK, (ii) the Member (Estate) (iii) RAJUK, (iv) the Deputy Director (Estate), RAJUK were impleaded as defendants. In the context, it is necessary to state that plaintiff, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, filed the suit for the principal relief as under: 

 "A. Pass a decree in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendants declaring that the plaintiff is legally entitled to get sale permission and the defendants are also bound to issue sale permission in respect of the scheduled property by receiving the proper transfer fees from the plaintiff as per rule of RAJUK." 

 36. The learned second Judge considering the evidence of the plaintiff as PW1 came to the finding that though PW 1 (Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza) claimed that he was an Executive Engineer, his testimony regarding service book, ACR and organogram clearly proved that he was not a service holder at all. In coming to the said finding, the learned Judge observed that "He stated that he was executive engineer but could not understand the ACR and organogram." The learned Judge came to further finding that the documents filed by the plaintiff exhibited in the suit clearly showed that those were prepared in the name of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar, which was admittedly the permanent address of Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, a different person. The learned Judge further held that the suit of the plaintiff for sale permission simplicity to sell the suit plot was not maintainable as he himself admitted in the plaint as well as in his deposition that he was out of possession and that Title Suit No.81 of 2006 filed by the heirs of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar for declaration of title and permanent injunction heard simultaneously by the same Court (the plaintiff was defendant No.3 in the suit) was decreed. The learned Judge rejected the objection raised by Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan who also appeared before the High Court Division that the trial Court erred in law "in adopting the evidence of PW1 as a (sic) evidence of DW1 in the respective cases" as such adoption was done in violation of section 33 of the Evidence Act, on the view that the said section had no manner of application as the plaintiff of both suits, i.e. Title Suit Nos.51 of 2004 and 176 of 2004 failed to prove the respective case. More so, from the record, it appeared that the defendants by filing application on 30-6-2009 prayed for adoption of their depositions given as PW 1 in Title Suit Nos.176 of 2004 and 51 of 2004 respectively as deposition of DW in Title Suit No.81 of 6 at their own risk." The learned Judge further held that the appellants were not entitled to raise objection as to the adoption of evidence before the Appellate Court as no objection was raised either before the trial Court or any such ground was taken in the Memorandum of Appeal and that no one was entitled to get benefit of his own wrong. On the above findings, the learned Judge concluded that the trial Court did not commit any error of law in dismissing the suit. 

 These two leave petitions have been filed by Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza and MA Hashem respectively against the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal Nos.346 and 357 of 2009 which were preferred against the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No.81 of 2006. First Appeal No.346 of 2009 was preferred by Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza and First Appeal No.358 of2009 was preferred by MA Hashem, who were defendant Nos.3 and 1, respectively in the suit. Both the appeals have been dismissed. 

 38. The learned presiding Judge observed that though defendant No.3 (also plaintiff in Title Suit No.176 of 2004) claimed that he was in possession in the suit plot, but "no where he ever stated how he was inducted into possession and when he was dispossessed." There was only a solitary statement in his deposition that in 1970, (it will be 1972) he sent his brother-in-law and the only son to the suit plot and thereafter, both of them disappeared. If that fact was true, then the defendant and other family members would have left no stone unturned to find out the whereabouts of his only son and brother-in-law, but nothing was done. PW 1 stated that he made a GD entry, but the copy of GD entry was not produced. The learned Judge observed that since the time of missing of his only son and the brother-in-law till the date of hearing of the appeal, the defendant did not take any step either to recovery the possession of the suit plot or for a declaration that he was the lawful owner thereof. Considering the documents of the plaintiffs, namely: allotment letter (exhibit-1); general power of attorney executed by the heirs of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar (exhibits-2, 3, and 3Ka) in favour of Eastern Housing Limited; matriculation certificate of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar (exhibit-4); intermediate certificate of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157 Bara Moghbazar (exhibit-4Ka); BSc Engineering certificate Part II of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar (exhibit-4Kha); BSc Engineering certificate of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar (exhibit- 4Ga); Pakistani domicile declaration of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza (exhibit-5); deed of sale executed in favour of AZM Sanaullah dated 24-9- 1957 (exhibit-6); deed of sale executed by AZM Sanaullah dated 24-9-1957 in favour of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza in respect of the property at Bara Moghbazar; deed of heba dated 17-8-1979 executed by Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza in favour of his wife, Selima Begum (exhibit-7); approved plan of DIT (exhibit-8); voter identity card of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza (exhibit- 9); passport of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza (exhibit-'9Ka); certificate issued by the Government of Canada in favour of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza (exhibit-10); promotion letters (exhibit-11 series); allotment letter of DIT in favour of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza (exhibit-12); receipts showing payment of installments (exhibits-12Ka to 12Gha); the letters written by Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar to DIT informing about the fact of payment of installments (exhibits 13 uma to 13Cha); letter written by the then DIT to Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza as to the delivery of possession of the suit plot and also asking him to deposit Taka 51 (exhibit-14); Standard lease deed of the suit plot (exhibit-15); letter of DIT approving plan (exhibit-16); photostat copy of approved plan of DIT (exhibit-16Ka); letter of House Building Finance Corporation sanctioning loan (exhibit-17); mortgaged deed executed by Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar in favour of House Building Finance Corporation (exhibit-17Ka); tenancy agreements between Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza and the tenants spreading over the period from 1967 to 2000 (exhibit-18 series); letters of WASA for water connection and bills showing payment of gas, electricity and WASA charges (exhibits-19 series); municipal assessment tax for the period 1967 to 1968 (exhibit-20); the receipts of tax as to the payment of tax of the Municipality for the period 2003 to 2004 (exhibit-20Kha); receipt showing payment ofland tax (exhibits-21-21 Na); RS Khatian No. 1174 recorded in the name of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar (exhibit-22); Memorandum and Articles of Association of Bengal Development Corporation Limited (exhibits-23-23Ka); audit reports of Uttara Bank Limited for the period 1996-2001 (exhibits-24-24Uma); letter of DIT to Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar regarding fees for changing the suit plot from residential to commercial (exhibit-25); letter issued by RAJUK to Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar approving the conversion of the suit plot into a commercial plot from residential plot (exhibit-26); certified copy of the general power of attorney executed by Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar in favour of Eastern Housing Limited (exhibit-27); approval letter of RAJUK in respect of the power of attorney given by Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza to Eastern Housing Limited (exhibit-28); approved plan (exhibits 29-29Kha); notices published in the Daily Janakatha (exhibits-30-30Kha); corrigendum published in the Daily Janakatha (exhibits 31-31Ka); Death certificate of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar (exhibit 32); news published in different news papers by Uttara Bank Limited on the death of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza (exhibit-33); Succession certificate issued by the ward Commissioner of Ward No.53, Dhaka City Corporation (exhibit-33Ka); Succession certificate issued by the 3'd Joint District Judge, Dhaka (exhibit-34); plaint of Title Suit No.51 of 2004 (exhibit-35); plaint of Title Suit No.176 of 2004(exhibit-36); pay bills (exhibits-37-37Ka); Passport No.B-57985 of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar (exhibit-38); came to the positive finding that the plaintiffs proved that from 1967 till the hearing of the suit, i.e. for more than 35 years, they had been in possession of the suit plot and such continuous possession gave them title and that the lessor, RAJUK always recognized the plaintiffs as the lessees and it did not challenge their title in the suit plot in any form. The learned Judge further held that the case of defendant No.3, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, could be considered if he were found to be in possession "but his case on possession is down right false" and by his own statement, it was proved that at no point of time, he was in possession thereof. Considering the documents filed by defendant No.3, namely: letter of allotment dated 21-3-1962, receipts showing deposit of installments against the suit plot, letter as to the delivery of possession of the suit plot, approved plan by RAJUK for construction on the suit plot and the certified copy of the RS Khatian (these documents were proved and marked as exhibits 1,2 series, 3, 6 and 9 respectively) further held that "the exhibits although resemble or appear to be true are not genuine or true, but he has manage(sic) to get those document which apparently original documents" to claim title to the suit plot. If the case of defendant No.3 that he was thrown out of his possession of the suit plot after he was inducted therein and that too when his only son with his brother-in-law disappeared in 1972, was true, he would have left no stone unturned to get back his son and brother-in-law and also the possession of the suit plot, but he only made a GD entry and moved the Parliamentary Standing Committee which had no business in the matter "of declaring title and getting possession of a property which can only be done by Court." Another aspect is that defendant No.3 gave his address "in his suit as of the disputed allotted suit plot which shows that he is a fake person as addressless person can be used by any person for any illegal purpose." The learned Judge further observed that it was the case of defendant No.3 that he entered into an agreement with MNH Bulu to sell the suit plot and to prove that fact defendant No.3 could examine Bhulu but he did not which shows that he lives in false in making out his case." The learned Judge found the documents of the plaintiffs genuine considering two vital and relevant facts (i) when on physical verification of the suit plot, a fraction chhatak/decimal was found to be in excess of the allotted plot, the then DIT directed their father (wrongly written as plaintiff) to pay for the excess land and by the 5th deposit excess amount of Taka 51 was paid and (ii) plaintiffs' predecessor, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Bara Moghbazar took loan from House Building Finance Corporation by mortgaging the suit plot as evidenced by exhibit-17. Defendant No.3 did not produce any paper to show that he was present when the suit property/plot was measured and in fact, he was never inducted into possession of the suit plot. 

 39. The learned second Judge considered the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, particularly, the documentary evidence (as have been noted hereinbefore while noting the findings of the learned presiding Judge) and came to the specific finding that the plaintiffs' predecessor, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, was the lessee of RAJUK and he had been exercising his right, title and interest over the suit plot from 1962 till his death within the knowledge of all others. The learned Judge came to the further finding that exhibits-15 (lease deed in original), 15(ka) and 15(kha) (signatures of the attesting witnesses) revealed that those were compared with the original standard lease deed kept in the custody of RAJUK and RAJUK recognized Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, as its lessee. Exhibit-14 dated 7-4-1962 showed that possession of the suit plot was handed over to the father of the plaintiffs. The learned Judge separately considered exhibit-12 series, which are the original allotment letter and original copies of receipts of the payments of installements by the plaintiff to the DIT against the suit plot; exhibit-17 , the loan sanction letter by Housing Building Finance Corporation and exhibiit-17Ka dated 17-5-1967, the mortgage deed by which the suit plot was mortgaged by the plaintiffs' father with the House Building Finance Corporation in order to obtain loan; exhibits-18, 19, and 20 series which are the tenancy agreement, the gas bill, electricity bill and City Corporation tax receipts and rent receipts respectively and came to further finding that it was proved "beyond any doubt" that the plaintiffs after getting lease of the suit plot from RAJUK have been in continuous and uninterrupted possession therein. The learned second Judge further considered exhibits-25 and 26 which proved that "earlier" the suit plot was residential plot and at the instance of the plaintiffs' father, it was converted into commercial plot and exhibits-27 and 28 which proved that after conversion, RAJUK accepted the legal transfer fees and exhibit-29, the approved plan of multistoried commercial building by Eastern Housing Limited as the attorney of the plaintiffs father and these showed that RAJUK accepted plaintiffs father, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza as its lessee and did not accept Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur and the living Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza (defendant No.3). The learned Judge came to further finding that other two Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza who claimed the suit plot admittedly were not in possession thereof and both of them made agreement for sale of the suit plot "not as admitted lessee of Rajuk because their papers and documents filed in Title Suit No.51 of 2004 and 176 of 2004 never produced before RAJUK' and claimed that they are the allottee of RAJUK." 

 41. In these four leave petitions, in fact, three suits are involved being Title Suit Nos.51 of 2004, 176 of 2004 and 81 of 2006. Before considering the propriety of the common submissions, we deem it proper to see the individual merits of the three suits. We shall do that serially. 

 42. The first suit which comes for consideration is Title Suit No.51 of 2004. In this suit, MA Hashem was the plaintiff and the suit was filed for specific performance of contract. The trial Court as well as the High Court Division dismissed the suit. It does not require any elaboration as regards the burden of the plaintiff to prove his case, because, by now, it is well settled that the plaintiff has to succeed on his own legs and he cannot succeed on the weakness of the defendant's case, if there be any. It is also well settled that even a suit is heard ex-parte, the plaintiff has to prove his case. 

 43. In a suit for specific performance of contract, the plaintiff has to prove that there was a valid contract entered into by him with the owner of the suit plot/the suit land, the consideration passed as a part performance of the contract and that the plaintiff was willing to perform his rest part as per the terms of the contract. Let us see how far the plaintiff proved the above things. 

 44. In the suit (Title Suit No.51 of 2004), the plaintiff impleaded one Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza as defendant No.1 showing his address at House No.31 , Lane No.6, Section 6/ A, Mirpur, Dhaka as his vendor and prayed for specific performance of contract against him. The other defendants, in the suit, were: Md Akhtaruzzaman, Director, Eastern Housing Limited, Chairman RAJUK and the People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka. Prayer was also made for a direction upon defendant No.1 to obtain necessary sale permission from RAJUK (defendant No.3) and for a further direction upon RAJUK to accord necessary permission for sale of the suit plot to the plaintiff. In the suit, the heirs (sons and daughters) of Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar filed an application for adding them as defendants asserting categorically that their father, late Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, was the owner of the suit plot who died on 2-2-2004. After the filing of the said application, plaintiff MA Hashem filed an application for substituting the heirs of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza bf 157, Bara Moghbazar as the heirs of defendant No.1, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur, The learned Joint District Judge rejected the application filed by the sons and the daughters of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar, but allowed the prayer of substitution made by the plaintiff. This substitution was not accepted by the heirs of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar and they filed a civil revision being No.358 of 2004 before the District Judge, Dhaka which was allowed by the learned Additional District Judge, 7111 Court, Dhaka and thus, they were added in the suit as the heirs of late Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar and not as the heirs of defendant No.1, that is, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur, but challenging this order passed in the civil revision, plaintiff MA Hashem filed Civil Revision No.4608 of 2004 before the High Court Division and eventually, the Rule was made absolute and the order passed by the learned Additional District Judge, was set-aside and thus, the .heirs of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar remained on record in Title Suit No.51 of 2004 as the substituted heirs of defendant No.1. However, the heirs of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza as defendant Nos. 1(a)-1(e) filed written statement categorically stating that their father, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar was the allottee of the suit plot and he never entered into any contract with MA Hashem to sell the same and Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur against whom the plaintiff filed the suit for specific performance of contract was a fake person. Therefore, burden was heavily upon plaintiff MA Hashem either to prove that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur was the actual allottee of the suit plot, who entered into the contract with him on 29-12-2002 to sell the same and as a part performance of the contract, advance money as claimed by him was paid to him or that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar, the father of defendant Nos.1(a) to 1(e), the actual allottee of the suit plot entered into the contract with him on 29-12-2002 to sell the suit plot and as part performance of the contract, advance payment was made to him. In this regard, it is to be noted that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, plaintiff of Title Suit No.176 of 2004, was not a party in this suit. Interesting thing is that though, in the plaint (of Title Suit No.51 of 1984), MA Hashim claimed that it is defendant No.1, i.e. Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur, who entered into the contract with him on 29-12-2002 to sell the suit plot to him, in the written statement filed by him in Title Suit No.81 of 2006, (the suit filed by the heirs of Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza) clearly admitted that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar was the actual allottee of the suit plot and the plaintiff of Title Suit No.8 of 2006 being his heirs were bound by the terms of the bainapatra executed by their father and thus, plaintiff MA Hashem gave up his plaint case that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur was the allottee of the suit plot and he entered into the contract with him on 29- 12-2002 to sell the suit plot. But the plaintiff did not make any corresponding amendment to the plaint, both in the body as well as in the prayer. From the judgment of the trial Court, it appears that it framed 5(five) issues, viz: 

 45. Of the five issues, issue Nos.3 and 4 clearly show that one of the crucial fact to be decided in the suit was whether the deed of agreement dated 29-12-2002 was executed by the actual allottee of the suit plot, namely: Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar or Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur. The other fact to be decided was whether defendant No.1 (Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur) was bound to register the kabala in respect of the suit plot on obtaining permission from RAJUK. In order to prove the case, the plaintiff examined three witnesses including himself as PW 1. PW s 2 and 3 were none but his employees. The trial Court discussing the evidence on record came to the specific findings, inter alia, that it is Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, a BSc Engineer of 157, Bara Moghbazar, who was allotted the suit plot and not Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur; at the time of allotment, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar was the Executive Engineer of C&B, Dhaka; from the plaint, it was clear that the address of defendant No.1, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, was given at House No.31, Lane No.6, section 6/1, Mirpur, Dhaka; plaintiff MA Hashem, in his deposition as PWl, admitted that as defendant No.1 was not registering the sale deed in respect of the suit plot, he through his lawyer issued a legal notice on 20-12-2003 to him, who duly received the same; though plaintiff MA Hashem in the written statement filed in Title Suit No.81 of 2006 (MA Hashem was defendant No.1 in the suit) categorically asserted that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar was the original allottee, he, as a witness, deposed that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur was the allottee of the suit plot and thus, the plaintiff gave two different versions as to the original allottee of the suit plot; the plaintiff made the agreement on 29-12-2002 with Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur for purchasing the suit plot, who was not the allottee of the suit plot; as the plaintiff did not enter into the agreement on 29-12-2002 with the original allottee to purchase the suit plot, his suit for specific performance of contract was not maintainable. The trial Court came to those findings, on detailed discussions of the evidence on record, both oral and documentary. The High Court Division as the last Court of fact discussed the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, in a more detailed manner and affirmed the said finding of the trial Court. The High Court Division came to the further findings that the plaintiff made prayer for specific performance of contract from defendant No.1 and also for a direction upon him to obtain necessary sale permission from RAJUK in his favour and had he disowned defendant No.1 than after substitution or addition of defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(e), the prayer and other incidental statements of the plaint ought to have been amended, but the plaintiff did not amend the plaint which shows that till hearing, he claimed original defendant No.1, i.e. Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur as his vendor. The learned Judges came to further finding that execution of bainapatra was suspicious and no money was transacted and when there was doubt as to the payment of earnest money, decree for specific performance of contract could not be passed. The learned Judges also came to the finding that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mjrpur and Engineer Md Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Gulshan were not the same persons (emphasis supplied); Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza died on 2-2-2004, whereas the plaintiff filed the suit on 8-2-2004 impleading Md Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza as defendant No.1 as his vendor and Md Akhtaruzzaman, a Director of Eastern Housing Limited, the attorney of Engineer late Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza as defendant No.2; at the time of filing of the suit and also for sometime thereafter, the plaintiff did not admit rather denied the existence, right, title and possession of Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar in the suit plot and later on, only to escape and justify his earlier false activities admitted "with a device that defendant Nos. 1 (a) to 1 (e) are the legal heirs of defendant No.1. i.e. Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reja of Mirpur"  and substituted the heirs of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur; the plaintiff neither made a contract for purchasing the suit plot with a genuine person nor the document submitted in Court were genuine and On the basis of those documents he could not get decree for specific performance of contract and that the total case of the plaintiff was nothing put got up story only to grab the suit plot on the basis of forged deed and paper with the help of a fake person. The learned Judges also opined that the identity of defendant No.1 could only be clarified by Showkat Ali who figured as a witness in the agreement and is also a relative of the plaintiff and used to live in the same holding with defendant No.1, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur, but he was not examined. The learned Judges gave further finding that the plaintiff not only failed to prove his own case but produced some forged and fabricated deeds and papers and that from the fact; and circumstances it was dear that the plaintiff produced exhibit:;-1. 2. 3. 4 and 5 in the Court "showing his vendor as custodian of those exhibit's who failed to appear before the Court and from the material on record it is proved that he is none but a fake person" and that exhibit-6 (the agreement) was nothing but the creation of forgery only to grab the suit plot. These are all findings of facts. 

 49. Title Suit No.l76 of 2004, giving rise to Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2198 of 2011, was filed by one Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza impleading the officials of RAJUK only for two reliefs (i) that he was legally entitled to get the sale permission of the suit plot and the defendants were bound to issue such sale permission on receiving the proper transfer fees from him and (ii) that the defendants were bound to dispose of the application filed by him on 18-2-2004 for sale permission of the suit plot within a specified time as to be directed by the Court claiming himself to be the allottee of the suit plot. He claimed that he was an Executive Engineer of C&B under the Ministry of Communications. But in support of his said claim, he did not file a single paper. The trial Court considering the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, dismissed the suit on the clear findings, inter alia, that the suit plot was allotted to Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza who was the Executive Engineer of C&B ; the plaintiff was a Diploma Engineer and it was not believable that he could join a big department like C&B as an Assistant Engineer in 1950/1952 and then promoted as Executive Engineer in 1956/57 The trial Court further observed that the plaintiff in his cross-examination admitted that though he served as an Executive Engineer in C&B, he did not open any  bank account, which also proved that he was not an Executive Engineer, because the salary of a first class employee is given through cheque and in the  absence of bank account* he could not draw his  salary and that he was not the allottee of the suit allot. Therefore, RAJUK could not give permission to him to sell the suit plot. RAJUK recognized Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar as the allottee of the suit plot and also approved Eastern Housing Limited as his attorney and that the suit was not maintainable. The trial Court further held that the suit plot was allotted to Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, who was an Executive Engineer of C&B and RAJUK did not recognize the plaintiff as the allottee of the suit plot. RS Khatian  No.11174 in respect of the suit plot was recorded  in the name of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar and plaintiff Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza as PW1 in his cross-examination  clearly stated that he never resided at 157, Bara  Moghbazar and while he deposed, he was residing at 911/1 Shewrapara as a tenant of one Monowara. The trial Court further held that no application was filed to RAJUK by the plaintiff on 18-2-2004 for permission to sell the suit plot to MNH Bulu. While dismissing the first appeal, the learned Judges affirmed the said findings of the trial Court, but giving their own reasonings. The learned Judges gave further finding that the plaintiff did not produce any copy of his application filed to RAJUK for sale permission of the suit plot. The learned Judges taking into notice of the fact that RAJUK in its written statement stated that "such file in the name of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza as mentioned is not traceable in the office of RAJUK" concluded that "so, it may be legally presumed that such application was notified and alternatively it may be presumed that the suit plot was not allotted to the plaintiff." The learned Judges came to further finding that documents filed by the plaintiff exhibited in the suit clearly show that those were prepared in the name  of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar which was admittedly the permanent address of Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun  Reza, a different person. The learned Judges further held that the suit of the plaintiff for sale permission simpliciter was not maintainable as he himself admitted in the plaint as well as in his deposition that he was out of possession and that Title Suit No.81 of 2006 filed by the heirs of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar for declaration of title and permanent injunction heard simultaneously by the same Court (the plaintiff was defendant No.3 in the suit) was decreed. The learned Judges came to further finding that though PW I (Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza) claimed that he was an Executive  Engineer, but his testimony regarding Service  Book, ACR, and Organogram clearly proved that he was not a service holder at all. The findings given by the trial Court as well as the High Court Division as to the actual allottee of the suit plot are so specific and well reasoned that we see no scope of touching with those findings. More interesting thing is that the whole case of the plaintiff was that he filed an application to RAJUK on 18-2-2004 to give him permission to sell the suit plot to MNH Bulu, but that application was not disposed of by RAJUK, which gave him the cause of action to file the suit. And, in fact, the plaintiff prayed for a relief to give direction to RAJUK to dispose of his said application within certain specific time fixed by the Court, but no such application was filed before the Court. Thus, the very foundation of the plaintiff's case had no existence. So, the plaintiff was not entitled to get any relief in the suit. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan and Mr AF Hasan Ariff, appearing for the petitioner, could not lay their hands on any of the material evidence on record to assail the findings jotted down hereinabove either on the ground of misreading or non-consideration of any material evidence by the Courts below and thus, term those as perverse. (The reasonings, given by the trial Court and the learned Judges of the High Court Division in coming to their findings have been exhaustively noted while summarizing their findings, so those are not repeated.) 

 50. However, Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan has raised a specific objection that in deciding the merits of Title Suit No.176 of 2004, the High Court Division did not consider the evidence of plaintiff, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza as PW 1 (deposition of PW1 was also adopted in Title Suit No.81 of 2006 as defendant No.3) that he applied to the Parliamentary Standing Committee to get possession of the suit plot and the Standing Committee heard him and saw his papers, but none appeared on behalf of the defendants (the defendants were RAJUK and its officials). Then the Parliamentary Standing Committee gave letter to RAJUK, who was the actual Humayun Kabir Reza (in Bangla it has been written কে প্রকৃত হুমায়ুন রেজা ছিল)? and on being asked by the Parliamentary Standing Committee, a report was sent to RAJUK from where it appeared that the plaintiff was the Executive Engineer, Design Division (nothing mentioned of which Department or Directorate) on the ground that the Parliamentary Standing Committee had no business to declare title and give possession of a property without considering that there was no legal bar in approaching the Parliamentary Standing Committee for the purpose and the report given to the Committee was an official one. The comments of the High Court Division as objected to by Mr Bhuiyan cannot be considered in isolation. From the judgment, it appears that the High Court Division made the comments after giving clear finding that though the only son and the brother-in-law of plaintiff, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, did not come back after they had allegedly gone to the suit property in December, 1972; till hearing of the appeal, he neither filed any criminal case nor took any step to recover the possession of the suit plot, nor informed the matter to RAJUK nor took any step for declaration of his title to the suit plot for the last 32 years. The High Court Division also took note of the fact that the plaintiff as PW 1 stated in his examination-in-chief that after the death of his son and brother-in-law, he did not even go to the suit plot. The High Court Division further observed that the application filed before the Parliamentary Standing Committee was neither proved nor filed and the file "which according to him was opened was not called for and therefore, disbelieved plaintiff's (Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza) story of approaching the Parliamentary Standing Committee and then made the comment. To us it also appears unusual and against the common course of natural events and human conduct that an actual allottee or actual owner of a plot at a posh area like Gulshan in Dhaka City shall not go to his owned land for 32 years and moreso. when a building was allegedly constructed thereon(emphasis supplied). We have gone through the evidence of PWl, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza. From his evidence, it appears that after examining him partly in Court on 13-3-2008 and 15-4-2008, he got him examined on commission. While examined on commission, on 8-6-2008, by the learned Advocate Commissioner, Jamaluddin Ahmed, he filed the photostat copy of the so called report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee along with other relevant papers (in Bangla it has been written (সংসদীয় কমিটির প্রতিবেদনসহ আনুষাঙ্গিক দলিলাদির) (17 pages), but this was not accepted as an exhibit and rightly so, as the same was not admissible in evidence in the absence of any proof that the same was made from the original. It is to be further noted that no one was examined to prove the report allegedly given by the Parliamentary Standing Committee. Though PW 1 in his examination-in-chief on 15-4-2008 stated that as per the order of the Parliamentary Standing Committee the report came, which was kept with RAJUK. But the report given by the Parliamentary Standing Committee was not called for from RAJUK; onus was squarely upon the plaintiff to prove the report by examining a competent witness as per the rules of evidence. In this connection, it is also very pertinent to state that plaintiff, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza though claimed that he joined the then C&B Department under the Ministry of Communications as an Assistant Engineer in 1952 and then was promoted as an Executive Engineer in 1960, in support of his said case, did not file any scrap of paper. Whereas, the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.81 of 2006 in support of their case that their father, late Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, was a BSc Engineer and was the Executive Engineer of C&B and went to Canada for higher training, filed all the relevant papers, such as, BSc Engineering certificate (exhibit-4Gha), certificate issued by the Government of Canada in favour of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza (exhibit-10), promotion letters (exhibit-11 series). So, we find no substance in the objection taken by Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan. 

 51. Title Suit No.81 of 2006 was filed by the sons and the daughters of late Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar. In the suit, the plaintiffs prayed reliefs, amongst others, for declaration of title to the suit plot and for further declarations that defendant No.2, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of House No.31, Lane No.2, Section 6/A, Mirpur, Dhaka, who executed bainapatra on 29-12-2002 as claimed by defendant No.1 and defendant No.3, (plaintiff of Title Suit No.176 of 2004) were not their father and that both the living Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza were the creations of defendant Nos.1 and 4 (defendant No.4 was MNH Bulu) and that the bainapatra dated 29-12-2002 showing defendant No.2 as its executor as claimed by defendant No.1 and the bainapatra dated 18-1-2004 executed by defendant No.3 in favour of defendant No.4 as claimed by him (defendant No.3) were fraudulent, collusive, illegal, without any consideration and in-executable (অকার্যকর) and were not binding upon them. 

 52. In the suit, plaintiff of Title Suit No.51 of 2004, MA Hashem and Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, plaintiff of Title Suit No.176 of 2004, were impleaded as defendant Nos.1and 3 respectively and Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur was impleaded as defendant No.2. The trial Court decreed the suit on the clear findings that the plaintiffs proved conclusively that the suit plot was allotted to Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157 Bara Moghbazar their father and he constructed building therein on obtaining loan by mortgaging the same with House Building Finance Corporation and had been in possession thereof by letting out the same to various tenants as apparent vide exhibit-18 series. Defendant No.3. Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza was not the owner of the suit plot. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence of MA Hashem examined in Title Suit NO.51 of2004 further held that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur neither was the allottee of the suit plot nor was in possession thereof. The agreement, even if, entered into by him with defendant No.1 was not executable. After the death of plaintiffs' father. Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157. Bara Moghbazar they became the owners of the suit plot and they were in possession thereof Defendant No.1 entered into a contract with fake Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur without permission of RAJUK and claimed possession in the suit plot and thus posed threat to the plaintiffs' possession therein as well as their title. So the suit was maintainable. Defendant No.1 in his written statement admitted that the plaintiffs' father was the owner of the suit plot and thus, admitted the plaint case. The trial Court came to the further findings that the RS record of the suit plot was recorded in the name of the plaintiffs' predecessor. Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza wherein his address had beenc cearly mentioned as 157. Bara Moghbazar which fact also confirmed that he was the allottee of the suit plot. The High Court Division, being the last Court of fact besides affirming the above findings of the trial Court, came to the finding that from 1967 till the hearing of the suit, i.e. more than 35 years, the plaintiffs had been in possession of the suit plot continuously and uninterruptedly and such possession gave them title and RAJUK, lessor always recognized the plaintiffs as lessees. In coming to the said finding, the High Court Division considered the documents filed by the plaintiffs, being 38 in number and the oral evidence as well. The High Court Division found the documents of the plaintiffs genuine. The High Court Division further held that defendant No.3 (plaintiff of Title Suit No.176 of 2004) claimed that he was in possession in the suit plot, but "no where he ever stated how he was inducted into possession and when he was dispossessed." The High Court Division further observed that had it been true that defendant No.3 sent his brother-in-law and the only son to the suit plot in 1972 and from there. both of them disappeared. then the defendant and the other family members would have left no stone untumed to find out their whereabouts but nothing was done. Although PWl Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza (examined in Title Suit No.176 of 2004) stated that he made a GD entry over the incident. but copy of the GD entry was not produced. The High Court Division further observed that since the time of missing of the only son and the brother-in- law of plaintiff, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza. till the hearing of the appeals. he did not take any step either to recover the possession of the suit plot or for declaration that he was the lawful owner of the suit plot. The High Court Division further found that though the letter of allotment dated 21-3-1962. receipts showing deposit of installments against the suit plot. letter as to the delivery of possession of the suit plot approved plan by RAJUK for construction on the suit plot and the certified copy of the RS khatian Cexhibits- 1. 2 series. 3. 6 and 9 respectively) produced by defendant No.3 resemble or appear to be true are not genuine or true but he managed to get those documents which apparently appear to be original documents just to claim the suit property. In this appeal, the High Court Division also considered the fact that though plaintiff, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza (of Title Suit No.176 of 2004) claimed to have filed application before the Parliamentary Standing Committee, such application was neither exhibited nor filed and that "the file which according to him was opened was not called for." The High Court Division further observed that though defendant No.3 claimed that he entered into an agreement with MNH Bulu to sell the suit plot for which he applied to RAJUK for sale permission, but Bulu was not examined. The High Court Division further found that the plaintiffs' father, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, was the lessee of RAJUK and till his death, he exercised his right, title and interest over the suit plot to the knowledge of all. Exhibit-14 dated 7-4-1962 showed that possession of the suit plot was handed over to the father of the plaintiffs. The High Court Division separately considered exhibit-12 series, the original allotment letter and original copies of receipts of the payments of installments by the plaintiffs' father to the DIT against the suit plot; exhibit-17 , the loan sanction letter by the Housing Building Finance Corporation and exhbiit-17Ka dated 17-5-1967, the mortgage deed by which the suit plot was mortgaged by the plaintiffs' father with the House Building Finance Corporation in order to obtain loan; exhibits-18, 19, and 20 series which are the tenancy agreements, the gas bills, electricity bills and City Corporation tax receipts and rent receipts respectively and came to the further finding that it was proved "beyond any doubt" that the plaintiffs' father after getting lease of the suit plot from RAJUK had been exercising his continuous and uninterrupted possession therein. The High Court Division further considered exhibits-25 and 26 which proved that the suit plot was converted into a commercial plot from residential one at the instance of the plaintiffs' father, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar; exhibits-27 and 28 which proved that RAJUK accepted the transfer fees for converting the suit plot as a commercial plot and exhibit-29 showed the approval of plan of multi- storied commercial building by Eastern Housing Limited as the attorney of the plaintiffs' father and these documents showed that RAJUK accepted the plaintiffs' father, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza as its lessee and did not accept Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur and the living Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza (defendant No.3) as the lessee of the suit plot. The High Court Division came to the further finding that other two Shamsul Kabir Humayun Rezas who claimed the suit plot admittedly were not in possession thereof and both of them made agreement for sale of the suit plot "not as admitted lessee of RAJUK because their papers and documents filed in Title Suit No.51 of 2004 and 176 of 2004 never produced before RANK and claimed that they are the allottee of RAJUK." Plaintiff, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza was a fake person. These are all findings of facts. 

 54. This suit being a suit for title along with other prayers, we have also perused the evidence on record and found that the findings, given by the High Court Division in concurring with those of the trial Court, based on proper consideration of the evidence on record. The documents filed by the plaintiffs in support of their case that at the time of allottment of the suit plot by the then DIT, their father was the Executive Engineer of the then C&B and that he used to live at 157, Bara Moghbazar and got possession of the suit plot, paid the installments against the suit plot to the then PIT, got the standard lease deed, constructed building on the suit plot by taking 10 a.m. from the House Building Finance Corporation and had been in possession thereof althrough by letting out the same to the various tenants and now they are in possession thereof through their attorney, Eastern Housing Limited, are so interlinked and clockwise that no prudent man can have any difficulty to come to the decision as to the truth of their claim of title and possession in the suit plot. And a single broad fact as admitted by defendant No.3, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza in his deposition as PW1 in Title Suit No. 176 of2004 (in this suit, hl1 was plaintiff and has evidence was adopted in Title Suit No.81 of 2006) that he did not go to the suit plot after December, 1972 when his only son and the brother-in-law disappeared, is enough to disbelieve his case that he was the actual allottee of the suit plot and also to conclude that he was trying to be an imposter just to claim the suit plot. In this regard, we are tempted to say that "possession follows title" and the very fact that the plaintiffs filed all the documents of possession, such as: RS Khatian prepared in the name of their father showing his address at 157, Bara Moghbazar, rent receipts, municipal tax receipts, bills of various utility services, the tenancy agreements first one being of the year, 1967, prima-facie, proved their possession in the suit plot, besides other documents already discussed earlier and the oral evidence: It is also necessary to state that defendant No.3 has failed to file any municipal tax receipts and utility services bills in respect of the suit plot to show that he ever asserted his title to the suit plot and possession therein. The trial Court rightly decreed the suit and the High Court Division committed no wrong in affirming the same. 

 57. We do not also find any substance in the second common submission. It appears that though no specific issue was framed by the trial Court in terms as formulated by the learned Advocate for the petitioners, it gave specific finding that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur was a fake person and the suit plot was not allotted to him and that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar was the actual allottee of the suit plot. The trial Court gave the further finding that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, plaintiff of Title Suit No.176 of 2004 and also defendant No.3 of Title Suit No.81 of 2006 was not the allotted of the suit plot. The High Court Division, being the last Court of fact, on detailed consideration of the evidence on record, adduced by the parties affirmed those findings of the trial Court and gave further specific finding that the plaintiff of Title SuitNo.51 of2004 produced some forged and fabricated deeds and papers; the documents filed by plaintiff, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, were not genuine or true. The High Court Division gave the further finding that plaintiff, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, was also a fake person. The High Court Division found the documents of the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.81 of 2006 genuine. The evidence adduced by the parties, particularly, those of the plaintiffs of Title Suit NO.81 of 2006, were quite sufficient to decide the issues/points and, in fact, both the Courts decided the points/issues as raised and formulated by the learned Advocate for the petitioners. From the findings of the Courts below, it is apparent that none of the Courts below found any difficulty in giving the finding as to who was the actual allottee and whose documents were genuine and whom RAJUK recognized as its allottee, the real issue in the suits. Therefore, the question of sending either the suit or the appeal back on remand as submitted by the learned Advocates, does not also arise at all. In this regard, we like to observe further that a suit or appeal cannot be sent back on remand as a matter of course or at the fancy of the parties, particularly, when the Courts below decided all the points including the one raised by the learned Advocates .
