The third and last common submission relates as to the adoption of the evidence by defendant Nos. 1 and 3 in Title Suit No.81 of 2006 adduced by them in Title Suit Nos.51 of2004 and 176 of 2004 in support of their respective case as made out in their written statement as defendants in the suit. The learned presiding Judge discarded the point with the finding as under: 

 The learned second Judge discarded the point with the finding that "It further appears from the record that the defendants by applications dated 30-6- 2009 prayed for 'adoption of their depositions given as PW 1 in title suit Nos.176 of 2004 and 51 of 2004 respectively as deposition of DW in title suit No.81 of 6 at their own risk. 

 59. The learned second Judge took the further view that as the respective plaintiff of Title Suit Nos.51 of 2004 and 176 of 2004 failed to prove their case, the provision of section 33 of the Evidence Act had no manner of "application in the instant appeal, in other word, it cannot be said that the trial Court erred in law in dismissing Title Suit Nos.51 of 2004 and 176 of 2004." 

 60. Before we examine as to whether the learned Judges were correct in taking the above views, in view of the provisions of section 33 of the Evidence Act, the context, in which the trial Court allowed the prayer for adopting the evidence adduced by defendant Nos.1 and 3 in their respective suit, has to be seen. As it appears from the records, three suits were heard by the same Joint District Judge simultaneously. It is true that in 3(three) suits, the plaintiffs were distinct and' separate and the defendants were also not same. But in Title Suit No.81 of 2006, the plaintiffs of the two other suits (Title Suit Nos.51 of 2004 and 176 of 2004) were defendants and the defendants of those two suits were also impleaded as defendants and the questions involved in the suits were virtually the same as have already been discussed earlier in other context. 

 61. In Title Suit No.81 of 2006, the plaintiffs were the sons and daughters of late Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar, who claimed that their father was the actual allottee of the suit plot. In this suit, MA Hashem, plaintiff of Title Suit No.51 of 2004, was impleaded as defendant No.1 and plaintiff of Title Suit No.176 of 2004, Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, was impleaded as defendant No.3 and Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur with whom defendant No.1, MA Hashem, claimed to have entered into a contract on 29-12-2002 to purchase the suit plot, was impleaded as defendant No.2; MNH Bulu with whom defendant No.3 allegedly entered into a contract to sell the suit plot was impleaded as defendant No.4; RAJUK and its officials were impleaded as defendant Nos.5-8 and Eastern Housing Limited was impleaded as defendant No.9. In this suit, defendant Nos.1 and 3 filed written statement stating similar facts as stated in the respective plaint (the case of the respective plaint and the written statement has been stated in detail while stating case of the parties). Defendant Nos.4 and 5-8 also filed written statement. In Title Suit No.51 of 2004, the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.81 of 2004 were substituted as defendant Nos.1(a) to 1(e) and they filed written statement stating similar facts as stated in the plaint of Title Suit No.81 of 2006. In Title Suit No.176 of 2004 filed by Shamsul Kabir Humayun, only RAJUK and its officials were made parties. From the pleadings of the parties, a common issue emerged that out of 3(three) Shamsul Kabir Humayun Rezas, who was the actual Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza and who was the actual allottee of the suit plot? The plaintiffs of Title Suit No.81 of 2006 examined 5(five) witnesses in support of the case that their father late Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157, Bara Moghbazar was the actual allottee of the suit plot and their father had been in possession thereof and after his death, they inherited the suit plot and they were in possession thereof and that their father did not enter into any contract with MA Hashem, plaintiff of Title Suit No.51 of 2004. Defendant Nos.1 and 3 who were plaintiffs of Title Suit Nos.51 of 2004 and 176 of 2004 respectively cross-examined each and every PWs(Defendant No.2 did not appear and contest the suit. Defendant No.4 though filed written statement ultimately did not show up). Defendant Nos. l and 3 neither examined themselves nor examined any other witness in this suit. However, they examined themselves and examined other witnesses in their respective suit being Title Suit Nos.51 of 2004 and 176 of 2004 respectively. It is also pertinent to note that the plaintiff of Title Suit No.51 of 2004 who was examined as PW1 was cross-examined by the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.81 of 2006 and defendant Nos.5-8 (RAJUK and its officials) and the plaintiff of Title Suit No.176 of 2004 also was cross-examined by the defendants, namely: RAJUK and its officials. On behalf of RAJUK, one of its officers was examined as DWI in Title Suit No.176 of 2004 and he was duly cross-examined by the plaintiff. On 30-6-2009, defendant Nos. l and 3 filed applications in Title Suit No.81 of 2006 to adopt their evidence adduced in their respective suit, which was allowed by the trial Court. Similarly, the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.81 of 2006 filed application in Title Suit No.51 of 2004 to adopt their evidence in the suit which they adduced in Title Suit No.81 of 2006 and the Court allowed the prayer. Similarly RAJUK also filed application in Title Suit Nos.51 of 2004 and 81 of 2006 to adopt its evidence adduced in Title Suit Not No.176 of 2004 and the Court allowed the prayer. It further appears from the record that no objection, whatsoever, was raised by any of the parties in adopting such evidence and the suits were disposed of accordingly. It is true that Title Suit No.81 of 2006 was filed subsequent to Title Suit Nos.51 of 2004 and 176 of 2004, but it was heard simultaneously with the other two suits. However, it may be kept on record that the examination of PW 1 in Title Suit No.51 of 2004 commenced on 2-4-2006 and examination of the witnesses was concluded on 29-5-2009, examination of witness in Title Suit No.176 of 2004 commenced on 13-3-2008 and was concluded on 12-8-2008 and examination of the witnesses in Title Suit No.81 of2006 commenced on 13- 3-2008 and was concluded on 30-6-2009. 

 62. A reading of section 33 of the Evidence Act shows that the evidence given by a witness in a judicial proceeding, or before any person authorised by law to take it, is relevant for the purpose of proving, in a subsequent judicial proceeding, or in a later stage of the same proceeding, the truth of the fact which it states. But to consider such evidence the conditions, which must be fulfilled, are that the witness is dead or cannot be found, or is incapable of giving evidence, or is kept out of the way by the adverse party, or if his presence cannot be obtained without an amount of delay or expense which, under the circumstances of the case, the Court considers unreasonable; provided that the proceeding was between the same parties or their representatives in interest; that the adverse party in the first proceeding had the right and opportunity to cross-examine; that the questions in issue were substantially the same in the first as in the second proceeding (Explanation given to the section is not relevant to decide the instant petitions, so omitted from being quoted.) One of the stringent conditions to take recourse to the section on the ground of incapability of a witness of giving evidence has to be proved. 

 63. In support of his contention, Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan has referred to the cases of Ali Haider vs the State (supra) and Allah Ditta vs the State (supra). Those two cases arose out a criminal trial. In the first case, the depositions of some of witnesses recorded by the Committing Magistrate were transferred to the Sessions record without summoning them on the ground that their evidence were of a formal nature and with a view to avoid unnecessary expenses to the State and the order of the learned Sessions Judge was acquiesced in by the learned Counsel for the accused and then the depositions of the witnesses examined during the committal proceeding were read over to the accused and were used against them. In the context, it was held that in a criminal case, the provisions of section 33 of the Evidence Act cannot be waived; the evidence of the witnesses, illegally admitted, must be excluded. It was also held that the defect was not curable under section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In the second case, the evidence of a witness named Lala examined during the committal proceeding was also transferred to the Sessions case under section 33 of the Evidence Act and order was passed admitting the evidence declaring that Lala's evidence could not be procured "without delay and unnecessary adjournment" without any evidence before the Court that the witness was incapable of giving evidence on the later date. The defence Counsel conceded that he had no objection to take recourse to section 33 of the Act and in those circumstances, it was held that the Court had misapplied section 33 of the Evidence Act. In that case, it was further held that the witness "could not be found" has to be proved by direct evidence of persons having personal knowledge. It was further held that the defence Counsel's consent did not do away with the necessity of the Court being satisfied by proof on the requirements of section 33. In holding so, in the second case, Cornelius, J who wrote the opinion on behalf of the Court, relied on the observations made by the Privy Council in the case of Chainchal Singh vs Emperor, AIR 1946 PC 1 to the effect: 

 "Where it is desired to have recourse to section 33 of the Evidence Act on the ground that a witness is incapable of giving evidence, that fact must be proved, and proved strictly. It is an elementary right of an accused person that a witness who is to testify against him should give his evidence before the Court trying the case, which then has the opportunity of seeing the witness and observing his demeanor and can thus form a far better opinion as to his reliability than is possible from reading a statement or deposition. It is necessary that provision should be made for exceptional cases where it is impossible for the witness to be before the Court, and it is only by a statutory provision that this can be achieved. But the Court must be careful to see that the conditions on which the statue permits previous evidence given by the witness to be read are strictly proved." 

 64. In both the cited cases, the witnesses were not examined in the trial Court and it had no advantage to see the demeanour of the witnesses and the accused had no chance to cross-examine them. But in the instant cases, the context as stated earlier is totally different. Defendant Nos.1 and 3 (petitioner of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1672 of 2011 and 2199 of 2011) by filing applications adopted the evidence adduced by them in the respective suit as plaintiffs after closing the examination of the plaintiffs' witness in Title Suit No.81 of 2006. And in Title Suit No.81 of 2006 in which their evidence was adopted and considered, they had the advantage to cross-examine the PWs. Therefore, the principle of law enunciated in the cases cited by Mr Bhuiyan, has got no manner of application in the instant cases. The depositions of the witnesses-examined in the two suits (Title Suit Nos.51 of 2004 and 176 of 2004) and the documents exhibited therein by the respective plaintiff, are definitely evidence within the meaning of section 3 of the Evidence Act. So, we do not see any bar under section 33 of the Act to consider the evidence adduced in the suits having been heard simultaneously and the common questions of facts and laws were involved. Moreso, the onus to prove the facts as asserted by defendant Nos. 1 and 3 in their respective written statement filed in Title Suit No.81 of 2006, was squarely upon them within the meaning of sections 101 and 102 of the Evidence Act and they opted not to examine any witness in Title Suit No.81 of 2006 in support of their case and adopted the evidence adduced by them in their own suits. In the context, we do not also see any illegality committed by the trial Court in allowing the prayer made by the respective defendant to adopt the evidence adduced in the respective suit and such a course, in no way, caused any prejudice to them. Therefore, the trial court did not commit any illegality in considering the evidence of the respective defendant adduced in the respective suit as plaintiff within the meaning of section 33 of the Evidence Act in coming to the finding as to the proof and disproof of facts involved in the suits and thus deciding their merits. In this regard, we consider it necessary to state the law that in the Code of Civil Procedure, there is no specific provision to allow a party in a suit or a civil proceeding to adopt evidence adduced by him in another suit or proceeding heard simultaneously or analogously, but section 151 of the Code has given inherent power to the Court to pass any such order to secure the ends of justice and in the instant cases by allowing the prayer of the defendants to adopt their evidence given as plaintiff in their respective suit in Title Suit No.81 of 2006, ends of justice has been served and that also prevented the abuse of the process of the Court. It is also a fact that the petitioners herein did not raise any objection, whatsoever, before the trial Court against the adoption of their evidence in their respective suit as a defence in Title Suit No.81 of 2006 and allowed the suits to be disposed accordingly, and the petitioners did not also take any ground in the Memorandum of Appeal in that respect as observed by the High Court Division. A party should not be allowed to change its position as per its own sweet will and cannot be allowed to make a summer sault or make a 'U' turn after the disposal of the suit and that there was no allegation of fraud as well. It appears to us that objection as to the adoption of the evidence given in Title Suit Nos.51 of 2004 and 176 of 2004, in Title Suit No.81 of 2006 citing section 33 of the Evidence Act was taken before the High Court Division for the first time during the hearing of the appeal just to delay the disposal of the suits by way of sending them back on remand to the trial Court giving them chance to adduce evidence,

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 to show cause as to why judgment and decree dated 12-5-2004 passed by learned Additional District Justice, 1st Court, Faridpur in Title Appeal No. 61 of 2003 allowing the appeal in-part by modifying judgment and decree dated 25-5-2003 passed by learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Faridpur in Title Suit No. 74 of 2000 decreeing the suit in-part should not be set-aside. 

 2. Facts, relevant for the purpose of disposal of this Rule, are that opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 74 of 2000 on 19-4-2000 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Sadar, Faridpur for a decree of partition of 0.50 acre land claiming saham of 0.1250 acre land in her favour. The case of the plaintiff in short is that 0.50 acre land belonged to Salim Jamaddar and after his death his four sons namely, Yeasin Jamaddar, Abdul Khaleque Jamaddar, Ismail Jamaddar, Habibur Rahman and three daughters, Shamsunnessa, Badrunnessa and Kamrunnessa inherited the land as per their respective shares. After death of Yeasin Jamaddar, his six sons namely, Mutahar, Moazzem, Enayet, Altaf, Mozaffar, three daughters, Badrunnessa, Zohra, Asiya and one wife Sakina inherited his share. Thereafter, RS Khatian No. 670 in respect of 0.50 acre land was prepared and finally published in the name of the heirs of Salim Jamaddar and Yeasin Jamaddar. Each son of Salim Jamaddar inherited 0.09 acre land and each daughter inherited 0.0450 acre land. Badrunnessa and Kamrunnessa settled their share measuring 0.09 acre land to their brother Ismail Jamaddar and thereafter, Ismail Jamaddar settled his land by pattan dated 15-4-1946 in favour of his four sons namely Yousuf, Yeakub, Ali Akbar and Haider. Khaleque Jamaddar sold his share to Sultan Kazi and thereafter, he re-purchased the same. Ali Akbar and Haider died while they were minors leaving behind their father Ismail Jamaddar. In the aforesaid way, Ismail Jamaddar became owner of 0.17 acre land and thereafter, died leaving behind two sons Yousuf, Yeakub and five daughters namely Nurjahan, Ayesha, Rokia, Rabeya, Kulsum and one wife Fuljan. Habibur Rahman died leaving behind one son Mahbubur Rahman. In the aforesaid way, the heirs of Yeasin Jamaddar, Ismail Jamaddar and Habibur Rahman became owners of 0.50 acre land and thereafter, they transferred the same by registered sale deed No. 3250 dated 8-3-1967 in favour of Sultan Miah, Abdur Razzak Miah, Enaruddin and Aneruddin and handed over possession thereof to them. While Sultan, Abdur Razzak, Enaruddin and Aneruddin were owners in possession of 0.1250 acre land each, Sultan and Abdur Razzak jointly transferred 0.1250 acre land in favour of Taijuddin by registered sale No. 2587 deed dated 26-4-1972 and .1250 acre land in favour of the plaintiff by registered sale deed No. 3176 dated 8-3-1976. In the aforesaid way, the plaintiff becomes owner in possession of 0.1250 acre land and SA Khatian was prepared with some mistakes. The plaintiff applied for mutation of her name but the concerned Tahsildar refused to do so. Cause of action of the suit arose on 30-3-2000 when the plaintiff requested the defendants to make partition of the suit property but they refused and, as such, the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit. 

 3. Defendant Nos. 1-2 jointly and defendant No. 3 separately filed written statements to contest the suit contending that the suit is not maintainable, barred by limitation and bad for defect of parties. The positive case of defendant Nos. 1-2 is that during RS operation 0.50 acre land of RS Plot No. 1500 and 0.61 acre land of RS Plot No. 1528 was jointly recorded in the name of Abdul Khaleque Jamaddar and others in RS Khatian No. 670 and on an amicable partition Mozaffar Hossain and others got 0.20 acre land of RS Plot No. 1500 and 0.20 acre land of Plot No. 1528 and while they were owning and possessing said 0.40 acre land settled the same to Amena Khatun by registered patta No. 1259 dated 21-2-1947 and handed over possession thereof to her and on the basis of the pattan and her possession total 0.40 acre land was prepared and finally published in the name of Amena Khatun in separate SA Khatian No. 363. Yousuf Ali Jamaddar and others got 0.31 acre land including 0.08 acre land from suit Plot No. 1500 and said 0.31 acre land was recorded in the name of Yousuf Ali Jamaddar and others in separate SA Khatian No. 730. Moreover, while Kazi Sultan Ahmed and others were owning and possessing 0.22 acre land SA Khatian No. 729 was prepared and finally published in their name. While Amena Khatun was owning and possessing 0.40 acre land transferred the same to Abul Fazal Khan @ Ali Miah by registered sale deed No. 3257 dated 4-7-1962 and handed over possession thereof to him who transferred the same to Sheikh Ramjan by registered sale deed No. 8289 dated 18-10-1976 and after mutating his name and paying rents thereof he transferred 0.20 acre land of suit Plot No. 1500 in favour of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by registered sale deed No. 5498 dated 20-10-1986 and handed over possession thereof to them and they have been owning and possessing the same by payment of rent upon separation of the holding by mutation case. Accordingly, the RS recorded tenants lost their title to .20 acre land out of 0.50 acre land. 

 4. Though in deed No. 3250 dated 8-3-1967, 0.50 acre land was shown to be transferred but the transferors (RS recorded tenants and their successors) had transferable rights to only 0.30 acre land and accordingly, Sultan, Razzak, Enarudin and Anerudin acquired title to 0.0750 acre land each and thereafter, Enarudin Matubbar transferred his share to Sheikh Tara by registered sale deed No. 6873 dated 11-7-1974 who thereafter, transferred the same to Khalil Molla by registered sale deed No. 5711 dated 24-5-1976. Anerudin Sheikh transferred his share to Gonjur Ali by registered sale deed No. 6006 dated 5-9-1972 who thereafter, transferred the same to Sheikh Zaved Ali by registered sale deed No. 7422 dated 27-8-1974 and thereafter, Sheikh Zaved Ali transferred the same to Hossain Matubbar by registered sale deed No. 3156 dated 3-2-1975 and Hossain Matubbar transferred it to Khalil Molla by registered sale deed No. 6037 dated 30-7-1977 and thereafter, Khalil Molla transferred the same to defendant Nos. 1-2 by registered deed No. 120 dated 3-1-1979. Though Enarudin and Anerudin purchased 0.25 acre land but they jointly acquired title to 0.15 acre land and as such the defendants got title to 0.15 acre land instead of 0.25 acre land through Enarudin and Anerudin Sheikh. Said Sultan and Razzak while owning and possessing 0.15 acre land transferred 0.1250 acre land in favour of Taijuddin @ Tajel by registered deed No. 2587 dated 26-4-1972 and after mutating his name and paying rents to the Government Sheikh Taijuddin died leaving behind two sons namely, Sheikh Tara and Sheikh Lal Miah, five daughters namely, Rahela Khatun, Amena Khatun, Komela Khatun, Sufia Khatun (defendant No. 3) and Roki Khatun and one wife namely, Ful Banu and they inherited .1250 acre land as per Muslim law of inheritance. Rahela Khatun sold her share measuring 0.0125 acre land to defendant No. 1 by registered sale deed No. 3901 dated 10-8-1991; Sheikh Lal Miah sold 0.0250 acre land to defendant No. 1 by registered sale deed No. 2686 dated 4-5-1992; Amena Khatun sold 0.0125 acre land to Sheikh Lal Miah by registered sale deed No. 5203 dated 5-9-1992 and after death of Komela Khatun her two daughters and husband Rema transferred 0.0125 acre land Jahangir Molla by registered sale deed No. 5585 dated 4-9-1995 and thereafter, Jahangir Molla and Sheikh Lal Miah sold 0.0250 acre land to defendant No. 1 by registered sale deed No. 2519 dated 15-5-1996. On the other hand, Sheikh Tara Miah and Ful Banu sold 0.04 acre land to defendant No. 1 by registered sale deed No. 2115 dated 12-4-2000 and handed over possession to him. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 became owner in possession of total 0.1025 acre land through Taijuddin. In the aforesaid way defendant Nos. 1-2 become owner in possession of total 0.20 + 0.15 + 0.1025 = 0.4525 acre land and has been owning and possessing the same by erecting dwelling houses and planting different trees therein and they also mutated their names in different mutation cases and have been paying rents and taxes thereof. After transfer of 0.1250 acre land to Taijuddin by sale deed No. 2587 dated 26-4-1975, Sultan and Razzak had title to and transferable right of only 0.0250 acre land and accordingly, the plaintiff acquired title to 0.0250 acre land by purchase from them vide sale deed No. 3176 dated 8-3-1976. Defendant No. 1-2 prayed for a separate saham of 0.4525 acre land. 

 7. Being aggrieved by said judgment and decree dated 15-4-2001 defendant Nos. 1-2 preferred Title Appeal No. 103 of 2001 and defendant No. 3 preferred Title Appeal No. 148 of 2001 before the learned District Judge, Faridpur which were transferred to learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Faridpur who, upon hearing the parties, allowed both appeals by common judgment and decree dated 7-4-2002 and set-aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and sent the suit back on remand for fresh trial to the trial Court. After remand, defendant No. 3 adduced one oral witness and also produced some documentary evidence to prove her case which were marked as exhibits. 

 8. After considering the evidence and materials adduced by the parties, the trial Court again decreed the suit in-part in preliminary form vide judgment and decree dated 25-5-2003 allotting 0.0250 acre land in the saham of the plaintiff, 0.4525 acre land in the saham of defendant Nos. 1-2 and 0.0225 acre land in the saham of defendant No. 3. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 61 of 2003 before the learned District Judge, Faridpur which was transferred to learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Faridpur who, upon hearing the parties, allowed the appeal in-part vide judgment and decree dated 12-5-2005 and modified the judgment and decree of the trial Court and allotted 0.1250 acre land in the saham of the plaintiff, 0.3525 acre land in the saham of defendant ''Nos. 1-2 and 0.0225 acre land in the saham of defendant No. 3. The plaintiff and defendant No. 3 did not challenge the judgment and decree of the Court of appeal. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the Court of appeal defendant Nos. 1-2 have preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the instant Rule and order of status-quo. 

 9. Mr Sk. Reajul Hogue learned Advocate appearing with Ms. Shishirkona, learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the Court of appeal, upon misreading and non-consideration of the evidence and misconception of law illegally allotted 0.1250 acre land in the saham of the plaintiff though her vendors had transferable right of 0.0250 acre land and in doing so did not discuss any evidence of the parties. Learned Advocate further submits that as the last court of facts, the Court of appeal did not evaluate or discuss any evidence independently and come to independent findings of fact or reversed the findings of fact of the trial Court but illegally reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court. Learned Advocate further submits that the Court of appeal erroneously held that complicated question of title is involved in the suit and a simple suit for partition is not maintainable but it decided the suit on merit and decreed the suit. Learned Advocate further submits that upon amicable partition among the RS recorded tenants, Mozaffar and others got 0.20 acre land out of 0.50 acre suit land and transferred the same to Amena Khatun by registered deed of pattan dated 21-2-1947 being No. 1259 and on the strength of said pattan separate SA Khatian No. 363 was prepared and finally published in the name of Amena Khatun and accordingly, the said pattan has been acted upon and title of 0.20 acre land vested to Amena Khatun, who thereafter, transferred the same to Abul Fazal Kha vide registered sale date dated 4-7-1962 and accordingly, the RS recorded tenants and their successors lost their title to 0.20 acre land. Learned Advocate further submits that defendant Nos. 1-2 acquired title to 0.20 acre land through Amena Khatun by successive transfers through valid registered sale deeds and mutated their names in respect of 0.20 acre land and have been owning and possessing the same for more than 12 years and accordingly, they have acquired adverse possession in respect of said 0.20 acre land. Learned Advocate further submits that by deed No. 3250 dated 8-3-1967 though 0.50 acre land was shown to have been transferred to Sultan, Abdur Razzak, Enaruddinn and Aneruddin but the vendors of said deed had title to and transferable right of only 0.30 acre land and after deduction of 0.20 acre land, Sultan and three others acquired title to 0.0750 acre land each instead of 0.1250 acre land each. Learned Advocate further submits that after transfer of 0.1250 acre land to Taijuddin by Sultan and Razzak by registered sale deed dated 26-4-1972 they had title to only 0.0250 acre instead of 0.1250 acre land and accordingly, the plaintiff got title to only 0.0250 acre land from Sultan and Abdur Razzak by sale deed No. 3176 dated 8-3-1976. Learned Advocate further submits that the trial Court upon evaluation of evidence of the parties came to the conclusion that the plaintiff is entitled to 0.0250 acre land but the Court of appeal without discussing any evidence of the defendant Nos. 1-2 illegally reduced their share to 0.3525 acre from 0.4525 acre land and illegally increased share of the plaintiff from 0.0250 acre land to 0.1250 acre land. Learned Advocate finally submits that the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment of reversal and, as such, liable to be set-aside. 

 11. As against the above contention, Mr Goutam Kumar Roy learned Advocate appearing for opposite party No. 1 submits that the Court of appeal, as the last Court of facts, upon considering the evidence and materials on record, rightly held that the plaintiff is entitled to 0.1250 acre land on the basis of sale deed dated 8-3-1976 and such findings of fact cannot be reversed in revisional jurisdiction. Learned Advocate further submits that the Court of appeal rightly held that the defendant could not prove pattan dated 21-2-1947 being No. 1255 and accordingly, they could not prove Amena's title to 0.20 acre land and since Amena Khatun could not acquire title to 0.20 acre land the defendants could not acquire title to said 0.20 acre land through Amena. Learned Advocate further submits that the Court of appeal upon considering the evidence held that Sultan Miah, Abdur Razzak, Enaruddin and Aneruddin acquired title to 0.50 acre land by registered sale deed dated 8-3-1967 from the heirs of Ismail and others and accordingly, the vendees of said deed acquired title to 0.50 acre land, in particular, Sultan and Razzak acquired title to 0.25 acre land jointly and after transfer of 0.1250 acre land to Taijuddin they had title to 0.1250 acre land which has been rightly transferred to the plaintiff by registered sale deed dated 8-3-1976 and, as such, the plaintiff has acquired title to said land not only by purchase but by adverse possession by owning and possessing the same by erecting dwelling hurts therein for more than 12 years. Learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiff paid rent to the Government as well as paid municipal taxes in respect of 0.1250 acre land and it is settled principle of law that rent receipts are evidence of possession and may be used as collateral evidence of title. Learned Advocate further submits that the trial Court, upon misreading and non-consideration of evidence of the parties illegally allotted 0.0250 acre land in the saham of the plaintiff and, as such, the Court of appeal committed no error of law in allotting 0.1250 acre land in the saham of the plaintiff by modifying the judgment of the trial Court. 

 15. The plaintiff in her plaint as well as deposition of PW 1 stated that Salim Jamaddar was owner of 0.50 acre land and after his death his four sons namely Abdul Khaleque and others got 0.09 acre land each and three daughters namely Badrunnessa and others got 0.0450 acre land each and thereafter, Badrun-nessa and Kamarunnessa transferred their 0.09 acre land in favour of their brother Ismail who settled the same to his four sons Yusuf and others and thereafter, his two sons who were minors died leaving behind their father Ismail and accordingly, Ismail acquired title to 0.17 acre land and on the other hand Abdul Khaleque sold his share to Sultan Kazi and thereafter, he re-purchased said 0.09 acre land. Further case of the plaintiff that the heirs. of Yeasin, Habibur Rahman and Ismail acquired title to 0.50 acre land on amicable partition among the recorded tenants and their co-sharers and thereafter, they 'transferred the same to Sultan, Abdur Razzak, Enaruddin and Aneruddin by registered sale deed dated 9-3-1967 being No. 3250. The plaintiff produced the certified copy of said deed of sale dated 9-3-1967 which was marked as Exhibit No. 4. The plaintiff did not produce any deed of so-called pattan by which Badrunnessa and Kamarunnessa transferred 0.09 acre land in favour of Ismail and any deed of pattan by which Ismail transferred the same to his four sons. Accordingly, title of 0.09 acre land by Ismail from Badrunnessa and Kamarunnessa and by Yusuf and his three brothers from Ismail has not been established. 

 16. Against the above contention of the plaintiffs the defendants claimed that on an amicable partition among the RS recorded tenants and some of their heirs, Mozaffar and five others ( four sons and one daughter of Yeasin) got 0.20 acre land from the suit plot and other co-sharers got rest land with other land of other khatian and then Mozaffar and five others sold the same vide registered pattan No. 1259 dated 21-2-1947 to Amena Khatun and while she was owning and possessing the same separate SA Khatian was prepared and finally published in her name. The defendant also contended that after such transfer the rest RS recorded tenants and their successors had only transferable right and title to 0.30 acre land and accordingly, by sale deed dated 8-3-1967 Sultan and his three brothers acquired title to 0.0750 acre land each. Defendant Nos. 1-2 claimed title to said 0.20 acre land through successive transfers from Amena Khatun by sale deeds. In support of the transfer of 0.20 acre land in favour of Amena Khatun by Mozaffar and five others defendants Nos. 1-2 produced original copy of pattan dated 21-2-1947 and its related Index from the Sub-registry Office which were marked as Exhibit Nos. Ka and Ka(1)1 without any objection from the plaintiff. The plaintiff and defendant Nos. 1-2 produced certified copy SA Khatian No. 363 showing preparation and publication of 0.20 acre land in the name of Amena Khatun which was marked as Exhibit 1-Ga. Defendant Nos. 1-2 also produced rent receipts in the name of Amena Khatun in respect of 0.20 acre land which was marked as Exhibit No. Kha(3). They further contended that Amena Khatun transferred 0.20 acre land by registered sale deed dated 4-7-1962 to Abul Fazal Kha who transferred it to Sheikh Ramjan by sale deed No. 8289 dated 18-10-1976 who mutated his name and paid rents to the Government and thereafter, he transferred said 0.20 acre land to defendant Nos. 1-2 by registered sale deed No. 5498 dated 20-10-1986. They produced original copy of sale deed No. 3257 dated 4-7-1962, marked as Exhibit-Ja; certified copy of sale deed No. 8289 dated 18-10-1976, marked as Exhibit-Jha; rent receipts showing payment of rent by Ramjan marked as Exhibit Nos. Kha(4)-Kha(5); original sale deed No. 5498 dated 20-10-1986 marked as Exhibit-Ja(1). The defendants also produced rent receipts in the name of defendant Nos. 1-2 showing payment of rent of the suit land by them, marked as Exhibit Nos. Kha(6)-Kha(9). All those documents were marked as exhibits without any objection from the plaintiff. 

 17. While deposing as PW 1 the husband of the plaintiff namely, Muhammad Lalon Fakir stated, "এস, এ ৩৬৩নং খতিয়ানে আমিনা খাতুনের নামে ১৫০০ দাগে ২০ শতাংশ রেকর্ড হয়েছে কি না জানি না।" He further stated in cross-examination "সুলতান মিয়া, আব্দুর রাজ্জাক, এনার উদ্দিন ও আনার উদ্দিন এস, এ রেকর্ডের পরে জমি কিনে। এদের খরিদের আগেই আমিনা খাতুন ২০ শতাংশ কিনে এবং তার নামে এস, এ রেকর্ড হয়।" From the testimony of P.W 1, it is clear that Amena Khatun took settlement of 0.20 acre land and SA khatian was prepared and finally published in her name and thereafter, Sultan, Razzak, Enaruddin and Anaruddin purchased land. Considering above admission of the P.W1 as well as other evidence, the trial Court observed that by registered pattan No. 1259 dated 21-2-1947 [(Pattan Exhibit No. Ka and Index Exhibit No. Ka(1)] some of the RS recorded tenants and their successors transferred 0.20 acre land in favour of Amena Khatun by that pattan she acquired title to 0.20 acre land and SA khatian No. 363 (Exhibit No. Ga=1) was rightly prepared and finally published in her name and she paid rent to the Government [Exhibit (Kha(3)], who transferred the same to Abul Fazal Kha vide registered deed of sale No. 3257 dated 4-7-1962 (Exhibit Ja) who transferred the same to Sheikh Ramzan vide registered deed of sale No. 8289 dated 18-10-1976 (Exhibit Jha) and upon mutating his name he paid rent to the Government [Exhibit Nos. Kha (4) and Kha(5)] and thereafter, he transferred the same to defendant Nos. 1-2 vide registered deed of sale No. 5498 dared 20-10-1986 [Exhibit ja(1)] and upon mutating their names they paid rents to the Government [Exhibit Nos. Kha (6) and Kha(9)]. On relying upon those documentary evidence the trial Court came to the conclusion that after transfer of 0.20 acre land by RS recorded tenants and their successors they had title to remaining 0.30 acre land and accordingly, by sale deed No. 3250 dated 8-3- 1967 (Exhibit No. 4 = Jha(1)] Sultan, Razzak, Enaruddin and Anaruddin acquired title to only 0.30 acre land. 

 18. The Court of appeal disbelieved the said pattan and index [(Exhibits-Kha and Kha(1)] on the ground that those could not be read out as those were illegible and, as such, Amena Khatun could not acquire title to 0.20 acre land. Except this finding the Court of appeal did not consider the SA Khatian No. 363 which has been prepared and finally published on the basis of said pattan in the name of Amena Khatun and did not consider the transfer deeds dated 4-7-1962, 18-10-1976 and 20-10-1986 by which Amena Khatun transferred 0.20 acre land to Fazal Miah, who transferred the same to Sheikh Ramjan and thereafter, Ramjan Sheikh transferred said 0.20 acre land to defendant Nos. 1-2. The Court of appeal did not consider the rent receipts [(Exhibits Nos. Kha(3)-Kha(9)] by which Amena Khatun, Sheikh Ramjan and defendant Nos. 1-2 paid rents to the Government. 

 19. It appears that the trial Court, upon proper consideration of the evidence of the parties in particular as per admission of PW 1, came to right conclusion that the RS recorded tenants and their successors transferred .20 acre land to Amena and thus they lost title to 0.20 acre land and defendant Nos. 1-2 acquired title to 0.20 acre land through Amena. But that the Court of appeal upon misreading and non-consideration of evidence and upon misconception of law came to the finding that defendant nos. 1-2 could not acquire title to .20 acre land through Amena Khatun and illegally reversed the findings of the trial Court in this regard. 

 20. The plaintiff produced certified copy of sale deed dated 8-3-1967 being No. 3250 (Exhibit-4) and claimed that by said deed the successors of RS recorded tenants and some of their successors have transferred 0.50 acre land in favour of Sultan, Razzak, Enaruddin and Anaruddin. This sale deed is admitted by the defendants in the way that after transfer of 0.020 acre land to Amena Khatun there was only 0.30 acre transferable land and by deed dated 8-3-1967 Sultan, Razzak, Enaruddin and Anaruddin acquired title to only 0.30 acre land. Since the RS recorded tenants and their successors earlier lost title to 0.20 acre land, the trial Court rightly held that Sultan, Razzak, Enaruddin and Anaruddin acquired title to only 0.30 acre land instead of 0.50 acre land by sale deed No. 3250 dated 8-3-1967 (Exhibit-4). The plaintiff claims that she purchased 0.1250 acre land from Sultan and Razzak by sale deed No. 3176 dated 8-3-1976. During trial, the plaintiff could not produce any rent receipts and mutation Khatian showing her possession in said 0.1250 acre land. Though the plaintiff adduced two oral witnesses to support her claim but the trial Court upon evaluation of the evidence of the plaintiff came to the conclusion that the plaintiff acquired title to only 0.0250 acre land. The Court of appeal, while reversing the finding of the trial Court held that the plaintiff adduced rent receipts which were marked as Exhibit Nos. 2(Ga) and 2(Ga)/1 but from perusal of the records it appears that those rent receipts were produced by defendant No. 3 to prove payment of rent by her predecessor Taijuddin in respect of 0.1250 acre land. Accordingly, the findings of the Court of appeal that the plaintiff produced rent receipts to prove her possession are against the evidence on record. 

 21. It is contended by the defendant No. 1-2 that Sultan and Razzak transferred 0.1250 acre land to Taijuddin by registered sale deed No. 2587 dated 26-4-1972 original of which was produced by them which was marked as Exhibit No. Ja(9) without any objection from the plaintiff. After purchase, Taijuddin paid rents to the Government (Exhibit Nos. 2(Ga), 2(Ga)/1J. Though the plaintiff claimed that said deed dated 26-4-1972 was a forged deed but she could not prove such plea by adducing any evidence. Since Sultan and Razzak acquired title to total 0.15 acre land by sale deed dated 8-3-1967 and after transfer of 0.1250 acre land in favour of Taijuddin, they had title to only 0.0250 acre land. Accordingly, the plaintiff acquired title to only 0.0250 acre land from Sultan and Razzak by sale deed No. 3176 dated 8-3-1976. The defendants in their evidence also admitted that the plaintiff has acquired title to only 0.0250 acre land instead of 0.1250 acre land. The Court of appeal, did not discuss or consider those evidences adduced/produced by the defendants and erroneously held that the plaintiff could prove title to and possession of entire 0.1250 acre land and illegally reversed the findings of the trial Court and allotted 0.1250 acre land in favour of the plaintiff by reducing share of defendant Nos. 1-2. 

 22. The defendants further contended that after death of Taijuddin, his wife Ful Banu Khatun, two sons Lal Miah, Tara Miah and five daughters, namely Rahela, Amena, Komela, Sufia (defendant No.3) and Roki/Rubia inherited 0.1250 acre land as Mahmedan Law of Inheritance and thereafter, Ful Banu Khatun and Tara Miah transferred 0.04 acre land by registered sale deed No. 2115 dated 12-4-2000 to defendant No. 1 original of which was produced and marked as Exhibit-Ja(15), Lal Miah transferred 0.0250 acre land to defendant No. 1 by registered sale deed No. 2686 dated 4-5-1992 original of which was produced and marked as Exhibit Ja(11). Rahela transferred 0.0125 acre land in favour of defendant No. 1 by registered sale deed No. 3901 dated 10-8-91 original of which was produced and marked as Exhibit Ja(10). Amena Khatun transferred 0.0125 acre land to Lal Miah by registered sale deed No. 5203 dated 5-9-1992 original of which was produced and marked as Exhibit-Ja(12). After death of Komela her husband Nazim and her two daughters transferred 0.0125 acre land to jahangir by registered sale deed No. 5585 dated 4-9-1995 original of which was produced and marked as Exhibit-Ja(13) and then Lal Miah and Jahangir transferred their purchased 0.0250 acre land in favour of defendant No. 1 by registered sale deed No. 2519 dated 15-5-1996 original of which was produced and marked as Exhibit-Ja(14). Roki Khatun transferred 0.0125 acre land to defendant No. 3 by registered sale deed No. 18 dated 4-1-1992 original of which was produced marked as Exhibit-2(Ka). On the other hand, Enaruddin transferred his share to Sheikh Tara by registered sale deed No. 6873 dated 11-7-1974 original of which was produced and marked as Exhibit-Ja(2). Aneruddin transferred his share to Gonjur Ali Sheikh by registered sale deed No. 6006 dated 5-9-1972 original of which was produced and marked as Exhibit-Ga(4). Gonjur Ali Sheikh transferred the same to Sheikh Zaved by registered sale deed No. 7422 dated 17-8-1974 original of which was produced and marked as Exhibit-Ja(5). Sheikh Zaved transferred the same to Hossain Matubbar by registered sale deed No. 3156 dated 3-2-1975 original of which was produced and marked as Exhibit-Ja(6) and thereafter, Sheikh Tara and Hussain Matubhar transferred their purchased land to Khalil Molla by registered sale deed No. 5771 dated 24-5-1976 and sale deed No. 6037 dated 30-7-1977 originals of which were marked produced and as Exhibit Nos. Ja(3) and Ja(7) and thereafter, Khalil Molla transferred said land to defendant Nos. 1-2 by sale deed No. 120 dated 3-1-1979 original of which was produced and marked as Exhibit-Ja(8). The defendants also produced rent receipts in the name of Taijuddin showing payment of rent of 0.1250 acre land which were marked as Exhibit No. 2(Ga)- 2(Ga)/1. Upon considering above title deeds and rent receipts, the trial Court held that the defendant Nos. 1-2 acquired title to and possession in 0.2525 acre land, defendant No. acquired title to 0.0225 acre land through Sultan, Abdur Razzak, Enaruddin and. Aneruddin by successive sale deeds as mentioned above and accordingly, allotted total 0.4525 acre land in favour of defendant Nos. 1-2 and 0.0225 acre land in favour of defendant No. 3. The Court of appeal without sifting the evidence and upon non-consideration and misreading of evidence adduced by the defendants in this regards came to its findings and illegally reversed the findings and decision of the trial Court and reduced the share of defendant Nos. 1-2 from 0.4525 acre to 0.3525 acre land. 

 23. In the case of Erfan Ali vs Joynal Abedin Mia 35 DLR (AD) 216 it has been held that rent receipts are evidence of possession and may be used as collateral evidence of title. Section 110 of the Evidence Act provides a presumption of ownership in favour of person who is in possession of the property and possession follows title. Moreover, as per section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, every entry in a record of rights prepared or revised under section 144 shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect. By producing SA Khatian No. 363 (Exhibit-Ga) defendant Nos. 1-2 contended that the SA Khatian was rightly prepared and finally published in the name of Amena Khatun on the basis of pattan dated 21-2-1947 (Exhibit-Ka). Though the plaintiff claimed that said deed of pattan was a product of forgery and the SA record was wrongly prepared and finally published in the name of Amena Khatun but she could not rebut the presumption of correctness of the SA Khatian by adducing any reliable evidence. Accordingly, it is to be presumed that deed of pattan dated 21-2-1947 has been acted upon and SA Khatian No. 363 was rightly prepared and finally published in the name of Amena Khatun. Though the plaintiff claimed that the title deeds by which defendant Nos. 1 and 2 claimed title to the suit land were forged documents but the original sale deeds were produced by the defendants and those were marked as exhibits without any objection from the plaintiff. Accordingly, it is to be presumed that those sale deeds are genuine documents. The defendants by producing oral and documentary evidence have been able to prove that they have been owning and possessing 0.4525 acre land for more than 12 years through their predecessors before filing of the suit and, as such, they have acquired title to and possession of 0.4525 acre land by way of adverse possession.

2. Both the Civil Appeals are directed by leave granting order dated 07.08.2016 passed in Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal No.2789-2790 of 2013 against the judgment and decree dated 29.07.2013 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revisions No.2078-2079 of 1999 making both the Rules absolute reversing the judgment and decree dated 05.04.1999 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Sylhet in Title Appeals No.83-84 of 1997 dismissing both the appeals affirming the judgment and decree dated 07.04.1997 passed by the Court of Additional Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet in Title Suit No.155 of 1993 dis-missing the suit and in Title Suit No.74 of 1993 decreeing the suit. 

 3. The relevant facts necessary for the disposal of both the civil appeals are that on 12.07.1993 the respondents No.1-2 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.155 of 1993 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet impleading the appellant as main defendant and respondents No.3-9 as proforma defendants praying for declaration of title over the 2nd schedule land and for recovery of Khas possession of the said land upon removing the houses and obstruction there from. 

 4. The case of the plaintiffs in Title Suit No.155 of 1993, in a nutshell, is that the land described in 1st schedule of the plaint originally belonged to Katanmoni Nath, son of Shankar Nath, who by a registered Kabala dated 25th Shrabon, 1359 B.S. corresponding to 10.08.1952 transferred northern half portion of the 1st schedule land in favour of Krishnamoni Dey, wife of Surendra Kumar Dey. Said Katanmoni Nath and Krishnamani Dey while in possession of the 1st schedule in equal share the record of right of the said land was correctly prepared in their names. Said Krishnamoni Dey sold her eight Anas share in favour of Samuj Miah, the predecessor of the pro-forma defendants No.2-7 by a registered Kabala dated 10.11.1973 and he had been possessing the same by constructing boundary wall at the eastern, western and northern side of their purchased land and by constructing dwelling house at the west of the said land. Said Katanmoni Nath having been the owner of 2nd schedule land on request of Roshomoy Datta, the husband of the defendant No.1 allowed him to reside at the western part of .01 acres of land out of 2nd schedule land by raising a mud-built but thereon. Thereafter, Katanmoni Nati died on 28th Chaitra 1366 B.S. corresponding to 11.04.1960 leaving behind his wife Kornomoni Nath as the only heir and became the owner of all the properties belonging to Katanmani Nath. Subsequently, Kornomoni Nath again got married with Prashanna Nath and she died on 12th Chaitra 1399 B.S. corresponding to 26.06.1993. Said Karnamani Nath was deprived of enjoying the 2" schedule land since she lost her life interest in the said land after entering into a second marriage. The right, title and interest of Katanmani Nath in the 2nd schedule land devolved upon the plaintiffs as reversionary heirs (brother's daughter's sons of Katanmani Nath) according to Hindu Law. The plaintiffs got mutated their names in respect of the suit land. The husband of the defendant No.1 used to live in a very small portion of the suit land having received per-mission from the plaintiffs. On the demise of the husband of the defendant No.1, the plaintiffs asked the defendant No.1 on several occasions to deliver vacant possession of the land while the defendant No.1 agreed to comply with the said request. Subsequently, the plaintiffs came to know at the middle of April, 1993 that the defendant No.1 being plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.74 of 1993 claiming the suit land as her purchased land. Thereafter, at the last part of April 1993 the plaintiffs again asked the defendant No.1 to vacate the suit land while she refused to do so since she claimed the title of the suit land by way of the alleged sale deed which is false, fraudulent and collusive being the said Kabala is an antedated and void document and on the basis of the alleged Kabala the defendant No.1 instituted Title Suit No.42 of 1992 against two fictitious women, who had no right, title in the suit land and she managed to get the said suit decreed on compromise by practicing fraud, upon the Court and subsequently by creating a new story the defendant No.1 instituted Title Suit No.74 of 1993 against the plaintiffs which cast cloud upon the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs and as such the plaintiffs have filed the suit. 

 5. The defendant No.1-appellant contested the Title Suit No.155 of 1993 by filing a Written Statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint. She con-tended, inter alia, that Katanmoni Nath as owner of the land of plot No.1208 executed a Bainapatra on 2nd Ashar 1367 B.S. in favour of the plaintiff on receiving Tk.50.00 out of the total consideration money of Tk.95.00 and delivered possession of the disputed homestead which is situated at the southern part of plot No.1208 and since then she had been possessing the same. Due to sudden death of Katanmoni Nath no Kabala was executed and registered according to the terms of the aforesaid contract for sale. On the demise of Katanmoni Nath his wife Kornomoni Nath executed a Kabala on 31.01.1963 in favour of the defendant No.1 regarding the land described in the schedule of the Bainapatra executed by her husband Katanmoni Nath. She excavated a tank at the eastern part of the plot No.1208 and converted the western part of the said plot as Bhiti land by earth-filling and constructed two dwelling houses thereon. She had been possessing the same beyond statutory period of limitation. The defendant No.1 filed Title Suit No.42 of 1992 in the Court of the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet against Kornomani Nath which was decreed on compromise on 21.11.1992. The plot number was wrongly written as 1207 instead of 1208 in the schedule of said Bainapatra and registered Kabala, but from the boundaries delineated in the schedules of the aforesaid two documents it is clear that the land of plot No.1208 was transferred in favour of the defendant No.1. Due to the afore-said mistake of mentioning plot No.1207 in the compromise decree dated 21.11.1992 passed in Title Suit No.42 of 1992 there arose a confusion and as such the defendant No.1 instituted Title Suit No.74 of 1993 to remove such confusion. Kornomoni Nath did not get married for the second time rather she became pregnant by leading immoral life with Prosanna Nath for which her life interest had not been lost. Being a woman of immoral character Kornomoni Nath departed to elsewhere. Krishnamoni Dey sold out the land of plot No.1207 to the defendant No.7 and her husband by a Kabala dated 25th Kartik 1380 B.S. and they had been possessing the land of plot No.1207 since the time of purchase. The plaintiffs brought the suit with a view to harass the defendant No.1 and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 6. On the other hand, the appellant as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.74 of 1993 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet impleading the respondents No.1-2, Kornomoni Nath and the respondent No.9 as defendants praying for a declaratory decree that the land described within the boundary of the deed dated 31.01.1963 executed in favour of the plaintiff by the defendant No.1 and the land stated in the decree of the Title Suit No.42 of 1992 appertain to the land of plot No.1208 although plot No.1207 was mentioned in the deed dated 31.01.1963 and the Title Suit No.42 of 1992. The averments made in the plaint of Title Suit No.155 of 1993 are identical to the same made in the written statement filed by the defendant No.1 in Title Suit No.155 of 1993. 

 7. The defendants No.3 & 4, who are the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.155 of 1993 contested Title Suit No.155 of 1993 by filing a written statement denying all the material averments made in the plaint sup-porting the self-same statements made in the plaint of Title Suit No.155 of 1993. The defendant No.2 also contested the Title Suit No.74 of 1993 by filing a separate written statement although supporting the claim of the defendants No.3 and 4. 

 8. Both the Title Suit No. 155 of 1993 and Title Suit No.74 of 1993 were heard analogously by the trial Court. Upon hearing both the suits, the trial Court was pleased to dismiss Title Suit No.155 of 1993 while decreed Title Suit No.74 of 1993 by a single judgment dated 07.04.1997. 

 9. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decrees dated 07.04.1997 passed by the trial Court in Title Suit No.155 of 1993 and Title Suit No. 74 of 1993 the respondents No.1 and 2 preferred Title Appeal No.83 of 1997 and Title Appeal No.84 of 1997 respectively before the learned District Judge, Sylhet which were eventually transferred to tie Court of Additional District Judge, 3r Court, Sylhet, who upon final hearing dismissed both the appeals by judgment and decree dated 05.04.1999. 

 10. Against the judgment and decree dated 05.04.1999 passed by the appellate Court in Title Appeal No.83 of 1997 and Title Appeal No.84 of 1997 the respondents No.1 and 2 filed Civil Revision No.2078 of 1999 and Civil Revision No.2079 of 1999 respectively before the High Court Division and Rules were issued. 

 13. Mr. A.M. Amin Uddin, learned senior Advocate appearing along with Mr. Didar Alam Kollol, Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant in both the appeals taking us through the judgment and decree of the High Court Division dated 29.07.2013 passed in Civil Revisions No.2078-2079 of 1999, judgments and decrees of the appellate Court as well as the trial Court, the other materials on record, contends that the High Court Division has committed illegality in totally misconceiving the case of the appellant upon misreading and misconstruing the evidence and materials on record and thereby misdirected beyond the law and facts of the case in passing the erroneous judgment making the Rules absolute occasioning serious miscarriage of justice and as such the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside. The learned Counsel contends further that appellant acquired title and possession in the suit land from the original owner Kotanmoni Nath by way of sale deed dated 31.01.1963. The learned Counsels contend next that Kornomoni Nath never got married for the second time and as such she did not lose her life interest in the suit land, but the High Court Division on mis-conception made the Rules absolute. The learned Counsels argue next that from the Local Investigation Report along with other relevant papers (Exhibits- 6 series) it is found that the land described both in the sale deed dated 31.01.1963 (Exhibit-z) and compromise decree (Exhibit-5(A)) would attract the land of plot No.1208, but the High Court Division ignoring the said documents most illegally made the Rules absolute. The learned Counsels referred to the case of Md. Alkas Ali and others vs. Mansur Ahmed Khan and others reported in 1983 BLD(AD) 126. The learned Counsels contend, in fine, that although the possession of the plaintiff is admitted by the defendants, the High Court Division could not appreciate the matter and most illegally set aside the judgment and degree of the appellate Court as well as the trial Court and as such the judgment and decree of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. 

 16. It is admitted that the land of plot No.1208 belonged to Katanmoni Nath while the land of plot No.1207 belonged to Krishnamoni Dey. 17. Needless to say that the plaintiff of Title Suit No.74 of 1993 contested the Title Suit No.155 of 1993 by filing a written statement while the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.155 of 1993 contested Title Suit No.74 of 1993 by filing a written statement. It is apparent from the record that both the Title Suit No.74 of 1993 and Title Suit No.155 of 1993 were tried analogously and the plaintiff of Title Suit No.74 of 1993 produced both oral and documentary evidences as plaintiff in both the suits while the defendants No.3 and 4 in the said suits produced both oral and documentary evidences as defendants in both the suits. 

 18. The case of the plaintiff of Title Suit No.74 of 1993 is that Katanmoni Nath being the owner of land of plot No.1208 executed a Bainapatra (contract for sale) on 2nd Ashar 1367 BS. in favour of the plaintiff (Lakshmi Rani Dutta) on receiving Tk.50.00 out of the total consideration money of Tk.95.00 and delivered possession of the said land to her. On the demise of Katanmoni Nath his wife Kornomoni Nath executed a Kabala on 31.01.1963 in favour of the plaintiff regarding the land described in the schedule of the Bainapatra. In the aforesaid Bainapatra and Sale Deed dated 31.01.1963 plot No.1207 was mistakenly written as the location of plot numbers had not been properly identified through investigation on the spot although the land of plot No.1208 was transferred in favour of the plaintiff by way of aforesaid deeds. Katanmoni Nath owned the land situated on the south side and the boundaries specified in the sale deed dated 31.01.1963 would attract the land of plot No.1208. Kornomoni Nath did not get married for the second time rather she became pregnant by leading immoral life with Prosanna Nath on account of which her life interest had not been lost. Being a woman of immoral character Kornomoni Nath departed to elsewhere. 

 19. Now let us examine how far the plain-tiff of Title Suit No.74 of 1993 has been able to prove her case. The document on the basis of which the plaintiff claims her title on the suit land is the sale deed dated 31.01.1963 which was exhibited as Exhibit-2, but admittedly plot No.1207 was stated in the said deed. To cure such mistake happened in the above sale deed the plaintiff claims that she instituted Title Suit No.42 of 1992 which was decreed on compromise on 21.11.1992. It also transpires that Kornomoni Nath was the defendant No. I in the Title Suit No.42 of 1992 and she deposed in the said suit in support of the compromise deed. The plaintiff filed the certified copy of the judgment and decree and Solenama (compromise deed) which were exhibited and marked as Exhibit-5 series. From the decree of Title Suit No.42 of 1992 (Exhibit-5(A)) it appears that plot No.1207 along with specific boundaries had been described in the decree although the plaintiff claims that the land described in the schedule of the sale deed dated 31.01.1963 as well as decree of Title Suit No.42 of 1992 (Exhibit-5(A)) are the same and they would indeed attract the land of plot No.1208. To dispel such confusion the plaintiff prayed for local investigation before the court and accordingly a local investigation was held. P.W.6 deposed in support of the Local Investigation Report and the defendants No.3 and 4 cross-examined him, but they could not show any contradiction. On going through the Local Investigation Report together with relevant papers in this regard (Exhibits-6 series) it appears that the land described both in the Exhibits-2 and 5(A) would attract the land of plot No.1208. 

 20. It is crystal clear from the foregoing discussion that due to demise of her husband Kornomoni Nath executed Sale Deed (Exhibit-2) in favour of the plaintiff (in Title Suit No.74 of 1993) in compliance with the terms and conditions of Bainamana. Thus, it is proved that the plaintiff acquired title and interest from Katanmoni Nath. But the defendants No.3 and 4 raised a question that the plaintiff could not acquire title by virtue of an unregistered deed. On plain reading of the Sale Deed (Exhibit-2) it is seen that the sale in question was settled at the consideration money of Tk.95.00. According to Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 the sale of immovable property the value of which is less than 100 taka can be made by an unregistered document. Therefore, the Sale Deed (Exhibit-2) is a valid instrument accruing title to the plain-tiff (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993). 

 21. Apart from the above, the plaintiff (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993) examined sever-al witnesses in support of the genuineness of the Sale Deed (Exhibit-2). P.W.2 is the scribe, who identified his signature in the said deed as Exhibit-2(A). P.W.2 stated in his deposition in the following way: 

 23. Regarding possession in the suit land i.e. land of plot No.1208 the plaintiff (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993) examined four witnesses. P.Ws.1, 2, 3 and 5 deposed sup-porting the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. Although those witnesses were cross-examined by the defendants No.3 and 4, but no contradiction had been made. Moreover, Exhibit-4 (D.P. Khatian) shows that Katanmoni Nath had the possession in respect of the land of plot No.1208. 

 24. Adverting to the case of defendants No.3 and 4 (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993), let us first scan the evidences adduced in support of their claim. The defendants No.3 and 4 claim that Katanmoni Nath died on 28th Chaitra 1366 B.S. corresponding to 11.04.1960 leaving behind his wife Kornomoni Nath as the only heir, who became the owner of the land of plot No.1208 belonging to Katanmani Nath. Subsequently, Kornomoni Nath again got married with Proshanna Nath and she died on 12th Chaitra 1399 B.S. corresponding to 26.00.1993. The time Kornomoni Nath got 2nu marriage she became divested-of suit land belonging to Katanmani Nath the said land devolved upon the defendants No.3 and 4 as reversionary heirs (brother's daughter's sons of Katanmani Nath) according to Hindu Law. 

 25. The crux of the contention between the plaintiff and the defendants No.3 and 4 (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993) indeed revolves around the question whether due to second marriage Kornomoni Nath lost her life interest in the land of plot No.1208 originally belonged to her husband Katanmoni Nath and the same devolved upon the defendants No.3 and 4 as reversionary heirs. On scrutiny of the record it is evident that the defendants No.3 and 4 could not prove by adducing satisfactory evidence as to the fact that at the time of execution of Sale Deed (Exhibit-2) Kornomoni Nath got married for the second time due to which she lost her life interest in the suit land. The defendants (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993) could not also adduce any document to prove the facts that on the death of Katanmoni Nath his brother Ratan i.e. the predecessor of the defendants No.3 and 4 became the owner the suit land. Rather, it is squarely proved that at the time of execution of the Sale Deed (Exhibit-2) Katanmoni Nath did not lose her life interest in the suit land due to the reason of second marriage or loosing chastity. 

 26. The defendants No.3 and 4 (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993) further claim that Katanmoni Nath died on 28th Chaitra 1366 B.S. corresponding to 11.04.1960 while the plaintiffs claim that Katanmoni Nath died on 15th Chaitra 1368 B.S. But there is no iota of evidence available on the record in support of the claim of the defendants whereas the plaintiff adduced the death certificate of Katanmoni Nath which was marked as Exhibit-7. It reveals from Exhibit-7 that Katanmoni Nath died on 15th Chaitra 1368 B.S. 

 27. There is another contention between the plaintiff and the defendants No.3 and 4 (In Title Suit No.74 of 1993) regarding the second marriage of the Katanmoni Nath. The defendants No.3 and 4 claim that after the death of Katanmoni Nath his wife Komomoni Nath entered into second marriage with one Proshonno Nath for which she lost her life interest in the suit land while the plaintiff claims that Kornomoni Nath never got married with Proshonno Nath although she used to led immoral life with Proshonno Nath. 

 33. Be that as it may, despite the proposition of second marriage of Komomoni Nath is accepted the same will not affect the title of the plaintiff if the said sale in favour of the plaintiff takes place before losing her life interest in the suit land originally owned by Komomoni Nath got married for the second time. From the foregoing discussion, it has abundantly proved that due to demise of Katanmoni Nath his wife Kornomoni Nath transferred the suit land in favour of plaintiff on 31.01.1963 by way of Exhibit-2 as per the terms and conditions of Bainapatra executed between the plaintiff and Katanmoni Nath while Kornomoni Nath had subsisting life interest on 31.01.1963. 

 39. Thus, D.W.5 claimed to know the fact of permissive possession from the husband of plaintiff although at one stage of his cross-examination he admitted that he was not present at the time of taking possession of 01 decimal land by Roshomoy Datta from Katanmoni Nath as permissive possessor. In the given situation the testimony of D.W.5 regarding permissive possession does not carry any evidentiary value and as such it is not proved that Roshomoy Datta was not a permissive possessor in 01 decimal land of suit plot No.1208. Apart from this, the defendants No.3 and 4 did not claim the plaintiff as illegal possessor in rest 24 decimal land of suit plot No.1208. 

 40. At this juncture, let us know what about the relief of the defendants No.3 and 4 in the land of plot No.1207 regarding which the plaintiff does not claim any title. On examination of the plaint of Title Suit No.155 of 1993 it reveals that the defendants No.3 and 4 of Title Suit No.74 of 1993 as plaintiffs in Title Suit No.155 of 1993 further claimed their relief in respect of the land of plot No.1207. 41. On perusal of the plaint of Title Suit No.155 of 1993 it is seen that the plaintiffs (In Title Suit No.155 of 1993) admitted the transfer of land of plot No.7 in favour of the defendant No.7 (In Title Suit No.155 of 1993) namely Samuj Mia. Apart from the above, D. W.1 stated in his deposition in the following way: 

 42. Therefore, admittedly after transfer of the land of plot No.1207 by Krishnamoni Nath in favour of Samuj Mia the defendants No.3 and 4 have no title in the said plot. 

 44. In the light of the foregoing discussion it is evident that the plaintiff of Title Suit No.74 of 1993 has been able to prove her title and possession in the suit land i.e. on plot No.1208 and as such she is entitled to get the relief as prayed for. On the other hand, the defendants No.3 and 4 (plaintiffs of Title Suit No.155 of 1993) have not been able to prove their title and possession in the suit land. The trial Court as well as the appellate court on proper appreciation of the facts and law lawfully decreed the Title Suit No.74 of 1993 suit and dis-missed the Title Suit No.155 of 1993, but the High Court Division most illegally set aside the judgments and decrees of the trial Court as well as the appellate Court.
