In the said suit these defendants claimed that Khiroda Shundari Daishya and Lalit Mohan Dash sold the suit property to Salimunnesa on 27.05.1954 and that Khatimunnesa, wife of Doctor Manjurul Haque @ Ali Ahmed was a tenant under Khiroda Shundari Daishya and Lalit Mohan Dash and that after transfer of the suit property she become a tenant under Salimunnesa. Title Suit No. 221 of 1964 was decreed on 25.12.1965 in favour of Rasheda Begum declaring the registered agreements being Nos. 6904 and 6905 dated on 16.11.1959 as cancelled and ineffective. The trial Court further declared the compromise applications filed in Money Suit No. 50 of 1959 and House Rent Control Case No. 598 of 1959 as cancelled. Doctor Manjurul Haque and Khatimunnesa than filed Title Appeal No. 50 of 1966 before the District Judge, Dhaka and the appeal was heard by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge and was dismissed. Thereafter, Majurul Haque and his wife filed Second Appeal No. 1095 of 1966 before the High court Division but the said appeal was dismissed. Then the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 59 of 1994 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for declaration of title to the suit land and also for declaration that the plaintiffs are not bound by the judgment and decree dated 15.11.1979 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979. The plaintiff also filed Money Suit No.73 of 2000 in the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for realization of compensation of taka 28,71,900/-(twenty eight lacs seventy one thousand and nine hundred) along with interest @ of 15% till realization, and the Money Suit was transferred to the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) and renumbered as Money Suit No. 2 of 2002. Both the suits were tried simultaneously and decreed in favour of plaintiffs, respondents herein. Thereafter, the defendants as appellants filed First Appeal No. 181 of 2004 before the High Court Division and the High Court Division by judgment dated 13 day of May, 2008 dismissed the appeals and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court. Whereupon, the present appellants filed CPLA. No. 1358-1359 of 2009 before this Division and this Division by order dated 13.05.2008 dismissed CPLA No. 1358 of 2009 arising out of Money Suit No. 02 of 2002 and LA No. 1359 of 2009 arising out of Title Suit No. 59 of 1994. Then the present appellants, who were defendants of the aforesaid suits filed Civil Review Petition No. 90 of 2010 before this Division. 

 "I. Whether the Gazette notification dated 2nd April 1956 No 4024 LR(sic No.4824 LR) and No.  4836 LR respectively under section 3 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act XXVIII of 1951) (hereinafter mentioned as the SA&T Act) as amended by E.P. Ordinance III of 1956, the rent receiving interest vested in the Government on 02.04. I 956 and exhibit-1 shows Khiroda Shundari Daishya held a Mirash Ijara  interest wider a private land lord and it conclusively proves that the certificate case No. 660 of 1952-53 issued by L.R. Government Acquired Estate are manufactured papers and exhibits-2 and 2(ka) are all also forged papers and the claim of title of the plaintiffs falls through. 

 (1) Admittedly, Khiroda Shundari Daishya and Lalit Mohon Dash were original tenants of the suit property under a private zamindar (জমিদার) i.e. landlord Lakshmi Narayan and others as per Exhibit- 1 i.e. C.S. Khatian. (2) The root of plaintiffs case is that their predecessor in interest Ali Ahmed Dr. Monjurul Haque had purchased the suit property in auction from the R.L. Government Acquired Estates in Certificate Case No. 660 of 1952-53 through exhibit 2 and got possession thereof from the said estate through exhibit 2(ka). 

 (V) the appellants' title to the adjacent land is based on the very auction purchase of the land appertaining to Tauzi No. 61/1 vide conveyance deeds No. 3827 dated 03.09.1954 and, therefore, the appellants have no scope to dispute that the said Tauzi was not at all acquired by the Government earlier than the general notification No. 4836 L.R. dated 2nd April, 1956. 

 (VIII)under the above facts and circumstances the appellants should not be allowed to dispute the statements in their own solemn deeds by the principle of 'estoppels by recitals in the deeds', and in that view of the matter, they should be debarred from disputing the similar facts with regard to the title of the respondents. 

 (XVII) The plaintiffs had been in uninterrupted possession of the suit property since their predecessor's time for more than 60 years and if anyone had purchased the suit property, then the said persons are to file suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession and not the plaintiffs. 

 34. We have examined the judgment of the trial Court dated 31.03.2004 passed in Title Suit No. 59 of 1994, the judgment and decree dated 12th and 13th day of May, 2008 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 181 of 2004, the judgment and order dated 06.05.2010 passed by the Appellate Division in CPLA No. 1359 of 2009, sale Certificate No. 660 of 1952-53 (exhibit-2), certificate of delivery of possession (exhibit-2(ka), Dhaka Gazette Extra-ordinary published by the authority on April 2, 1956, Gazette Extra-ordinary dated 12.02.1954 and the judgment and decree passed by various Courts in various suits, appeals, etc. and the connected materials on record. 

 35. From the judgment of trial Court in Title Suit No. 59 of 1994 decreeing the suit and the judgment of First Appeal No. 181 of 2004 passed by the High Court Division dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment of the trial Court, it appears that the trial Court and High Court Division by elaborate and threadbare discussions on all the issues involved in the suit filed by respondent Nos. 1 and 2-plaintiffs decided merits on the issues on the basis of evidence on record. Both the courts concurrently found that the plaintiff-appellants could prove their title to and possession in the suit property till they were forcibly dispossessed by the defendants. The courts also disbelieved the defendant-appellants case. The CPLA was also dismissed by this Division with reasoning on merit. 

 59. Moreover, admittedly the plaintiffs' predecessor in interest Doctor Monjurul Hoque @ Ali Ahmed had been in possession of the suit property by virtue of those documents as the defendants failed to prove monthly tenancy of Ali Ahmed or his wife under Khiroda Shundari Daishya or anyone else. Admittedly, the plaintiffs had also been in possession of the suit property, till they were dispossessed during the pendency of the suit. Possession follows title. 

 67. The proposition of law enunciated in the said decision can hardly be disputed. But in the instant case both the trial Court as well as the Appellate Court (High Court Division) considering the documents and all the facts and circumstances of the suit/appeal decided it in favour of the plaintiffs. The High Court Division on examination of the documents held as under: "We have examined the sale certificate along with the said form and the rule but we have not found any major deviation or non-compliance with the said form and the rule to make the sale certificate or voidable. We are of the view of that the moment the auction sale was confirmed it took its effect from the date of its sale on 20.06.1953 and it was also acted upon with the delivery of possession of the auction sold property. After all these years the defendants cannot be allowed to challenge the same and that too by way of oral submission through their learned Advocate and thus, to deny plaintiffs title to the suit property." 

 73. We have already seen that in fact the Rup Lal Government Acquired Estate was the owner of 7 annas share of the Tauzi and out of it .568 ajutangsha of land was sold in auction. Moreover, the plaintiffs were admittedly in possession of the suit property. Therefore, if any one claims title to or ownership of the same or part of it, they shall have to file a suit for declaration of title, partition and possession. The defendants, under no circumstance were entitled to evict the plaintiffs from the suit property.

parties:
Abdus Sobahan Miah being dead his heirs 1(a). Reazuddin and others…..Appellants. (In both the appeals)
Vs.
Abdur Rashid Khan being dead his heirs Md. Sohrab Ali Khan and others…..Respondents (In both the appeals)
full_judgment:
3. That the present appellants (in both the appeals) and one Saleha Khatun instituted Title Suit No.31 of 1991 in the 2nd Court of Assistant Judge, Barisal, (originally Title Suit No. 224 of 1985 in the 1st Court of the then Munsif, Barisal) seeking declaration that the auction sale of the suit land as mentioned in schedule 'Ka' to the plaint in Certificate Case No. 472(KT)/1983-84 is fraudulent, collusive, illegal and not binding upon them. On the other hand, the present respondent Nos. 1 and 2 also instituted Title Suit No. 35 of 1991 in the 2nd Court of Assistant Judge, Barisal, (originally Title Suit No. 241 of 1985 in the First Court of the then Munsif, Barisal) against the present appellants and proforma respondent Nos.3-14 (in both the appeals) as defendants, seeking declaration of their title in the suit land and for further declaration that the decree dated 10.8.1959 passed in Title Suit No.220 of 1959 of the 2nd Court of Munsif, Barisal is fraudulent, illegal and not binding upon them. 

 4. It is stated in the plaint of Title Suit No. 31 of 1991 that the suit land originally belonged to Amorendra Nath and others who settled the same with one Abdus Sobahan and Abdul Hamid Howlader; that the said Abdus Sobahan died leaving behind his only son, the plaintiff No.1 and Abdul Hamid Howlader died leaving behind plaintiff Nos.2 to 5 as heirs. It is alleged that when the suit land was wrongly recorded in SA Khatian they instituted Title Suit No. 220 of 1959 and obtained a compromise decree on 10.8.1959, on the basis of which the plaintiffs got the suit land recorded in their names and since then they have been possessing the same. It is further alleged that the defendants fraudulently created an auction sale proceeding in respect of the suit land in Certificate Case No. 472 (KT)/83-84 but did not acquire any title or possession in the same. Hence, the suit. 

 5. On the other hand, the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 35 of 1991 (the present respondent Nos. 1 & 2) in their plaint stated that the suit land belonged to Amorendra Nath and others and the same was put in auction in Certificate Case No. 472(KT)/83-84 and defendant Nos.13 to 16 purchased the same; that the sale was confirmed and the auction purchasers were given possession of the same. The plaintiffs (present respondent Nos.1 and 2) purchased the suit land from the auction purchasers by registered kabala dated 11.4.1985 and have been in possession of the same since then. It is further alleged that the defendants (plaintiffs of Title Suit No.31 of 1991) instituted false Title Suit No. 220 of 1959 and obtained a forged and collusive compromise decree on 10.8.1959 by practicing fraud upon the court. Hence, Title suit No. 224 of 1985 (original Title suit No.31 of 1991) should be dismissed and Title suit No. 241 of 1985 (original Title suit No. 35 of 1991) should be decreed. 

 7. The learned Assistant Judge, after hearing both the suits analogously, dismissed both the suits by judgment and decree dated 19.02.1992. Then the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 35 of 1991 (present respondent Nos. 1 and 2) preferred Title Appeal No. 53 of 1992 and the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.31 of 1981 (present appellants) preferred Title Appeal No.135 of 1992. The learned Subordinate Judge (Now Joint District Judge) after hearing both the appeals analogously, allowed Title Appeal No. 135 of 1992 and thereby decreed Title Suit No. 31 of 1991 and dismissed Title Appeal No. 53 of 1992 and thereby affirmed the dismissal of Title Suit No. 35 of 1991 by judgment and decree dated 27.4.1994. As against that, the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 35 of 1991 (present respondents) moved the High Court Division and obtained two Rules in Civil Revision Nos. 2431 and 2432 of 1994. 

 8. The High Court Division after hearing both the parties, made the Rule issued in Civil Revision No. 2432 of 1994 absolute and thereby dismissed Title, Suit No. 31 of 1991 filed by the present appellants and made the Rule issued in Civil Revision 2431 of 1994 absolute in part and thereby decreed Title Suit No. 35 of 1991 (filed by the present respondent Nos. 1 and 2) in part declaring only to the extent that the judgment and decree dated 10.08.1959 passed in Title suit No. 220 of 1959 is illegal, void and not binding upon the present respondents, by the impugned judgment and order dated 16.5.2007. 

 10. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, the learned senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellants of both the appeals submits that the respondents filed title suit No.35 of 1985 praying for declaration of title to the land mentioned it schedule 'ka' to the plaint on the basis of auction purchase and also praying for a declaration that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 220 of 1959 as illegal and void and the trial court after having found the alleged auction purchase fraudulent and void dismissed the suit and the said judgment and decree of the trial court was affirmed by the appellate court. But the High Court Division affirmed the judgment of two lower courts regarding acquisition of title by that alleged auction purchase but committed error in passing part decree so far it relates to the validity of Title Suit No. 220 of 1959 without considering the fact that since the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 35 of 1991 failed to establish their title to the suit property they have no locus standi to challenge the decree obtained by the plaintiffs in Title Suit No. 220 of 1959. He further submits that the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.31 of 1991(i.e. the present appellants) filed the suit in respect of 1.40 acres of land of Plot No. 21 and .85 acre of land of Plot No.3 on the basis of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 220 of 1959, the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 35 of 1991(i.e. the respondent Nos. 1 and 2) herein, filed their suit in respect of 1.40 acres of land of Plot No. 21 only, but the High Court Division committed error in passing a part decree in favour of the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 35 of 1991 in respect of entire suit land of Title Suit No.31 of 1991.So the judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. 

 11. Mr. Abdul Quiyum, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents submits that the lower appellate court did not reverse the finding of the trial court as regards fraud in respect of the disputed decree of Title Suit No. 220 of 1959 but reversed the judgment of the trial court relying upon the Bank of Calcutta Ltd. vs. Debendra Nath Singh and others reported in 19 DLR 400, which is not applicable in this case. He also submits that the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 31 of 1991 (the present appellants) have no locus standi to challenge the auction of the defendants as the so called settlement in 1358 BS, which is the basis of their title, is not proved by them. He further submits that the courts below misconstrued the evidence of PW-1 who proved mutation by the defendant respondents after the auction purchase within the knowledge of the plaintiffs, so the auction was not fraudulent and as a result the appellants are not entitled to get decree as prayed for. 

 12. On consideration of the submissions advanced on behalf of both the parties and on perusal of the impugned judgment and order and the materials on record it appears that, admittedly, the suit land belonged to Amarendra Nath and others. The plaintiffs of Title Suit No.31 of 20,09, (hereinafter mentioned as appellants claimed that Abdus Subhan Mia, (the plaintiff appellant No. l) and Abdul Hamid Hawlader (predecessor of Plaintiff appellant Nos. 2 to 6) took settlement of the suit land from Amarendra Nath and others; but they did not disclose the date or year of such settlement in their plaint. PW-1, Abdus Sobhan Miah, in his deposition stated that they took settlement from Baidhyanath in the year 1358 BS; but no other PW corroborated PW-1 in this respect nor has the settlement been proved by producing either Patta or Kabuliyat or any other written document. Under the Bengal Tenancy Act, though settlement may be granted orally without any written instrument but in case, if any question arose as to genuineness of such settlement then burden always lies upon the person claiming as such to prove the same settlement by proper oral evidence. But in the present case the appellants have failed to prove such settlement by any proper evidence either oral or documentary. Thus when the settlement, the basis of appellants title, is not proved by proper evidence, they cannot claim title through auction purchase. 

 13. The learned advocate for the appellants claimed that the suit land was not recorded in the names of the settlement holders in the SA Khatian and as a result they filed Title suit No. 220 of 1959 and obtained a compromise decree and by that decree the appellants made the record corrected and thereby included their names in the record and relying upon such submission the appellate court decreed Title Suit No. 31 of 1991 only on the basis of the said compromise decree [Exhibit-2(ka)] passed on 10.8.1959. But on examination of the plaint of Title Suit No. 220 of 1959, the solenama (Exhibit-2) and the Sole decree [Exhibit-2(Ka)] it transpires that there were two plaintiffs and seven defendants in the said suit but none other than Amarendranath (one defendant) and the sole plaintiff No.1, Abdul Hamed, signed the said solenama and the plaintiff No.1 alone put his signature at the bottom of the same. Interestingly neither the other six defendants nor the plaintiff No. 2, Abdul Subhan Miah, signed the said solenama. Moreover, the solenama was not proved by either party of the suit and there is no explanation as to why others did not sign that solenama. On the other hand PW-2, Subudh Chandra Majhi, in his cross examination admitted that “বাবুদের সহিত পত্তনের সময় কথা হইয়াছে যে, মোকদ্দমা করিলেই সোলে করিয়া দিবে। ঐ সময় অন্য বাবুরা বাড়িতেই ছিল। 

 14. Moreover, it also appears that Title Suit No. 220 of 1959 was filed in 1959 and the same claimed to have been decreed on compromise on 10.8.1959 but the Vokalatnama of the said suit appears to have been accepted on 5.5.1985 which is illusive and rather creates doubt. It also appears that no notice was served upon the original owners of the suit land and the defendants of that suit did not appear in the court before signing the Solenama. That's why the trial court found the Vokalatnama of the said suit to be forged one. Again, on perusal of the sole decree [Exhibit-2(ka)] it appears that the suit was disposed of on compromise on 10.08.1959 bit the said decree appears to have been signed by the learned Judge on 19.08.1958. Thus, it is not clear how the decree was prepared and signed one year before passing of the same. These abundant discrepancies in the decree of Title Suit No.220 of 1959 clearly prove that the solenama was not only a fraudulent one but also collusive one and as a result such illegal decree cannot confer any title upon the appellants. 

 16. On the other hand the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.35 of 1991 (hereinafter mentioned as present respondents) claimed that the suit land was put in auction in Certificate Case Nos. 472(KT)/1983-84 and 387(KT)/1976- 77which was purchased by defendant Nos. 1-3 and 5 who took possession of the same through court on 12.10.1984 and since then they have been possessing the same. Subsequently, on 11.04.1985 they transferred .85 acre of land out of the said auction purchased land to this respondent who was given possession of the same. But the courts below found that they failed to prove the sale certificate in support of such auction sale/purchase, also failed to prove delivery of possession and service of notice under sections 7 and 46 of the Public Demand Recovery Act. Though the plaintiffs of Title suit No. 220 of 1959 claimed that they purchased the same from the persons who purchased such land in auction they failed to prove that auction by producing proper evidence. DW-1, Abdur Rashid Khan, deposed that he got possession of the suit land in 1985 but DW-2, Sultan Howladar, admitted in his cross examination that ‘One Gobinda Babu possessed the suit land till 1991' Interestingly DW-4, Razni Kanta Baliar, in his cross examination stated that the plaintiffs (the present respondents) have been possessing the suit land for 20/21 years. On the other hand PW-5, Wazed Ali, in his cross examination stated that the plaintiffs (present respondents) have been possessing the suit land for about 14/15 years. From the aforesaid evidence and discussion it is abundantly clear that the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 35 of 1991 have totally failed to prove their possession in the suit land. 

 17. The learned Advocate for the appellants, on the face of the respondents' Title Suit No. 35 of 1991 for declaration of their title to the suit land on the basis of auction purchase in the year 1985 and also for a declaration that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 220 of 1959 is illegal and void submitted that since they failed to prove the auction purchase they cannot get a decree for declaration that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 220 of 1959 is illegal and void. It is true that the respondents filed their Title Suit No. 35 of 1991 for two declarations, one for declaration of title to the land described in schedule-I to the plaint and another for two declarations, one for declaration of title to the land described in schedule-I to the plaint and another for declaration that the decree passed in title suit No. 220 of 1959 is fraudulent, collusive and not binding upon them. These two prayers are separate and independent and they filed that suit by paying separate court fees for these two separate prayers. Though they filed to prove their title to the land described in schedule-I to the plaint they have successfully proved that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 220 of 1959 is fraudulent, illegal and collusive. 

 So, they can get part decree to the extent of their second prayer. Hence, the High Court Division Committed no wrong in decreeing the suit in part to extent of declaring the decree passed in the Title Suit No. 220 of 1959 to be fraudulent, void, illegal and not binding upon them. 

 18. The appellants further claimed that they filed their Title Suit No. 31 of 1991 in respect of 2.25 acres of land in plot Nos. 21 and 3 but the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 filed Title Suit No. 35 of 1991 in respect of 1.40 acres of land only in plot No. 21 along with a prayer for declaring the decree of Title Suit No. 220 of 1959 fraudulent and void etc. So, the decree passed by the High Court Division is not maintainable in the eye of law. It is required to mention here that though the respondents’ first prayer was in respect of 1.40 acres of land their second prayer for declaration was in respect of the whole suit land i.e. 2.25 acres of land including 1.40 acre of land described in schedule-1 which was the subject matter of Title Suit No. 220 of 1959. So, the claim of the learned Advocate for the appellants finds no legal ground in this respect. 

 19. So, the trial court and the lower appellate court after examining the evidence and materials on record rightly dis-missed both the suits to the extent to which the plaintiffs failed to prove and the High Court Division also rightly affirmed the judgment and order of those two lower courts. But, the High Court Division in its revisional jurisdiction rightly observed that the evidence on record clearly proved that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 220 of 1959 was fraudulent and collusive and as a result the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.35 of 1991 can get part decree to that extent in that suit.

parties:
Shahidul Haque Bhuiyan (Md.) and others ------ Appellants
Vs.
Chairman First Court of Settlement and another ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
3. In respect of other appeal filed by Abdus Sobhan, one Moriam Bapari was the CS recorded tenant of the disputed buildings. Subsequently, Sofar Uddin, Sheikh Sahed Ali and others who were the tenants took settlement from the Zaminder in 1916. Abdus Sobhan inherited the property and as he was minor when the record was prepared it has been recorded in the name of some persons who have no right or title. Abdus Sobhan instituted Title Suit No. 183 of 1972 after coming to know that the then Sub-Divisional Officer was taking attempts to take possession of the property and obtained an injunction. The property is not an abandoned property. Abdus Sobhan, thereafter, by separate deeds transferred some land in favour of Zakia Sultana and Lutful Huda on 22-7-1974. He also sold some other land in favour of Ayub Ali, Md Islam Bhuiyan and some other persons on 22-11-1973, 22-2-1973, 2-4-1974, 14-3-1974 and on other dates. They are now in possession of the same. The enlistment of the property in the abandoned `Kha' list is illegal. 

 4. The above facts disclose two rival claims by two sets of claimants over the same property. One set is claiming the land by way of purchase and gift from the recorded owners, and the other set is claiming by way of inheritance and then transfer by different deeds by one of the alleged heirs on the ground that he got the same exclusively by way of amicable partition. If one version is accepted then the other version cannot be believed. These two versions cannot go simultaneously. None of the groups is claiming clean title and exclusive ownership. The first group also claims benami transaction and the other group is claiming amicable partition among the co-sharers by which one co-sharer exclusively got the property and then he transferred. Under the above admitted facts, the issue which exfacie discloses is whether under the existing law the appellants in both the sets are entitled to any relief under section 7 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985. Before dealing with the issue let us consider the submissions made by the learned Counsel of both the groups. 

 5. In Civil Appeal No. 10 of 2003, Mr. M Amirul Islam submits that the High Court Division erred in law in not interfering with the judgment of the Court of Settlement which refused to release of property in failing to consider that the authority released another property situated at Puran Paltan area in favour of the same owner on being satisfied that Rafi Tehrani was in Bangladesh on the day of promulgation of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 (PO 16 of 1972) and therefore, the property cannot be enlisted as abandoned property. The other point canvassed by the learned Counsel is that there was always a dispute between Rafi Tehrani and Abdus Sobhan since 1972 over the property but Abdus Sobhan's claim was rejected by the trial court in Title Suit No. 31 of 1972. Whereas, in Abdus Sobhan's suit being Title Suit No. 183 of 1972 Rafi Tehrani was impleaded as defendant and this fact proves that Abdus Sobhan has no right or title in the property. On the other hand, the learned Counsel appearing for Abdus Sobhan argues that the law of abandoned property is an administrative law and under the parent law, article 7 provides a statutory notice required to be served for taking possession of the property. Similarly Rule 3(1) also requires the service of notice. Since no prior notice was served, which is a precondition for enlistment of the property in the list and the same having given the jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement, the High Court Division erred in law in not excluding the property from the list of abandoned building, inasmuch as, the Court of Settlement has limited jurisdiction to deal with the property. 

 6. I am not persuaded with the submissions made by the learned Counsel of both the parties, rather the submissions disentitled both the groups from any relief under section 7 of the Ordinance. The Court of Settlement on consideration of the rival claims by two groups clearly held that "the petitioner in Case No.586 of 1999 (appellant in Civil Appeal No.77 of 2003) never admitted that Rafi Tehrani possessed the case property nor this petitioner (Abdus Sobhan) has admitted in his evidence as PW 1 that Raft Tehrani ever possessed the case property. PW 1 Abdus Solihan in Case No.586 of 1988 said that he heard that Raft Tehrani lived in the Ispahani Colony. There is no Ispahani colony situated in the case property. This shows that Rafi Tehrani never lived at Maghbazar, Dhaka". These findings are based on undisputed evidence on record claimed by the respective claimants. These findings negated the claim of the claimants, inasmuch as, they are not legally entitled to any relief under section 7(1) of the Ordinance. Under the scheme of the law the Court of Settlement has no power to decide counter claims made by the parties in the similar manner a civil court can decide. In view of Sub-Section (2) of section 10, though the Court of Settlement has all trappings of a civil court - it does not possess all powers of a civil court, inasmuch as, sub-section (1) of section 10 says the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are not applicable and it has powers of a civil court for (a) summoning witness (b) directing production of a document (c) calling for public record and (d) issuing commission for examination of witness or document, and nothing more. 

 17. The Court of Settlement has been given no power to decide the disputed fact or title relating to the said property. The Court of Settlement can inquire into as to the abandoned character of any buildings and make such order as it deems fit declaring the building not abandoned property or a direction to hand over possession to the claimant if it is found that the possession has been taken illegally. The Court of Settlement is not a court invested with all the powers deter-mining the title of the rival claimants. It is a tribunal established to determine whether the building has been legally enlisted as abandoned property or not. See Bangladesh vs The Chairman, Court of Settlement, 17 BLD (AD) 301 = 50 DLR (AD) 93. 

 18. In the cases in hand admittedly there are rival claimants and therefore, the Court of Settlement has no jurisdiction to resolve the dispute of the rival claims of the parties the determination of which requires determination of title in the property. In this regard the learned Counsel of both the parties have made no effort to repel the admitted rival claims made by the parties. They consciously avoided the said point whenever their attention was drawn in that regard. Their reply is that after the order of release the parties will resolve their dispute in appropriate forum. Both the applicant groups claim deletion of buildings from the list of abandoned buildings but they did not clarify to whom the possession will be delivered. Admittedly they are not in possession of the entire buildings which they have admitted. Secondly, both the groups cannot possess the same buildings at a time. They are not claiming joint possession. When there is conflicting title over the disputed property, the remedy lies in a forum other than the one provided by the Ordinance. 

 20. As to the question whether the owner was in Bangladesh after 25th March, 1971, will be considered later on. Now let us consider the legal matrix of the issue. Sub-section (2) of section 5 states that the lists published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence on the facts that the publication of the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have been vested in the government as such. There is no dispute that the disputed property has been enlisted in the `Kha' list. Therefore, there is presumption that the buildings have been vested in the government as abandoned property until and unless rebuttal evidence is produced by the claimants. Till the claimants can prove that they have right or interest in the property, there is conclusiveness of abandoned nature of the property. It is presumption of law. A presumption of law is a rule of law that a particular inference shall be drawn by a court of law from a particular circumstance. The rebuttable presumptions are intendments made by law, but unlike them, they only hold good until disproved. 

 22. Sub-section (2) of section 5 clearly says that the lists published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included were abandoned property and have been vested in the government. Therefore, a heavy onus cast upon the appellants to prove that the buildings are not abandoned property. The High Court Division and the Court of Settlement on consideration of the materials on record held that the appellants have miserably failed to establish that the buildings are not an abandoned property. This apart, in the face of counter claims about the ownership of the buildings which justifies in coming to the conclusion that the appellants have been claiming the property on the basis of forged deeds, inasmuch as, two inconsistent versions cannot go together. If one version is accepted the other version is bund to fall through or the vice versa. There is no scope under the scheme of the Ordinance to determine by the tribunal that Honse Ara or Abdus Sobhan had title and possession in the property. On the question of onus, references may be made in this connection are the cases of Ministry of Works vs Abdul Jalil, 48 DLR (AD) 10, Bangladesh vs Md Jalil, 49 DLR (AD) 26, KM Zaker Hossain vs Ministry of Works, 8 BLC (AD) 27, and Hezerullah vs Chairman, 3 BLC (AD) 42. 

 24. Article 7(2) provides service of notice upon the person in possession of the property within seven days by the Deputy Commissioner or the authorized person for taking possession. Similar provision has been inserted in clause (b) of section 4 of the Ordinance with the exception that under the latter provision if the possession is to be taken such notice be issued upon him. In order to bring the case under Article 7, the appellants must prove that they are in possession of the building but if they fail to prove possession, the claim of service of notice upon them is redundant for, if they are not in possession how the government can infer that they have right or interest in the buildings. More so, section 4 is a non-obstante clause overriding the provisions contained in the President's Order 16 of 1972. The rules frames under the President's Order cannot supersede the parent law. In the premises, the High Court Division is perfectly justified in holding that the appellants are not entitled to any notice since they are not in possession of the property. In this regard, the Court of Settlement held that the question of non-service of notice required under section 4(1)(b) of the Ordinance was not challenged in the case. Similar views have been taken in Rowshan Ara vs Bangladesh, 59 DLR (AD) 165. It has been held that if the property has assumed the character of abandoned property, 'the listing of the property in question, even if without service of notice as per provision of Ordinance No.54 of 1985, is not material as the property because of non-service of notice of listing in the list of abandoned properties would not cease to be an abandoned property

 31. As regards decrees, it has been strenuously argued that in view of the decrees passed in Title Suit Nos. 31 of 1972 and 425 of 1978, the High Court Division erred in law in not holding that the disputed property was illegally declared as abandoned property. The Court of Settlement on perusal of the plaints and other materials on record came to a definite finding that the decrees were obtained by practising fraud upon the court. The Court of Settlement is perfectly justified in holding as such. It is now settled that even without challenging a decree if it can be shown that any decree has been obtained by fraud a court in a collateral proceeding can ignore such decree. A judgment obtained by fraud or collusion may be treated as nullity. Even the executing court may refuse to execute a void decree without any formal proceedings to set aside the same if it can be shown that on the face of the decree it has been obtained by fraud. It is the party against whom it is offered as shield may prove that the court which gave it had no jurisdiction. If a judgment or decree is vitiated on the ground of fraud the defendant can also resist the decree. 

 32. Section 44 of the Evidence Act was included with the object of avoiding multiplicity of proceedings. It is in order to show that a judgment obtained by fraud from a court is wholly vitiated and has no binding force either on the court passing it or on the party against which it is passed. Other object is that the party against whom the judgment was obtained through fraud should not be compelled to institute another suit and not permitted to move the court from which the judgment was obtained through fraud by raising a defence in the proceedings initiated. A judgment obtained by perjury cannot attain finality and it can be challenged at any time by any interested party by filing an application or by way of defence on the ground that the decree was vitiated by fraud. Reference in these connections are Asmat Ara Begum vs Hajira Bibi, PLD 1964 Peshawar, 283; Rajib Panda vs Lakhan Sendh Mavapatra, 27 Cal 11; Bansi vs Dhap (1902) ILR 24 All 242; Parbati vs Gajraj, AIR 1937 All 28; Prayag vs Siva, AIR 1926 Cal 1; Hare Krishna vs Umesh, AIR 1921 Pat 193; Ranganath vs Gobinda (1904) ILR 28 Bom 639; Jamiruddin vs Khadejanessa, AIR 1929 Cal 685; Gurajada Vijaya vs Padmanabhani, AIR 1955 AP 112, section 1714 of Taylor 's Evidence; Reg vs Sadler's Company (1868) 11 ER 1088; Tribani Mistra vs Ram Pujan Mistra, AIR 1917 Patna 13. In Gram Panchayat of Village Naulakha vs Ujagar Singh, AIR 2000 SC 3272, the Supreme Court of India approved the views taken in those cases and observed "Thus in order to contend in a latter suit or proceeding that an earlier judgment was obtained by collusion, it is not necessary to file an independent suit as stated in Jagor Rami's case for a declaration as to its collusive nature or for setting it aside, as a condition precedent." What's more, the government was not party in those suits and therefore, those exparte decrees are not binding upon them. It can ignore them. Therefore, the Court of Settlement has rightly held that since the decrees were obtained by fraud, these decrees are not binding upon the government.
