A reading of the judgments passed in Title Appeal No. 196 of 1984, Civil Revision 76 of 1987 and Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal No. 297 of 1992 it is primafacie clear that the plaintiffs suit was dismissed as complicated questions of title were involved, but all the courts found their possession in the suit property. It is also a well settled legal proposition that in a suit for permanent injunction regarding an immovable property the court shall see whether the plaintiffs are in exclusive possession of the suit property and it can see title of the plaintiffs incidentally, so all the courts rightly refrained from giving any finding as to the title of the parties to the suit property as well as the auction purchase by Ali Ahmed on 20.06.1953. When all the 3 (three) courts dismissed Title Suit No. 329 of 1980 on the categorical finding that complicated questions of title being involved the suit was not maintainable then how the stray observations even if any made regarding the auction purchase by plaintiffs vendor's predecessor Ali Ahmed can be said to be a constructive res-judicata to nonsuit the plaintiffs, the instant suit being one for title along with the consequential reliefs. We are of the view that in order to non suit the plaintiffs from maintaining a suit of the instant nature on the plea of constructive res-judicata as conceived of in explanation IV to section 11 of the Code the defendants were obliged to prove that in the earlier suit the plaintiffs did not at all plead their title on the basis of the auction purchase by their vendor's processor Ali Ahmed or that there was a conclusive decision in the previous suit on the title of the plaintiffs or the auction purchase but the plaintiffs could prove none. At the risk of repetition we hold that since no issue as to the title of the parties to the suit property and the auction purchase by Ali Ahmed was raised and decided in neither of the suits fought by the parties and the plaintiffs vendors vendor having pleaded in the very first suit his own right title to the suit property it cannot be said that the plaintiffs claim was barred by the principle of constructive res-judicata. So, we find no substance in the submission Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, on the first point and hold that the instant was quite maintainable in law. 

 21. Now let us see whether the plaintiffs proved their title to the suit property. The whole basis of the plaintiffs title to the suit property was the auction purchase by Ali Ahmed on 20.06.1953. Further case of the plaintiffs was that the sale was confirmed on 24.08.1953, the sale certificate was issued on 19.11.1953 and Ali Ahmed got possession of the suit property through court 20.01.1954 and since then he had been in possession thereof. After the death of Ali Ahmed his wife Khatibunnesa inherited his entire property and on her death Abdul Mannan, her full brother inherited the same. In support of the said case of the plaintiffs they filed the sale certificate (exhibit 2) and the writ of delivery of possession (exhibit 2 (ka). In the written statement exhibit 2 and 2 (ka) were not challenged as spurious or forged. In the deposition of D.W. 1 only a general denial was given to the effect: 

 22. From exhibit 2 it is clear that the sale was confirmed on 24.08.1953. From exhibit 2 it is further clear that the entire suit land measuring .568 ajutangsha was sold in auction and not 7 (seven) annas share out of the suit plot. From exhibit 2 it further appears that the said 568 ajutangsha was the 7th annas share of the "হিস্যে" of the touzi being No. 61/1 of Dhaka Collectorate. `Touzi' refers to a page of the register of the tenant. When a property is sold in auction giving specific description thereof and mentioning the area how can it be said that 7 (seven) annas share out of the plot mentioned in the schedule of the sale certificate was sold. Mr. A. J. Mohammad vehemently argued that since in the compromise applications dated 16.11.59 filed in Title Suit No. 50 of 1959 and House Rent Case No. 598 of 1959 and in the two registered agreements of the same date Ali Ahmed claimed to have purchased 7 (seven) annas share out of the suit land, in no case the plaintiffs could claim more than said 7 (seven) annas share of the suit property. But we do not find any substance in the said submission of Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, our reason being that when the alleged agreements and the compromise applications were cancelled at the instance of the defendant's predecessor Rasheda Begum in Title Suit No. 221 of 1964 how reliance could be put on the said agreements and the compromise applications. Further as those were not filed in the instant suit neither the trial court had any chance to see the recitals therein nor this court has any chance to go through the same to verify the submission of Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali. In the plaint the plaintiffs claimed the entire suit property which is clearly mentioned in the sale certificate as well as in the writ of delivery of possession, but the defendants never challenged the identify of the suit property or the area of the suit property. 

 23. The submission of Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali that auction purchase by Ali Ahmed being after the transfer of the suit property to Salimunnesa by the admitted rightful owners, namely, Khiroda Sundari Shaha and Lalit Mohan Das Shaha no title accrued to him appeared to us absolutely fallacious. Because, though the auction sale took place on 20.06.53, yet the number of the certificate case shows that it was started in 1952 being No. 60 of 1952-53. It is also very pertinent to keep in mind that before auction sale notice under section 7 of the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 (the Act) must have been served after observing the other requirements as mandated in sections 4, 5 and 6 of the Act. The said provisions of the Act deal with filing of certificate for public demand payable to the Collector, requisition for certificate in other cases and the filing of certificate on requisition. Rules framed under section 38 of the Act have provided the details as to how the notice under section 7 of the Act shall be served. Section 8 of the Act has clearly stipulated that from and after the service of notice of any certificate under section 7 of the Act upon a certificate debtor any private transfer or delivery of any of his immovable property situated in the district in which the certificate is filed, or of any interest in any such property, shall be void against any claim enforceable in execution of the certificate and the amount due from time to time in respect of the certificate shall be a charge upon the immovable property of the certificate-debtor, wherever situated, to which every other charge created subsequently to the service of the said notice shall be postponed. Section 9 of the Act has clearly provided for filing petition denying the liability and section 10 thereof has spelt out about the hearing and determination of such petition. The defendants in their written statement did not specifically challenge the auction sale, what they pleaded was that Ali Ahmed having earlier claimed that he purchased 7 (seven) annas share of the suit plot the plaintiffs could not claim the entire suit property. Whether the certificate of demand and certificate of requisition were filed before the certificate officer prior to the alleged sale by Khiroda Sundari Daishya and Lalit Mohan Shaha to Salimunnessa are questions of fact and as the defendants did not challenge the certificate proceedings in which Ali Ahmed auction purchased the suit property the plaintiffs were not required to prove all those facts. In support of the plaintiffs claim of title through auction purchase by Ali Ahmed they having filed the sale certificate and the writ of delivery of possession their onus was discharged. Further, as per the own admission of the defendants that Ali Ahmed disclosed the fact of auction purchase as far back as in 1959 when he allegedly created two deeds of agreements and two applications for compromise filed in Money Suit No. 50 of 1959 and in House Rent Case No. 598 of 1959 which were ultimately cancelled in Title Suit No. 221 of 1964, but Rasheda Begum never took any attempt to set aside the said auction purchase by Ali Ahmed. In this regard we like to observe that in a revenue matter proceeding follows the land not the person, so even if Khiroda Sundari Daishaya and Lalit Mohan Shaha sold the suit property prior to the auction sale but that shall not automatically make the auction sale a nullity. It was obligatory upon Rasheda Begum to take step to set aside the sale. In this regard we like point out that rule 39 of the Rules as detailed in schedule 11 to the Act which have binding effect in view of the provision of section 38 of the Act (hereinafter refereed to as the Rules) has clearly provided that if any claim is preferred to or any objection is made to the attachment or sale of, any property in execution of a certificate, on the ground that such property is not liable to such attachment or sale, the certificate officer shall proceed to investigate the claim or objection. Rule 40 has provided that the claimant or the objector must adduce evidence to show that (in case of immovable property) at the date of service of the notice under section 7 of the Act he had some interest in, or was possessed of, the property attached. Rule 41 has given power to the certificate officer to release the property from attachment or sale. Rule 43 has provided that the party against whom an order is made may instant a suit in a civil court to establish the right which he claims to the property in dispute, but subject to the result of such suit (if any) the order shall be conclusive. But Salimunnessa or Rasheda Begum did not take shelter under the said provisions of law to set aside the sale. In the Act or in the rules nothing has been provided for as to when an auction sale shall take its effect, but we can easily take the aid of section 65 of the Code which reads as under: 

 24. It is true that the auction sale in question was not held in execution of a decree of a civil court, but we do not see any wrong in borrowing the concept from the Code it being a civil proceeding and appeared to us quite akin to an auction sale held under the Code in execution of a decree. Mr. Mohammad Ali like a drowning man who catches a straw tried to challenge the auction sale by submitting that the sale certificate does not tally with Form 28 and Rule 74 of the Rules, so on such defective sale certificate the plaintiffs could not claim their title to the suit property. On such submission of Mr. Mohammad Ali we have examined the sale certificate along with the said form and the rule but we have not found any major deviation or noncompliance with the said form and the rule to make the sale certificate void or voidable. We are of the view that the moment the auction sale was confirmed it took its effect from the date of its sale on 20.06.1953 and it was also acted upon with the delivery of possession of the auction sold property. After all these years the defendants cannot be allowed to challenge the same and that too by way of oral submission through their learned Advocate and thus to deny plaintiffs title to the suit property. 

 25. Admittedly the plaintiffs had been in possession of the suit property which was clearly found by all the courts in connection with the proceedings which arose out of Title Suit No. 329 of 1980 of the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka. The plaintiffs by amending the plaint prayed for recovery of khas possession of the suit property and also for mesne profit stating categorically that the defendants dispossessed them and their tenants therefrom forcibly on 16.09.1997. All along plaintiff's case was that their predecessor's predecessor Ali Ahmed got possession of the suit property through court on the basis of his auction purchase and in support of their said case they filed the writ of delivery of possession, exhibit 2 (ka). From exhibit 1 (ka) and 1 (kha) it appears that the S.A. and R.S. khatians were prepared in the name of Ali Ahmed. Exhibit 5 shows that plaintiffs names were mutated and a new khatian being No. 197 was opened in their names. Exhibit 6-6 (Na) series show that Ali Ahmed paid rents to the government and then the plaintiffs paid rents to the government after mutation of their names. Exhibit 7-7 (Nia) series show that the holding in respect of the suit property was recorded with the Dhaka City Corporation in the name of the plaintiffs and they paid City Corporation tax. Exhibits 8. 9 and 10 series show that it is the plaintiffs who paid the utility bills such as Dhaka Was a, gas and electricity in respect of the suit property. Exhibits 11 and 12 series show that the plaintiffs inducted tenants in the suit property who paid rents to them. And those documents primafacie proved that it was Ali Ahmed and the plaintiffs who exercised their right of ownership in the suit property and had been in possession thereof uninterruptedly since the delivery of possession on 20.01.54 by virtue of the auction purchase. On the other hand, the contesting defendants failed to file a single scrape of paper to show that their so-called vendor Rasheda Begum and before that Salimunnesa ever exercised their right of ownership and possession in the suit property or that Ali Ahmed or his wife had ever attorned Salimunnessa as land lord after purchase from Khiroda Sundari Daishya and Lalit Mohan Shaha or they ever paid any rent to Rasheda Begum attorning as their land lord. Not only that the defendants also failed to file/produce any original deed of their alleged vendor Rasheda Begum. It is a well settled legal proposition that though the khatians and rent receipts are not the documents of title, yet they can very much be used for collateral purpose to prove title. The very fact that S.A. and R.S. khatians were prepared in the name of Ali Ahmed and he paid rents to the government and after his death the plaintiffs paid rents and they also paid other utility bills proved their title to the suit property. It is also a salutory legal proposition that possession follows title, so even if it is presumed for argument's sake that the plaintiff's vendor's vendor Ali Ahmed purchased the 7th share of the suit plot as argued by Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, yet due to the long and continuous uninterrupted possession in the suit property since 20.01.1954, the plaintiffs acquired absolute title to the suit property. 

 26. From the judgment passed in Title Suit No. 221 of 1964 it is apparent that Rasheda Begum filed Money Suit No. 50 of 1959 in the Court of the then Munsif 3rd Court, Dhaka for realization of arrear rent and also House Rent Case No. 598 of 1959 in the same court for eviction of her tenant and although Ali Ahmed allegedly took attempt to nullify the result of the said suit and the house rent case by filing two compromise petitions and eventually the said two compromise petitions were declared cancelled in Title Suit No. 221 of 1964, yet thereafter no step was taken by her either to realize arrear rents from Ali Ahmed and his wife Khatibunnesa or to evict them from the suit property. From exhibit 13 it appeared that Rasheda Begum filed Title Suit No. 106 of 1970 on 13.04.70 in the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka against Khatibunnesa and others for declaration of title and injunction. Exhibit 13 further shows that the said suit was dismissed for default on 28.06.72. The said fact was asserted in the plaint as well as in the deposition of p. w. 1. Rasheda Begum did not take any step to set aside the said order of dismissal by filing an application under Order 9, rule 9 of the Code. Exhibit 14, the application filed by the plaintiffs for the certified copy of the plaint of said Title Suit No. 106 of 1970 also shows that the said order of dismissal was passed on 28.06.72; the certified copy of the plaint could not be supplied as the record was destroyed. Rule 9 of Order 9 of the Code has clearly spelt out that where a suit is dismissed wholly or partly under rule 8 of Order 9 of the Code the plaintiff shall be precluded from bringing a fresh suit on the same cause of action. Section 12 of the Code has clearly debarred a plaintiff from instituting a further suit in respect of any particular cause of action where he is precluded by rules from instituting a further suit. In this regard we may also refer to the provision of sub rule (3) of Rule 1 of Order XXIII of the Code which is as under: 

 27. Thus, it appeared to us that in fact, Rasheda Begum defendant's so-called vendor abandoned her claim to the suit property by not taking any step to set aside the order of dismissal of Title Suit No. 106 of 1970. It is true that it is not the defendants who have come for title, but when they set up a specific case of their title to the suit property through Rasheda Begum by obtaining an ex-parte decree for specific performance of contract and tried to justify their possession in the suit property we can very much see whether their vendor had any right and title to the suit property. From the above, it is clear that Rasheda Begum failed to establish her title to the suit property, so how the defendants could claim title to the suit property through Rasheda Begum in their defence to deny the plaintiffs title when they proved their story of acquisition of title and possession in the suit property by filing documents without any gape right from the auction purchase of the suit property by, Ali Ahmed. In this regard it is also very pertinent to state that the plaintiffs in theft plaint categorically stated that after a few days of the liberation of Bangladesh Resheda Begum left Bangladesh for Pakistan Via Nepal and did not enter into any contract with the defendants to sell the suit property, but they created a forged bainapatra. P.W.1 also deposed in court to the said effect. But the defendants failed to produce any evidence whatsoever to show that at the time of bainapatra which was allegedly executed on 12.08.72 or thereafter Rasheda Begum was in Bangladesh. Rather, the evidence of D.W.1 in his cross-examination to the effect: 

 corroborates the plaintiff's case that at the relevant time of execution of the alleged bainapatra by Rasheda Begum and during the period of filing of Title Suit No. 62 of 1979, at the time of passing of the decree as well as up to the execution and registration of the kabala in favour of the defendants she was not in Bangladesh. Our view is further strengthen from the further fact that Title Suit No. 106 of 1970 brought by Rasheda Begum was dismissed for default on 28.06.72, had she remained present in Bangladesh after liberation then she would not have allowed the suit to be dismissed for default. Further though the defendants filed the bainapatra, yet none proved the same and none deposed as to the fact of passing of consideration to Rasheda Begum as part performance of the contract. Since the plaintiffs were not party in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979 filed by the defendants and they were claiming title to the suit property on the basis of a decree passed therein the plaintiffs had every right to challenge the propriety of the decree passed in the suit, particularly when they prayed for a declaration to the effect that they were not bound by the judgment and decree passed therein. As the plaintiffs challenged the bainapatra allegedly entered into by Rasheda Begum and the ex-parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979 as fraudulent the onus was upon the defendants to prove that the bainapatra was genuine and the decree in the said suit was obtained in a regular course on due service of summons of the suit upon Rasheda Begum in Bangladesh but they failed to discharge the said onus. It is also very significant to state that the defendants could not file any original title deed of their alleged vendor Rasheda Begum which also creates primafacie doubt about their case of bainapatra entered into by Rasheda Begum. 

 28. We conclude by holding that the plaintiffs proved their 16 (sixteen) annas title to the suit property. 

 30. So, the plaintiffs could not be evicted from the suit property other that due process of law. The defendants levied Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka for execution of the decree. The defendants admitted in the written statement that though the bailiff went to the suit property yet he could not deliver possession thereof to them because of the resistance put by the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs specific case was that the defendants dispossessed them and their tenants forcibly on 16.09.97 and looted away the goods for which they amended the plaint and prayed for recovery of khas possession along with other reliefs including mesne profit. Whereas the defendant's case was that the plaintiffs of their own delivered vacant possession of the suit property to them on 05.10.97 on receipt of, a sum of taka 16,60,000/00 on 30.09.97 on the basis of a salish/mediation done by Hajee Md. Selim, the local member of the parliament and the other respectable people of the locality. Defendant's further case was that Abdul Majid, father of the plaintiffs acknowledged the receipt of the said amount of money in writing in a paper by putting his signature which was subsequently signed by plaintiff No. 2 on 05.10.97. P.W.1 categorically denied the said assertion of the defendants. In support of the forcible dispossession by the defendants from the suit property the plaintiffs besides examining plaintiff No. 2 as p.w.1 also examined 3 (three) other witnesses and filed documentary evidence. P.W.1 in his examination-in-chief categorically stated that while the suit was pending the defendants entered into the suit property along with 20/30 terrorists and dispossessed them and looted away the goods which included gold ornaments. The defendants also looted away the goods of their tenants. P.W.1 further stated that over the said incident their father lodged a complaint with Lalbag Police Station which gave rise to Case No. 32 (9) 97. On behalf of the 'bharatias' Wazir Ahmed also lodged a general dairy with Lalbag Police Station being No. 940 dated 16.09.97. The certified copy of the First Information Report (FIR) was filed and marked as exhibit 16 and the copy of the general diary was filed and marked as exhibit 17. The p. w. further stated that the news of their illegal eviction from the suit property and the looting away of goods therefrom were published in the daily Inquilab and the Bhorer Kagaj on 18.09.97 and 20.09.97 respectively. The copies of the said news papers were filed and marked as exhibits 18 series. P.W.1 further deposed that on 30.09.97 the defendants by force obtained a writing from his father in a white paper to the effect that he received taka 16,60,000/00 and then on 05.10.75 also obtained a similar writing from him in the same paper though they did not receive any money. In cross-examination p.w.1 further asserted that no salish took place on 30.09.97 at the house of the ex-member of the parliament. Hajee Selim at the presence of the plaintiffs and the Ward Commissioner and they did not put their signature on receipt of a sum of taka 16,60,000/00 (sixteen lacs sixty thousand). P.W.1 further asserted that his signature was obtained in the receipt on 05.10.97 by force. P.W.2, Abdul Majid, the father of the plaintiffs categorically stated in his examination-in-chief that Rasheda Begum was never the owner of the suit property and she never possessed the same and Title Suit No. 106 of 1970 filed by her for declaration of title was dismissed for default. This P.W. further stated that on 16.09.97 the defendants being accompanied by 20/25 goondas dispossessed the plaintiffs and their bharatias by force and looted away the goods. After eviction the defendants took him to court forcibly and got the suit withdrawn on the threat that if he did not withdraw the suit they would kill his sons (the plaintiffs). On 30.09.97 the defendants took him to their office and then got a paper written by him to the effect that he received taka sixteen lacs and sixty thousand. At first it was written as 16,000/00. He further stated that he did not receive any money from the defendants. P.W.2 denied the defendant's case that he, on 30.09.97 in presence of the former member of the parliament Hajee Selim and others demanded taka 20,00,000/00 (twenty lacs) from the defendants as compensation and on receipt of taka 16,60,000/00 delivered possession of the suit property and withdrew the civil and criminal cases. This p. w. corroborated P.W.1 on all other points. By cross-examining these two P.W. s the defendants could not at all shake the credibility of their testimony in examination-in-chief. 

 33. The defendants examined 9 (nine) witnesses, of them D.W.1 is defendant No. 2. D.W.1 admitted that the plaintiffs had been in possession of the suit property but asserted that the plaintiffs were not the owners of the suit property. D.W.1 asserted in his examination-in-chief that on 30.09.1997 at the mediation (ম��্যস্থতায়) of the former local member of the parliament Hajee Md. Selim, Ward Commissioner of Ward No. 61, Hajee Md. Masum, ex-ward Commissioner of Ward No. 60 Mosharaf Hossain and the others, namely, Janab Lal, Janab Md. Uzir (p.w.3), Md. Yousup, Md. Aziz, Md. Shawkat, Md. Mesbahuddin including the plaintiffs, their mother, their maternal uncle Abdul Gani, the plaintiffs father admitted that it was the defendants who were entitled to get the suit property and on demand of compensation to leave the suit property as well as to settle somewhere else Hajee Selim settled the amount of compensation at taka 16,60,000/00 on the further condition that the plaintiff's father would withdraw the cases both civil and criminal and that in the very salish they paid the said amount which was received by the plaintiffs, their father and maternal uncle. D.W.1 further asserted that Abdul Majid in his own hand wrote in a paper to the effect that he received the said amount and put his own signature which was also signed by the plaintiffs maternal uncle Abdul Gani on 30.09.97 and thereafter plaintiff No. 2 wrote similar thing on 05.10.73 in the said paper and then he put his signature. D.W.1 further asserted that after receiving the money on 30.09.97 the plaintiffs shifted their goods from the suit property to the house of their maternal uncle from 01.10.97 to 04.10.97 and then on 05.10.1997 delivered possession of the suit property to them. D.W.2 is one Md. Islam. He did not say a ward about the salish/settlement and payment of money on 30.09.97 at the mediation of Hajee Selim and others. He stated that the plaintiffs and their father delivered possession of the suit property to the defendants on 05.10.1997 and he was present at the said time. After 7/8 months therefrom the process server from the court went to the suit property and having found the defendants in possession gave the report which he signed. In cross-examination he stated that Din Mohammad father of defendant No. 2 was his tenant. In the suit land there were shops and the plaintiffs also used to live there. He further stated to the effect: 

 42. The evidence of the D.W.S does not inspire confidence in our mind to believe defendant's case that the plaintiffs voluntarily handed over possession of the suit property to them on 05.10.1997 on receipt of a sum of taka 16,60,000/00 (sixteen lacs sixty thousand), on 30.09.97, as it sounded absurd to us that when the plaintiffs fought upto the Appellate Division to maintain their possession in the suit property by filing Title Suit No. 329 of 1980 in the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka against the defendants and then filed application in Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980 so that they could not be evicted through the execution of the said case and fought upto this Division they would leave the same on receipt of a sum of taka 16,60,000/00 the suit being ready for peremptory hearing. Defendant's story of delivery of possession by the plaintiffs also appear to us against the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business in relation to the facts of the case as articulated in section 114 of the Evidence Act. If the plaintiffs handed over the vacant possession of the suit property to the defendants voluntarily then why there should be “ভাংচুর” as deposed by P.W.3 and evident from exhibits 16, 17 and 18 series. Had such a huge amount been paid as a. prize for the compromise then it would have been written in a form of document signed by both the parties and duly witnessed by the witnesses stating in detail the terms of compromise and the fact of voluntary delivery of possession. And what prevented the defendants to take step to file a compromise application in the suit to dispose of the same as per terms of the compromise. We have seen the alleged writing of Mr. Abdul Majid as to the receipt of taka 16,60,000/00 allegedly paid to him by the defendants as a settlement to leave the suit property as incorporated in the additional paper book. It is to be noted that original money receipt was not filed but from the evidence of D.W.1 it appeared that the same was written on the pad of Hajee Selim local member of the parliament. Though a photostat copy of the same was allegedly filed when D.W.1 was examined, we could not find out the same from the record. However, the said writing is as under: 

 43. The very writing as relied upon by the defendants as a proof of their payment of taka 16,60,000/00 to the plaintiffs appeared to us shocking and repulsive. It is unbelievable that when the bailiff from the Court failed to deliver possession of the suit property due to the resistance put by the plaintiffs they would hand over vacant possession of the same to the defendants on the basis of a mere money receipt written on a pad of a local member of the parliament; and that to in four lines having no reference to the suit property and the names of the parties. None of the persons who were allegedly present in the salish including the local member of the parliament Hajee Selim and the local Ward Commissioner was examined in court. What business the local member of the parliament had to meddle in the matter when both the suit and the execution case were pending in Court. Further, from the evidence of the D.W.S it is apparent that the alleged salish was held only on one date, that is, on 30.09.97, if that be so, how is that on the same sitting such a huge amount could be arranged and given by the defendants. How did they know that there would be a settlement on that very date and they would be required to pay the said amount. How is that in the alleged money receipt Abdul Majid put his signature on 30.09.97, whereas defendant No. 2 put his signature on 05.10.97. Moreno, if possession of the suit property was delivered voluntarily as claimed by the defendants then there must be a paper showing delivery of possession by the plaintiffs or their father executed in favour of the defendants. In this regard it is very pertinent to state that after the plaintiffs failed to resist the proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980 by filing an application under Order XXI, rule 99 of the Code they filed an application in the suit on 28.11.94 for temporary injunction praying for restraining the defendants from evicting them from the suit property till disposal of the suit. On the said application a notice was issued upon the defendants asking them to show cause within 10 (ten) days as to why an order of temporary injunction as prayed for shall not be granted. As the said application for temporary injunction could not be heard and the defendants were taking desperate attempt to dispossess them the plain-tiffs on 14.09.97 filed an application under section 151 of the Code praying for an order of temporary injunction with a prayer for ad-interim injunction so that they could not be evicted through the proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980. Copy of the said application was duly served upon the learned Advocate of the defendants. The court below fixed the said application for hearing on the next date, that is, on 07.10.97. In the meantime the plaintiffs were evicted on 16.09.97 and the reason for such action by the defendants is obvious. P.W.1, categorically asserted the said facts in his deposition but he was not cross-examined on the said facts. The fact of forcible dispossession is also borne out from the photographs taken from the suit property after the eviction and exhibit 18 series which show that the structures on the suit property were damaged by resorting to vandalism. D.W.1 also admitted that he did not protest the news item published in the two dailies, namely, the Bhorer Kagaz and the Inquilab in that respect. From the evidence as discussed hereinbefore, it appeared to us that the defendants by taking law in their own hands dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit property forcibly just to frustrate the result of the suit which is very much deplorable and shocking and if such action of the defendants is countenanced to that would bring the whole legal system of dispensation of justice through court into jeopardy. 

 44. The fact that there was a one storied building, 10 (ten) family rooms and 13 (thirteen) shops in the suit property and after taking possession of the suit land those were demolished are also admitted by the D.W.S apart from the evidence of the p. w. s particularly,P.W.3, an independent and disinterested witness as already discussed hereinbefore. Therefore, we find no reason to disbelieve plaintiffs case that because of their forcible dispossession from the suit property by the defendants on 16.09.97 and then demolition of the 10 (ten) family quarters and 13 (thirteen) shop rooms they were deprived of monthly rent from the tenants and so they were entitled to get the mesne profit as decreed by the court below.

full_judgment:
These three Rules were issued in Civil Revision Nos. 2525 of 2005, 2526 of 2005 and 2527 of 2005 arising out of Title Appeal No. 145 of 1996 against the Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 (original Title Suit No. 180 of 1990), Civil Revision No. 2526 of 2005 arising out of Title Appeal No. 144 of 1996 against the Title Suit No. 16 of 1995 (original Title Suit No. 137 of 1994) and Civil Revision No. 2527 of 2005 arising out of Title Appeal No. 143 of 1996 against the Title Suit No. 72 of 1994 (original Title Suit No. 194 of 1990) calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 15-2-2005 and 22-2-2005 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Jhenidah, in Title Appeal Nos. 143 of 1996, 144 of 1996 and 145 of 1996 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 30-6-1996 and 7796 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Jhenidah, in Title Suit Nos. 60 of 1994, 16 of 1995 and 72 of 1994 decreeing the suit should not be set aside. 

 3. The short fact of the case is that the plaintiffs-petitioners brought the Title Suit No. 180 of 1990 in the Court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Jhenidah for a declaration that the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 283 of 1988 on 3-6-1990 in favour of the respondent-opposite party in respect of 14 decimals of land under suit Plot No. 1057 of SA Khatian No. 90 of Mouza Teordah No. 254 was collusive, inoperative, illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff-petitioners who claimed themselves to be necessary parties was not in pleading in Title Suit No. 283 of 1988. Title Suit No. 283 of 1988 was brought by defendant-opposite party for declaration of his title in 14 decimals of said land. The said suit was transferred to the Court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Jhenidah for trial and the Title Suit No. 180 of 1990 was renumbered as 60 of 1994. 

 4. The plaintiff-petitioners case, in brief, is that 25 decimals of land under SA Khatian No. 90, Mouza Teordah No. 254 was taken on lease by one Mubarak Mridha from CS recorded tenant Ratikanta and others. While he was possessing thereof he sold the same to Abdur Rashid Miah by a registered kabala dated 2-3-1965. While Abdur Rashid was in possession thereof by mutating his name and by payment of rent thereof he sold the same to the plaintiff petitioner Nos. 13 by three separate kabalas dated 12-11-86. The plaintiff-petitioner No. 4, the father of plaintiff-petitioner, possessed the suit land on their behalf along with other lands of the suit plot by paying rent and, by mutating their name and amalgamating the same with his other adjoining nonsuited lands under his own Plot Nos. 1058 and 1059 by establishing a paddy crushing mill and Chatal thereon. On 8-7-91 respondent-opposite party secretly managed to obtain the ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 283 of 1988 and thereafter threatened to dispossess the plaintiff-petitioners from the 14 decimals of said land by virtue of the said ex parte decree dated 3690. So the plaintiff-petitioners brought the Title Suit No. 180 of 1990 and thereafter the said suit was renumbered as Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 which was filed for declaration that the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 283 of 1988 is not binding on them. The suit was dismissed by his judgment and decree dated 21-11-1991. The plaintiff-petitioners filed the Title Appeal No. 216 of 1991 against the dismissal order. The appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Jhenidah who was pleased to allow the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court and by the said judgment the Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 was sent on remand to the Trial Court for fresh trial analogously with Title Suit No. 72 of 1994 (a suit brought by respondent-petitioner Lutfur Rahman for declaration of his title in 14 decimals of land and for partition by metes and bounds) by taking into consideration the evidence, documents already filed by either party and by giving an opportunity to the parties to adduce further oral evidence, if necessary. Accordingly, the Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 was analogously tried with Title Suit No. 72 of 1994 brought by the plaintiff-petitioners for their declaration of title in 14 decimals of land, all these three suits between the same parties over the same suit land. 

 5. The case of the defendant (respondent-opposite party) Lutfur Rahman is that the suit land along with other lands originally belonged to TC Tude under whom Rati Kanta and Makhan Sundari Dasya were the tenants. They defaulted in payment of rent, TC Tudi obtained a rent decree against them. Subsequently, he sold 14 decimals of said land to Didar Baksh and Chan Khan, Ratikanta and Makhan Sundari again defaulted in payment of rent and again the land was put to auction for sale on obtaining rent decree. Didar Baksh and Monaim purchased the same in auction and went into possession thereof. Thereafter, they sold 14 decimals of land to Abdul Gani on 20-6-60. While in possession thereof Abdul Gani sold the same to respondent-opposite party Lutfar Rahman who went into possession of the land and constructed building thereon. Plaintiff-petitioners threatened to dispossess Lutfar Rahman from the said building on 6th Sravan, 1397 BS so he brought the Title Suit No. 72 of 1994 and prayed for injunction, but show cause notices were served upon the plaintiff-petitioners but they constructed building on the said land in spite of serving of such notice. Plaintiff-petitioners were never in possession of the said 14 decimals of land before hand. The defendant-opposite party in their additional written statement also stated that the record of right in respect of the said land in the name of Mobarak Mridha was wrongly recorded. He also denied the allegation that Abdur Rashid was in possession of the said land. But the plaintiff-petitioners are in possession of the said land and by constructing godown and Chatal thereon. So, according to him, plaintiff-petitioner's false Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 and Title Suit No. 16 of 1995 are liable to be dismissed and the case brought by him as plaintiff being 'Title Suit No. 72 of 1994 needs to be decreed. 

 6. During the trial the Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 was dismissed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Jhenidah by his judgment and order dated 21-11-91. 

 8. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Jhenidah tried the Title Suit No. 60 of 1994, Title Suit No. 72 of 1994 and 16 of 1995 analogously and by taking into consideration all the documents already filed and examining the evidence on record decreed the Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 and Title Suit No. 16 of 1995 brought by the plaintiff-petitioners and dismissed the Title Suit No. 72 of 1994. He also declared title of the plaintiff-petitioners to the said land and further declared that the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 283 of 1988 is inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff-petitioners by his judgment dated 30-6-96, in other words, the plaintiff-petitioners obtained the judgment and decree of both the cases in his favour and the case of the defendant-opposite parties were dismissed. 

 9. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree the defendant-opposite party preferred the Title Appeal Nos. 143 of 1996, 144 of 1996 and 145 of 1996 against the judgment and decree of the learned Senior Assistant Judge. Additional Court, Jhenidah dated 30-6-96 in respect of Title Suit No.72 of 1994, Title Suit No. 16 of 1995 and Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 respectively. This revisional application is related to Title Appeal No; 145 of 1996 arising out of Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 which is in respect of plaintiff-petitioner's prayer for declaration that the ex parte decree obtained by the defendant-opposite party in Title Suit No. 283 of 1988 is not binding upon the plaintiff-petitioners. Thereafter, the lower Appellate Court heard all the three appeals analogously being Title Appeal Nos. 143 of 1996, arising out of Title Suit No. 72 of 1994, Title Appeal No. 144 of 1996 arising out of Title Suit No. 16 of 1995, Title Appeal No. 145 of 1996 arising out of Title Suit No. 60 of 1994. The learned lower appellate Court allowed all the appeals and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court and in Title Appeal No. 143 of 1996 on the prayer of the appellants lawyer before the Appellate Court who submitted that as a matter of fact the lawyer who conducted the Title Suit No. 72 of 1994 before the trial Court could not produce some important documents and the plaint also needs to be amended, therefore, if the appeal is sent on remand to the trial Court for proper adjudication of the eases justice would be met. On the prayer of the lawyer of the appellants of Title Appeal No. 143 of 1996 the lower appellate Court sent all the appeals on remand to the trial Court for fresh trial directing the trial Court by giving an opportunity to both the parties to adduce evidence and produce documents and amend the plaint, if necessary. 

 10. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree dated 15-2-2005 and 22-2-2005 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Jhenidah, in Title Appeal Nos. 143 of 1996, 144 of 1996 and 145 of 1996 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 30-6-96 and 7-7-96 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court Jhenidah, in Title Suit Nos. 60 of 1994, 16 of 1995 and 72 of 1994 the respondent-petitioner preferred the instant revisional application before the High Court Division under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule. 

 11. Mr Muhammad Nazrul Islam with Mr Syed Al-Asafur Ali, appearing on behalf of the respondent-petitioners, submits that the learned lower appellate Court is absolutely wrong and erroneous in sending the case back on remand unnecessarily for fresh trial which will take a long time to dispose of the suit causing hardship to parties. Next, he submits that the appellate Court committed an error of law by passing further order of allowing fresh evidence when fresh evidence has already been adduced by the plaintiff-petitioners and also examined more witnesses by the plaintiff-petitioners and the defendants also. He further submits that the lower appellate Court committed an error of law by giving an opportunity to the defendant-opposite party to fill up the lacuna by taking fresh evidence who miserably failed to prove his case even at the time of fresh trial earlier when the case was remanded for retrial in Title Appeal No. 216 of 1991. The learned Counsel finally, submits that the lower appellate Court only to shirk his responsibility sent the case on remand for fresh trial to the trial Court where there is a Provision under section 117 of the Code of Civil Procedure that the appellate Court is absolutely empowered to examine and take evidence, if necessary, for proper adjudication instead of sending the case back to the trial Court for causing unnecessary delay. 

 14. In view of the discussion made above and the facts and circumstances of the case and also the legal position, the judgment and decree dated 15-2-2005 and 22-2-2005 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Jhenidah, in Title Appeal No. 145 of 1996 heard analogously with Title Appeal Nos. 143 of 1996 and 144 of 1996 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 30696 and 7796 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Jhenidah, in Title Suit Nos. 60 of 1994 heard analogously with Title Suit No. 16 of 1995 and 72 of 1994 decreeing the suit and the order of remand for sending the suits to the trial. Court for fresh trial is hereby set aside and the lower appellate Court is directed to rehear the appeals as expeditiously as possible preferably within 3(three) months and dispose of the appeals in accordance with law, if necessary, by examining witnesses and taking additional evidence, without sending the suits to the trial Court for fresh trial.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Syed Abu Kowser Md. Dabirush-Shan

parties:
Matiar Rahman ----- Appellants
Vs.
Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property Lands and Buildings ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
2. The appeal was filed against the judgment and order dated June 29, 1982 of the 1st Court of Additional District Judge, Bakerganj in Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1980 allowing the same. The aforesaid miscellaneous case was registered upon an application filed under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the respondent herein in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 seeking review of the judgment and decree dated 31-12-79 affirming the judgment and decree dated August 22, 1973 passed in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 decreeing the same. The suit was filed seeking decree for permanent injunction and for declaration that the property in suit is not enemy property i.e. vested property. 

 3. The appellant filed Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 seeking the relief as stated hereinbefore stating, inter alia, that he obtained decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge, Bakerganj) and on the basis of the said decree got his name recorded in the revenue record, that the defendant No. 2 illegally declared the property in suit as enemy property and he having had come to know about the said fact filed objection on November 5, 1970 and that the defendant No. 2 rejected the said objection and thereupon, treating the land in suit vested property, threatened the appellants to evict them from the land in suit. 

 4. The suit was contested by the defendant No. 2 alleging that the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 was fraudulent one and that the same was filed impleading dead persons and that the appellant obtained the compromise decree therein showing dead persons as parties to the compromise. It was also the case of the defendant No. 2 that part of the property in suit along with building and tin shed was requisitioned and the same is possessed by the defendants. The defendant also denied the possession of the plaintiff in the land in suit. The definite case of the defendant No. 2 is that the property in suit was treated as enemy property on February 18, 1967 since the owners of the property migrated to India, that recorded owner Sreenath Chatterjee died on July 24, 1947 and, as such, decree obtained in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 showing said Sreenath Chatterjee as party to the compromise was illegal. 

 5. The trial Court on consideration of the materials on record held that plaintiff acquired title in the land in suit on the basis of the decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 and thereupon got his name mutated in the revenue record and paid rent, that the defendant failed to establish his contention that the decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 was obtained against the dead persons. The trial Court also found possession of the plaintiff in the land in suit and thereupon decreed the suit with the finding that the order of treating the property in suit as enemy property is illegal. The trial Court restrained the defendant No. 2 permanently from interfering with the possession of the plaintiff. 

 6. The defendant No. 2 went on appeal, Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973. The appellate Court by the judgment and decree dated December 31, 1979 dismissed the appeal and thereby affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court passed in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 of the 2nd Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge) Barisal on August 22, 1973. 

 7. As against the judgment and decree in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 the respondent herein i.e. the appellant in the aforementioned appeal, filed an application under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure seeking review of the appellate judgment contending that at the time of hearing of the suit and the appeal the appellant i.e. the respondent herein, could not place material documents i.e. death certificate of Sreenath Chatterjee and the record of the Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959. 

 8. In the petition for review it was stated that the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 is claiming the property on the basis of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970, which was filed averring that the land in suit orally was settled to him by the recorded tenants, that the suit i.e. Title Suit No. 634 of 1970, was contested by the defendant No. 2, i.e. petitioner in the review petition, whereupon Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1980 was registered, primarily contending that the recorded tenants of the property left for West Bengal, India and thereupon the property in question was treated as enemy property and that some of the recorded tenants died long before obtaining decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970, that the solenama on the basis of which Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 was decreed was a fraudulent one and that the said solenama was said to have been signed by persons who died long before filing of the Title Suit No. 198 of 1970, that the government is in possession of the property on the basis of Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959, that during the trial as well as at the time of hearing of the appeal in spite of exercising due diligence could not bring on record the vital papers, i.e. the record of the Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 and the death certificate of Sreenath Chatterjee, who died on July 24, 1947. 

 9. The application for review was opposed by the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 i.e. plaintiff-respondent in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973, contending that the death certificate of Sreenath Chatterjee sought to be produced before the Court by the petitioner is forged and that the petitioner had all the opportunities to produce the death certificate and the record of the requisition case before the trial Court as well as before the appellate Court but he did not do so and that the petitioner is guilty of serious laches and negligence and, as such, the review application filed seeking production of the papers for the consideration of the Court, which he could have produced earlier, should not be allowed as the petitioner is guilty of laches and negligence. 

 11. As against the order of the 1st Court of Additional District Judge Bakerganj allowing the Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1980 the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 moved the High Court Division in appellate jurisdiction, First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 9 of 1982. The High Court Division dismissed the appeal upon observing " The learned Court Of appeal below in the circumstances of the case held that the petitioners could not produce the death certificate and the record of the Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 at the time when the decree was passed in spite of exercise of due diligence and the petitioners have been aggrieved and accordingly, allowed the application for review under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and passed order for re-hearing of the appeal. I have already pointed out that the application under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was simply allowed and an order was passed for re-hearing of the appeal i.e. Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973. So that appellant's claim that the judgment and decree dated 31-12-1979 passed in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 affirming the judgment and decree dated 22-8-1973 passed in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 of the 2nd Court of Munsif, Barisal were set aside is not correct. The appeal being Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 as per order of the Court of appeal below be re-heard". 

 13. The learned Counsel in support of the appeal submitted that respondent was required to seek remedy against the decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 and unless the said decree is set aside plaintiff's right, title and interest in the land in suit remains fortified and the genuineness of the decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 can no way be the subject matter of the appeal re-hearing whereof has been ordered by the appellate Court and affirmed by the High Court Division, that the respondent has chosen wrong forum to agitate the question of obtaining the decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 against the dead persons, that there is no scope to consider the review application in view of the provision of Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as the facts alleged for review were very much within the knowledge of the respondent, particularly the record of the Requisition case and, as such the same having not been produced before the  Court or step having not been taken for production thereof before the Court, it cannot be said that after due diligence the said record could not be produced before the Court, that facts pleading which the review application was filed were pleaded in detail in the written statement and that as the same demonstrate that the facts sought to be placed before the Court through the review application were very much within the knowledge of the respondent and he having had not taken step for production thereof, either before the trial Court or the appellate Court, the High Court Division as well as the lower appellate Court were in error in allowing the review application in total disregard of the provision of Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, that the issue raised as to matter of death of Sreenath Chatterjee could have been brought before the Court by leading oral evidence but having had not done so in spite of the fact that in the written statement in detail the said issue was raised and, as such, the High Court Division as well as the appellate Court were in error in allowing the review application and thereby in allowing the respondent to bring on record the fact which could have been brought on record at the time of trial as well as at the time of hearing of the appeal and thus, the action of the High Court Division as well as of the appellate Court in the name of the re-hearing of the appeal is nothing but given premium of the laches or negligence to the respondent. 

 17. In the instant case as it appears from the judgment of the High Court Division and the appellate Court that the review was sought to be brought before the Court for the certified copy of the death register relating to the fact of death of Sreenath Chatterjee said to have died on July 24, 1947, one of the owners and the recorded tenant of the land in suit and who was a signatory to the compromise petition on the basis of which Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal was decreed and thereby title of the appellant herein in respect of the land in suit was declared and further, the record of Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 was not within the knowledge of the respondent herein. 

 18. The law relating to the review as in Order XLVII, rule 1 is that a review of a decree or order may be sought on the discovery of an important matter or evidence which after exercise of due diligence was not within the knowledge of the person seeking review or could not be produced by the person who is seeking review at the time of hearing of the case and the decree was passed. In the instant case as is seen from the written statement of the defendant No. 2 (herein respondent) that the facts on the basis of which review of the judgment and decree passed in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973, which was preferred against the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 decreeing the suit, which was a suit for permanent injunction and for a further declaration that the property in suit is not enemy property (now vested property) was sought were categorically stated therein. In the written statement it was categorically asserted by the respondent herein that Sreenath Chatterjee one of the recorded tenants of the land in suit died on July 24, 1947. The fact of requisition of part of the property was also stated in the written statement. 

 19. In the afore state of the matter in our opinion the facts i.e. record of the Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 and the fact of alleged death of Sreenath Chatterjee on July 24, 1947 were very much within the knowledge of the respondent herein who sought for review of the decree passed in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973. We are of the view as the facts averred in the written statement i.e. requisitioning of the property in suit, by initialing Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 and the alleged death of Sreenath Chatterjee were within the knowledge of the respondent herein and, as such it can reasonably be held that the respondent being in possession of the facts and in possession of the materials made the statements in the written statement about requisition of property and death of Sreenath Chatterjee. In that view of the matter, it cannot be said that the respondent at the time of passing the decree in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 was not aware of the said materials and was not in possession of the papers on the basis of which review has been sought, since the respondent having had not been in possession of the materials relating to requisition of the property in Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 and the materials relating to death of Sreenath Chatterjee, he would not have asserted the fact of death and the date as July 24, 1947 and, as such, there is no reason-able ground for the respondent to produce the said papers at the time of hearing of the appeal, review of the judgment and decree whereof was sought by filing the application for review alleging the facts i.e. record of the Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 and the certified copy of the death register relating to the death of Sreenath Chatterjee which were very much within the knowledge of the respondent and, as such, it cannot be said that the said facts could not be discovered at the time of hearing of the appeal "after the exercise of due diligence", since in the background of the facts averred in the written statement it can reasonably be said that the respondent was very much in possession of the materials for the production whereof review application has been filed seeking review of the decree passed in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 and there being no explanation why those materials could not be produced before the Court at the time of passing the decree sought to be reviewed, we are of the view the appellate Court ought not to have entertained the review application and thereupon passed the order allowing the review for rehearing of the appeal. 

 20. On perusal of the judgment of the High Court Division it is seen that the said Division affirmed the order allowing the review application upon observing "the learned Court of appeal below in the circumstances of the case held that the petitioners could not produce the death certificate and the record of the Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 at the time when the decree was passed in spite of exercise of due diligence and the petitioners have been aggrieved and accordingly, allowed the application for review under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and passed order for re-hearing of the appeal. I have already pointed out that the application under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was simply allowed and an order was passed for re-hearing of the appeal i.e. Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973, so that appellant's claim that the judgment and decree dated 31-12-79 passed in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 affirming the judgment and decree dated 22-8-1973 passed in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 of the 2nd Court of Munsif, Barisal were set aside is not correct. The appeal being Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 as per order of the Court of appeal below be re-heard". On perusal of the aforesaid observation of the High Court Division and the view expressed by the said Division it appears that the said Division has misconstrued, in the background of the facts on record, the provision of review as in Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that view of the matter, in our view, the High Court Division was in error in maintaining the order of the appellate Court allowing the prayer for review for re-hearing of the appeal. The law relating to review and the time tested ground(s) entitling one of the parties in the judgment has been re-stated in the case of Basharatullah, being dead his heirs: Fazle Karim and others vs Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 9 = 48 DLR (AD) 178 wherein it has been held : 

 22. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division as well as from the order passed by the trial Court allowing the application for review that the respondent, who was the petitioner in Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1980, sought review for consideration of the genuineness of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 on the ground that the said decree was obtained without impleading the respondent and further, for bringing the fact before the Court that the decree in the said suit was obtained upon impleading the dead person, particularly Sreenath Chatterjee who is said to have died on July 24, 1947 and as such the compromise decree obtained in the aforementioned title suit was not a genuine one. The matter of death of Sreenath Chatterjee on July 24, 1947 has been sought to be brought before the Court by producing death certificate. Suffice it to say the genuineness of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 was not an issue in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 of the 2nd Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge, Barisal) as against whereof Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 was filed and dismissed. Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 was filed seeking the decree for permanent injunction and for a declaration that the property in suit is not an enemy property (now vested property). The said declaration was sought on the basis of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970. The respondent under the law was required to seek relief against the decree passed in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 for establishing its contention that the decree was not genuine since the same allegedly to have been obtained impleading a dead person as defendant and consequently, obtaining of compromise decree on the basis of the compromise entered into between the plaintiff herein appellant and the defendant. Since the subject matter of the Tile Suit No. 634 of 1970 out of which Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 arose was quite different and distinct from the relief sought through review of decree in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973, i.e. seeking of relief against the decree passed in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970, the respondent was required to file separate suit seeking setting aside of the decree earlier obtained by the appellant in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970. The High Court Division and the appellate Court lost sight of the matter that respondent's endeavour to have the relief against the decree passed in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 upon resorting to review of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 166 of 1973 was misconceived one and also was not legally well founded. 

 23. In view of the aforestate of the matter we find merit in the submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant that respondent was required to seek remedy against the decree passed in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 by instituting a separate suit and that the respondent by resorting to review had chosen a wrong forum for ascertaining the question of genuineness of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 19-8 of 1970. 

 24. It has already been mentioned herein-before that the application for review was not legally well conceived one since the facts alleging which review was sought were very much, in the background of the averments made about those facts in the written statement of the respondent filed in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970, within the knowledge of the respondent. It also may be mentioned that there was specific plea in the written statement Sreenath Chatterjee died on July 24, 1947 but the respondent did not take any step to establish the said fact. From the averments made in the written statement is seen that the respondent was in possession of the materials in support of alleged death of Sreenath Chatterjee on July 24, 1947 and in that view of the matter for re-agitating the said fact upon resorting to review was not legally competent. The contention, as stated hereinbefore, upon making which leave was obtained, in our view, in the background of the materials on record, appears to be of merit, primarily question of genuineness of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 was not an issue in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 out of which Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 arose, second issue as to genuineness of the decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 could only be the subject matter of a suit seeking declaration about the said decree i.e. decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 and in no way can be the matter for adjudication within the scope of Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 as framed and the review as sought. We have already mentioned hereinbefore that, the ground upon which review was sought does in no way conform to the requirement of the provision of law as in Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure for maintaining an application for review or entitling a person to seek review against a decree, the order of the High Court Division affirming the order of the appellate Court passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1980 allowing the application filed seeking review for re-hearing of the appeal was not maintainable.

lawyer:
Mahmudul Islam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record--For the Appellant. 

Shafiq Ahmed, Senior Advocate (Tabarak Hossain, Advocate with him) instructed by AKM Shahidul Huq, Advocate-on-Record---For the Respondent No. 1. 

Respondent Nos. 2-6---Not Represented.
parties:
Ruhul Amin ------ Appellant
vs
Official Liquidator, Mahaluxmi Bank Ltd ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Tafazzul Islam J: This appeal by leave, at the instance of the proforma defendant No. 6, is directed against the judgment and order dated 9-5-1984 of the High Court Division passed in Suit No. 1 of 1981 decreeing the suit upon declaring that the property described in the schedule of the plaint belonged to Mahaluxmi Bank Ltd (in liquidation), the bank, and that the defendants have no right, title or interest in the land in suit, the registered deed of sale No. 5870 dated 29-9-1958 executed by Madhabi Lata Lala in favour of the defendant No. 2, only insofar sale of the suit plot is concerned, is null and void, the bank would be entitled to recover khas possession of the suit property by evicting the defendants and removing structures from the suit property except the defendant No. 4, who shall pay to the bank such sum as may be determined by the Court on an application to be filed by the Officer Liquidator of this bank or the said defendant No. 4 to perfect its title to that portion of the suit property which is in its occupation and the said defendant may recover his said sum from defendant Nos. 1 and 3 and the defendant Nos. 1, 5 and 6 may negotiate with the Official Liquidator of the bank for realisation of possession of those parts of the suit property which are in their possession on payment of such sum as may be agreed upon subject to the approval of the Court upon an application by either the Official Liquidator or the defendant Nos. 1, 5 and 6 to be concluded within 1 year from the date of drawing up of the order of the Court failing which the official Liquidator would be at liberty to execute the instant order of the Court. 

 2. The respondent No. 1, the Official Liquidator of the bank, filed the above suit seeking declaration that the suit property belongs to the bank and the defendants have no right, title, interest and possession in the same and that if the suit property or part thereof is found to be not in possession of the bank then restore possession of the same in its favour on the averments that Sarada Kripa Lala was the owner of the suit property, that is RS Plot No. 2956 in RS Khatian No. 776 corresponding to CS Plot No. 1748 (Part under CS Khatian No. 41 comprising 8.81 acres of land of Mouza East Nasirabad, Chittagong and he, in the year 1929, as security against loans granted to him by the bank, mortgaged the same with the bank along with his other properties, by way of depositing of title deeds and also delivering the possession of the suit property to the bank; then the bank filed an application for mutation of the suit property along with other properties and the Khashmahal Tahsilder, Sadar, Chittagong by order dated 7-1-36 passed in Judicial Miscellaneous (JM) Case No. 236 of 1936-37 mutated the name of the bank in the suit property; Sarada Kripa Lala having failed to repay the loans, the bank filed mortgage suit and obtaining decree filed Mortgage Execution Case No. 51 of 1952 and therein purchased the suit property along with other mortgaged properties; one Haroon Matin filed Money Suit No. 5 of 1957 against the bank claiming Taka 21,000 as damages stating that he, along with Allah Rakha Bai, took lease of the suit property as well as six other plots from the bank for 99 years and subsequently it transpired that the bank had no title on the properties leased to them and the bank, by misrepresentation, leased the same to them and then on obtaining decree dated 14-2-1959 in the above suit, Haroon Matin filed Money Execution Case No. 25 of 1959 wherein he, in collusion with the  then officials of the bank, managed to auction purchase the suit property as well as other six plots in the name of his father, the defendant No. 2; after the bank was wound up by order dated 18-3-1960, the Official Liquidator of the bank filed Pauper Miscellaneous Case No. 100 of 1960 to set aside the above auction sale of the properties of the bank which, subsequently being transferred to the High Court, Dhaka in terms of section 61 of the Banking Companies Ordinance, 1962, was renumbered as Transferred Suit No. 1 of 1981 and, after hearing, the High Court, Dhaka, by judgment and order dated 22-12-1966, decreed the suit declaring the above leases in favour of Haroon Matin and another as well as the subsequent auction purchase of the suit property in the name of defendant No. 2 in Money Execution Case No. 25 of 1959 as null and void with the observation that the officials of the bank, who were in charge of the litigation, had colluded with Haroon Matin. As against that, Haroon Matin filed Letters Patent Appeal No. 4 of 1967 and a Division Bench of the High Court Dhaka by judgment and order dated 31-3-1977 dismissed the above appeal. 

 3. As it appears in 3 ILR it has been held that where a plaintiff seeks to recover possession of property from which he has been dispossessed and bases his claim on the ground of purchase and also upon the ground of a twelve years' possessory title, he is entitled to succeed if he proves his possession, even if he fails to prove his purchase. In the above case, the possession of the plaintiff in the case land has been proved not only by the evidence of the plaintiff but also by the admission of the defendant. 

 19. In the above cases the plaintiff proved his long possession over 12 years beyond any doubt. 

 20. In 14 ILR the plaintiff sued to recover possession of certain land, alleging that it was lakhiraj land, which he had purchased from a third party and the Court of first instance having found that he had not proved the title he alleged but proved twelve years' possession decreed the suit. On appeal, the lower appellate Court having found that though 12 years adverse possession had been proved but since acquisition of title by adverse possession was not alleged in the plaint and no issue was raised as to it, the plaintiff was not entitled to succeed. But on appeal the High Court held that as the suit was one for possession and the defendant had express notice in the lower appellate Court that the plaintiff relied on the title of adverse possession, and as the defendant took no objection on the ground that he should be allowed an opportunity to call evidence to rebut it, and as he had consequently not been prejudiced by the course adopted by the lower Appellate Court, the decree of trial Court should be confirmed.

So, in the instant case even if the bank proves possession over period of 12 years, they will not succeed if the title remained with the defendant No. 1.

In the aforesaid case there was no assertion either in the plaint or in the deposition regarding adverse possession and no issue was also framed regarding acquiring of title by the plaintiff on the basis of adverse possession.

The High Court Division held that the gratuitous conferment of title was uncalled for in a suit for partition and that of the precise title to which the plaintiff lays his claim is not supported by evidence on record, the Court cannot find out another source of title for him, by way of gratuitous relief.

A mere suggestion in the relief clause that there was an uninterrupted possession for "several 12 years" or that the plaintiff had acquired "an absolute title" was not enough to raise such a plea. Long possession and the prayer clause is not a substitute for a plea. 

 29.
