The defendant Nos. 5-8 being a purchaser during tendency of the suit, their title will be governed according to section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act.

parties:
Moulana Serajul Haque ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Md Saifullah ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
2. The petitioner as plaintiff in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 836 of 1998 instituted Title Suit No. 222 of 1992 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Chandpur for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession against the respondents on the allegations inter alia that he is the owner of the suit property. The respondent No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 93 of 1985 for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession on the selfsame ground of ownership. 

 3. The area of suit land is 1/2 decimal of land with a shop on the same and both the parties claim ownership over the same. Md Saifullah, respondent No. 1 in both the appeals instituted Title Suit No. 93 of 1985 (defendant of the Title Suit No. 222 of 1992) has claimed that the property appertained to CS Plot No. 313, while Moulana Serajul Haque plaintiff in Title Suit No. 222 of 1992 has claimed that the suit land appertained to CS Plot No. 312. Both the suits were for declaration of title and for recovery of khas possession. 

 4. The case of Md Saifulla as plaintiff of Title Suit No. 93 of 1985 and Defendant of Title Suit No. 222 of 1992, in brief, is that the land appertaining to SA Khatian No. 425, Plot No. 313 of Mouza Karaish, PS Kachua, District-Chandpur originally belonged to Rajani Kanta Majumder. After the death of Rajani Kanta Majumder his only son Ramesh Chandra Majumder became owner and let out the suit land to the plaintiff about 20 years ago and subsequently on 1-9-1976 he sold the suit property to the plaintiff by a registered kabala. The plaintiff possessed the same by running shop thereon. On 10-6-1979, the defendants forcibly entered into the suit land and dispossessed the plaintiff. There was a salish in which the defendants admitted their guilt and signed a Rajinama promising to deliver back possession of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff. On 31-12-1979 again the defendants forcibly entered into the suit land and dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit property. The plaintiff then filed Title Suit No. 112 of 1980 in the Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Chandpur under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act for getting back possession of the suit property. The learned Munsif (now Assistant Judge) on 30-12-1982 decreed the suit. Against the said decision the defendants preferred Civil Revision No. 109 of 1982 before the learned District Judge, Comilla which was rejected on 29-11-1983. The defendants then preferred Civil Revision No. 386 of 1983 before the High Court Division and the Rule was made absolute on 30-7-1984 with the finding that the suit is triable by the village Court. The plaintiff then filed civil petition before the Appellate Division being Civil Petition No. 351 of 1984 for leave to appeal but it was also rejected on the same finding. As the defendant claimed ownership in the disputed property this has cast cloud upon the title of the plaintiff. As such the plaintiff instituted the present suit being Title Suit No. 93 of 1985. 

 5. In Title Suit No. 93 of 1985 the defendant Moulana Serajul Haque filed written statement claiming that the suit property originally belonged to Harendra and Nagendra who sold the same to Azgar Ali by registered kabala dated 10-11-1962 and subsequently Azgar Ali gifted the suit property to his son the defendant Serajul Haque. The defendant Nos. 2-3 and Mukbul Hossain the predecessor of defendant Nos. 4-10 got the land by registered deed of gift dated 31-12-1975 and since then the defendants have been possessing the suit property. The plaintiff created forged and fabricated kabala deed in respect of the suit property showing Ramesh Chandra as executant. In fact Ramesh Chandra had no right, title or possession in the suit property. The plaintiff could not claim any right, title and interest or possession in the suit property on the basis of said forged and collusive kabala and the defendants also never dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit property. The plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 112 of 1980 under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act on absolutely false claim and allegations and the said suit was dismissed up to the Appellate Division. The plaintiff most collusively filed Title Suit No. 93 of 1985 against the defendants beyond their knowledge and suppressing the summons obtained the ex parte decree. The defendants thereafter filed a Miscellaneous Case No. 45 of 1985 under Order IX rule 13 CPC for setting aside the said ex parte decree and ultimately got forged decree set aside. In the meantime the decree holder put the decree into execution and got delivery of possession. 

 6. The case of Moulana Serajul Haque as plaintiff in Title Suit No. 222 of 1992, in short, is that the suit property originally belonged to Kali Kumar Bordhan who had no son. He had only three daughters. After his death his grandson by daughter Rabindra Chandra Majumder got the lands of the suit plot No. 312 in his share. Rabindra Chandra Majumder sold 1/2 acres of land to the plaintiff Moulana Serajul Haque, by a registered kabala dated 8-11-1984 and delivered possession. The plaintiff and other purchasers from Rabindra Chandra Majumder filed Title Suit No. 288 of 1984 in respect of .05 acres of land of the suit plot No. 312 including the suit land in the Court of Assistant Judge, Kachua. In that suit the land of suit plot No. 312 was measured by local Revenue Officer and it was found that the suit property appertains to plot No. 312. However, the said Title Suit No. 288 of 1984 was decreed on 23-2-85 declaring the title of the plaintiff in .05 acres of land of the suit plot no. 312. Subsequently on 1-6-85 the plaintiff of the Title Suit No. 288 of 1984 executed and registered a deed of partition amongst themselves in respect of the entire land of suit plot No. 312. In that partition suit plaintiff Moulana Serajul Haque was allotted the present suit land in his share. The plaintiff got his name recorded in Khariji Khatian No. 322 of 1984 and paid rent regularly. The plaintiff also got permission from the proper authority to construct two-storied building on the suit property. The defendant Md Saifullah has denied the plaintiff's right, title and interest in the suit property. Hence the plaintiff was constrained to file Title Suit No. 90 of 1986 before the Court of Assistant Judge, Kachua for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and also permanent injunction against the defendant and got a decree on 29-4-87. Against the judgment and decree the defendant Md Saifullah preferred Title Appeal No. 90 of 1987 but the appeal was ultimately dismissed and thus the judgment in Title Suit No. 90 of 1986 stands still valid. The learned Court of Appeal before which is the final court of fact, stated that the boundaries of the land which have been given in the schedule of both the suits are same. There is no dispute that the suit land of both the suits is the same. The contesting parties also have claimed that the suit land in both the suits relates to the same land. The plaintiff of Title Suit No. 222 of 1992 Moulana Serajul Haque has claimed that he previously filed Title Suit No. 90 of 1986 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Kachua in respect of the selfsame land against the defendant Md Saifullah and got a decree on 20-4-1987. The defendant Md Saifullah unsuccessfully contested the suit up to the appellate stage and in his presence Title Suit No. 90 of 1986 was decreed declaring plaintiff's title in the suit land. These facts are not disputed. The trial Court in the judgment of Title Suit No. 90 of 1986 stated that there was local investigation of the suit land by an Advocate Commissioner to ascertain the exact location of the suit land and the Advocate Commissioner in presence of both the plaintiff, and defendant measured the suit land and found that the suit land appertained to plot No. 312 and submitted his report accordingly. The defendant Md Saifullah did not take any step against the judgment passed by the appellate Court against him in the higher forum. So the judgment in which he was a party is very much binding upon him and the decree still stands valid. It may be stated here that in Title Suit No. 90 of 1986 on local investigation it was found that the suit land appertains to plot No. 312 and the Court found that the same belongs to Moulana Serajul Haque. It may be pointed out here that the suit land of Title Suit No. 90 of 1986 and the present suit are the same. Thus it appears that so long a valid decree passed by a competent court on contest against the defendant Md Saifullah stands the same is binding on him who is present plaintiff of Title Suit No. 93 of 1985. 

 7. The findings of the High Court Division are that the present Title Suit No. 222 of 1992 filed by the same plaintiff of Title Suit No. 90 of 1986 is barred by resjudicata as the subsequent suit was filed for the selfsame land. It may be stated that the Title Suit No. 90 of 1986 was filed for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and for permanent injunction in respect of ½ decimal of land of plot No. 312. Title Suit No. 45 of 1991 subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 222 of 1992 was filed for recovery of khas possession as in the meantime the plaintiff was dispossessed as claimed by him. So, we are unable to agree with the findings of the High Court Division that the subsequent suit was barred by resjudicata. We are also of the view that Title Suit No. 222 of 1992 having been filed within 12 years from the date of dispossession the suit was quite maintainable as the title of Moulana Serajul Haque was earlier declared by a competent court in Title Suit No. 90 of 1986 and the decree was upheld up to the appellate stage and the decree stands still valid. 

 8. In the above facts and circumstances we are of the view that the High Court Division on a wrong approach to the facts and evidence and materials on record arrived at an erroneous decision and made the Rule absolute and the judgment and decree passed by the District Judge, Chandpur in Title Appeal No. 140 of 1994 were set aside and those of the Assistant Judge in Title Suit No. 222 of 1992 were restored. Rule in Civil Revision No. 4184 of 1996 was also made absolute and the judgment and decree passed by the District Judge, Chandpur in Title Appeal No. 139 of 1994 were also set aside and the judgment and decree passed by the Assistant Judge, Chandpur in Title Suit No. 93 of 1985 restored. 

 9. For the reasons and discussion above both the appeals are allowed without any order as to costs. The judgment and order dated 19-3-1998 passed in Civil Revision Nos. 4183 of 1996 and 4184 of 1996 by the High Court Division are hereby set aside and those of the learned District Judge, Chandpur passed in Title Appeal No. 139 of 1994 and 140 of 1994 are restored.

lawyer:
Mr. Harendra Nath Nondy, Advocate ----- for the defendant-petitioners
Mr. Nurul Amin, with Mrs. Sakila Rowshan, Advocates ----- for the opposite party No. 1
parties:
Janab Ali Mondal and others
Vs.
Md. Anowar Hossain and others
full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider, J:- The defendant petitioners obtained this Rule calling upon the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 11.2.1999, passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Jhenidah, in Title Appeal No. 78 of 1996 reversing those dated 23.4.1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) 1st Court, Jhenidah, in Title Suit No. 58 of 1986 should not be set aside and/or pass such other of further order or orders as may be deemed fit and proper. 

 2. The case of the defendant-petitioners in short, is that on 29.12.1980 the opposite party no. 1 instituted Title Suit No. 1678 of 1980 for declaration of his title in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Jessore, against the present opposite party Nos. 2 to 5 i.e. the heirs of Godai Molla, Thereafter when Jhenidha became a new district the suit was transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Jhenidah on 16.3.1986 and renumbered as Title Suit No. 58 of 1986. The plaintiff alleged that the suit property along with other properties originally belonged to one Kunjo Bihari Ghose under the Superior land Lord Raja Bhushan Dev Roy Bahadur. Kunjo Bihair Ghose while possessing the suit land died leaving behind his only son Rashik Lal Chose who inherited the same and subsequently settled 7.08 acre of and orally, with the plaintiff on 10th Ashar, 1350 B.S. and since then the plaintiff has been possessing the same peacefully. The plaintiff also stated in his plaint that he entrusted one Godai Mollah to help him in recording his name in the S.A. record but the plaintiff came to know on 20th Chaitra 1386 B.S. corresponding to 3.4.1980 that instead of recording the plaintiffs name Godai Mollah got his own name recorded in respect of the suit land in the S.A. Record. Thus after coming to know about such wrong recording he instituted the present suit on 29.12.80. Subsequently by amendment dated 22.3.87 the present petitioner No. 1 Jonab Ali Mondal was added as defendant No. 5 and thereafter by order dated 16.6.1987 defendant No. 6 to 12 who are petitioner’s No. 2 to 7 and opposite party No. 7 herein, were added as defendants. 

 3. The defendant No. 5 i.e. the present petitioner No. 1 appeared and contested the suit by filing written statement denying all material allegations of the plaint contending inter alia that admittedly the suit land originally belonged to Kunja Bihari Ghose under Raja Promotha Bhushan Deb Roy Bahadur. But the said defendant claims that Kunja Bihari Ghose, while possessing the suit property settled the same in favour of Godai Molla by oral settlement. Subsequently Kunja Bihari Ghose surrendered his interest in favour of the superior Land Lord Raja Promotho Bhushan and since then Godai Molla being accepted as a tenant continued to pay rent in the Sheresta of the superior Land Lord. The defendant petitioner claims that one Rajab Ali and some others instituted Title Suit No. 150 of 1953 in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Jhenidah against Codai Mollah and obtained a collusive sole decree which was challenged. by Godai Molla in Title Suit No. 78 of 1955 of the same Court wherein the said sole decree was set aside against which Rajab Ali and others unsuccessfully moved up to the High Court of East Pakistan. The contention of the contesting defendant is that during the Rent Role Verification the suit property was correctly recorded in the name of Godai Mollah who subsequently transferred the entire property to Babar Ali, Khelafot, Ator and Khotejan. Some of these transferees in their turn transferred some of their shares to some other persons including defendant No. 6. The defendant No. 5 further claims that the said purchasers are all possessing the suit land in ejmali for more than 12 years. It is the specific case of the defendant No. 5 that the plaintiff never got possession in the suit land and as such he has no title therein thus the suit is liable to be dismissed. It appears from the record that defendant Nos. 7,8,10 and 12 entered appearance in the suit and by an application dated 21.3.1990 they adopted the written statement filed by defendant No. 5. 

 4. Upon hearing, the parties and perusing the evidences on record the trial court was pleased to dismiss the suit by its judgment and decree dated 23.4.1996. Holding that the plaintiff as well as the defendants failed to prove their title in the suit land but, however, the learned Judge found both the parties in possession of the suit land. 

 5. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree, the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 78 of 1996 in the Court of District Judge, Jhenidah. But the defendants did not challenge the finding of the trial court as regards disbelieving Godai Molla's title in the suit land by "Bondabasta" as well as the title of the defendants on the basis of the said unfounded "Bondabasta" and also the finding of the plaintiffs part possession of in the suit land by preferring any appeal nor the defendants filed any cross objection in the appeal filed by the plaintiff. However, the aforesaid appeal of the plaintiff appellant was ultimately heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Jhenidah, who allowed the same on contest and reversed the findings and decision of the trial court and thereby decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 11.2.99. Against which the present Rule has been obtained by the contesting defendant petitioners. 

 6. Mr. Harendra Nath Nondy, the learned advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that the suit is barred by limitation as P.W.1 i.e. the plaintiff himself admitted that he tried to record his name in the S.A. record according to him in Jessore area S.A. survey started in 1956 and published in 1957 and knowledge of wrong recording must be during that time; thus institution of the suit in 1980, nearly after 23 years of plaintiffs knowledge of wrong recording is hopelessly barred by limitation. Secondly, he submits that P.W. 1st admission that other than 3 Katas of his paternal property he did not purchase or acquire any property supports the suggestion of the defendants that the plaintiff had no right, title and interest in the suit land and hence he did not record his name. Thirdly, he submits that recording of Godai's name being existing for long 30 years, and supported by the dakhilas, the presumption should have been that the defendants have title and possession in the suit land. According to him the rent receipts filed by the defendants are corollary evidences of title and possession and thus the rent receipts of the defendants following the title of Godai Molla being not considered by the courts below the findings and decision arrived at are erroneous and as such liable to be set aside. Relying on the case of Erfam Ali Bs. Joynal Abedin Mia and others reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216 he submits that when on finding of fact not based on evidence or is based on utterly inadequate evidence or inconsistent with the evidence on record, the High Court is justified in interfering with the same when such misreading of evidence is apparent. According to him the finding of the court of appeal below being based on inadequate evidence the same has resulted error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr. Nondy then submits that the Court of Appeal below misread and misconstrued the evidences of P.Ws. (who were produced as witnesses, without issuing summons) and came to an erroneous decision without considering that out of the five witnesses, three of them stated that they do not know the suit and. Thus he submits that the finding and decision based on such evidences which are not legally admissible are liable to be set aside. He submits that Rashik Lal Ghoseson of Kunja Behari Ghose, was produced as P.W. 4, who admitted that his father Kunju Bihari Ghose surrendered possession of the suit land to the superior Land Lord and as such the court of appeal below without considering this aspect of the evidence, came to an erroneous finding that the plaintiff has been able to prove his case, which is erroneous. The next contention of Mr. Nondy is that the courts below did not consider Exhibit 'C', the judgment passed in Second Appeal No. 572 of 1997. Lastly he submits that the learned Judge failed to consider that without asking for consequential relief simple declaration of this nature is not maintainable. Thus according to him the judgment and decree complained of is erroneous and has resulted error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and as such the same are liable to be set aside. 

 7. On the other hand, Mr. Nurul Amin appearing with Mrs. Sakila Rowshan, learned Advocates for the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 at the outset submits that this revisional application filed by the added defendants is not maintainable because Ainuddin the defendant No. 6 who has been shown as petitioner no. 3, neither contested the suit by filing any written statement nor preferred or contested the appeal but he deposed as D.W. 2 wherein he neither claimed his on title and possession in the suit land nor he proved the title and possession of any other defendant and as such he having no interest in the suit land cannot have any grievance against the judgment and decree and as such cannot be a petitioner in this revisional application, Defendant no. 5 who is the petitioner no. 1 herein has not properly disclosed his title or possession in the suit land nor he proved his title and possession by producing sufficient documentary evidences to substantiate his case and the other defendants having adopted defendant no. 5's case did not take sufficient steps to prove their title and possession as such this revisional application is not maintainable. Moreover, without filing any appeal or cross objection against the findings of the trial court as regards disbelieving the title of Godai Molla as well as the title and exclusive possession of the defendants they are not in any way aggrieved and they have no locus standi to file the revisional application and disturb the finding of the appellate court which is the last court of fact. Mr. Amin then submits that the petitioner now cannot argue that rent receipts are corollary evidences of title and possession before this court because Godai's title as well as the defendants title having not been proved before the court below by producing any convincing and cogent evidence, which they could also do in the appeal and the defendants having not preferred any appeal challenging those findings, the same remained undisturbed by the last court of fact, thus they cannot now argue contrary to the concurrent findings of fact. 

 8. Mr. Amin secondly submits that the plaintiff having title and possession through Rashik Lal Ghose, the only son of the admitted owner Kunja Behari Ghose since 1350 B.S. and the possession of the plaintiff having been found concurrently by both the courts below the question of seeking consequential relief does not arise at all. In reply to the submission of Mr. Nonday as to non-consideration of Exhibit-'C' Mr. Amin submits that the courts below rightly did not take the same into consideration as neither the plaintiff nor his predecessors were parties in the said decree rather the same was passed against a 3rd party who is not a party in the present suit and as such the said decree is not at all binding upon the present plaintiff. On the point of limitation Mr. Amin submits that the trial court though dismissed the suit but upon discussing the evidences on record, did not find that the suit is barred by limitation and the said finding having not been challenged in the appeal or reversed by the lower appellate court the same cannot be argued before this court Moreover, relying on the case of Abdul Hafiz and another Vs. Lal Meah and others reported in 8 BLD 497 he submits that the plaintiff is not bound to institute a suit for declaration that the entry in the record of rights is wrong rather he can wait and sue when his right is invaded. Thus he submits that on 20 Chaitra 1386 B.S. corresponding to 3.4.1980 A.D. when the plaintiff came to know about the invasion of his title by the defendants claim through the wrong recording he instituted the suit on 29.12.1980 and as such the same is very such within time and not, in any way, barred by limitation. About the next contention of Mr. Nondy that a finding of fact when not based on evidence or based on merely inadequate evidence or inconsistent with the evidence on record the High Court can interfere when misreading of evidence is apparent. Mr. Amin submits that the said principle also does not help Mr. Nondy, in any manner, because relying upon the evidences available on record the courts below came to a definite finding that the defendants failed to prove their title or exclusive possession in the suit property and it cannot be argued now that the evidences were inadequate or inconsistent when the said finding was not challenged in higher court. There were opportunities for the defendants to adduce further evidence if any, if appeal under the law but they having not availed that opportunity at the appropriate stage now they cannot take advantage of the above principle. 

 9. Mr. Amin next submits that Exhibit-1, the C.S. Khatian bears the name of Kunja Behari Ghose as a Rayoti Tenant which cannot be surrendered simply by oral pronouncement without compliance of the provisions of sections 85, 86 and 87 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Thus the statement of Rashik Lal P.W.4 as to surrendering the tenancy by his predecessor to the superior Landlord cannot be construed as complete evidence and as such the petitioner cannot take any advantage of the said statement. Mr. Amin submits that the court below very carefully considered all the evidences on record specially Exhibit-'A' series the rent receipts and came to proper finding that the defendants failed to prove their title no matter Goddai Molla's name was in the record for a certain period but without filing any rent receipt or any other document his title is not proved. Lastly, Mr. Amin submits that for argument sake if it is found that the plaintiffs title through his predecessor's settlement in 1350 B.S. is not valid, which is not at all admitted rather found to be proved as valid by the last court of fact, even then possessing the suit property since 1350 B.S. as proved by P.Ws. and found by both of the courts below, the plaintiff has a good and valid title by way of adverse possession and the plaintiff had been enjoying the same and also transferred some portion of it to different persons and now he is possessing the rest of it along with 3 Khathas of his paternal property. In support of his contention he relied on the case of Sadak Ali Vs. Suruj Ali and other reported in 7 DLR 94 and on case of Sheikh Abdul Majid and others Vs. Dhudar Chandra Chose and others reported in 16 DLR 287. Thus according to him the judgment of the court of appeal below having been based on proper consideration and appreciation of all the material evidences available on record and upon proper scrutinizing the same, is a correct judgment and as such there is nothing to interfere with the same. 

 10. On hearing the learned Advocates for both the parties at length and on perusal of the materials on record it appears that the defendants did not file any appeal or cross objection challenging the findings of the trial court as regards disbelieving the title of Godai Molla as well as the title of the defendants in the suit land and as such the said finding being not reversed by any competent court the same remains as a final finding of fact thus the defendants cannot claim their own title and possession under the revisional jurisdiction, contrary to what has been found by the courts below. In several decisions it is clearly said that only the error of law cannot be a ground for interference under section 115(1) of the Code but it is also the duty of the petitioner to prove that such error has caused error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. Under such circumstances Mr. Nondy the learned Advocate for the defendant petitioners frankly admits that it is difficult to attract section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside the impugned judgment on the ground that the error, if any found, has occasioned failure of justice to his clients. He rather admits that having not challenged the finding on title and possession of the trial court it is difficult to say that the impugned judgment has resulted error in the decision occasioning failure of justice to his clients. So in the present Rule only point remains to see whether the court below has committed any error in holding that the plaintiff has been able to prove his case by sufficient evidence, not beyond that. 

 11. It appears from the record that the plaintiff produced five witnesses and some documentary evidences to prove his case and relying upon all the evidences on record and considering the same the courts below disbelieved the title of Godai Molla as the defendants failed to produce or prove the alleged "Bondabasta Nama" and also failed to prove the date of settlement by Kunja Behar' in favour of Godai Molla or any other date of settlement subsequent thereto by the superior Landlord Raja Promatha Nath Roy as alleged, by producing any oral or documentary evidence nor the defendants filed any evidence to prove that Godai or his successors, ever paid rents to the Landlord before transferring the property to the present defendants. Documents they have produced in this respect is Exhibit-`A' series which show that some rents were paid by one Ainuddin a non-contesting defendant having no interest in the suit land to the Government amongst which the earliest receipt is found to be dated 17.7.1981 which is subsequent to the institution of the present suit though shown to have been paid for the years 1379-83 B.S. and the other receipts are of different dates during the pendency of the suit not prior to that. As such there is no evidence on record from which the courts below could arrive at a decision that Godai Molla had a valid title and after his death his heirs inherited the same and transferred it to the defendants. On the contrary the plaintiff's title through Rashik Lal, son of Kunja Behari Ghose, the admitted C.S. recorded tenant of the suit and, has been proved by Rashik Lal himself as P.W.4. On perusing Exhibit 1 and 2 series it appears that after Kunja Behari Ghose his son and successor Rashik Lal himself as P.W.4 became the owner of the suit land and continued to possess the same and settled the same to the plaintiff on receiving rents from him. Exhibit 2 series, the rent receipts of 1350 to 1357 B.S. received by Rashik Lal having been produced before the Court and admitted by Rashik Lal, clearly show that there is no discrepancy in this respect that the suit land has been transferred to the plaintiff who paid rents to Rashik Lal. Relying on the case of Safar Mia and other Vs. Ajufannessa and others reported in 22 DLR 259 it can very well be said that when no less than the settler himself i.e. in this case Rashik Lal, the son of the admitted recorded tenant Kunija Behari, appears and admits the rent receipts then the primary of the same is already made and the burden of proving contrary or otherwise of those receipts thereafter is thus shifted to the persons who challenges the same. In Md. Yasin's case reported in 2 BCR 16 it has also been held that there is no dispute on the proposition that the onus to prove the tenancy lies heavily on the persons who claim the same. In the present case the onus of proving the transfer from the admitted tenant Kunja Behari Ghose through his son Rashik Lal Ghose to the plaintiff lies on the plaintiff and to prove the same the plaintiff produced Rashik Lal himself who proved that on the demise of Kunja Behari, he as his son, transferred the property to the plaintiff in 1350 B.S. on receipt of rents. He proved the rent receipts, Exhibit-2 series in support of his contention which are the documents showing payment of rent for the years 1350, 1352, 1354 and 1357 B.S. respectively. The signatures in those receipts dakhilas having been proved by Rashik Lal himself, those are rightly taken into consideration by the court of appeal below which decree the suit. Though the defendant petitioners tried to draw some contradictions in the genuinely of those rent receipts by cross examining P.W.6 one Sanaullah but surprisingly Rashik Lal the person claiming to have signed the said dakhilas have not been cross examined on the validity of the same. Thus it appears that the plaintiff proved the transfer in his favour by sufficient evidence. It appears that admittedly, nothing has been produced by the defendants before the court to prove Godai's title by way of settlement by Kunja Behari Ghose or the superior Landlord nor any evidence has been led to prove payment of rent from Godai time till filing of the suit in 1980 to prove that Godai Molla or any of the subsequent transferees paid rents in support of their title or possession in the suit land except Exhibit-'A' sense which is subsequent to institution of the suit which has already discussed earlier. However, in no manner the said rent receipts prove that Godai or his successors had title or paid rent in the suit property or that the present set of defendant except Ainuddin, ever paid rents. Thus such rent receipts paid by another person who is subsequent to the institution of the suit cannot be considered as corollary evidence of title and possession of the defendants and as such, the 35 DLR case, in any view of the matter, does not come to any assistance to the defendant petitioners. Thus in the absence of any such evidence on record the courts below rightly found that Godai and or the defendants claim through him do not have any title in the suit land. 

 12. The question of surrendering or abandoning the settlement to the superior Land-lord by Kunja Behari Ghose, a reaiyat, though stated by P.W. 4 Rashik Lal, if found to be correct even then the same cannot be construed to have been done in accordance with the provisions of law because the provisions of sections 85, 86 and 87 of the Bengal Tenancy Act has not been complied with. Though Rashik Lal stated that his father surrendered possession to the superior Landlord that is nothing but a statement made by a person again 82 years without any link with the entire evidence as such the same cannot be construed as a complete evidence that possession was surrendered to the superior Landlord nor the same is an admission because his whole contention in the evidence is that upon taking joma and receiving rents he settled the suit property and delivered possession to the plaintiff. Whatever might be the statement of P.W.4 unless the provisions of sections 85, 86 and 87 of the B.T. Act are complied with the surrender cannot be proved under the law. The defendants having not taken any step to prove such surrender or abandonment of the Tenancy by Kunja Behari Ghose by adducing any evidence the allegation, of surrendering and or the statement made by Rashik Lal, will not ipso facto prove the defence case. 

 13. The defendant petitioners took a plea that none of the witnesses were summoned by the court but it appears from the record that other than P.W. 2 this question was not put to any other witnesses thus it cannot be construed that they were produced without being summoned by the court. Moreover, P.W.2 in his cross categorically stated that upon receipt of summons, through the peon of the court, he has come to depose. So the contention of Mr. Nondy that the evidences o the P.Ws are not proper evidence to be considered does not have any leg to stand. However it appears that P.W. 2 has proved plaintiffs possession in the suit land for last 45/46 years and he never saw Godai Molla possessing the same other P.Ws. also corroborated him. Only thing which the defendant petitioners tried to prove as could be gathered from the cross, is that some of the P.Ws. could not describe the suit land but however, when Rashik Lal categorically deposed that he has transferred the suit land to the plaintiff and he has received rents from the plaintiff and the plaintiffs possession being proved by other witnesses there remains no doubt in the mind of the court below to hold that the plaintiff has been able to prove his title and possession in the suit land. On the other hand the evidence led by the defendants, in no way, proves the title of the defendants rather Exhibit 1 and 2 series having clearly proved the title and possession of the plaintiff, and his predecessors, the court of appeal below rightly passed the impugned judgment and as such no error has been committed in passing the same occasioning failure of justice. 

 14. Mr. Nondy could not point out any misreading of evidence in the judgment of the lower appellate court for which the above principle laid down in 35 DLR could be attracted. The principle laid down in the 35 DLR case is not in revision under section 115 of the Code where the scope is very limited. But however, in the said decision it has also been observed "Misreading of evidence, not miss appreciation can be interfered with and partial misunderstanding of a document not a case for High Court's interference". Thus on this score also the above citation does not come for any assistance of the petitioner. On the contrary relying on the case of Md. Yasin and others Vs. Kamini Kumar Shome and others reported in 2 BCR 216 it can be said that mere payment of rent to the Government on the strength of unfounded entry in the record of rights will not create valid tenancy in favour of the defendants and extinguish the title, if any, of the plaintiffs. Thus Exhibit `A' series does not in any way help the defendants to prove their case. 

 15. It is true that the plaintiff is to prove his title in all the cases. But it is now settled that the plaintiff is not always required to prove his title to the hilt rather if he is able to prove his title better than that of his adversary it is enough. Moreover, adverse possession in law is subsisting right of a party, which the law protects and which can be enforced against a person who does not prove a better title. Thus it appears that the plaintiff, in this case have been able to prove better title against the defendants and having possessing the suit land since 1350 B.S. he is as such, entitled to a decree. The defendants having failed to produce any evidence as to settlement made by Kunja Behari to Godai Molla or after the alleged surrender settlement by superior Landlord to Godai they actually failed to prove Godai's title in the suit land and Rashik Lal, the son of Kunja Behari Ghose having proved the transfer in favour of the plaintiff which is corroborated by other witnesses the court below rightly decreed the suit upon finding plaintiff's title and possession in the suit land. 

 18. Considering the facts and circumstances stated above. I do not find any merit in the Rule. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court Jhenidah, in Title Appeal No. 78 of 1996 is affirmed.

parties:
Gouri Das and ors ----- Appellants 
Vs.
ABM Hasan Kabir and others  ----- Respondents
book_ref: 55 DLR (AD) 52,23 BLD (AD) 160,11 BLT (AD) 87,2 ADC 449,2 ADC 635,7 MLR (AD) 231
full_judgment:
2. These appeals arose out of two title suits being Title Suit No. 171 of 1985 and Title Suit No. 133 of 1981. 

 3. The Title Suit No. 171 of 1985 was filed by the respondent, ABM Hasan Kabir as plaintiff impleading predecessor-in-interest of the defendant appellants and others for a declaration of title and recovery of khas possession. 

 4. Haripada Das, predecessor of the defendant appellants as a plaintiff, filed Title Suit No. 133 of 1981 impleading Ava Rani Aich, ABM Hasan Kabir and other defendants for a declaration of title and recovery of khas possession. 

 5. There was a third Title Suit being Title Suit No. 303 of 1980 renumbered as Title Suit No. 172 of 1985 filed by the respondent ABM Hasan Kabir challenging the order of the Chairman of the Municipal Committee treating the holding as enemy property. 

 7. Against Title Suit No. 171 of 1985, Title Appeal No. 260 of 1988 was filed and against Title Suit No. 133 of 1981, Title Appeal No. 20 of 1999 was filed. Both the appeals were heard together and dismissed by the District Judge, Comilla affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court by his judgment dated 18-3-1991. Against Title Suit No. 172 of 1985 no appeal was preferred. 

 8. The plaintiff respondent's case in Title Suit No. 171 of 1985 is that, the property mentioned in the schedule 1 of the plaint originally belonged to three brothers, namely, Mahim Chandra Aich, Satish Chandra Aich and Opendra Chandra Aich who became owners of the same on the basis of a kabuliyat dated 31st Baishak, 1332 BS. Thereafter, by amicable partition between themselves Mahim Chandra Aich got the land mentioned in the schedule 1 of the plaint and was in exclusive possession of the property for more than 50 years by constructing building and huts thereon. Mahim Chandra Aich died leaving his only son, Binayendra Aich who was also in actual physical possession of the suit property for more than 12 years. He died leaving behind his wife Ava Rani Aich and two sons, namely, Dharanindra Aich and Bijoy Krishna Aich. Bijoy Krishna relinquished his claim in his paternal property. Thus Ava Rani Aich and Dharanindra Aich remained in possession of the suit property of late Binayendra Aich in assertion of their right, title and possession thereon. The record of right was finally published in the name of their heirs. They sold the suit land by registered kabala dated 31-1-1972 to the plaintiff-respondent No.1, ABM Hasan Kabir who went into possession of the first schedule property of the plaint along with other suit properties which was under possession of the defendant appellants as monthly tenants. The defendant appellants agreed to pay monthly rent to the plaintiff. Thereafter, on demand of the rent, the defendant appellants refused to pay rent and finally on 2-11-1981 denied the right, title and interest of the plaintiff in respect of the suit property. Hence, the Title Suit No. 171 of 1985 was initiated. 

 9. The defendant appellants contested the suit by filing written statement denying all material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that they were never monthly tenants under the plaintiff-respondent or his vendor. They claimed that they were tenants under Hari Prasad Das to whom they have been paying rent since 1972. Hari Prasad Das took settlement of the suit land from Binayendra in the year 1940 and possessing the same on payment of ground rent as non-agricultural tenant. Hari Prasad was still residing in the suit property with his family members. Binayendra was never in possession of the suit land and after his death, his sons and wife never inherited the suit property and by mistake in RS khatian name of Ava Rani Aich was recorded with respect to the suit land. It is also claimed that the defendant-appellants never paid any rent to the vendor of the plaintiff-respondent and they never promised to pay rent to the plaintiff-respondent after the latter claimed to have purchased the suit land and the plaintiff-respondent never demanded any rent from the defendant-appellants So, the plaintiff-respondent has got no right, title and possession of the suit land. 

 10. The defendant-appellants landlord, Hari Prasad Das, earlier filed Title Suit No. 133 of 1981 for declaration of title on the basis of settlement in the same suit property, described in schedule 1, claiming that his father Baroda Prasad Das took settlement of the land from Binoyendra Aich in 1940 and constructed huts thereon and possessed the same by residing in some huts and letting out others to monthly tenants. After the death of Baroda Prosad Das, he had possessed the suit property for more than the statutory period of limitation and acquired an indefeasible non- agricultural tenancy right. 

 11. The Government as defendant in Title Suit Nos. 171 of 1985 and 133 of 1981 appeared and claimed that the suit property had vested as an enemy property. 

 12. Title Suit No. 172 of 1985 was filed by AB Hasan for declaration that the creation of a municipal holding in the name of Hari Prasad in respect of six huts standing in the suit land was illegal. 

 13. The trial Court after hearing three suits analogously dismissed the suits and also held that the suit property was not an enemy property. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the trial Court both the plaintiffs in the aforementioned suits filed title appeal before the District Judge, Comilla being Title Appeal Nos. 260 of 1988 and 20 of 1989 which were heard analogously and dismissed by the judgment and decree dated 18-3- 1991. Against which Civil Revision Nos. 2407 and 7793 of 1991 were preferred before the High Court Division. Rules were obtained and finally a Single Judge of the High Court Division made the Rule absolute in Civil Revision No. 2407 of 1991, but discharged the Rule in Civil Revision No. 7793 of 1991 by his judgment dated 15-1-1995. 

 "The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in failing to consider and decide the specific case of the petitioners as to acquisition of non-agricultural tenancy right in the suit property by possession for more than the statutory period upon erecting huts and residing therein, after taking settlement from the admitted owner Binayendra Aich in 1940. In view of the findings of the courts below as to the petitioner's continued possession from the time of their predecessor-in-interest, Had Prasad Das and the law contained in section 7 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. High Court Division erred in making the Rule in Civil Revision No. 2407 of 1991 absolute and in discharging the Rule in Civil Revision No. 7793 of 1991 without any finding on the petitioner's case of title. Lastly, the courts below having found long possession of the petitioners, presumption should be in their favour as to the lawful character of such possession, unless the contrary is proved and holding such possession to be proof of settlement by the admitted owner Binayendra Aich in favour of Hari Prasad Das in 1940 as claimed by the petitioner." 

 18. The defendant-appellants' claim that their landlord Hari Prasad Das's father Baroda Prasad Das took settlement from BinoyendraAich in 1940 and, as such, it cannot be said that the origin of their tenancy for residential purpose was unknown. But, in fact, they could not produce any paper in support of their claim. Further, they do not claim to have constructed any permanent structure on the land to the knowledge of Baroda Prasad Das, from whom they took the settlement. On the other hand, they claim that Baroda Prasad Das erected twelve huts in plot No. 947 and used to reside in some huts with his family and used to possess the other huts through monthly tenants. Upon these facts no substantial findings can be made out that any pucca building on the land was built to the knowledge of the landlord to justify the presumption of permanency of tenancy. The defendant-appellants also claim that the Municipal holding was also created in his father's name and he has been paying municipal taxes regularly. Admittedly, all the courts have found them in possession but they could not produce any patta kabuliyat in support of the alleged settlement in favour of Baroda Prasad Das from Binoyendra Aich in the year 1940. Three typed receipts have been marked as exhibit I series in Title Suit No. 133 of 1981 to prove the payment of ground taxes to Binayendra Aich. In these receipts it is mentioned that Rs. 60.00 was received by Binayendra Aich in respect of ground tax and municipal holding Nos. 185, 186 and 152(a) of Bazrapur Mohalla of Comilla Town. All the courts below held that from these receipts it could not be said that Baroda Prasad took settlement of the said land from Binayendra Aich. We do not also find any reason to disagree with them. Thus the defendant appellants failed to establish uniform payment of rent raising difficulties in the way of presumption of permanency of tenancy. 

 19. Mr Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel, referred to section 7(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, to advance his argument of adverse possession. Under the section a tenant must show that he had been holding the property in question for a period of not less than twelve years without any lease. Mere suggestion of uninterrupted possession for "12 years" or that the plaintiff had acquired "an absolute title" is not enough to raise such a plea. (1) To claim adverse possession it must be specifically pleaded in the plaint, (2) hostile title must be asserted, (3) adverse possession must be adequate in continuity, (4) Evidence must be adduced to show when possession became adverse so that the starting point of limitation against the party affected can be found. But in the instant case' there was no attempt to prove since when the adverse possession has started. There is no evidence here when possession became adverse as long possession is not necessarily adverse possession. 

 20. Lastly, Mr Khandkar Mahbubuddin, has relied on 29 CWN 138, 128 and 43 CWN 828 to show that if a person is in possession of a land for a very long time, there is a presumption in his favour under section 110 of the Evidence Act. There is no dispute as to the proposition of law. But we are to see whether the facts upon which reliance has been placed unequivocally point to long possession by the defendant appellants of the suit property. The presumption under section 110 in this case would apply only if two conditions are satisfied viz, that the possession of the person claiming long possession is not prima facie wrongful and secondly, the title of the person, in this case the plaintiff-respondent, against whom the long possession is claimed is not proved. The courts below found that the defendant-appellants are in possession but they could not prove their title or that they are not in possession to the knowledge of the real owner upon denying his title or any kabuliyat or deed of settlement. On the other hand, the plaintiff-respondent has proved their title by registered kabala executed on 13-11-1978 for valuable consideration. This kabala has not been disbelieved by the courts below. This hits at the root of the claim by the defendant- appellants on the suit land on the basis of long possession since their claim of title of the suit property has been disbelieved by the courts below. No doubt the defendant-appellants' possession for a long time and by succession are material. But the claim of long possession remains precarious because of the finding of title of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff- respondent by courts below.

full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: This Rule was obtained by defendant Nos. 1 and 10 upon making a revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against judgment and decree dated 30-3-2000 passed by Additional District Judge, Court No. 2 at Barisal in Title Appeal No. 148 of 1996 affirming those dated 8-7-96 passed by Subordinate Judge, Court No. 1 in Title Suit No. 33 of 1995 in decreeing the suit. 

 2. Opposite party Nos. 1 to 3 and Mojibar Rahman, predecessor-in-interest of opposite party Nos. 4 to 13 as plaintiff instituted the suit for confirmation of their possession upon declaration of title by adverse possession in the suit land measuring about 0.092 acre of land comprised of holding No. 269/265 of No. 9 Hatkhola Ward of the Barisal Municipality fully described in the schedule to the plaint. Plaint case, in short is that the suit land originally belonged to Atul Behari Shaha and others, and in 1927 they orally settled the land with Hafizur Rahman Bhuiya alias Habu Khalifa, father of the plaintiffs at a rental of Taka 4 and put him into possession. Habu Khalifa possessed the land in his own right by raising dwelling house and living therein with his family up to 1965 when he died leaving the plaintiffs as his successors and heirs. In 1960, Habu Khalifa already orally gifted the land to the plaintiffs and delivered possession and the plaintiffs have since then been in possession of the suit land. After the death of Habu Khalifa, the plaintiffs constructed three more dwelling houses on the suit land. Plaintiffs also sank a deep tubewell in the land. One Hafez Noor Mohammad however got his name recorded in RS khatian No. 220 without the knowledge of the plaintiffs and SA Khatian was also prepared following the wrong entries of RS record. In fact, Hafez Noor Mohammad had got no right, title or possession in the suit land. As Hafez Noor Mohammad never asserted any sort of right or interest over the suit land, they did not need to take any steps. The plaintiffs have possessed the suit land for more than 70 years on assertions of their own right and title and adversely against and to the knowledge of all and such hostile possession have perfected their title in the suit land. 

 4. Defendant Nos. 1 and 10 contested the suit by filing two separate written statements. Case of the defendant No. 1, in brief, is that both RS record and SA record of rights were correctly prepared in the name of Hafez Noor Mohammad as kolkorsha raiyat. Then, Hafez Noor Mohammad died leaving three sons. Matiur Rahman, Nurul Huda Miah and Nurul Hoq Miah, two daughters, Mabia Khatun and Rahima Khatun and a wife, Afserunnessa as his only heirs and legal representatives. Then Matiur Rahman and others agreed to sell the suit land to Habib Box and Nabijan Miah and executed a registered agreement on 28-8-56 and put them in possession in part performance of the agreement and ultimately, through their attorney Md Yousuf executed and registered a deed of sale on 7-7-57. At the time, Hafizur Rahman alias Habu Khalifa was a tenant in a portion of the suit land. Habib Box and Nabijan Miah got their names mutated on 20-6-75 and possessed the suit land by paying rents and municipal and other taxes. In Title Suit No. 253 of 1981 for partition, Nabijan Miah got 0.029 acre of land and the rest fell to the share of the heirs of Habib Box. Subsequently, defendant No. 1, his brothers and mother instituted Title Suit No. 67 of 1983 and defendant No.1 got 0.052 acre of land with the structures thereupon. Defendant No.1 thereupon got a separate Khatian No. 600 in respect of his share and he is living. Defendant Nos. 2 to 4 are possessing their share through monthly tenants, namely, Abdur Rahid (DW 2) and plaintiff No.1. Plaintiff No. 1 paid rents up to June, 1992 but thereafter stopped paying rents. Thereafter, serving a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on 29-5-95 tenancy was terminated and instituted SCC Suit No. 10 of 1995 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge at Sadar in Barisal for eviction of plaintiff No.1. 

 8. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner, submits that in the absence of proof of adverse possession in the suit land, the trial Court erred in law in decreeing the suit. He submits, in view of its own finding that the plaintiffs got land by way of settlement from the original rent receivers, the trial Court erred in law in decreeing the suit declaring title of the plaintiffs by adverse possession in that once entry into the land is established to be of lawful origin that never becomes adverse. Plaintiffs also failed to prove their possession hostile. The Court of appeal below fell in serious error in affirming such decree. 

 9. He submits that the defendants proved their constructive possession through their tenants DW 2 Abdur Rashid and DW 3 Mofizur Rahaman and lease agreements exhibits 'Ta' and 'Tha' at least in a part of the suit land but the trial Court decreed the suit in respect of the entire suit land. In support, he cites the decisions in the cases of Golam Ilahi vs Md Waris Khan, 10 DLR (FC) 174; Abdur Kader vs Noor Mohammad, 36 DLR (AD) 261; Hazera Begum vs Rousahan Ara, 39 DLR (AD) 22; Achal Reddy vs Ramakrishna Reddiar; AIR 1990 (SC) 553=(1990) 4 SCC 706; Abdul Jalil Miah vs Niropama Ritchil, 49 DLR (AD) 61= 1997 BLD (AD) 63 and Salma Khatun vs Zilla Parishad 51 DLR (AD) 257. 

 10. On the other hand, Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Counsel opposes the Rule submitting that the plaintiffs have proved their long, continuous and uninterrupted possession in the suit land since 1927 first by way of settlement by their father Hafizur Rahman Bhuiya alias Habu Khalifa and then, by the plaintiffs by open and overt enjoyment of the land against the whole world. Defendants totally failed to prove their possession in any part of the suit land as was found by the Courts below. Defendants also failed to prove their case of monthly tenancy. DW 2 and DW 3 are the tenants of the plaintiffs and the trial Court has correctly found that they were gained over during the proceeding of the suit, which would be evident, from exhibits 'Ta' and 'Tha'. He relies upon the decisions in the cases of Mahaprabhu Ram vs Gopal Ram 42 DLR (AD) 154; Jogendra Nath vs Amulya Chandra, 44 DLR (AD) 147 and Abdus Sattar vs Abdul Rahman, 44 DLR (AD) 100. 

 11. Only issue facing us is whether the Court of appeal below is well founded in affirming the decree of the trial Court in declaring the title of the plaintiffs in the suit land by adverse possession. To appreciate the conflicting submissions of the learned Counsels on adverse possession, we should first consider when adverse possession creates title and extinguishes a lawful title. We first see the decisions relied upon by the learned Counsels. 

 "Now the principle of law is that possession is not to be considered adverse if its origin can be referred to a lawful title whenever that is possible, because a person who claims to have entered into possession as a trespasser will be presumed not to have done so if at the time he so entered he had some lawful title to possession. This rule is an application of the wider principle which presumes against crime, wrong and fraud of every kind. Of course, the rule applies only where the facts are in doubt and not where the circumstances under which possession was assumed are known." 

 14. In Abdul Kader vs Noor Mohammad. 36 DLR (AD) 261. the plaintiffs instituted the suit for declaration of title and possession in the suit property and for further declaration that the compromise decree obtained in Title Suit No. 107 of 1966 was fraudulent, void and not binding upon them, and also for injunction, mainly on the basis of an agreement of sale from the original owner, Noor Mohammad Bepari. Three sets of defendants opposed the claims of the plaintiffs. Defendant No. 1 claimed to have acquired the suit land by successive settlements from the original owner and also on the aforesaid compromise decree. Various suits instituted earlier for cancellation of the compromise decree failed. Defendant Nos. 3 to 5 claimed through successive purchases from the said owner while defendant No. 6, the Government, claimed to have requisitioned the suit property on 23-7-47 and allotted it to class-IV employees. In affirming the decision of the Courts below of dismissal of the suit, Mr Fazle Munim CJ, was of the view. "In the present case there is no evidence to show that the plaintiff-appellants ever claimed any title to the suit property on adverse possession, nor when their possession became hostile to Noor Mohammad Bepari the owner of the suit property. Also they never asserted hostile title against him. On the contrary, it is admitted by the appellants that they entered the suit premises with the permission of the owner who, however, allowed it to be requisitioned by the Government for the accommodation of Government employees. From the Government papers produced by the learned Additional Attorney-General, it is seen that the suit premises are still under requisition. Moreover, the present suit is not for declaration of plaintiff’s title by adverse possession, but for declaration that the compromise decree obtained by some of the respondents in Title Suit No. 107 of 1966 in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka is fraudulent, void and not binding upon them. In this suit, therefore, plaintiff-appellants are not entitled to any relief whatsoever." 

 15. In Hazera Begum vs Roushan Ara. 39 DLR (AD) 22 the suit of the plaintiffs for partition on declaration of title in respect of their share was resisted by the defendants pleading adverse possession. All the Courts found that the property was joint and the plaintiff’s co-sharers, and the defendants failed to prove ouster or exclusion of the plaintiffs from possession of the property. Accordingly, the suit was decreed and the Appellate Division finally affirmed the decree. 

 17. In Mahaprabhu Ram vs Gopal Ram. 42 DLR (AD) 154. the plaintiff sought for partition to the extent of eight annas share by way of inheritance from his father, which was resisted by his first cousins saying that the plaintiff had no right, title or possession in the suit land. Before the Appellate Division, title was claimed by adverse possession as well. In dispelling such claim and in affirming the dismissal of the suit, Mr Mostafa Kamal, J as his Lordship then was, took the view. 

 "The appellant never prayed for partition on the basis that he or his predecessor acquired title to the suit property by adverse possession. Title by adverse possession has to be specifically pleaded and proved. The appellant's case was one of acquisition of title by settlement. The trial Court found that the case of settlement has not been proved, but it conferred title on the appellant on a gratuitous finding of adverse possession in his favour, unwarranted by pleadings. This gratuitous conferment of title was uncalled for in a suit for partition where the plaintiffs’ claim of title is to be looked into incidentally. If the precise title to which he lays his claim is not supported by the evidence on record, the Court cannot find out another source of title for the plaintiff by way of gratuitous relief." 

 "The parties are concluded by the finding of the Division Bench that the transaction of July 10, 1946 between Dasu Reddi and Varada Reddi is only an agreement for sale and not an oral sale of the property. If that be so the possession of Varada Reddi in pursuance of such an agreement of sale and in the expectation that there would be a complete divestiture of all the rights of the owner in his favour on execution of a regular sale deed, until the execution of the sale deed, was only possession on behalf of Dasu Reddi. Such possession having been within a period of 12 years prior to the present suit, the plaintiff succeeds in having established the possession of his predecessor-in-interest within 12 years prior to the date of the suit. The plaintiff is, therefore, entitled to a decree in his favour. The decision of the letters patent bench of the High Court is correct and we confirm the same. The appeal is accordingly dismissed with costs." 

 "In the case of an executory contract of sale where the transferee is put in possession of the property in pursuance of the agreement of sale and where the parties contemplate the execution of a regular registered sale deed the animus of the purchaser throughout is that he is in possession of the property belonging to the vendor and that the former's title has to be perfected by a duly executed registered deed of sale under which the vendor has to pass on and convey his title. The purchaser's possession in such cases is of a derivative character and in clear recognition of and in acknowledgement of the title of the vendor. The position is different in the case where in pursuance of an oral transfer or a deed of transfer not registered the owner of a property transfers the property and puts the transferee in possession with the clear animus and on the distinct understanding that from that time onwards he shall have no right or title to the property. In such a case the owner of the property does not retain any vestige of right in regard to the property and his mental attitude towards the property is that it has ceased to belong to him altogether. The transferee after getting into possession retains the same with clean animus that he has become the absolute owner of the property and in complete negation of any right or title of the transferor, his enjoyment solely as owner in his right and not derivatively or in recognition of the title of any person. So far as the vendor is concerned both in mind and actual conduct, there is a total divestiture of all the right, title and interest in the property. This applies only in a case where there is a clear manifestation of the intention of the owner to divest himself of the right over the property. On the other hand, in the case of an executory contract the possession of the transferee until the date of registration of the conveyance is permissive or derivative and in law is deemed to be on behalf of the owner himself." 

 20. Abdul Jalil Miah vs Niropama Ritchil, 49 DLR (AD) 61=1997 BLD (AD) 63 arises out of a suit for declaration of title by adverse possession. The plaintiff claimed to have entered into possession in 1963 on the basis of an agreement of sale executed by defendant No. 1 and continued to be in such possession adversely against the world. Defendant No.2 opposed the claim on the basis of decree of title she obtained by way of inheritance from her mother against defendant No. 1 who happened to be her father. Her further case is that she let the suit premises to the plaintiff on a monthly lease and he paid rent to her up to the middle of 1975. The trial Court found that defendant No. 1 had no saleable interest in the suit land and so possession of the plaintiff could not be construed as lawful, which was continuous since 1963 within the knowledge of defendant No. 2 rightful owner and that the plaintiff acquired a good title by adverse possession. The Appellate Division however found the period of adverse possession falls short by three years to mature into a good title. In affirming the decision of this Division in dismissing the suit, Mr BB Roy Chowdhury, J was of the following view. 

 "when the plaintiff after getting into possession retains the same with clean animus that he has become the absolute owner of the property in complete negation of any right or title of the true owner thereof i.e. defendant No. 2, his enjoyment would be solely in assertion of hostile title. 

 "In order to claim title by adverse possession it is incumbent upon a person to prove that he has been in continuous possession of the disputed property over the statutory period of 12 years in assertion of his hostile which the plaintiff has failed to prove." 

 21. Jogendra Nath vs Amulya Chandra, 44 DLR (AD) 147 arises out of a suit for partition. The plaintiff claimed partition on the basis of a will but the defendants opposed the claim by adverse possession. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the conclusion that the plaintiff’s title was extinguished by adverse possession of the uncles of the plaintiff and their transferees. This Division affirmed the decision. In confirming the decision of this Division, the Appellate Division was of the view. 

 22. In Abdus Sattar vs Abdul Rahman, 44 DLR (AD) 100, the suit was instituted for declaration of title and recovery of possession in respect of four annas share by way of settlement was resisted by the defendants who got admittedly twelve annas share of the holding by settlement but claiming possession in entire 16 annas of the holding for over the period of 35 years. Accepting the adverse possession of the defendants in respect of said four annas share, this Division reversed the concurrent decree of the Courts below and dismissed the suit. On the following view, the Appellate Division confirmed the decision of this Division, 

 23. In Salma Khatun vs Zilla Parishad, 51 DLR (AD) 257 the plaintiff instituted the suit for declaration of title on the basis of successive transfers from one Noor Hossain who got settlement from the Zilla Parishad. SA record of rights stands in the name of said Noor Hossain. The Zilla Parishad resisted the claim saying that they never settled the land with Noor Hossain nor received any rent from him. Plaintiff created papers to grab the property of Zilla Parishad. Trial Court decreed the suit. But this Division dismissed the suit. The Appellate Division affirmed the decision of this Division, on the view, 

 " ... the plaintiffs could not file any paper to show the alleged raiyati right of Noor Hossain on the basis of settlement or lease taken from defendant No. 1. The High Court Division was well founded in law in holding that under the circumstances the plaintiffs have established a case of possession but not of title. When they are in possession claiming raiyati settlement they cannot set up adverse possession either. They are not entitled to a declaration of title." 

 24. Adverse possession is a mixed question of fact and law, in the sense. that the fact of adverse possession is to be gathered from surrounding circumstances and then, to decide whether such possession creates title in favour of the person in such possession. What constitutes adverse possession in law is also now well settled by the pronouncements of highest judicial authorities. Besides the above cases, in Secy of State for India in Council vs Debendra Lal Khan, (1933) 61 IA 78: 1934 All LJ 153 (PC) the Privy Council laid down that it is sufficient that the possession must be overt and without any attempt at concealment so that the person against whom time is running out if he exercises due vigilance, to be aware of what is happening and if the rights of the Crown have been openly usurped it cannot be heard to plead that the fact was not to its notice. In P Lakshmi Reddy vs Lakshmi Reddy, AIR 1957 (SC) 314, the Supreme Court of India observed that it should be nec vi, nee clam, nec preeario-that is, the possession required must be adequate in continuity, in publicity and in extent to show that it is possession adverse to the competitor. In Annasaheb Bapusaheb Patil vs Balwant, (1995) 2 SCC 543; AIR 1995 (SC) 895 it again observed that a claim of adverse possession being a hostile assertion involving expressly or impliedly in denial of the title of true owner, the burden is always on the person who asserts such a claim to prove by clear and unequivocal evidence that his possession was hostile to the real owner and in deciding such claim, the Courts must have regard to the animus of the person doing those acts. Once adverse possession for over the statutory period of limitation is established, the person in such possession becomes entitled to a decree since it is one of the accepted modes of acquisition of title in property. 

 26. Further case of the plaintiffs is that their father was in the nature of humble disposition, he did not care to know about the record of rights nor he paid any rents. RS and SA khatians though record the name of Hajji Noor Mohammed but neither he nor his any heirs ever asserted any claim whatsover over the suit land. Nor even the rent receivers or anybody on their behalf claimed any interest in the suit land. Defendants also did not claim any interest over the suit land till the issue of the legal notice in 1995. Consequently, the plaintiffs continued to possess and enjoy the suit land since 1927 on assertion of their own rights and interest continuously, openly, overtly, and adversely against the world including the defendants. Such adverse possession for more than 70 years has perfected their title in the suit land. 

 27. On the other hand, defendant Nos. I and 10 claims that Hajji Noor Mohammed took settlement from said Atul Behari Saha and others and RS and SA record of rights were correctly prepared in his names. Then, Nsbijan Mia and Habib Box purchased the suit land from the heirs of said Hajji Noor Mohammed by registered deed dated 7-7-57 and go their names mutated in mutation case No. 107(II) K.T/74-75 on 20-6-75. By way of a compromise decree in Title Suit No. 253 of 1981 dated 4-9-82 Nabijan Mia got 0.029 acre of the suit land and in other compromise decree dated 17-1-84 passed in. Title Suit No. 67 of 1983 defendant No.1 got the rest of the suit land measuring about 0.052 acre. Defendant No. 1 got the land mutated in his Khatain No. 600. 

 31. On elaborate consideration, the trial Court has held that the documents as adduced by the defendants in support of their title were mere paper transaction. The decrees as mentioned hereinbefore were also created by fraud and forgery. It has clearly found that no heir of Hajji Noor Mohammed executed the deed dated 7-7-57, exhibit 'Ga'. In order to decide the issue facing us, we find no need to go into detail on such findings. What we find is that the Courts below did not commit any error in excluding those documents in deciding the issue. 

 32. On the evidence on record, and in the circumstances of the case, the trial Court has come to a conclusion that the plaintiffs have acquired right and title in the suit land first by settlement and then, by way of adverse possession. By independent consideration, the Court of appeal below appears to have affirmed such finding. 

 33. Mr Quayum challenges this conclusion and the decree passed upon such conclusion in submitting that once possession lawfully i.e. by way of settlement commences, such possession can never transform into an adverse possession. He heavily relies upon the decisions in the cases of Most Golam Ilahi vs Md Waris Khan and Salma Khatun vs Zilla Parishad. The principle he wants to stand on is a very well-known standard, namely, the possession to become adverse must have commenced in wrong and maintained against right. But this is not the only and conclusive criterion for adverse possession as we have found in the above cases. In Achal Reddy vs Ramakrishna Reddiar; the Supreme Court of India has observed that where a transferee enters either on the basis. of an oral transfer or a deed of transfer into possession of a property and retains such possession with a clean animus that he has become the absolute owner of the property and in complete negation of any right or title of the transferor, his enjoyment is solely as owner in his right and not derivatively or in recognition of the title of any person. Such possession must be held to be adverse and if he continuously possesses for the statutory period of 12 years and if the true owner fails to institute a suit for possession, then the title of such true owner under section 28 of the Limitation Act becomes extinguished. Consequently, the person in such possession becomes entitled to own the property as his own. 

 34. As stated above, in 1927 Habu Khalifa, father of the plaintiffs, entered into possession of the suit land on the basis of an oral settlement, and possessed till his death in 1965 with clean animus, that he became the absolute owner of the suit land and in complete negation of any right or title of any person including the rent receivers and then, on his death the plaintiffs have similarly been continuing and enjoying their possession on assertion of their own right and title overtly and openly and without any attempt at concealment. Such long continuous possession with clean animus of an absolute owner must be held to be hostile to anybody including the defendants. To make such possession hostile, and consequently, adverse the plaintiffs were never required to announce/publicise their hostility by beat of drums. 

 35. In view of the above legal position, the findings of the trial Court that the plaintiffs have acquired right and title in the suit land by long, continuous and overt possession for more than 70 years are well founded. So, the Court of appeal below did not commit any error of law or procedure in affirming the decree of the trial Court upon such conclusion by the impugned judgment and decree, which have not resulted in any failure of Justice.

caseno: Appeal from original decree No. 267 of 1981
parties:
Aftabuddin Ahmed & another
Vs.
Rebeya Khanam Chowdhury and another
full_judgment:
Md. Awlad Ali, J:- This is an appeal by the plaintiffs from the judgment and decree dated 11.9.81 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 130/79 dismissing the suit. 

 2. The plaintiffs brought the suit for declaration of title to the suit land, confirmation of possession and for further declaration that the decree in Title suit No. 72/1947 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet and decree in Title Suit No. 56/1959 of the 1st Court of Munsif, Sadar, Sylhet which is upheld in Title Appeal No. 561/1961 by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Sylhet are fraudulent, illegal, null and void and not binding upon the plaintiffs and also for a decree for perpetual injunction restraining the defendant No. 1 from interfering with the plaintiffs possession in the suit land by executing the decree in Title Suit No. 56 of 1959. 

 3. The plaint case, in short, is that the land described in the 1st schedule of the plaint along with other land belonged to late Gopika Ramani Roy. He granted permanent pattani settlement of the said land to Krishna Kumar Dey Purokaistha by pattani deed dated 20.12.1925. Krishana Kumar died leaving two sons, Dinesh Chandra Dey Purokaistha and Paresh Chandra dey Purokais that as his sole heirs. The said two sons granted Dar pattani settlement of the first schedule land to Narendra Krishna Dutta by registered patta and Kabuliat dated 3.1.1930. Narendra Krishna Dutta entered into possession of the land and constructed residential quarters thereon and he possessed the land with structure through a monthly tenant named Surendra Kumar Das, a pleader of Sylhet District Bar. Dinesh and Paresh mortgaged the first schedule land and other lands to defendant No. 1, the Sylhet Cooperative land Mortgage Bank Ltd. by Mortgage deed dated 27.10.1930. The Derpattani holder Narendra Krishna Dutta also mortgaged the first schedule land and the structures to Sylhet Industrial Bank Ltd. by a registered deed of mortgage dated 20.3.1939. The mortgagor failed to pay the mortgage money and the mortgagee, the Sylhet Industrial Bank Ltd. filed Title Suit No. 33 of 1940 in the Vid Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet and obtained a decree. The said decree was put into execution in Title Execution Case No. 41 of 1942 and in execution preceding the decree holder Bank auction purchased the first schedule land and structures on 13.11.1943. The auction sale was confirmed and the delivery of possession was taken by the auction purchaser. The Sylhet Industrial Bank Ltd. could not take actual possession in the land and Surendra Kumar Das continued to remain in possession of the land. Surendra Kumer Das purchased the first schedule properties including in the benami of his sons Subendu Krishna Das Chowdhury and Sudhendu Kishore Das Chowdhury by Kabala dated 17th Aswin, 1351. B.S. and Surendra Kumar Das possessed the premises in his own right. It is asserted that Surendra Kumar Das left Sylhet after partition of the Subcontinent in 1947 letting out the premises to Sailesh Chandra Roy and Suresh Chandra Roy and possessed the premises through the said tenants. Then Surendra Kumar died in India sometimes prior to 9.5.1951 leaving six sons as his heirs. Out of the six sons four sons, namely, Swapon Krishna Das Chowdhury, Subrata Krishna Das Chowdhury, Susanta Krishna Das Chowdhury and Salil Krishna Das Chowdhury contracted to sell the first schedule land and structures to Rais Ali at a price of Tk. 1500 and on receipt of Tk. 1200 the said four sons executed a bainapatra on 3.4.1958 in favour of Rais Ali and put him in possession of the properties. The said four sons failed to execute the sale deed although the purchaser Rais Ali paid the balance amount of Tk. 300. Rais Ali having been in possession of the contracted land and structures for more than statutory period acquired hostile title by way of adverse possession in the property.
