Rais Ali himself resided in the property and also possessed through tenants. Thereafter Rais Ali sold eastern half of the first schedule land along with the structures to the plaintiff No. 1 by two kabalas dated 13.9.77 and 19.9.77. Rais Ali also sold the western half of the said property to the plaintiff No. 2 by two kabala dated 14.9.77 and 20.9.77 respectively and put the plaintiffs in possession of the said properties with the Bharatia Nurul Haque Chowdhury. The tenant Nurul Huq Chowdhury on 20.9.77 vacated the first schedule and since then the plaintiffs have been possessing the first schedule land and residing in the building on the eastern side of the land. The plaintiffs have been possessing the first schedule land for more than statutory period in their own right and adversely to others. On 24.9.77 Mr. A Sadrul Amin Chowdhury, an Advocate Commissioner along with Process Server of the Court went to the suit land and asked the plaintiffs to vacate the properties on the plea that the defendant No. 1 obtained a decree for khas possession in respect of the suit land against one Akaddas Ali Laskar in T.S. No. 56 of 1959. As the plaintiffs have been in possession in their own right they refuied to vacate the suit land. Thereafter the plaintiffs made search, inquiries and came to learn that the defendant No. 1 purchased the suit land and other lands from the defendant No. 2 and then secured a decree against Akaddas Ali in Title Suit No. 56 of 1959. The plaintiffs also came to learn that Sylhet Cooperative Land Mortgage Bank Ltd. obtained a decree against Dinesh, Parash, Surendra Kumar Das and two of his sons, namely, Subendhu Krishna Das Chowdhury and Sudhendu Kishore Das Chowdhury in Title Suit No. 72 of 1947 of the 2nd Court of Subordiante Judge, Sylhet and that the Bank filed Title Execution Case No. 54 of 1954 and obtained delivery possession on 27.12.1954 symbolically. The plaintiffs also learned that defendant No. 1 filed Title Execution Case No. 33 of 1977 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Sadar, Sylhet for taking delivery of Khas possession of the suit land. It is the further case of them plaintiff that in Title Suit No. 72 of 1977 the defendant No. 2 stated that Surendra Kumar Das purchased the first schedule land and structure’s in the benami of his sons Subendhu Krishan Das Chowdhury and Sudhendu Kishore Das Chowdhury and thus admitted that Surendra Kumar Das was the real purchaser of the Is' schedule land and structures from the Sylhet Industrial Bank Ltd. During the pendency of Title Suit No. 72 of 1947 Surendra Kumar Das died, his heirs were not substituted and as such the decree is null and void, Defendant No. 2 derivence right, title and interest in the first schedule land and defendant No. 2 had no saleable interest and the defendant No. 1 has acquired no right, title and interest in the said land by her alleged purchase. The decree obtained in Title Suit No. 56 of 1959 in respect of second schedule of land is collusive and fraudulent and the plaintiffs are not bound by that decree. 

 4. The defendant No. 1 Rabeya Khanem Chowdhury contested the suit by filing written statement. In the preliminary objection in term alia, the defendant pleaded that the suit is barred by limitation. The defendants case is that 1st Schedule land belonged to Kumar Gupika Raman Roy and Redhika Mohan Dutta having 9 annas and 7 annas share respectively. Krishna Kumar Dey Purakaistha took. Permanent pattani settlement from the said owners by two deeds dated 21.12.1925 and 17.3.1926. The first schedule land along with other lands were mortgaged by Dinesh and Paresh Chandra Dey Purakaistha to the defendant No. 2, the Sylhet Cooperative Land Mortgage Bank Ltd. The mortgaged money having not been paid by the mortgagers the Bank obtained a mortgage decree and in execution of the decree Bank purchased the said land in Title Execution Case Nos. 180 of 1936 and 182 of 1936. The sale certificate was granted on 18.11.1936 and the possession was delivered on 16.3.1937 to the said Bank. Subendhu Krishna Das Chowdhury and Sudhendu Kishore Das Chowdhury purchased the schedule land from Sylhet Industrial Bank Ltd. with their own money and for their own benefit and their father Surendra Kumar Das had no interest in the land purchased by them. As Surendra Das has been in possession of the structures he was impleaded along with his two sons as defendant in title Suit No. 72 of 1947. The said Title suit was decreed on 12.5.1952 and decree was awarded for recovery of Khas possession. That Suredra died prior to 9.5.1951 is not correct. The decree obtained in Title Suit No.72 of 1947 was put into execution being Title execution Case No. 54 of 1954 and pursuant to that proceeding delivery of possession was given to the defendant No. 2 Bank and the defendant No. 2 Bank and the defendant No. 2 sold the suit land along with other land by registered kabala dated 7.11.1955 to the defendant No. 1. Thereafter the defendant No. 1. Instituted Title Suit No. 56 of 1959 in the Court of Munsif, Sadar, Sylhet against Akaddas Ali and Abdul Musabbir in which Subendu and Sudhendu were impleaded as defendants. Akaddas Ali contested the suit on the plea interalia, that surendra Kumar Das had purchased the land in the benami of his two sons, Subondu and Sudhendu and Surendra Kumar Das died at Shilchar before the Title Suit No. 72 of 1947 was decreed leaving behind six sons and he got the suit land by way of exchange with the sons of Surendra Das. The said suit was dismissed by the Trial Court on 31.8.61 and the defendant No. 1 professed Title Appeal No. 561/61 which was allowed on 12.4.63 by the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet and the title of the defendant No. 1 was allowed on 12.4.63 by the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet and the title of the defendant No. 1 was declared and also a decree for recovery of khas possession was granted in favour of defendant No. 1 as against the appellate decree Akaddas Ali preferred second appeal No. 968 of 1963 before the honourable High Court and the appeal was dismissed on 13.7.76. The defendant No. 1 then filed Title Execution Case No. 33 of 1977 on 27.8.77 in the Court of Sadar Munsif for execution of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 56 of 1959 and the writ of delivery of possession was issued on 20.9.77 and the learned Advocate Commissioner and the process server of the Court went to give delivery of possession of the suit land but could not execute the writ because of the obstruction by the plaintiffs set up by the judgment debtor. The defendant No. 1 being the decree holder applied on 26.9.77 for police help and also applied on 3.11.77 under Order 21 Rule 97 C.P.C. for direction to give delivery of khas possession and the notices were served upon the plaintiffs in the said execution case and the plaintiffs appeared and filed objection on 27.12.77 claiming that they purchased the suit property from Rais Ali. The learned Munsif after hearing the parties passed any order on 21.3.1978 under Order 21 Rule 98 to the effect that the resistance or obstructions by the plaintiffs was without any just causes and directed delivery of khas possession by evicting the plaintiffs. Thereafter the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 129 of 1978 on 27.3.1978 for declaration of their title but the plaint of the suit was rejected for non-payment of deficit Court fees. The plaintiffs also preferred Civil Revision No. 425 of 1978 before the High Court Division and the Rule issued in the revision case was discharged on 25.7.78 with the finding that the plaintiffs had been set up by the judgment debtors of Title Suit No. 56/59 and they have no right, title and interest in the suit land and the judgment debtors in collusion with Assaduddin and Aftabuddin and Rais Ali have created the alleged bainapatra dated 3.4.1958 and the four registered kabalas obtained by the plaintiffs are collusive, false and fabricated. The judgment debtors with the help of the plaintiffs have been delaying and defeating the rightful claim of the defendant No. 1. 

 6. Mr. Azizur Rahman Chowdhury, the learned Advocate repreenting the appellants having placed the plaint, written statement and some documentary evidence, particularly. Ext. 8, Exts. 9 series and Ext. 10, has contended that Surendra Kumar Das purchased the suit property in the benami of his two sons which is admitted in the plaint of Title Suit No. 78 of 1947 and he has specifically pointed out the relevant portion of Ext. 8 the plaint of that suit to show that the defendant No. 2, the Bank admitted Surendra Kumar Das to be the real purchaser of the first schedule land he contends that if Surendra Kumar Das had been the real owner in that case the persons who entered into a contract with Rais Ali on 3.4.58 inherited the property belonging to Surendra Das and Rais Ali having obtained the bainapatra to purchase the property remained in possession and possessed the property uninterruptedly for more than twelve years and thereby acquired hostile title in the suit land, and Rais Ali having acquired title under the law transferred the suit properties to the plaintiffs by four kabalas dated 13.9.77, 19.9.77, 14.9.77 and 20.9.77 respectively, delivered possession to the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs having acquired title by registered instrument have been in possession in their own right and adversely to others, the decree obtained by the defendant No. 1 in Title Suit No. 56 of 1959 is not binding upon the plaintiffs and the execution proceeding in Title Execution Case No. 33 of 1977 cannot be proceeded with against the plaintiffs for eviction of the plaintiffs from the suit property. He has also in order to establish that the property belonged to Surendra Kumar Das referred to Ext. 9 series and Ext. 10 being the receipt showing payment of Municipal taxes in the name of Surendra Das and also the demand notice issued by the Municipal Authority to Surendra Kumar Das. In the whole of his contention Mr. Chowdhury has laid much stress on the benami nature and character of the property which was purchased in the name of Subendu Krishna Das Chowdhury and Sudhendu Kishore Das Chowdhury the two sons by registered instrument dated 17th Aswin, 1351 B.S. In order to further establish the benami nature of transaction and to prove that Surendra Kumar Das was the real owner of the property, although purchased in the name of his two sons, an application under Order 41 Rule 27 C.P.C. has been filed by the appellants annexing papers showing Municipal assessment in the name of Surendra Kumar Das before the institution of Title Suit No. 72 of 1947. It is argued that if the extract from the municipal assessment Register is accepted as additional evidence that would amply prove that Surendra Kumar Das was the real owner of the property. As regards benami transaction he has placed reliance in the case of Nurjahan Begum, wife of Mahmdur Rahman vs. Mahmudur Rahman Mullick being dead his heirs and legal representatives, reported in 34 DLR (AD) 61 and particularly referred to paragraph 9 of the cited case whose it has been stated as follows: 

 7. He has further argued that the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 72 of 1947 against dead person being a nullity is not executable under the law. He has referred to the evidence of P.W. 2 Jegesh Chandra Bhattacharjee a clerk of Sylhet. District Bar who deposed that on 9.5.51 he was the clerk of the Bar Association. The said witness produced a resolution dated 9.5.51 Ext. 1 relating to the condolence meeting held connection with the death of Surendra Kumar Das to prove that Surendra Kumar Das died long before the decree in T.S. Suit No. 72/1947 was passed. 

 8. Mr. Mahbubey Alam with Mr. J.N. Das and Mrs. Razina Chowdhury, the learned Advocates have appeared for the respondents. Mr. Mahbubey Alam referring to Ext. B, the judgment in Second Appeal No. 968/63 has contended that the issue or question of benami transaction has been conclusively decided by the High Court and it was established in that judgment Ext. B that the two sons of Surendra Kumar Das were the real owners of the property in question. In the judgment dated 13th July, 1976 passed in S.A. No. 968/63 which arose from Title Suit No. 56 of 1959 the main question that was resolved whether the deed standing in the name of two sons of Surendra Kumar Das was a benami purchase by Surendra and it was found that the document by which the said two sons purchased the disputed land was not banami document but was a genuine document showing the actual state of affairs and that they were bound by the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 72 of 1947 and though Surendra was a party in Title Suit No. 72 of 1947 but he did not file any written statement. 

 10. The points which fall for our determination are whether the decree in Title Suit No. 72 of 1947 and the decree in Title Suit No. 56 of 1959 are binding upon the plaintiffs and whether the plaintiffs have acquired any title in the suit land by way of adverse possession which may entitle the plaintiffs to seek a decree for perpetual injunction restraining the defendant from interfering with the plaintiffs possession by executing the decree in Title Suit No. 56 of 1959. 

 11. It appears from the plaint of Title Suit No. 72 of 1947 Ext. 8 that Surendra Kumar Das was impleaded as defendant No. 4 and his two sons Subendhu Krishna Das and Sudhendu Krishna Das were impleaded as defednants and the suit was for declaration of title and recovery of Khas possession and that suit was decreed and khas possession was delivered to the Sylhet Co-operative Land Mortgage Bank Limited, the plaintiff in that suit. The present plaintiffs are claiming through Surendra Kumar Das but Surendra Kumar Das neither filed any written statement in the said suit nor contested the suit to establish his position that he was the real owner. Therefore, the conclusion would be that the claim which. Surendra himself could not establish and did not establish anybody claiming under him cannot question the validity of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 72/47. The judgment and decree given in Title Suit No. 72/47 is the basis of the title of the defendant No. 1 who purchased the suit land on 7.11.55 from the defendant No. 2 Bank and then filed the Title Suit No. 56 of 1959, that judgment according to section 41 of the Evidence Act is a judgment in rem. 

 13. Mr. Chowdhury has contended that the plaintiffs who acquired the right, title and interest from the heirs of Surendra Kumar Das were not impleaded as parties or defendants in Title Suit Nos. 72/47 and 56/59 and therefore the decree obtained in those suits are not binding upon the plaintiffs. 

 15. According to the foregoing principles and in view of the fact that Surendra Kumar Das was a defendant in Title Suit No. 72/47, such judgment is a conclusive proof of the ownership of the Bank namely the Syleht Co-operative Land Mortgage Bank Limited. The plaintiffs having derived title from Surendra Kumar Das are bound by that judgment and consequently by the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 56/59 which was upheld in S.A. No. 968/63 by the High Court. Plea of benami having been concltisively decided in the Judgment of the Second Appeal such plea can not be res judicata inspite of the fact that the present plaintiffs were no party to the previous litigations. Process of eviction of the unauthorised occupier of the suit property having been initiated long before the alleged bainapatra dated 3.4.58 the claim for acquisition of hostile title either by the prodecessor of the plaintiff or the plaintiffs has no legal foundation.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Syed Muhammad Dastagir Husain

caseno: First Appeal No. 128 of 1987 (FAT No. 359 of 1987).
parties:
Shahani Bibi being dead her heirs: Mohammad Azim and others ------ Appellants
Vs.
Nur Islam being dead his heirs: Doly Islam and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J: By this First Appeal, the plaintiff-appellant challenges the decisions of the trial Judge dismissing her suit for declaration of Title simpliciter over the property described in the schedule to the plaint. The suit was dismissed by the judgment dated September 19, 1987 followed by a decree of the Third Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. 

 The appellant as plaintiff on 11-12-1979 laid suit being Title Suit No. 893 of 1979 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka which was, on transfer, re-numbered as Title Suit No. 574 of 1981 of the Third Court of Subordinate Judge in Dhaka. The subject matter of the suit appearing from the schedule to the plaint is 0.44 1/2 acres out of 0.89 acres of land on the northern portion of Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114 under Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124 within Mouza-Brahman Chiran under Police Station Tejgaon now Motijheel, District-Dhaka, State Acquisition Plots being 471 entire and 473 portion. 

 3. Averments made in the plaint are that Cadestral Survey Plot No. 112 measuring an area of 0.53 and Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114 measuring an area of 0.89 acres of Mouza-Brahman Chiran, Police Station-Tejgaon, District-Dhaka belonged to Sk Mainuddin who sold the same orally to Chand Bepari for a consideration of Taka 75.00. Chand Bepari breathed his last leaving behind, among others, two sons, Sultan Hossain and Abed Sheikh, two daughters Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Bibi. Saburannessa Bibi, Johara Bibi and some other heirs of Chand Bepari instituted a Suit being Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 for partition of the property including the aforesaid two plots left by Chand Bepari against Sultan Hossain and others in the Fifth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. In the said suit Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Bibi got final decree and they took possession of the partitioned property through court. Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Bibi sold their shares in several plots including the above stated two plots in favour of Kari Samiruddin Ahmed by a registered deed of conveyance dated 10-4-1922 who took over possession of the purchased land. Samiruddin, thereafter, on 30-5-1929 gifted half of the aforesaid plot Nos. 112 and 114 to Munshi Md Nowab Ali by a Deed of Gift dated 30-5-1929 and handed over the possession of the gifted property to the donee, Nowab Ali who subsequently transferred half of the Plot Nos. 112 and 114 to Sarama Sundari Guha by a registered Deed of Sale dated 5-1-1930. Sarama Sundari Guha got the northern portion of plot Nos. 112 and 114 by amicable partition among the co-sharers and, thereafter, sold the same to one Ramjan Ali by a registered Deed of Sale dated 8-12-1938. Ramjan Ali died leaving behind wife Faizun Nessa Bibi, 5 sons Abbas Ali, Ahmed Ali, Ansar, Abdur Razzak and Md Giasuddin and 2 daughters Amena Khatun and Sahara Khatun. 0.34 acres of land of plot No. 114 stood recorded in the name of Faizunnessa in State Acquisition Khatian Plot No. 473 and 0.37 acres of land of plot No. 114 was recorded in the name of Shamsuddin Mia who purchased from Asabuddin Mia and Abbasuddin Mia purchased from the heirs of Nowab Ali Mia and 0.18 acres of land of the said plot stood recorded in the name of the Province of East Pakistan in Khatian No. 1. 

 4. Further statements are that Faizunnessa and other heirs of Ramjan Ali transferred 0.311/2 acres of land to the plaintiff and 0.13 acres of land to Md Sona Mia from plot No. 114 by two separate registered sale deeds dated 16-2-1965 and the transferees were put into possession of the transferred land. Sona Mia, subsequently, transferred his 0.13 acres of land in favour of the plaintiff by a registered deed of sale dated 12-11-1966 and put later in possession of the same. The plaintiff, thus, in the manner stated above acquired title on 0.44 on 0.44½ acres of land in the northern portion of Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114. The plaintiff got her name recorded in the Record of Right in place of Faizunnessa with respect to 0.34 acres of land from the Revenue Officer and got 10½ acres of land recorded through civil Court in a proceeding under section 143A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The plaintiff paid rent with respect to the suit land upto the year 1383 BS The plaintiff has been all along in possession of the suit land since purchase and through labourers has been growing cauliflowers and paddy, etc. thereon. The defendants put forward claim on the suit land being the grand-sons and daughters of the Cadestral Survey recorded owner Mainuddin Sk who lost his interest on the suit land in the decree recorded in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916. The defendants got no right, title and interest in the suit land at any point of time. The wrong record of the suit land in the names of defendant Nos. 1-5 had cast cloud on the title of the plaintiff on the suit land and hence the suit. The cause of action of the suit arose on 20-11-1979 when the plaintiff came to know about the wrong record. 

 6. Averments made in the written statement filed by the defendant Nos. 1-9 are that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and manner. The suit is barred by limitation and principles of waiver and estoppel. The suit is bad mis-joinder and non-joinder of parties. The suit land is vague and indefinite. The plaintiff nor her predecessors had ever been in possession of the suit land and the suit is hit under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The suit property belonged to Sk Mainuddin whose name had been correctly recorded in the Cadestral Survey Record of Right and Sk Mainuddin had been possessing the suit property by constructing but and cultivating the land and enjoying the usufructs therefrom. Sk Mainuddin died leaving behind 2 sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Hali. There had been no partition suit amongst the co-sharers of Chand Bepari and no possession was taken of plot Nos. 112 and 114 through court by the Decree Holders. The Deed of Gift in favour of Md Nowab Ali and the subsequent transfer by Nawab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha in respect of 2 decimals of land of plot No. 114 is bogus. Ramzan Ali by purchase from Sarams Sundari Guha also did not acquire any title nor possession in the suit property. The suit property was all along vacant nal land and most of the year the same remained under water. The suit property had been in possession of the defendants since their fore-father and the same stood recorded in their names in State Acquisition and Revisional Settlement Khatian. Rents had been paid with respect to suit property. The defendants are the heirs and successors of Abdul Halim and Abdus Sattar who were the sons of Sk Mainuddin. Plaintiff got no right, title and interest in the suit land and the title deeds of the plaintiff are false, collusive and without consideration. 

 7. Statements made in the written statement of the defendant Nos. 10-17, in brief, are that the suit is not maintainable in its present form. The plaintiff got no cause of action for laying the suit. The plaintiff being completely out of possession of the suit property, the suit is not maintainable without the prayer for recovery of khas possession thereon on payment of ad valorem court fee according to the market value of the suit property. The suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The positive case set up by these defendants, is that in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 of the Fifth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, Saburennessa Bibi and Johara Bibi, the alleged two daughters of Chand Bepari did not get the land of Cadestral Survey plot No 112 and 114 in their shaham nor did they get possession thereof through final decree. Saburennessa Bibi and Johara Bibi did not get any exclusive or separate Shaham for their share and the land of Cadestral Survey plot Nos. 112 and 114 never fell in their Shaham of the said partition suit. The deeds of transfer of the predecessors of the plaintiff are false, fictitious, collusive, fabricated documents and never acted upon and those were mere paper transactions. The predecessor transferees did never exercise any acts of possession on the suit plot No. 114. The alleged sale of northern half of Cadestral Survey plot Nos. 112 and 114 by Sarama Sundari Guha in favour of Ramjan Ali is a myth. The deed of transfer in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha dated 5-1-1930 was in respect of only 0.2 acres of land from Cadestral Survey plot No. 114. The two sale deeds dated 16-12-1965, one in favour of the plaintiff and the other in favour of Sona Mia are false, fictitious, collusive and fabricated documents and those were never acted upon and they were mere paper transactions. 

 8. Further pleading is, that Mainuddin Sk, who was also known as Mainuddin Kochoan, acquired the property of Cadestral Survey plot Nos. 114 and 112 from Sultan Hossain, son of Chand Bepari quite some time before the final publication of Cadestral Survey Record of Right and during the preparation of the said Record of Right, Mainuddin''''s name had been correctly recorded in CS Khatian No. 124. Out of the two Cadestral Survey plots, plot No. 112 with an area of 0.53 acres was the homestead of Mainuddin Sk and the other Cadestral Survey plot No. 114 having an area of 0.89 acres was nal land which always remained under deep water for several months during the rainy season and those remain unfit for cultivation for those months. Mainuddin Sk used to grow various kinds of vegetable during winter and dry season on the said plots. Mainuddin Sk having been in exclusive possession of the property of cadestral survey plot No. 114 died leaving behind two sons, Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim and the two brothers were in exclusive possession of the land of the said Cadestral Survey plot. Abdus Sattar died leaving behind his only son Abdul Mannan, defendant No. 6, Abdul Halim and Abdul Mannan were exercising acts of possession on the land of plot No. 114 by producing various kinds of vegetables after the recession of the rainy season. Abdul Halim died leaving behind one son Nurul Islam alias Nur Islam, defendant No. 1, three daughters Rezia Khatun, defendant No. 2, Tarana Begum defendant No. 3 and Hasina Begum defendant No. 5, and wife Begum Bibi defendant No. 4 and they used to exercise acts of possession on the land of plot No. 114 by growing paddy, various kinds of vegetable through Bargadars and hired labourers. The defendant Nos. 1-5, thereafter, having been in actual and physical possession of the land of Cadestral Survey plot No. 114 transferred land of the said plot in favour of the added defendant Nos. 10-17 for valuable consideration by several deeds of conveyance of different dates. The transferee defendant Nos. 10-17 are in actual possession of the land in respect of their respective shares in total denial of right, title and possession of all persons including the plaintiff. The particulars of the purchase of land by the defendant Nos. 10-17 have been given in a chart in the written statement. Clear assertion had been made by the defendants that the plaintiff never acquired any title to the suit property nor did she ever possess the land or any part thereof. 

 "Chand Bepari died leaving behind two sons, Sultan Hossain and Abed Sk wife, Shahar Banoo Bibi @ Saker Bibi and five daughters Sayora, Saburonnessa, Johra Bibi, Marium and Rahamonnessa. Rahamonnessa died leaving behind her husband Abdul Gaffor and daughter Mayyara Bibi. After the death of Chand A   Bepari his eldest son Sultan Hossain sold the above plots to Mainuddin Kochwan and other lands to several other persons and Sultan Hossain sold much more than his inherited share. The other heirs of Chand Bepari, Sk Abed, his mother and sister including Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Khatoon & heirs of deceased sister brought Title Suit No.167 of 1916 for partition of all the properties left by Chand Bepari including CS Plot Nos. 112 and 114 of Brahman Chiran against Sultan Hossain and the purchasers from Sultan Hossain including Sk Mainuddin @ Mainuddin Kochwan who was defendant No. 21 of the said suit and Mainuddin Kochwan filed written statement in the said suit claiming the lands recorded in CS Plot Nos. 112 and 114 of Mouza Brahman Chiran and he died during the pendency of the suit. His heirs i.e. two sons Abdus Sattar and Azim @ Abdul Halim and wife Shaheron Bibi were substituted and the claim of the defendant No. 21 was disallowed by the learned Court. In the said suit, the plaintiffs including Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Khatoon got in their allotment the lands of CS Plot Nos. 112 and 114 and other properties and they got possession of their allotment through Court. The CS record of the said plots has, therefore, no legal force and validity". 

 2. Has the plaintiff right, title and interest in the suit property? 

 3. Is the plaintiff entitled to get the decree as prayed for? 

 4. To what other relief, if any, is the plaintiff entitled? 

 12. Both the plaintiff and the defendants led evidence, both oral and documentary in support of the respective claims/contentions. A good number of documents had been exhibited from both the sides. Of course, many of the documents did not appear to have been proved and exhibited in accordance with the provisions of the Evidence Act. Some documents had been exhibited without any objection and some documents had been exhibited with objection. 

 18. Defendant No. 16 is DW 1. This witness stated in his evidence that Mainuddin Sk was the owner of the suit land and the CS Record of Right stood is his name. He purchased 5 kathas of land from the suit property by way of three deeds of conveyance from the heirs of Abdul Halim. He got his name mutated in the connected Record of Right and paid rent and got Rent-Receipts. He constructed house on his share of the purchased land and the Municipal Holding stands in his name and he paid Municipal taxes to the authority concerned. He denied the suggestion put forward from the plaintiff side that his vendors had no title and possession over the suit land. 

 a) From the certified copy of the Decree of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916, Exhibit 1 it appeared that there were 8 schedules of land from Ka to Jha. Description of the land in Exhibit 1 had been shown by boundary and it was not possible to ascertain whether the schedule of Exhibit 1 attracted the suit plot No. 114. The plaintiff also did not state in her plaint as to which of the schedules of Exhibit 1 was the suit land and there was also no attempt from the side of the plaintiff to prove which of the schedules of Exhibit 1 was the suit land. PW 1 in his cross-examination stated that he could not say who got which plot of land. 

 b) From Exhibit 2 series (Final Decree, Field Book, Map, etc. of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916) it appeared that Advocate Commissioner in his Field Book had shown one Abdus Sattar in possession of the schedule Cha and Ta (ত) land of that partition suit and since the plaintiff failed to show that the said decree was executed within 12 years it could not be presumed that Abdus Sattar was dispossessed from the possession as found by the Advocate Commissioner. 

 g) Exhibit 13 is the Dakhila alleged to have been granted by the Superior Landlord in favour of Ramjan Ali but no attempt was made by the plaintiff to call for counter-foil of Rent Receipt and no witness was produced to prove the said Rent Receipt and the Record of Right and payment of rent, do not confer any title. 

 i)	Since the suit was for declaration of title over the suit property, the court was to decide first whether the plaintiff got title on the suit property. Title of the plaintiff had been traced from the Final decree passed in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 of the Fifth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka over the properties especially Cha and The (3) property detailed in the schedule to the plaint in favour of the plaintiffs of the said Suit including Saburennessa and Johara Bibi, plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 of the suit, daughters of Chand Bepari and the claim of Mainuddin Kochwan, the defendant No. 21 of the said suit on Cha and The (TO property stood rejected and the plaintiff by virtue of the subsequent Transfer from the Decree-Holders Saburennessa and Johora Bibi stepped into their shoes and the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error in holding that the plaintiff got no title on the suitland. 

 ii)	The plaintiff, along with the title, could successfully prove her possession on the suit property from the period of their predecessor, the Decree-Holders of the previous Title Suit and the Court failed to assess the legal evidence adduced from the side of the plaintiff on the factum of possession and thus committed a substantial error in recording the finding that the plaintiff failed to prove her possession on the suit land and the suit is hit by proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act for not seeking consequential relief in the form of recovery of khash possession over the suit property. 

 iii) The presumption attached to the SC Record of Right in the name of Mainuddin Kochwan had been successfully rebutted by the plaintiff and Decree of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 is a rebuttable piece of evidence and the court fell into an error in holding that no rebuttable evidence could be adduced by the plaintiff to show that CS Khatian was wrongly prepared and the CS Khatian got a presumptive value. 

 i) The plaintiff through legal evidence signally failed to prove title and possession over the suit property and the judgment under challenge is well-founded both on law and fact and, as such, no interference is called for by this Court in the exercise of its appellate jurisdiction. 

 ii) From the certified copy of the Decree of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 it is not at all possible to ascertain whether. Exhibit 1 attracted suit plot No. 114, description of which had been given by boundary. Plaintiff also did not state in the plaint of the instant suit as to which of the schedules of the Decree was the suit land and there was no attempt from the side of the plaintiff-appellant to prove which of the schedules of the Decree, Exhibit 1, was the suit land and, thus, CS plot No. 114 cannot be said to have fallen in the shares of Saburennessa and Johora Bibi, the daughters of Chand Bepari and the plaintiff cannot trace her title to CS Plot No. 114. 

 iii) There is nothing on record to show that the Decree in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 was executed within 12 years of the Decree as provided in section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the said decree is of no avail to the plaintiff. In support of the said contention, Md Abdur Rahim and others vs Sree Sree Gredhari Jeo, 27 DLR 72 and ADC (Revenue) Pabna vs Md Abdul Halim Mia, 48 DLR (AD) 141 has been referred to. 

 iv) In the previous Title Suit No. 167 of 1916, the substituted defendant Nos. 21 Kha and 21 Ga were minors and the minor substituted respondent No. 21 Ga Abdul Hakim had been shown to have been represented by his minor brother defendant No. 21 Kha Abdus Sattar and the said minor defendant was not even represented duly by an appointed guardian and the decree against him is void and inoperative in law and the same cannot be enforced against them. Support for this contention has been sought to be drawn in Ram Chandra Arya vs Man Singh and another, AIR 1968 SC 954. 

 v) Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 abated as a whole in the absence of due substitution of the heirs of deceased defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sk and abatement is an automatic process and does not require any formal order of the court. Province of East Pakistan vs Haji Muslimullah and others, 29 DLR 762, Wall and others vs Manish Ali and others, 17 DLR (SC) 536, Master Abdul Aziz vs Abani Mohan Mukherjee and others, 30 DLR (SC) 221 and Shefar Alam Nizamee vs Mrs Karima Begum Haridunnessa and others, 40 DLR 422 has been referred to for the said contention. 

 vii) In the Sale deed executed by Nowab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundoi Guha, Exhibit 5, there is overwriting of plot No. 114 in place of plot No. 124 and the land transferred by the said sale deed is 0.02 acres of land and the chain of devolution of interest given by the plaintiff is, thus, broken and it goes against the plaint case and the learned Subordinate Judge correctly found that Munshi actually sold 0.02 acres of land from CS plot No. 124 and since the chain of devolution of interest and title has been disrupted at the stage of Exhibits 4 and 5, plaintiff cannot acquire title on the basis of alleged title allegedly acquired by Sarama Sundari Guha and others. 

 viii) From Exhibit 2 series (Final decree, Field Book, Map etc.) of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 it appeared that Advocate Commissioner in his Field Book had shown one Abdus Sattar in possession of Schedule Cha and Tha (3) land of the said suit and since the plaintiff failed to show that the said decree was executed within 12 years, it cannot be presumed that Abdus Sattar who was found in possession of schedule Cha and Tha (3) land was dispossessed. 

 33. In approaching the appeal and before examination of the merit of the contentions it needs taking notice that in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916, the defendant No. 1 Sultan Hussain was the son of Chand Bepari who was the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs of the stated suit including plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 Saburennessa Bibi and Johra Bibi who are the predecessor-in-interest of the present plaintiff. The defendant Nos. 2-30 including the defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan were transferees from defendant No. 1 Sultan Hussain. Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim were the two sons of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan and Abdul Halim is the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant Nos. 1-5. The defendant Nos. 10-17 are transferees from defendant Nos. 1-5. It is also to be borne in mind that the subject matter of the present suit is Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114 of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124 corresponding to State Acquisition Plot No. 471 and portion of plot No. 473 and the plaintiff as the transferee by way of two Sale Deeds claims acquisition of title on the suit property on the basis of a Decree passed in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 of the Fifth Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka on schedule Ka, Uma and Cha-Tha (ত) property specifically schedule property as Cha and Tha (ত) and the said schedule properties were described by boundary alone in the plaint. 

 34. The fundamental questions which arise in this appeal is, whether the plaintiff-appellant acquired any title on the basis of her purchase and whether she could prove her title and possession over the suit property by legal evidence and the decisions of the trial Judge on those fundamental questions are sustainable or not. 

 35. The plaintiff traces her title from the Preliminary Decree and the Final Decree, Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 series, awarded in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916. On a perusal of the Preliminary Decree, Exhibit 1, the plaintiff No. 1 was awarded 3 Annas 2 Gondas and 2 Dontis, plaintiff No. 2 was awarded 2 Annas. Plaintiff Nos. 3, 4, 5 and 6 were awarded 1 Anna 11 Gondas and 4 Dontis each and the plaintiff Nos. 7-9 were awarded 1 Anna 11 Gondas and 4 Dontis. In that way plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 Saburennessa and Johora Bibi, the predecessors-in-interest of the present plaintiff, were given 3 Annas 2 Gondas and 8 Dontis share and the defendant No. 1 Sultan Hossain, the Vendor of defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan, was given 3 Annas 2 Gondas 8 Dontis share. The plaintiff of the said Title Suit claimed for partition of the property of schedule Ka-Tha (ত) Their claim for partition of schedule Kha to Gha property stood dismissed. Preliminary Decree for partition of the properties in schedule Ka, Uma, Cha to Tha (ত) was ordered to be made between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 as far as it might be practicable. Advocate Commissioner was appointed to effect partition in terms of the Preliminary Decree. Map, Field Book, Chitta, etc. had been prepared by the learned Advocate Commissioner and the Report along with the Map, Field Book, Chitta etc. had been submitted to the court. It transpires from the Report of the learned Advocate Commissioner that the plaintiffs of the said suit filed an application before the Court to have one compact allotment for the shares of all of them and, accordingly, he prepared a compact shaham for the shares of all the plaintiffs of the suit. In the Field Book the land of schedule Cha and Tha (ত) were shown to be under the possession of Abdus Sattar son of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan defendant No. 21 of the said suit. The land of Tha (ত) schedule had been shown as Homestead. Final Decree was, thereafter, drawn up and all the plaintiffs including the plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5, Saburennessa and Johara Bibi were awarded a compact allotment of 12 Annas 17 Gondas 3 Karas and 1 Dontis share and the defendant No. 1 Sultan Hossain was awarded 3 Annas 2 Gondas and 8 Dontis share. From the Final Decree it manifests that the plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 of the said suit, Saburennessa and Johara Bibi who are the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff were not awarded any specific property of any specific share and thus it cannot be at all said that they got any specific property of specific share including the property of schedule Cha and Tha (ত) as claimed by the plaintiff. In the present plaint there is no averment that the Cadestral Survey plot No. 114 attracted property of schedule Ka, Uma, Cha-Tha (ত) respectively especially schedule Cha and Tha (ত) property of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916. From this also it cannot be suggested that any of the schedule property such as Ka, Uma to Tha (ত) had been transferred to the plaintiff. It is pointed out here that Exhibits 7 and 8, the Title Deeds of the plaintiff, boundary is given. But on perusal of the said boundary given in the said two Title Deeds, the boundary given in the schedule Ka, Uma, and Cha to Tha (ত) land of the previous title suit does not at all appear to be identical with the boundary of the schedule land detailed in the said two Title Deeds. No attempt was made from the side of the plaintiff to have the land of the schedule Ka, Uma, and Cha to Tha (3) property relaid with the land recorded in Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114 by a survey trained Advocate Commissioner. 

 36. Argument had been put forward from the side of the plaintiff-appellant that the identity of the suit land had not been challenged in the written statement presented by defendant Nos. 1-9 and defendant Nos. 10-17 and, as such, defendants are estopped from raising the plea of identity of the suit land. True it is that the plea of identity of the suit property had not been specifically taken in the written statement yet. There is a statement to the effect that suit land is vague. But the fact remains that the sheet anchor of the plaintiffs title is the Decree passed in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 and the title of the plaintiff is traced from that decree and in the said decree the land in the schedule Ka, Uma, and Cha and Tha (ত) had been described by boundaries and onus, therefore, definitely is upon the plaintiff to substantiate that the land described in the schedule Ka, Uma, and Cha Tha (ত) especially schedule Cha and Tha (ত) of the said Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 very much attracted the present suit plot No. 114 of the present suit. 

 38. It has been pressed from the side of the plaintiff-appellant that an application on behalf of the plaintiff was filed on 7-9-87 for holding a Local Investigation to have the suit property re-laid with the schedule property of the previous Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 and the learned Subordinate Judge on the said date i.e. on 4-7-1967 illegally rejected the application taking the view that the said application was directed just to delay the disposal of the suit. 

 39. On perusal of the record it transpires that the suit was set down on 27-6-1967 for hearing argument of the contending parties. The hearing of argument was adjourned and 28-6-1967 was fixed for hearing argument. On that date argument of both sides was heard and 4-7-1967 was fixed for further argument. Further argument was, thereafter, heard on 9-7-1967. 10-8-1967 was again fixed for hearing further argument. Then again 7-9-1967 was fixed for hearing further argument. On that date the defendants presented written argument before the court. The plaintiff then rose to the occasion and filed application for holding local investigation. It was too late for the plaintiff to wake up at the stage of further hearing the argument of the suit. The order rejecting the said application for holding Local Investigation does not appear to have suffered from any illegality. We are of this considered view that the plaintiff slept and slept in taking proper steps in the matter of holding Local Investigation for relaying the suitland with the land detailed in the schedule of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 and the application was directed to cause delay in disposal of the suit. 

 40. Another contention has been also advanced from the side of the plaintiff-appellant that the defendant No. 6 of the present suit land a Suit being Title Suit No. 261 of 1982 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka wherein the present plaintiff was defendant No. 8 and the defendant No. 6 admitted that the schedule Cha and Tha (5) land of Exhibit 1 are the land of Suit Khatian No. 124. It appears that the said suit was withdrawn on the question of formal defect in the plaint. In the said Title Suit No. 261 of 1982 all the defendants of the present suit specially the defendant Nos. 10-17 were not parties. The plaintiff of the suit could not be examined nor the averments made in the plaint of the suit could be confronted to the plaintiff as because in the event of withdrawal of the suit there was no scope left for the said plaintiff to have been examined in the court not to speak of any confrontation with respect to the plaint of that suit. Law is settled that the previous statement of any person cannot be taken into consideration if that person is not examined as witness in the court and the said statement not confronted with the previous statement as enshrined in section 145 of the Evidence Act. This contention, thus, stands rejected as being without any merit. 

 41. From the above it, thus, manifests that the plaintiff signally failed to discharge the burden that lay on her or, in other words, failed to prove that the property detailed in the schedule including schedule Cha and Tha (ত) property of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 attracted Cadestral Survey Plot No. 144 of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124 which is the suit property of the present suit. Unless the plaintiff proves that the property stated in the schedule of the previous suit attracted the present suit plot (Cadestral Survey Suit Plot No. 124), the plaintiff cannot at all claim title on the present suit property and her title cannot be also declared thereon. The learned Trial Judge noticed and considered this vital aspect of the case and arrived at a correct decision. We are in total agreement with the said adjudication of the matter. 

 42. Next comes another pertinent question which also strikes the case of the plaintiff at the root. It is well established that possession in law is prima facie evidence of title. In the plaint of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 in paragraph No. 4 it was stated that the defendant No. 1 Sultan Hossain who is no other than the son of Chand Bepari, on different dates, transferred some properties in favour of different persons and inducted them into possession of the same, Relevant portion of paragraph No. 4 is extracted below: 

 43. From the averment made in paragraph No. 4 of the plaint it is clearly manifested that the defendant No. 1 Sultan Hossain, the son of Chand Bepari, the defendant Nos. 2-30, the transferees from defendant No. 1 including defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan were in possession when the plaint of the suit was presented before the court. The learned trial Judge in the judgment of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 recorded the positive finding that the schedule property including Cha and Tha (ত) property were in possession of different defendants. It had been already stated that Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan was defendant No. 21 of the suit. In preparing Final Decree the learned Advocate Commissioner physically held investigation and found Abdus Sattar, son of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan and predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 6-9 of the present suit, in possession of schedule Cha and Tha (ত) property. The learned Advocate Commissioner submitted his Report, Field Book, Chitta, etc in the court which are Exhibit 2 series. In the Field Book Abdus Sattar was shown in possession of schedule Cha and Tha (ত) property. The admitted position is, that the defendants of the said suit were in possession of the schedule property and Abdus Sattar, the predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 6-9 was in possession of the schedule Cha and Tha property and the Decree Holder plaintiffs were admittedly out of possession. Here it is needed to state that Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan, the defendant No. 21 having been dead during the pendency of the suit, his two sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim alias Azim were substituted as defendant Nos. 21 Kha and 21 Ga. Abdus Sattar was the eldest son and Abdul Halim was the youngest son. The possession of one brother was the possession of another brother. The possession of Abdus Sattar on the schedule property especially schedule Cha and Tha (ত) property was also the possession of his brother Abdul Halim. It is pointed out here that Abdul Halim is the predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 1-5 who are the Vendors of the defendant Nos. 10-17. No Title Execution Case appeared to have been laid to induct the Decree Holders of the previous suit in possession of the decreed land including Cha and Tha schedule Cha and Tha schedule land on evicting the defendant No. 1 Sultan Hussain and the transferee defendant Nos. 2- 30 and Abdus Sattar, the heir son of defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan. 

 44. It is well settled that decree, if not put into execution within the period prescribed by law, the same stands barred and becomes non-executable. The present plaintiff having failed to show through legal evidence that the Decree passed in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 was executed within the prescribed period of limitation it cannot be at all suggested that the Decree Holders including the plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 of the said suit, Saburennessa and Johura Bibi, the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiff got into possession of the decreed land. In Md Abdur Rahim and others vs Sree Sree Gredhari Jeo 27, DLR 72 as referred to from the side of the defendant-respondents it has been posited that an application for execution has to satisfy first Article 182 of the Limitation Act being the earliest period prescribed and then also section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure which prescribed the maximum period of limitation and if the Execution Petition is hit by any of the two provisions it is to fail. The said case was noticed and considered by the Appellate Division in ADC (Revenue) Pabna vs Md Abdul Halim Mia, 48 DLR (AD) 141. The Appellate Division approved the proposition of law enunciated in 27 DLR 227 Case. In the said cases Execution cases were filed and the question of limitation, therefore, arose. But in the case before us no Execution Case appeared to have been filed in the court for executing the decree for the purpose of inducting the Decree Holders including plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5, Saburennessa and Johara Bibi of the said suit into possession of the property stated in the schedule of the plaint. The question of limitation, therefore, becomes very much immaterial in the present suit. The learned trial judge on a proper discussion and consideration of the legal evidences and materials on record recorded the correct finding that since the plaintiff failed to show that the said decree was executed within 12 years it could not be presumed that Abdus Sattar was dispossessed from the possession as found by the Advocate Commissioner. In full agreement with the decision arrived at by the learned Trial Judge we are of the view that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 was never executed and the Decree Holder plaintiffs including plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 Saburennessa and Johara Bibi could not get into possession on the decreed land specially Cha and Tha (ত) land on evicting the persons i.e. the defendants of the suit including the sons of defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan, the substituted defendant Nos. 21 Kha Abdus Sattar, the predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 6-9 and Abdul Halim, substituted defendant No. 21 Ga, the predecessor-in-interest of defendants Nos. 1-5, the transferors of the defendants No. 10-17. 

 45. We now turn to a vital contention addressed before us on behalf of the defendant-appellant which is, that Mainuddin Kochwan, the defendant No. 21 of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 having been dead during the pendency of the suit, his heirs, two minor sons. Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim, were not, properly and legally substituted and the minor Abdul Halim had been shown to have been represented by his another minor brother Abdus Sattar and no court guardian as required under the provision of Order XXXII rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure had been at all appointed and, as such, the decree against the said two minor defendants without having been properly represented by a court guardian is void and inoperative and the decree so passed was not binding upon them. The said contention has been attempted to be controverted by the plaintiff-appellant raising the plea that in the written statement filed by the defendants nowhere there is an averment that Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim, the two sons of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan, were minors. 

 49. Keeping in view the principles of law indicated above let us deal with the substantial point so debated. Defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 died during the pendency of the Suit leaving behind one wife Sahana Bibi, and two minor sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Azim alias Abdul Halim respectively. The said heir wife Sahani Bibi had been substituted by the plaintiff as defendant No. 21 Ka and the two minor heir sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim had been substituted as defendant No. 21 Kha and 21Ga. The minor defendant No. 21 Ga Abdul Halim had been shown to have been represented by his minor brother substituted defendant No. 21 Kha Abdus Sattar. The defendant No. 21 Kha Abdus Sattar being a minor was absolutely incompetent to represent his minor brother Abdul Halim, the defendant No. 21Ga. The plaintiffs of the previous suit fraudulently had shown minor defendant No. 21Ga Abdul Halim to have been represented by another minor brother the defendant No. 21 Kha. On perusal of Exhibit I and Exhibit 2 series it transpires that in the plaint, the Preliminary Decree and the Final Decree, the substituted defendant Nos. 21 Kha and 21Ga had been described as minors and they were not at all represented by any guardian appointed by the court as mandated under Order XXXII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Their address were not shown. The suit was decreed ex parte against the minor defendant Nos. 21 Kha. The decree passed in the suit against them being totally unrepresented by a guardian appointed by the court was wholly without jurisdiction and the same was a nullity. The said decree having been without jurisdiction and nullity could not and cannot be enforced against them and also against the present defendant No.1-9 who are their heirs and also the transferee defendant Nos. 10-17. In Ram Chandra Arya vs Man Singh and others, AIR 1968 (SC) 954 relied on from the side of the defendant-respondents, a decree against one Ramlal, a lunatic had been passed in contravention of the provisions of Order XXXII, rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure and a Sale had been held in execution of the said decree. The Lunatic was not represented by a guardian appointed by the court. The Supreme Court of India stated thus: It is now well settled principle that, if a decree is passed against a minor without appointment of guardian, the decree is a nullity and is void and not merely voidable. This principle becomes applicable to the case of a lunatic in view of rule 15 of Order 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The decree has A) be treated as without jurisdiction and the Sale deed in execution of that decree also be held to be void: We are in respectful agreement with the proposition of law stated in the said authority. 

 51. We now propose to meet the plea taken from the side of the plaintiff-appellant that in the written statement filed by the defendants, nowhere there is any statement that Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim, the two sons of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan, were minors. The plea taken is devoid of any substance. The plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 themselves substituted Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim as minors defendant Nos. 21 Kha and 21 Ga and now it does not lie in the mouth of the plaintiff who stepped into the shoes of the plaintiffs of the said suit that they were not minors. 

 54. Turning now to the question whether the plaintiff, on the basis of her two title deeds, Exhibit 7 and 9, and other supporting evidences, can be said to have acquired title on the suit property and whether she could prove her possession thereon. It appears that the Decree-Holders, Saburennessa Bibi and Johara Bibi by Exhibit 3 transferred the suit property in favour of Kari Samsuddin from schedule No. 6 of the said deed and they transferred the land of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 123 and not the land of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124. PW 1, the son of the plaintiff in his evidence stated that Saburennessa and Johara Bibi sold the land of plot Nos. 112 and 114 of Khatian No. 123. He also testified that the Khatian No. 123 had been wrongly stated in the said Exhibit 3. It transpires, further, from Exhibit 4, the Deed of Gift by Kari Shamsuddin in favour of Munshi Nowab Ali, the said Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 123 appeared. Exhibit 5 is the Sale deed by Munshi Nowab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha. From Exhibit 5 it manifests that Munshi Nowab Ali transferred 0.02 acres of land of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124. Vehement argument had been put forward from the side of the defendant-respondents that in Exhibit 5, CS Plot No. 124 had been made 114 by interpolation. The plaintiff-appellant filed an Index showing the plot numbers transferred in the Sale deed No. 118 which is Exhibit 5. Though the Index had not been admitted into evidence and marked as Exhibit but this court feels inclined in taking judicial notice of the said Index. On a careful perusal of the said Index it appears that there is mention of deed No. 118. In Exhibit 5, the Sale deed by Nowab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha bore Deed No. 118 and plot Nos. 112 and 114 appear there. So, it is difficult to accept the contention raised from the side of defendant-respondents that Cadestral Survey Plot No. 124 had been made plot No. 114 by interpolation. 

 55. Let us now address ourselves to a substantial aspect of the matter. Exhibit 5 is a document produced from the side of the plaintiff-appellant and the same is the document of the plaintiff-appellant. On a close and careful scrutiny of the said Exhibit 5, it manifests that Munshi Nowab Ali transferred 0.02 acres of land in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha and Sarama Sundari Guha acquired title only with respect to 0.02 acres of land. She was not at all competent to transfer 0.44½ acres of land to Ramjan Ali and Ramjan Ali also could not acquire title on any other property more than 0.02 acres and'''' in that way Ramjan Ali also having acquired no title on any land more than 0.02 acres was quite incompetent to transfer 0.44½ acres of land in favour of the plaintiff by a deed of conveyance, Exhibit 7 and also in favour of Sona Mia by another deed of conveyance, Exhibit 8 and Sona Mia having also acquired no proprietary right over purchased property, was also incompetent to transfer 0.13 acres of land in favour of plaintiff by a Sale deed, Exhibit 9. From the above it became evidently clear that the chain of title stands disrupted and the plaintiff could not and did not acquire any title on 0.44 acres of land. The learned trial Judge duly discussed and considered the above vital aspect of the matter and recorded the well-founded decision. 

 56. Exhibit 10 is the certified copy of the Mutated Khatian in the name of Faizunnessa, the wife of Ramjan Ali with respect to 0.34 acres of land. Exhibit 12 is the corrected Record of Right standing in the name of the plaintiff on the basis of an order of the Revenue Officer dated 30-4-1972. Exhibit F is the objection laid by Nurul Islam and others, the heirs of Abdul Halim who are defendant Nos. 1-5 raising objection against the Record of Right prepared in the name of Faizunnessa recording her name in the Record of Right. Exhibit 9 is the Report of Badar Amin who on holding Local Inspection found objector Nurul Islam and others in possession of the land. Exhibit F (1) is the Order dated 27-10-1978 passed by the Revenue Officer allowing the objection. In the said order the name of Faizunnessa was ordered to be struck off and there was further order for correcting the record in the name of the objectors, Nurul Islam and others. Exhibit ''''H'''' is the corrected Record of Right standing in the named of Nurul Islam and others. In the event of the striking off the name of Faizunnessa from the Record of Right and recording the names of Nurul Islam and others in the Record of Right by the order of the Revenue Officer dated 27-10-1978, the Record of Right in the name of the plaintiff fell to ground as because the plaintiff was to rise and fall with Faizunnessa. Exhibit 11 is the certified copy of the order dated 7-11-1970 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 294 of 1969 of the First Court of Munsiff, Dhaka allowing the case ex parte wherein the Record of Right was ordered to be prepared in the name of the plaintiff with respect to 0.10½ acres of land. It appears that only the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka was made opposite party in the Miscellaneous Case and the heirs of Mainuddin Sheikh alias Kochwan, the defendant Nos. 1-9 were not made opposite parties. Therefore, the order passed in the Miscellaneous Case for recording the name of the plaintiff without impleading the defendant Nos. 1-9 who are the heirs of Mainuddin Sheikh alias Kochwan cannot be binding upon them and the said order is of no avail to the defendant Nos. 1-9 and also to the defendant Nos. 10-17 who are the transferees from them. Exhibit 13 is a private Rent Receipt allegedly granted in favour of Ramjan Ali by the alleged Naib of the alleged Landlord. Exhibit 13(a), 14(a) and 14(b) are Government Rent Receipts showing payment of rent. But it is to be remembered that mere mutation and payment of rents do not confer any title on any person. 

 60. The learned trial Judge on a proper discussion and consideration of the evidences and materials brought on record correctly recorded the decision that the plaintiff failed to prove her title on the suit land and also failed to prove possession and the plaintiff having not prayed for the relief of recovery of khas possession on the suit property, the suit is not maintainable as being hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. We, on a careful perusal of the pleadings of the respective parties, a discreet analysis of the legal evidences both oral and documentary and also taking into consideration all the materials brought on record, are of this considered view that the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff had no possession on the suit property and the plaintiff also got no possession thereon and the predecessor-in-interest of the defendants Nos. 1-9 had been although in possession of the suit property and the defendant Nos. 1-9 exercised acts of possession thereon and the defendant Nos. 10-17 having stepped into the shoes of the defendant Nos. 1-9 by way of purchase are in possession of the suit property. 

 61. We now turn to the submission advanced on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant that the presumption attached to the Cadestral Survey Record of Right in the name of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan stood rebutted by legal evidence from the side of the plaintiff-appellant and the decree passed in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 is a rebuttable piece of evidence. 

 62. For the purpose of appreciating the soundness of the contention raised, the provisions of section 103(B)(5) of Bengal Tenancy Act may be noticed. Section 103(B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act enjoins that every entry in a Record of Right finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect. 

 63. Cadastral Survey Record of Right is the oldest Record of Right in our country. Onus of proving that Cadestral Survey Record of Right is wrong is on the person who alleges it. The plaintiff-appellant challenged the correctness of the Cadestral Survey Record of Right and so onus is definitely upon the plaintiff to show that entry in the Record of Right as prepared under section 103 (B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is wrong. In Aminuddin Biswas vs Miajan Biswas, 12 DLR 103 it has been held: The presumption of correctness as available on the strength of section 103(B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act has got to be rebutted by the person who alleges it : In this context it needs be stated that where a person relies upon the entry in the Record of Right for the basis of his title he is not required to show the basis of the entry in the Record of Right. It is also to be noted that the presumption attached to the Cadestral Record of Right prepared under section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is not rebutted on the reason that there is no evidence for the basis of the entry. In Alauddin Munshi and others vs Mainuddin Talukder and others, 14 DLR 725 it has been posited: Merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the record of right, the presumption is not rebutted in view of the provision of the Bengal Tenancy Act and also the procedure laid down in the several sections of the Bengal Tenancy Act followed by the officer concerned while preparing the final records of rights. There must be further evidence to show that the evidences are incorrect : In Akrab Ali and others vs Zahiruddin Karia and others, 30 DLR (SC) 81, the presumption of the correctness of an entry in the Record of Right has been considered. It has been laid down by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court that according to section 103(B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act every entry in the Record of Right finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect. It had already been pointed out that in the plaint of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 in paragraph 4 there is clear averment that the defendant No.1 Sultan Hossain and the defendants 2-30 who are the transferees from defendant No.1 were in possession of the entire suit property detailed in the schedule of the said suit. The learned Advocate Commissioner found Abdus Sattar in possession of Schedule Cha and Tha (3) land and in the Field Book he noted the possession of Abdus Sattar on the said Cha and Tha (3) land. There is no evidence that the decree of partition Suit had been executed on evicting the defendants especially the heirs of defendant No. 21, Abdus Sattar and the Decree-Holder plaintiffs specially plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 of the said suit, Saburennessa and Johara Bibi got into possession of the decreed land. The Cadestral Survey Record of Right was finally published in the district of Dhaka round about the year 1929, perhaps before the amendment of Bengal Tenancy Act in 1929. The plaintiff has not adduced any evidence at all what was the state of possession of the suit land at the time of preparation of Cadestral Survey Record of Right. The decree of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 having not been executed at all, the said decree cannot be said to be a rebuttable piece of evidence rebutting the presumption of the correctness of the Cadestral Survey Record of Right standing in the name of Mainuddin Sheikh alias Mainuddin Kochwan. The presumption of the correctness of the entry in the Cadestral Survey Record of Right does not appear to have been rebutted by the plaintiff-appellant. The learned trial Judge on consideration of the legal evidences and materials on record recorded the finding that no rebuttable evidence could be adduced by the plaintiff to show that CS Khatian was wrongly prepared which, in fact, got presumptive value. No exception can be taken to the said decision arrived at by the trial Judge. 

 64. Then comes the argument put forward on behalf of the defendant-respondents that the Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 abated as a whole in the absence of due substitution of the heirs of deceased defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheik alias Mainuddin Kochwan and abatement does not require any formal order of the court and the same is automatic. The argument is absolutely misconceived and not tenable in law. 

 65. It cannot be said that there was no substitution of the heirs of deceased defendant No.21 Mainuddin Sheikh. The heirs of deceased defendant No. 21 including his two minor sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim were very much substituted in the suit as substituted defendant No. 21 Kha and 21 Ga. The legal predicament which occurred in the substitution can be said that since they were minors they were required to be represented by a guardian appointed by the court as mandated under Order XXXII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But no guardian ad-interim had been appointed for them by the court. So, the question is not of non-substitution, rather the same is the proper representation of the two minor substituted defendants, Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim. The question of recording an order of abatement in that Title Suit, therefore, cannot at all arise in the present suit and this court in adjudication of the present Title Suit also got no jurisdiction to record any order for abatement of the said Title suit wherein Final decree had been passed in the year 1920. Some precedents has been placed before us on the point of abatement of the suit but we do not intend to make an idle parade of discussing those precedents as none of those are relevant on the subject matter and got no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case before us. It is to be borne in mind that each and every judgment must be read as applicable to the particular facts proved or assumed and the generality of the expressions used must be read as qualified by the particular facts of the case and the issues raised therein. The contention so rose having been absolutely misconceived and devoid of any substance, thus, fails. 

 "The facts or facts which give a person a right to judicial redress or relief against another. The legal effect of an occurrence in terms of redress to a party to the occurrence. A situation or state of facts which would entitle party to sustain action and give him right to seek a judicial remedy in his behalf. Fact, or a state of facts, to which law sought to be enforced against a person or thing applies. Facts which give to one or more relations of right-duty between two or more persons. Matter for which action may be maintained. Unlawful violation or invasion of right. The right which a party has to institute a judicial proceeding". 

 "every fact which it would be necessary for the plaintiff to prove, if traversed, in order to support his right to the judgment of the court, but does not comprise every piece of evidence which is necessary to be proved." 

 "the whole bundle of material and essential facts which it is necessary for the plaintiff to prove in order to entitle him to succeed in the suit". 

 70. The expression "cause of action", thus, means the entire bundle of facts which a plaintiff has to prove in order to be eligible for the grant of relief. In other words, it can be stated that the facts that are alleged in the plaint and which are required to be proved without proof of which the plaintiff would not be entitled to a judgment, constitute the cause of action. Equally it can be said that a cause of action presupposes the existence of a right in the plaintiff which right has either been infringed or is threatened to be infringed. The right must be a substantive right, or it may pertain only to procedure, but the right must be there. Whether any particular facts constitute a cause of action has to be determined with reference to the facts of each case and with reference to the substance rather than the form of the action. Cause of action cannot be construed in an isolated way and the whole averments made in the plaint are to be seen and taken together to see whether any cause of action has been disclosed or not. It is the plaint as a whole which is to be construed and not the terminology or for that matter, a few stray references. 

 71. Bearing the principles stated above we have to approach the controversy which is whether cause of action has been disclosed in the plaint. True it is that there is no averment in the plaint that the Title of the plaintiff on the suit property had been invaded by the defendants giving an immediate action for laying the suit before the court. The cause of action of the suit had been alleged from the knowledge of the Record of Right in the name of the defendants. It is also true that there occurred some fundamental defects and infirmities in the plaint. But it cannot be suggested that the plaint did not consist of material facts giving rise to a cause of action for the plaintiff to lay the suit in the court. In Ram Awalamb and others vs Jata Sankar and others, AIR 1969 Allahabad 526 (F13) relied upon on behalf of the defendant-respondents, the principle of law is that in each and every case the cause of action of the suit shall have to be scrutinized to determine whether the suit is solely cognizable by a revenue court or is impliedly cognizable only by a revenue court or is cognizable by a civil Court. The said case is of no assistance to the defendant-respondent inasmuch as the facts of the present case are altogether different from the facts of the said case and law laid therein is also inapplicable. The contention that the plaint did not disclose a cause of action appears to be meritless and the same stands rejected. 

 (a) For the specific performance of any contract relating to the transfer of any immovable property or for declaration of title to or assertion of ownership of any such property. 

 74. The question now comes whether the suit for declaration of Title as is contemplated in clause (a), of Article 6 is the kind of suit out of which the present appeal arises. 

 75. Keeping the dominant purpose of the enactment in view it is evidently clear that the words "any such property" as used in clause (a) of the Article will not be referable to any immovable property, but to any immovable property which is the subject matter of a contract relating to transfer. We are of this considered view that the provision of Article 6 of the President Order No. 142 of 1972 has no manner of application in a Suit for declaration of title like the present one and the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, as such, is not at all necessary party and the suit cannot fail in not impleading the Government of Bangladesh as defendant. The contention raised from the side of the defendant-respondents being without any substance, fails. 

 76. We now propose to direct our attention to one legal aspect which is admissibility of documents as Exhibits. Many of the documents produced by the plaintiff were not admitted into evidence and exhibited in accordance with the provisions contained in the Evidence Act. A good number of documents has been exhibited with the certified copies. Exhibits 3, 4, 5 and 6 are all certified copies of the original documents and those copies were not even of 30 years old. The certified copies of those documents were obtained on 15-10-1979, 15-12-1978, 4-12-78 and 7-7-1979. The suit was registered on 11-12-1979. The certified copies of those documents i.e. the Deeds of Transfer were not admitted into evidence and exhibited in fulfilment of the requirement of law mandated in the Evidence Act. Exhibit 13 is a Rent Receipt allegedly granted by the Superior Landlord in favour of Ramjan Ali, the Vendor of the plaintiff and the said Rent Receipt is definitely a private document which was required to be proved in accordance with law but that was not so in this particular case. 

 87. Admittedly PW 1 is not a party to the suit. Rather his mother is a party to the suit who is no other than the plaintiff. It does not also appear at all that PW 1 is an attorney on the basis of a power executed by plaintiff in his favour to give testimony on her behalf in support of the plaint case. PW 1, Md Azim, thus, was an incompetent person to give testimony on behalf of the plaintiff in support of the plaint case and the plaint case, therefore, stands disproved. 

 88. Viewed in the perspective of the foregoing discourse and after giving our anxious consideration to all pros and cons of the case and on taking note of catena of decisions pronounced by the apex Court from time to time, the irresistible conclusion flows is, that since the plaintiff-appellant signally failed to prove her title and possession on the suit property and the defendant-respondents could successfully prove their title and possession thereon through legal evidence, plaintiffs suit was to meet the inevitable fate of dismissal and the learned trial. Judge was well justified in dismissing the suit and the judgment under challenge in this appeal having been well reasoned and well founded both on law and fact does not at all warrant any interference by us in the exercise of our appellate authority.
