full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 15.11.1984 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Narayangonj in Title Appeal No. 185 of 1982 reversing the judgment and decree dated 26.6.1982 passed by the Munsif, 2nd Court, Narayangonj in Title Suit No. 177 of 1979 decreeing the suit. 

 2. The petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 177 of 1979 in the Court of Munsif, Narayangonj for permanent injunction against the defendants restraining them from illegally entering into the suit lands. The plaintiff’s case is that the suit land along with other lands under C.S. Khatian No. 261 of Mouza Fatullah originally belonged to Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi in equal share. Sonaton Baroi died leaving leaving behind son Shyam Charan Baroi as his heir Ramananda Boroi died leaving 3 daughters. Mohan Mala Biswas, Hari Dasi Baroi and Seba Dasi Baroi as his heirs. By an amicable partition amongst the heirs of Sonaton and Ramananda, the said heirs of Ramananda got the suit plot i.e. C.S. plot No. 393 along with northern half of C.S. plot No. 436 of C.S. khatian No. 261 and they have been in peaceful possession of the suit land and the northern half of the C.S. plot No. 436. The further case of the plaintiff is that the S.A. Khatian of the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of Shyam Charan which was corrected by compromise decree dated 15.1.75 in Title Suit No. 290 of 1974 of the second Court of Munsif at Narayangonj wherein the right, title, interest and possession of the heirs of Ramananda in the suit plot and the northern half of plot No. 436 was declared and established. While the said Mohan Mala and her two sisters along with their sons were owners in possession of the suit plot along with northern half of the plot No. 436, they enured into a registered agreement dated 4.7.74 to sell the said lands for a consideration of Tk. 25,000/- and received taka 21,000/- as earnest money and delivered possession of the said lands to the plaintiff. Subsequently on 18.2.75 the vendors of the plaintiff executed and registered a saf kabala deed in favour of the plaintiff on receiving the balance consideration of taka 4,000/- from the plaintiff. The plaintiff excavated a tank in the southern portion of the suit land and stacked earth on the northern portion of the suit land for the purpose of manufacturing bricks and has been rearing fishes in the tank. The plaintiff mutated her name in S.A. Khatian in respect of the suit land by mutation case No. 35 FA/75-76 dated 22.7.75 and has been paying rents for the suit land in her name. The name of the plaintiff was duly recorded in the present R.S. Khatian No. 612 of Mouza Fatullah in respect of the suit land. The defendants have/had no right, title, interest and possession over the suit land. The defendants tried to enter into the suit land in the middle part of the month of September, 1979 but could not succeed on account of timely resistance put up by the plaintiff. The defendants gave out that they would enter into the suit land. Hence the plaintiff filed the suit. 

 3. The defendant opposite parties’ No. 1-3 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement alleging inter-alia that the suit for mere permanent injunction is not at all maintainable as the plaintiff has got no title and possession in the land in question. Their case is that the suit land originally belonged to Sonaton Baroi who died leaving behind his only son Shyam Charan Baroi Shyam Charam Baroi and his son Radha Ballav by a bainapatra dated 20.11.63 agreed to sell the suit property to Mohiuddin father of the defendant No. 1 to 3 and delivered possession of the same to Mohiuddin Ahmed. To enforce the agreement Mohiuddin Ahmed filed Title Suit No. 77 of 1969 for specific performance of contract. The said suit was decreed on 28.1.76 and Kabala was obtained through court on 3.2.78 and got possession of the land in question through court on 11.7.79. The contesting defendant thus contended that they have title and possession in the suit land. 

 4. The learned Munsif after recording evidence and hearing arguments of both the sides decreed the suit and being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the trial court the defendant opposite parties preferred Title Appeal No. 185 of 1982 before the learned District Judge, Narayangonj. The said appeal on transfer was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Narayangonj on 16.11.1984 and by the impugned judgment and decree he was pleased to set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial court and dismissed the suit. The plaintiff petitioner being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the appellate court below preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule. 

 5. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff petitioner submits that the judgment of the learned appellate court below is not a proper judgment of reversal because the appellate court below being the final court of fact has not controverts the reasoning and discussion of the trial court inasmuch as the learned appellate court below has not considered and discussed the entire evidence oral and documentary on record and as such this error of law on the part of the appellate court below caused erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that 'the learned appellate court below misread the C.S. khatian No. 261 exhibit 3 C in asmuch as he failed to read the word “গং” after Sonaton Baroi and also failed to read the word “বরাত” in C.S. Khatian No. 76 and the total non-consideration of these material words vitiated the findings of the appellate court below. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned appellate court below erred in law in deciding the question of title of the suit plot in favour of the defendants by wrongly holding that the properties of the disputed C.S. Khatian 76 exhibit 3C belong to Sonaton Baroi, the predecessor of the defendants along although it has been held that the suit is not maintainable for its involvement of complicated question of title. The learned Advocate referring to exhibit 3B and 3C further submits that the learned appellate Court below erred in holding that the learned Munsif is not justified to observe that the land originally belonged to Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi in equal shares. The learned Advocate with much emphasis submits that the learned appellate court below failed to consider and discuss the various exhibited documents filed by the plaintiff petitioner such as exhibits 1,1A, 2-2A, 3, 3A, 3B, 4A, 5, 6, 6A and also the oral evidence of 5 P.Ws. and those have proved the plaintiff's title and possession in the suit land and as such there is erroneous decision in the matter by the appellate court below occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that exhibit IA, bainapatra and exhibit 3A, S.A. Khatian, exhibit 2-2A rent receipts, exhibit 3 R.S. khatian exhibit 4, 4A containing an admission of Satya Ranjan son of Randha Ballav about the possession and title of the plaintiff petitioner's vendors in the suit plot and evidence of P.Ws. clearly proved the plaintiff's possession and title in the suit land and as such the learned appellate court contrary to those evidence on record erred in dismissing the suit. The learned Advocate finally submits that the defendants could not produce their alleged bainapatra dated 6.11.1963 showing their alleged possession since 1963 and that the defendants case of possession being self contradictory and that D.W.1 and 2 could not give the boundary of the suit plot inasmuch as D.W.1 and 2 are the defendant Nos. 1 and 4 respectively and as such the appellate court below erred in setting aside the decision of the trial court which decreed the suit considering the evidence and materials of the plaintiff vis-a-vis those of the defendants. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate, in support of his contention refers to and relies on the decisions namely (1991)11 BLD (AD)245,37D.L.R.79,PLD1976 (SC)784, 35DLR216 and 6 DLR 271. 

 6. Mr. Nurul Hoque, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant opposite parties submits that the correct position in that Sonaton Baroi was the sole 16 annas owner of the land of C.S. Khatian No. 261 as will appear on mere reading of the said Khatian exhibit 3C and in a suit for permanent injunction it is of paramount importance that the plaintiff must prove his title to the suit property and unless the plaintiff can show that he has some legal rights and the defendants have legal obligation not to disturb lawful possession of the plaintiff a suit for permanent injunction can not be maintained and in the instant case exhibit 3C clearly shows that the suit land solely belonged to Sonaton Baroi. The learned Advocate further submits that Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi are sons of two different persons and Ramananda Baroi was not a co-sharer of Sonaton Baroi and as such the question of amicable partition amongst the heirs of Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi does not arise at all. He further submits that these two persons being stranger to one another the question of any amicable partition between their heirs and such possession on the basis of the said alleged amicable partition does not arise. The learned Advocate further submits that the so called amicable partition if any, was falsely created and the same appears to have been created near about the time when the plaintiff was creating her documents. The learned Advocate further submits that the Title Suit No. 290 of 1974 cannot be a legally tenable suit for correction of S.A. record twelve years after finalization of the said record in 1962 and the trial court failed to take notice of this aspect of the case. Mr. Nurul Huq further submits that the compromise decree was collusive and untenable decree which cannot confer any right, title, interest and possession in favour of the heirs of Ramananda Baroi who was nobody having any interest in the suit land. The learned Advocate further submits that the story of excavation of the tank by the plaintiff is also a cock and bull story which the learned Munsif was hesitant in believing the same reading of the evidences of P.W. 3 and the trial court found major contradiction in evidence along with possession but gave his finding of possession in favour of the plaintiff petitioner without making any comment about the evidence of the D.Ws. which is not a legal decision on assessment of the evidence of both the parties as is called upon to do by the courts of facts and the trial court failed to follow the provisions of the Order 20 Rule 4(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Nurul Huq, the learned Advocate further submits that the mutation in the name of the plaintiff in Mutation Case No. 35/PA/75-76 dated 22.2.75 was not done in a lawful proceeding after service of notices as required under the law. There was no record to show that such mutation was lawfully made, the same was done during pendency of the title suit between the defendants and Satta Ranjan Baroi and as such record is hit by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. The recording of the plaintiff's name in the R.S. record was consequential effect of the illegal mutation of the plaintiff's name. In view of the decree obtained by the defendants in Title Suit No. 77 of 1969 the intervening all acts are hit by the doctrine of lis-pendense. The learned Advocate further submits that the trial court misread the C.S. khatian as was rightly found by the learned appellate court below. Mr. Nurul Hoque further submits that the prima facie title of the plaintiff and her possession was not legal finding inasmuch as the khatian No. 261 cannot be construed to show that Sonaton and Ramananda were the joint owner and such contention would be violative of the provisions of section 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act. The learned Advocate finally with much emphasis submits that in the instant case a complicated question of title is involved and the same cannot be decided without evidence in a properly framed suit and in that view of the matter also the learned appellate court below rightly dismissed the suit. Mr. Nurul Hoque, the learned Advocate has referred to and relied on the following decisions namely 1991 BLD (AD) 245, 10 DLR 193. 1982 BCR (AD). 

 7. Before I enter into the merit of this rule I would like to consider the legal aspect of the case. It appears from the trend of the earlier-judicial pronouncements that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff is to prove exclusive possession of the suit land and incidentally a prima facie title to the suit land. If these two requirements are fulfilled by the plaintiff only the he is entitled to a decree for permanent injunction. If we look to section 110 of the Evidence Act we find that this section embodies the well known principle of Roman law that possession in prima facie proof of ownership and when, therefore, a person is in possession of the property the presumption of ownership is highly in his favour and under section 110 of the Evidence Act the onus of proving that he is not the owner is on the person who affirms that he is not the owner. Similarly section 9 of the Specific Relief Act also protects the possessory right of a person. Title cannot be pleaded in bar in a suit of this nature and the court does not adjudicate upon the title of the parties in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act. It is thus, clear that even a tress passer can recover his possession if he is dispossessed from immovable property without his consent. If this be so then why a person who is already in possession of an immovable property claiming to be the owner will be required to prove his title to the property in order to protect his possession. In my opinion the correct legal position is that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff need not prove his title to the property as a condition precedent to succeed in an action for permanent injunction It is sufficient if the plaintiff can prove his prior and present possession of the suit land i.e. in a suit for permanent injunction possession is of paramount consideration and the fate of the suit veer round the proof of possession by the plaintiff. 

 8. From a review of the judicial pronouncements of the Superior Courts of this subcontinent it appears that in order to succeed in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff has to prove his exclusive possession and prima facie title. The same trend has undergone a change. Now the superior court emphasize much on the factum of possession and not on the title. It is now well settled that if a man is in continuous possession in the suit he is entitled to protect his right by way of permanent injunction. It has been held in 4BLD127 that a person in long possession can be evicted only in due process of law. Even the rightful owner cannot evict him with force. If he cannot be evicted with force he continues to be in possession and he can resist invasion of his possession by everyone including the rightful owner. If the rightful owner threatened his possession he can pray for an equitable relief of injunction to protect his possession and the remedy of the rightful owner lies in bringing appropriate suit for establishing his right and for recovery of possession. 

 9. The case reported in 10 DLR 193 was referred to in the said case but it was not followed. In the said 10 DLR case the plaintiff failed to prove his exclusive possession and that was the main ground for refusing the prayer for permanent injunction. Similarly our Appellate Division in the case reported in 4 BLD (AD)285 held that if the plaintiff failed to prove his title in a suit for permanent injunction that will not disentitle him to a decree for permanent injunction if he can prove possession. 

 10. There are other decisions in that line of both the divisions namely in the case reported in 37 DLR 79 it has been held that law nowhere enjoins that a suit for permanent injunction cannot be maintained without seeking a declaration of title, only because questions of title are raised. As in a partition suit so also in a suit for injunction questions of title may well be raised but that does not mean that without seeking declaration of title a simple suit for partition or a simple suit for injunction cannot be maintained when the plaintiffs are in possession of the land. 

 11. In the case reported in 11BLD (AD) 245 which has been referred to and relied on by both the sides it has been held that in a simple suit for permanent injunction with regard to a disputed landed property, the relief is available to a person who is in possession. The court may enquire incidentally into the respective claims of the parties to the suit for determining whether the plaintiff has got prima facie case i.e. whether he is in possession of the disputed property and entitled to the specific relief of permanent injunction. In that decision it has been further held that if the dispute involves complicated questions of title, the plaintiff must establish his title by filing a regular suit for declaration of title. 'A simple suit for permanent injunction should not be allowed to be used as a testing device for ascertainment of title. 

 12. Similarly in the case reported in 1982 BCR (AD) 321 it has been held that in a suit for permanent injunction it is not necessary for the plaintiff to prove his title to the suit property, he is entitled to get a decree of permanent injunction on the basis of his possession. 

 13. So it is crystal clear that suits for permanent injunction are merely concerned with the factum of possession and not with the nature and character of possession or capacity of the possessor. If the plaintiff is found to be in possession of the suit land he is entitled to get injunction. The principle of Division Bench ruling of the Kerala High Court reported in AIR 1966 (Kerala) 179, also seems to support the view, namely, that a person in possession even if wrongful is entitled to maintain his possession even against true owner, till eviction by due process of law. So the recent judicial pronouncement in this regard is that in a suit for permanent injunction the question of title is of no significance if in a properly framed suit the plaintiff can prove his exclusive possession of the suit land there is no doubt that he is entitled to protect his possession by way of permanent injunction against the whole world including the real owner. In the case reported in PLD 1976(SC) 785 it has been held that it is opened to the plaintiff to frame his suit and couch his relief in any manner within the law. He can sue for relief for declaration of title or permanent injunction or for both or even for declaration and permanent injunction as a consequential relief to suit his own requirement in accordance with law. In that case it has been observed that in this sub-continent declaratory decrees are granted under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act 1972, it lays down that any person is entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property. may institute a suit against any person denying his title to such character and the court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled and the plaintiff need not ask for any further relief, provided that no court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff being able to seek further relief then a declaration of the omits to do so. On the other hand the specific relief by way of perpetual injunction may be granted by the court in accordance with the provisions contained in sections 54 and 56 under Chapter X of the Specific Relief Act. In this connection section 54 inter-alia lays down that a perpetual injunction may be granted to prevent the breach of "obligation" existing in favour of the applicant, whether expressly Of by implication. The term "obligation" is defined in section 3 of the Act as "including every duty enforceable by law" so that when a legal duty is imposed on a person in respect of another, that other is invested with the corresponding legal right. In general under the first paragraph of section 54 of the Act, injunction may be granted by the court to an applicant to prevent the breach of an existing legal right vested in him. It is not always necessary for him to sue for the declaration of his title as a substantive relief and asked for the injunction as a consequential relief only. 

 15. Keeping these principles of law in mind let us now scrutinize and examine the impugned judgment and see how far it is sustainable in law. On a perusal of the impugned judgment it appears that the learned appellate court below observed that "It is admitted that to have a relief in the way of permanent in-junction it is the duty of the plaintiff to prove unclouded title and possession in the suit land in default to prove any one of the two will deprive the plaintiff from the cheap relief in the way of permanent injunction. So in a suit for permanent injunction first of all I am to see how far the plaintiff respondent has been able to prove her unclouded title in the land in question which will go to qualify her to have an order of permanent injunction to protect her alleged physical possession in the land in question". 

 16. From this observation of the learned appellate court below it is crystal clear that the learned appellate court below misdirected himself and treated the instant suit not as a suit for permanent injunction rather treated it as a suit for declaration of title and the said observation is apparently in conflict with the decisions which I have already referred to above. It is, thus, clear that the appellate court below in the instant case travelled beyond the scope of the suit and treating it as a suit for title put much emphasis on the question of title rather than the question of possession. 

 17. It further appears from the impugned judgment that the learned appellate court below found that the suit plot No. 393 of C.S. khatian No. 261 of mouza Fatullah comprising an area of 1.10 decimals of land originally belonged to Sonaton Baroi alone and this finding of the appellate court below is based on c.s. Khatian No. 261 exhibit 3C in respect of the suit plot No. 393 which speaks that the suit land belonged to Sonaton Baroi alone as a “রায়তী স্থিতিবান”. The learned trial court found that the land recorded in c.s. khatian No. 261 belonged to Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi in equal shares and the learned appellate court below has reversed that finding observing that in exhibit 3C there is no mentioned that Ramananda Baroi is also 8 annas owner of that jote but this finding of the appellate court below cannot be sustained in law inasmuch as exhibit 3C the c.s. Khatian No. 261 itself shows that Sonaton Baroi and others are the owners and in the column of rent it is written ১৫৯ নং মৌজায় ৭৬ নং খতিয়ানে মোট ৭ ।।৯ পাই Exhibit 3B the c.s. khatian 76 shows that Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi are the owners of the land recorded in that khatian. Of course, in khatian No. 76 plot No. 83 is recorded whereas the suit plot is recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 261. It is submitted by Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner, that বরাত mean reference and by referring to the relevant provisions of Technical Rules and Instructions of the Settlement Department, 1957 it has been shown that when tenant have land in different plots in different mouzas the full rent should be entered in one khatian only and cross-reference should be made in all the khatian and as such in the instant case the c.s. Khatian No. 76 and c.s. khatian 261 is to be read together and treated as one document and from this the trial court rightly arrived at a finding that Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi were equal sharer of the said jote. He has referred to the definition of "jote" as contained in section 5 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. "Jote' does not necessarily mean the interest of a cultivator, or an occupancy holding; it is only a general term and may mean a raiyati, under raiyati or any sort of holding for the purpose of cultivation. It simply connotes a tenancy. So if exhibit 3B and 3C are considered together it appears that the finding of the trial court is at least correct with regard to the prima facie title of the predecessor in interest46of the plaintiff petitioner in the suit land and the observation of the learned appellate court below cannot be maintained in view of the fact that in arriving at such a finding that Sonaton Baroi is the sole owner of the c.s. Khatian No. 393 is based on misreading of exhibit 3B as well as 3C because in exhibit 3C itself in column of owner it is written "owner is Sonaton Baroi and others and in the column of rent it is written “১৫৯ নং মৌজায় ৭৬ নং খতিয়ানে মোট ৭ ।।৯ পাই ” and the learned appellate court has failed to take notice of the contents of exhibit 3C and 3B and totally misread exhibit 3C and therefore the finding of the learned appellate Court below that Sonaton Baroi is the Sole owner of the suit land is absolutely contrary to the materials and evidence on record. At least there is prima facie evidence to show that both Sonatan Baroi and Ramananda were 8 annas share of the land recorded in 2 Khatians namely C. S. Khatian No. 261 and 76. On top of that the R.S. Khatian also stand in the name of the plaintiff petitioner. It is submitted that this R.S. Khatian has been published in the year 1974 in the district of Narayanganj by virtue of section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This RS. Khatian also has a presumptive value and this R.S. Khatian has been published after conducting field survey. In that view of the matter also it can be said that the plaintiff petitioner has been able to prove his prima facie title and possession in the suit land. If these 3 documents are considered along with the oral evidence of all the P.Ws. and D.Ws. it appears that the finding of the trial court that the plaintiff has been able to prove her prima facie title and exclusive possession in the suit land cannot be assailed. I, thus, find that the finding of the appellate court below that C.S. plot No. 393 entirely belonged to Sonatan Baroi is erroneous and contrary to the materials and evidence on record. 

 18. It further appears from the impugned judgment that the learned appellate court below did not give his finding on all the documents on the ground that in a simple suit for permanent injunction all those things need not be discussed and in that view of the matter he did not give has definite finding on exhibit 4, 4A and other documents filed by the plaintiff petitioner in support of her title and the learned appellate court below has rightly refrained himself from making any positive finding as to the legality and validity of these documents as in the instant suit the court is not called upon to adjudicate on the title rather the court is to see as to whether the plaintiff petitioner is in possession of the suit land and whether she is entitled to protect her possession by way of permanent injunction. The learned appellate court below arrived at a finding that the instant suit involves a complicated question of title and it cannot be decided in a suit for permanent injunction. It is true that in a suit for permanent injunction title cannot be gone into and it cannot be adjudicated upon but if it is found that the suit as framed comes within the ambit of section 54 of the Specific Relief Act the plaintiff is entitled to get a decree of permanent injunction inasmuch as in a suit for permanent injunction the question of title is of no significance at all. 

 19. It also appears on a perusal of the impugned judgment that although the learned appellate court below refrained himself from giving any positive finding on the question of title of the parties to the suit land, nevertheless, it has observed that the findings and decisions of the trial court in respect of the title of the suit land is erroneous and as such the learned appellate court below held that the suit is not maintainable but this finding of the appellate court below cannot be sustained in law in as much as in a suit for permanent injunction the fate of the suit cannot depend on the question of title of the plaintiff. The finding of the learned appellate court below that the acquisition of title of the plaintiff petitioner through heir of Ramananda Baroi cannot be considered to be good and no relief can be given to the plaintiff petitioner in the instant suit for permanent injunction is unwarranted and uncalled for in asmuch as in arriving at such a finding the learned appellate court below travelled beyond the scope of the suit. 

 20. Regarding physical possession of the suit land the appellate court below relying on the deposition of two D.Ws. and writ issued in pursuance of the Title Execution Case No. 19 of 1976 has arrived at a finding that at least the defendants have been able to prove symbolical possession in the suit land after successful termination of the Title Suit No. 77 of 1969 in their favour but in arriving at such a finding the appellate court below lost sight of the two c.s. khatians being khatian No.76 and khatian No. 261 and the R.S. khatian exhibit 3 and rent receipts exhibit 2-2A and the oral evidence of P.Ws. which conclusively proved the possession of the plaintiff petitioner in the suit land. It thus appears that the finding of the learned appellate court below that the defendants have been able to prove at least their symbolical possession of the suit land does not inspire confidence and the finding of the trial court on that point is backed by sufficient materials and evidence on record both oral and documentary. 

 21. It appears on a perusal of the impugned judgment that the learned appellate court below misdirected himself and treated the instant suit as a suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in asmuch as he has observed that the plaintiff petitioner has failed to prove her unclouded title and possession in the suit land. It thus appears to me that the learned appellate court below absolutely misappreciated the scope of the suit and travelled beyond the scope of the instant suit and arrived at such finding which is contrary to the established principles of law and in that view of the matter also the findings arrived at by the appellate court below at least on possession cannot be sustained. 

 22. One of the grievances of Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur is that the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment of reversal. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner has argued that the impugned judgment passed by the appellate court below is not a proper judgment of reversal in as much as the object of the Rule 31 of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure has not been complied with by the appellate court below. This contention of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner appears to be well founded. The object of Rule 31 of Order 41 of the Code is to see that a Judge does not act callously or even mechanically. Its purpose is to put the Judge on the right track and to the extent Rule of Procedure can do it, to see that he acts judicially. It enables the High Court to Judge whether the appellate court below had independently considered the case with a consciousness of relevant points which arose for adjudication. It is also to afford the parties opportunity of knowing the grounds of decision to enable them to exercise the right of revision and to enable the High Court Division in revision to see whether lower appellate court has properly appreciated and decided the case. Appellate judgment reversing the judgment of trial court should be adequate and satisfactory. It must contain definite findings on the questions involved and must give reasons for reversing the decisions of the trial court. In fact judgment of reversal may often need a little more discussion of facts, evidence and points involved in the case so as to embody in it convincing reasons for reversing the findings of the courts of first instance. It should cover almost entire grounds covered by the judgment appealed from. It must express opinion on all points on which the lower court has based its conclusion. It is not necessary for lower appellate court to mention each and every particular item of evidence in its judgment provided it is clear upon reading of the judgment itself that all relevant evidence has been substantially considered by the appellate court below. The appellate judgment may not meet all reasons given in the judgment of the trial court while setting it aside. The appellate court must advert to the findings and reasoning’s assigned by the trial court. These principles had not been followed by the appellate court below in as much as in some places appellate court grossly misread the evidence and the impugned judgment suffers from non-reading and non-consideration of the materials and evidence on record. The trial court discussed the evidence on the point of possession with regard to both oral and documentary evidence and after close scrutiny of the same have relied on the testimonies of the P.Ws. and discarded the testimonies of the D.Ws. on that point. The appellate court below failed to consider the assertions made by the parties in respect of possession of the suit property and also failed to notice the fact that in the instant case the defendants have failed to produce the agreement by virtue of which they have filed Title Suit No. 77 of 1969 and got an exparte decree and they have not been able to prove the said agreement even in the instant case. The learned appellate court below also failed to take notice of the fact that the case of possession is self contradictory inasmuch as in the said suit for specific performance of contract the defendant opposite parties have asserted that they have entered into possession of the suit land in 1963 in pursuance of bainapatra whereas in his evidence the D.W. 1 who is the defendant No. 1 asserted that they entered into possession of the suit land, through the court after execution of the decree of Title Suit No. 77 of 1974. The trial court dealt with the matter in detail but the learned appellate court below did not advert to it in its judgment. In 14 BLD (AD)229 it has been held by their Lordship that the appellate court whether reversing or affirming the decision of the trial court must independently consider the evidence on record but in the case of affirming the findings of the trial court, the narration of the entire evidence and reiteration of the reasons given by the trial court are not essential. In such a case expressions of general agreement with those of the trial court are generally considered sufficient. But in the case of reversal of the judgment the consideration of the evidence, of necessity, has to be thoroughly and more elaborate. But in the instant case it is crystal clear from the impugned judgment that the learned appellate court below failed to advert to the evidences both oral and documentary adduced by the plaintiff petitioner and the learned appellate court below also failed to reverse the finding of the trial court by giving cogent reason therefor. It has been held in the case reported in 15 BLD (AD) 120 that while exercising revisional power under section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code the High Court usually does not go into the question of fact but when the appellate court reverse the judgment of the trial court on non consideration of the materials on record and without adverting to the reasoning on which the trial court gave its judgment, the High Court may be justified to interfere with the findings of fact arrived at by the appellate court when it finds that non-consideration of such evidence has materially affected the appellate court judgment occasioning failure of justice. In the light of the aforesaid principles of law also the impugned judgment cannot be sustained in law. 

 It thus appears that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff is entitled to get an order in his favour only when the plaintiff can prove that the defendant is under an obligation either not to do an act which is threatened by him or to do an act which he refuses to do. In other words the defendants must be under a legal obligation either to do an act and not to do an act. He further submits that in that view of the matter if it is a contesting claim of title in a disputed property the plaintiff cannot resist the defendant from disturbing him with his possession of the defendant can show that he has legal right to the suit land. This argument is very much convincing but I cannot accept the same in view of the decisions of our Appellate Division as has already been referred to above. In the light of the aforesaid decisions it appears to me that in a suit for permanent injunction if the plaintiff can show his exclusive possession of the suit land, even independently of his title, he is entitled to get an order of injunction against the defendant. 

 24. From my aforesaid discussion it is crystal clear that in a suit for permanent in-junction there is no scope to adjudicate upon the question of title of the parties although the court can incidentally can go to the question of title. In that view of the matter the court should be conscious in making any observation touching the merit of title of either parties. On a scrutiny of the trial court's judgment it appears that the trial court has made certain observations which are actually relevant in determining the question of title. It has already been found that title is of no significance in a suit for permanent injunction and as such the observation made by the trial court regarding title of the parties are unwarranted, uncalled for and must be expunged. So, the finding of the trial court that "It gives a strong presumption that they merely created a document of title to and possession over the suit land by filing the aforesaid execution case for delivery of possession" and the finding of the trial court that "On perusal of the documents it appears that as per C.S. Khatian both Sonaton and Ramananda are equal shares (8 annas each) in the land of suit khatian" are expunged. 

 25. In this connection it may be stated that the observation of the trial court with regard exhibit 4, 4A, 5, 3, 3A, 2-2A, 1 and 1A that is all the documents exhibited by the plaintiff before the trial court should not be treated as a positive finding as to the genuinely or otherwise of the aforesaid deeds as in a suit for permanent injunction the court need not and should not enter into the question of title. The observations of the trial court with regard to the aforesaid documents are merely incidental and neither of the courts below had any jurisdiction at all to adjudicate upon the legality or validity of these documents in the instant suit. The validity and legality of these documents will be determined in a properly framed suit and these observations of the trial court will not stand on the way of either party in future in a properly framed suit and in that view of the matter the validity and legality of these documents are kept open to be adjudicated upon in future in an appropriate suit. 

 26. In view of my aforesaid discussion I find substance in this revisional application. In the result the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree dated 15.11.84 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Narayangonj in Title Appeal No. 185 of 1982 are set aside and the judgment and decree dated 26.6.1982 passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Narayangonj in Title Suit No. 177 of 1979 are restored.

parties:
Hazera Begum and others ------ Appellants.
 Vs
Roushan Ara Begum and others ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
Respondents filed Title Suit No. 163 of 1968 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka, against the defendants praying for partition of the suit lands on declaration of the plaintiffs title in certain share of the suit lands. 

 3. Plaintiffs case is that after the death of Hedayet his daughter and widow left the property to the care of Jobeda who possessed the property for and on behalf of the co-sharer and the plaintiffs are thus in constructive possession of the suit land. The ejmali character or the suit land has been causing inconvenience, hence the suit for partition with a prayer for declaration of the plaintiffs title. 

 4. Defendants 1 to 7 contested the suit by filing a written statement. They claimed through late Alfazuddin Ahmed who purchased the property from Jobeda Khatun in 1939, Their case was that Jobeda alone possessed the entire suit land exclusively and adversely in open assertion over the title thereto. Hedayet never possessed the suit land. Jobeda Khatun earlier mortgaged by way of conditional sale 7 pakhis of laud in 1935 and subsequently sold the said laud to Alfazuddin Ahmed in 1939. Thus Alfazuddin acquired  by purchase the entire suit land. Till his death in 1962 he executed as many as 7 registered kabuliyats during the period of 1936-1961 and after his death his heirs defendants 1 to 7 had been possessing the land on payment of rent exclusively for more than 12 year; in assertion of their hostile title to the knowledge of all including the heirs of Hedayet Baksha. 

 6. The appellate court below, however. decreed the suit after setting aside the Judgment and decree of the trial court and decreed the suit of the plaintiffs for partition, on declaration of the title to the extent of 5 pakhis 2 gondas 2 karas and 2 krants out of the lands shown in the schedule. 

 9. Alfazuddin Ahmed died on 12.11.62 The suit was filed in 1968. As noticed that the heirs of Hedayet Baksha are now the plaintiffs and the heirs of Alfazuddin Ahmed are the defendants. The trial court came to the conclusion that the plaintiffs had failed to prove their case and the suit was hopelessly time barred, and as such the plaintiffs are not entitled to get any decree. Further Hedayat and his heirs were never recognised as tenants by the landlords and as such Hedayet Baksha or his heirs never acquired any interest in the suit property. 

 10. The appellate court, on the other band, came to the conclusion that the right, title and interest by Hedayet Baksha in 6½  pakhis of land out of tile suit land had been subsisting and they had not been extinguished in any manner and consequently the plaintiffs inherited their legal share from Hedayet and they are entitled to get the same. The appellate court below further found that the defence has totally failed to prove that they ever set up a hostile title against the plaintiffs or their predecessor to their knowledge more than 12 years before the institution of this suit. Evidence of P.Ws. 1,3 and 4 was considered, which showed that the plaintiff’s had knowledge of the sale of the suit land by Jobeda Khatun although there was no evidence when the plaintiffs derived the knowledge of the same. Knowledge of Rehat Baksha, who was the husband of the sister of Alfazuddin as attesting witness of Exts. E. and E(1) could not be the knowledge of the plaintiff. Considering this relationship the appellate court below observed "there is no doubt that he was very much well affected to Alfazuddin Ahmed," Alfazuddin Ahmed immediately after his purchase created temporary lease by as many as 7 kabuliyats exts. B series through different persons in respect of the suit laud from 1936 to 1961. The appellate court below commented that by successive transfer by Exts. B series he thought, wrongly though "that he would thereby be in a position to extinguish, the title of Hedayet and his heirs." The appellate court below carefully considered the evidence and came to the conclusion that the right, title and interest of Hedayet Baksha had subsisted and his heirs are entitled to demand partition. Accordingly, the suit was decreed. 

 "The exclusive possession of Jobeda Khatun as alleged has not been proved and there is no finding by the court of fact in that behalf to attract the question of limitation to the instant suit." 

 The High Court Division repelled the contention of adverse possession and considered the possession of a co-owner becomes adverse to other co-owners from the moment when there is an outer or exclusion, that is, an assertion of a hostile title by one co-owner as against the others and that to the knowledge of the latter. It was noticed that these elements bad not been proved by the defendants. Sole possession is not exclusive or adverse possession, Reliance was placed on long line of decisions specially in the case of Bindu Bala De Vs. Rebati Mohan De reported in 4 DLR 293. In this view of the matter. the order and judgment of the appellate court below was affirmed and the suit was decreed. 

 12. Mr. S.R. Pal, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellants argued since 1939 Alfazuddin is in possession after his purchase Vide Exts. F and F (1) and therefore, his possession will be adverse to the plaintiffs. Mr. Pal argued that the defendants were in possession openly and to the knowledge of the plaintiff and such overt act is enough to constitute as ouster. Reliance was placed on some highest authorities claiming title by adverse possession 46 I.A. 46 and 61 LA. 78. Mr. Pal further argued that conception or Hindu caste cannot be imported in the facts of this case nor of law of agency can be applied, inasmuch as, no relevant evidence was given on that point. The question of equity does not come, it is contended, since it is the law that should be applied. Mr. Pal argued heavily on two decisions 23 Bom 137 and AIR 1942 Mad (F.B.) 622. 

 14. Now the second phase: on 10.8.38 Qayum sold his mortgaged land to Alfazuddin and on 12.4.39 Jobeda Khatun sold her mortgaged land to Alfazuddin. Now third phase: from 1939 to 1962 it seems that the parties were not at loggerheads. It was only in 1968 that the suit was filed. Mr. Ahmed argued that there is no trouble so far as the defendants are concerned because it is the matter between the relations and the suit land is situated at a distance of one mile of the plaintiffs' residence. Evidence was given that the plaintiffs got usufruct from the defendents, Finding of fact of the appellate court below and the High Court Division are that Hedayet had a title. Till Hedayet's death no case of adverse possession was made out and after Alfazuddin's purchase he became a co-sharer. Therefore, the question of adverse possession does not arise. Mr. Ahmed contended that the criticism tint plaintiffs obtained usufruct from time to time is not based on the pleading does not merit consideration, in as much as, positive evidence had been given by the plaintiffs that they not only had cordial relationship with Jobeda Khatun and Atfazuddin, but they were given also the usufruct from time to time. Evidence is there even in 1965 that usufruct was demanded from Jobeda. In this view of the evidence it is contended that the defendants had failed to make out achy case of adverse possession. 

 15. The plaintiff’s case was that the suit lands are ejmali and a co-sharer’s possession of ejmali property is the possession of all co-sharers. Since it has become inconvenient to possess the land in ejmali they brought the suit for partition. The defendants case was that Jobeda had been possessing the entire 20 pakhis of land in her exclusive raiyati rights on payment of rent in her name for the entire and on open assertion of hostile right and title against others. Hedayet, brother of Elahi Baksha staking advantage of illiteracy of the pardanashyn Jobeda Khatun fraudulently managed to create the kabuliyat in question and put forth a claim over the suit property in an attempt to make illegal gains" and Alfazuddin purchased the entire 20 pakhis for good consideration and since his purchase possessed the same "openly and publicly adversely to all subject to the right of Jobeda Knatun and Abdul Qayum for repurchase." In the additional written statement a further stand was taken that though Jobeda drove out Hedayet on detection of the fraud "who appeared to have fraudulently joined in a kabuliyat taking advantage of his position and no heir of Hedayet ever possessed any part of the suit land aid they had no right title or interest in the suit property. 

 18. The High Court Division rightly took the view that possession of a co-owner became adverse to others co-owners from the moment from when there is an ouster or exclusion. Reliance was placed in the case of Maharaja Bhupendra Ch. Singha Sarma & ors. Vs. Sudhindra Ch. Singha & ors reported in 5 D.L.R. 251. The appellate court below also worded a finding that there was nothing to suggest ouster or exclusion of the plaintiffs from possession. Sole possession is not exclusive or adverse possession. The appellate court below took the view that Hedayet possessed the suit land jointly with Jobeda. These findings of the courts below are founded on the evidence and taking into consideration of the facts and circumstances the question emerged whether the possession of the defendants were so hostile and adverse openly so as to justify the claim of adverse possession. Even if there are apparent show of adverse possession whether those circumstances were sufficient to defeat the title of the real owner only because some lack of vigilance can be attributed to the plaintiffs and would in such circumstances relieve the defendant from discharging their onus in support of their claim of adverse possession The onus is very heavy. It is for the defendant to discharge this so as to build up a claim of adverse possession. A thin veneer of adverse possession or semblance of it viewed from the distance would not be sufficient for the defendants to succeed without discharging their heavy onus. They have to do more that their possession was so open and hostile to the knowledge of all that the plaintiffs must have known the notorious fact that the plea of adverse possession is being raised up. When the relationships are such that the co-sharers are led to believe in certain circumstances which are not uncommon as fact of We will those circumstances be taken as evidence of knowledge of adverse possession. Long line of decisions show that is not the case. Plaintiffs' evidence that they got share of their crop from Alfazuddin and prior to that from Jobeda cannot be disbelieved when viewed in the light of relationship. Mere non-payment of rents and even non-sharing of profit would got justify a case of adverse possession. 

 Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.--I have gene through the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother, B.H. Chowdhury-J, but I regret my inability to agree with him. I would therefore give my own judgment as follows: This is defendants' appeal. The principal question therein is whether the High Court Division is well founded in law and fact in rejecting their contention that the plaintiff's suit for title and partition is barred by limitation under Article 144 of the Limitation Act in view of their alleged adverse possession of over 30 years as Stranger-Purchaser of the whole of the joint property. 

 23. The suit land measuring 20 pakhis, equivalent to 5.21 acres, originally belonged to one Younus Bepari. Plaintiffs' (respondents) case is that this laud was settled in raiyati right to Jobeda Khatun and Hedayet Baksh under a registered kabuliyat dated 2 June 1920; share of Jobeda Khatun was 14½  pakhis and that of Hedayet Baksh was 6½  pakhis. Both Jobeda and Hedayet Baksh possessed the land jointly. Hedayet, who lived in Jobeda's house in village Kaliganj left this village and settled in village Zinjira a few miles away but he continued to possess the land jointly with Jobeda till he died sometime in 1933-1934 AD. On his death his widow and two daughters (who are the plaintiffs)along with his brother Rabat Baksh and sister Jarina inherited his 6½  pakhis and since then they had been in constructive possession of the land through Jabeda.  Jabeda transferred five pakhis of land front her share to her son Abdul Qaayum by a registered Deed of Gift dated 5 September 1934. Thereafter, both Jobeda and her sea Quaiyum mortgaged their respective shares to Alfazuddin, predecessor-in-interest of defendants-appellants Nos. 1 to 7 by two separate Deeds of Mortgage dated 22 October 1935. The mortgage was followed by sale to the mortgagee under two registered Sale-deeds one dated 10 August 1938 and the other dated 12 April 1939. Since then Alfazuddin possessed the joint property as a co-sharer of the plaintiffs. Now inconvenience of joint possession being felt the plaintiffs filed the suit for simple partition to the extent of 5 pakhis 2 gondas. On objection hazing been raised the plaint was amended and a prayer far establishment of title was included in the plaint. 

 24. The suit was resisted by the defendants, who are heirs of Alfazuddin, by a written statement. They totally denied any title of Hedayet Baksh from the very beginning of the kabuliyat dated 2 June 1920. Their case is that the settlement under the kabuliyat was taken by Jobeda alone with her own money and for her own benefit and interest, but Hedayet Baksh who was brother of Jobeda's husband and was brought to her house to look after her affairs on her husband's death, fraudulently got his name inserted in the kabuliyat. That is why Hedayet was not recognized as a tenant by the landlord nor his name was mutated in the landlord's Sherista nor did he possess the land nor paid any rent but jobeda alone possessed the entire land and paid rent first to the landlord and then to the Government after State Acquisition. By the two Mortgage-deeds (as referred to above) Jobeda and her son Quaiyum, had first mortgaged the entire suit land to Alfazuddin and thereafter sold the entire land to him by two registered Sale-deeds whereupon Alfazudditn who was a stranger, entered into possession as owner and possessed it all through openly in assertion of his own title to the exclusion of the plaintiffs and others including Hedayet's brother Rahat and sister Jarina; from the date of settlement in 1920 till the filing of the suit in 1968 no claim of partition or for any usufruct of the land was made by Hedayet and after his death by his heirs, the plaintiffs; the suit was filed malafide as a test case for grabbing the property; the suit was barred by limitation. 

 24A. Plaintiffs examined 4 witnesses but adduced no documentary evidence except the admitted kabuliyat dated 2 June 1920 (Ext 1). Defendants examined 4 witnesses and produced a number of documents including seven registered Barga-kabutiyats, 18 Rent receipts and some khatians besides the undisputed Mortgage Deeds and Sale Deeds in favour of Alfazuddin. On consideration of these materials the trial Court found that except Hedayet's name appearing in the kabuliyat, Ext 1, there is no evidence whatever that he took settlement of the land along with Jobeda, that Hedayet was neither recognized as a tenant by the landlord nor did he pay any rent nor did he participate in any usufruct of the land and that it is Jobeda who alone possessed the land allthrough till she and her son transferred the entire suit land first by mortgage and then by out-right sale to Alfazuddin. The trial Court further found that Alfazuddin possessed the entire land to the exclusion of the plaintiffs claiming title for himself and that even if Hedayet had originally got any title to the extent of 6 ½   pakhis under the kabuliyat. Ext. 1, his title was extinguished by adverse possession of Jobeda and her transferee. On appeal, the learned District Jude reversed these findings and held that Hedayet had got his title to the extent of 6 ½  pakhis under the kabuliyat and possessed the land jointly with Jobeda and after transfer of the land to Alfazuddin, me plaintiff's possessed the land through Alfazuddin who was their co-sharer whose possession was not adverse to the plaintiffs. This finding bas been concurred in by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division against whose decision this appeal has been preferred as already stated in the judgment of my learned brother B.H. Chowdhury. J. 

 25. Mr. S.R. Pal, learned Advocate for the defendants- appellants, has seriously assailed the decision of the learned Single Judge rejecting the appellants contention of adverse possession from the beginning of the settlement, more particularly from 1935 when Jobeda and her son mortgaged the entire land to Alfazuddin, a stranger. The learned Counsel does not dispute the general principle of law that possession of a co-sharer in a joint property is possession on behalf of other co-sharers as well and that joint possession Continues till other co-sharers are completely ousted by exclusive possession in assertion or hostile title, publicly and openly for a period of 12 years; but he contends that the position is quite different in the instant case where a stranger entered into possession on the claim of exclusive title for the whole of the property. The possession of such a stranger transferee, the learned counsel contends, is adverse light from the beginning who in fact is not a co-sharer. As to knowledge of the co-owners about adverse possession, the learned Counsel contends that it is not necessary that the person claiming adverse possession on claim of hostile title should bring the matter to the knowledge of his transferor's co-sharers but it is sufficient that he possessed the land openly without any attempt to conceal it from the co-sharers and that he possessed it on claim of his exclusive title, The learned Counsel further contends that even if the stranger purchaser's title was defective or invalid still it does not matter so far as his possession is concerned and that the adverse possession begins right from his entry into possession. In the instant case the learned Counsel contends, the plaintiffs were fully aware of the defendants  possession on claim of title of the whole of the suit land. 

 26. Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-respondents, has stoutly defended the High Court Division's decision and contended that Alfazuddin by entering into possession of the suit land became a co-sharer with the plaintiffs no matter his sale-deeds evidenced transfer to him of the entire ejmali land; the sale-deeds are invalid to the extent of the plaintiff's share and as such they continued to be co-sharers in the joint property and that joint-possession shall be presumed to continue till the defendants prove complete ouster of the plaintiffs by adverse possession for 12 years. The learned Counsel has pointed out that plaintiffs predecessor Hedayet, had acquired title in the suit land to the extent of 6½  pakhis ad that this title could not have been extinguished except upon complete ouster on claim of hostile title a case which was not established by the defendants in this suit. 

 27. As it appears clearly, a. review of the evidence is necessary to determine the real question involved in this appeal, particularly when it centres found loss of title by adverse possession which is itself mixed question of law and fact. The first  point is whether Hedayet had acquired any title by kabuliyat Ext. 1 dated 2-6-1920 A.D. on the face of it he did acquire 6 ½  pakhis along with Jobeda Khatun Whose share was 13 ½  pakhis; whereas defendants totally denied such title, Widow of Hedayet (P.W.3) is one of the plaintiff. In her deposition she claimed that her husband had paid salami and acquired his interest under the kabuliyat but regarding the sources of salami or whether her husband got any means to procure this money she did not say anything. On the other hand, evidence adduced by both D.W. 1. son of Alfazuddin and P.W.1, son-in-law of P.W.3 read along with pleadings of both the parties, clearly shows that Hedayet (brother of Jobeda's husband) bad neither any land nor any house of his own that whatever ancestral landed property he had lie sold it away and resided in the house of Jobeda and after his exit. from that house he lived in the house of his father-in-law in a different village, Zinjira, a few miles away from Jobeda's village in which the suit-bud was situated. Jobeda on the other hand got sufficient resources both from her father and her late previous husband and that at her request Hedayet lived in her house from where he was driven out by her. This claim of the defendants in the written statement has not been disputed. Therefore evidence on record does not give any indication about Hedayet's means to pay for the salami, Be that as it may for the sake of argument I would take that he had paid the salami for his share and acquired title to the extent of 6½  pakhis of the property. But us to possession, evidence of P.W.3 is that Hedayet possessed his share jointly with Jobeda. Such possession, even if accepted continued only for a year or two, for he left the village Kaliganj where the land lay and settled in Zinjira from where he could have possessed only through Jobeda, But admitted fact is that his name was not mutated in the landlord's Sherista nor did he pay any rent nor his name was recorded in the Petty Settlement khatian Ext D (1) which was published some time in 1933. Ext. D(1) recorded Jobeda's name as owner in-possession to the extent of 13 ½  Pakhis in one of the two khatians, The trial Court held that non-participation in any profits from the land, non-payment of any rent and non-recording of his name either in tile landlord's sherista or In any record-of-rights showed that he got no title in the land tinder the kabuliyat which was not acted upon in his case. But the appellate Court took the view that since Hedayet was a co-sharer under the kabuliyat non-participation in profits or non-payment of rent would not extinguish his title. This is true, hut if Jobeda's title was hostile from the very beginning, then by her adverse possession Hedayet's title had extinguished by the time he died, I shall, however not take this view as Hedayet's name appeared in the kabuliyat and presume that he was  a co-sharer of Jobeda with or through whom he possessed his share and that the joint possession continued even after his death and see the subsequent development. 

 28. There is no dispute that Jobeda and her son Quaiyum transferred their entire interests first by mortgage in 1935 and then by sale in 1938-39 to AIfazuddin a stranger. Under these documents Alfazuddin entered into possession of the entire land asserting title over it and if this fact was known to Hedayet's heirs, then Alfazuddin's possession became adverse from the date of his entry into possession. The learned District Judge took the view that for adverse possession it must be brought to the notice of co-sharers and that in this case there was no evidence of such knowledge. This observation is not correct for besides these plaintiffs (who are two daughters and the widow), Hedayet left one brother Rabat Baksh and one sister Jarina as his heirs. Rahat Baksh and Jarina never claimed any share in the land as co-sharer of Alfazuddin. On the contrary Rahat Baksh was a witness to the Sale-deeds, Ext. E and E(1), by which Alfazuddin purchased the entire suit, land including his (Rahat) own interest, if any, therein. The learned District Judge observed that Rahat had married Alfazuddin sister and as such he intentionally kept the matter concealed from the plaintiffs acting in collusion with Alfazuddin. This observation is based on mare conjecture. For no where in the plaint or in the evidence the plaintiffs took such a plea that Rahat had married Alfazuddin's sister and acted in collusion with Alfazuddin or that he bad intentionally suppressed the fact of transfer of the land. Rather P.W. 2. Firoza one of the two daughters of Hedayet sated that her uncle Rahat  Baksh "used to maintain us "Rahat was a government servant and understood the implication  of the transfer to the entire suit land to a stranger under Sale-Deeds. His interest in the land  as common with the plaintiffs interest and he had no reason to keep the transfer suppressed. It is D.W. 1, son of Alfazuddin, who asked whether Rahat had married his father's sister and his answer was in the affirmative. But even if Rabat had married Alfazuddin's sister, there is no evidence that the marriage took place before this transaction, for if he had married after he attested the Transfer Deed then he had no reason to suppress it. In the absence of any plea taken by the plaintiffs, the learned District Judge went off the track to make out a case as to suppression of fact by Rahat. 

 32. Another piece of evidence of defendants possession is seven registered Barga Kabuliyats, Ext. B series. Evidence of D.W. 1. which is supported by P.W. 4, is that his father possessed the land though different bargaders. He produced these Barga Kabuliyats Executed by the respective Borgaders over a period of 25 years, the first one being dated 2-6-36 and the last one being dated 4-4-02. These bargaders delivered adhi-share not to the plaintiffs but to Alfazuddin alone. We find no basis for the observation of the learned District Judge that these Barga Kabuliyats might have been created for the purpose or fabricating evidence of title. 

 33. From the evidence discussed above, I find two distinct stages of possession of the laud, first one from 1920 to 1934 that is, from the date of Kabuliyat Ext. 1 till the death of Hedayet, and the second one from the time of Hedayet's death till the filing of the suit in 1968, more particularly from transfer of the land to Alfazuddin in 1935. For the sake of argument I would accept that Hedayet was a co-sharer under Ext. 1 in 1920 and also that he was in constructive possession of his share through Jobeda and then see whether the law of adverse possession came in operation against his heirs from 1935 when Alfazuddin, a stranger, on claim of 16-annas title, began to possess the  land alone. A co-sharer's possession is possession on behalf of all co-sharers and this possession is presumed to continue till other co-sharers are ousted completely by exclusive possession openly on claim of hostile title by another co-sharer. This principle of law was propounded by the Judicial Committee of tile Privy Council in the case of Corea Vs. Apuhamy AIR 1914 PC 243, in which Lord Macnaughten cited the dictum of V.C. Wood In Thomas vs. Thomas that possession is never considered adverse if it is referred to a lawful title. Similar view had been expressed  much earlier by Lord ,Denman C.J. in Culley  v. Doe Dem Taylerson. 11A & E. 1008 (1840) in the following terms: 

 Mr. Khondaar Mahbubuddin Ahmed argued that in spite of Alfazuddin's Mortgage-Deeds and Sale-Deeds showing transfer of the whole of the land to him, plaintiffs share remained unaffected and they continued as co-sharers of Alfazuddin and as such it is only their complete ouster, the onus of which lies on the defendants, that their title could be lost by adverse possession. 

 35. In support of their respective contentions the learned counsels cited a great number of decision. In Bhavrdo  v. Rakhmin,  23 Bom 137 (F.B.), some co-parceners of a joint family estate alienated  by mortgage and safe "certain defined and distinct portions" of the joint estate to a stranger who began possession claiming exclusive title. In a suit for partition by other co-perceners the plea of adverse possession taken by the alignee  was accepted by the court. In that case Article 127 of the Limitation Act was not held applicable as this Article applies only in cases between the members of a joint family and net to the case of a stranger in whose case Article 144 applies. As to the purchaser's possession it was held : 

 "The answer, we think, must be than as he enters as owner and in right of his conveyance, his possession is adverse to them also. In the eve of law, all the co-parceners though for the sake of convenience they may be in separate possession of portions of the joint estate, are the owners of the whole estate including the alienaled portion. It may be and indeed is the case that such a purchaser by his purchase does not get a good title to the land conveyed to him by a Sink co-parcener, but only the qualified right laid down in Pardurang v. Bhaskar (supra), and he is liable under some circumstances even to be evicted if the co-parceners take the requisite steps within the statutory period Nevertheless, his exclusive possession does not en that account case to be adverse. He, entering as owner, his possession must, we think, necessarily be adverse to the true owners. Adverse possession depends upon the claim to title under which the possessor holds and not upon a consideration of the question in whom the true ownership is vested whether in a single person or in many jointly." 

 "To constitute a plaintiff's title by adverse possession, the possession required to be proved must be adequate in continuity, in publicity, and in extent, and is displaced by evidence of partial possession by the defendant," 

 Mr. Pal contends that the defendants case fully fits into this principle as laid down and fulfills all the requirements of acquisition of title by adverse possession. In the case before us the principle as to acquisition of title by adverse possession has not been invoked by the plaintiffs, but it has been invoked by the defendants to maintain their possession under mortgage-deeds followed by sale-deeds for over a period of 30 years, a possession which was open without any concealment and in the exercise of hostile title. 

 38. The next case relied upon by Mr. Pal is Bharat Pillai V. Jeebarahmal, 46 IA, PC 285. There, possession of one co-shares was held to be adverse against the other co-sharer of a joint property. The Judicial Committee took note of the general principle that one tenant in common could not maintain an ejectment suit against another tenant in common in ordinary circumstances bra, the Committee held, where the letter tenant had not been in participation of rent and profits for a condonable length of time and other circumstances concurred then the court should hold ouster 'of the latter tenant. Mr. Pal has tried to reinforce his argument that if a stranger enters upon possession of any ejmali property either in whole or in part under any conveyance executed by one of several co sharers, then though the conveyance is invalid the stranger's possession is adverse right from the beginning and this possession ripens into title on the expiry of the statutory period of 12 years. In Lala Hem Chand V. Lala Peary Lal and others, AIR 1942, PC 64, a defendant claimed title by adverse possession on the basis of a trust which was held to be void on the ground of vagueness as to its contents. The plaintiffs' suit for ejectment was dismissed and it was held: 

 40. Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, as already state above, does not agree that a stranger purchasing the whole of an ejmali property is not a co-sharer. He contends that such a purchaser, whether he purchases whole of the ejmali property or any share thereof, is also a co-sharer and his possession is governed by the general principle that a co-sharer's possession is possession on behalf of all other co-sharers. He has referred to the case of Muzaffar Khan Vs. Yousuf Khan., PLD (1959) . SC 9. in which the vendee of a co-sharer of an undivided property was held to be a co-sharer and is entitled to pre-emption under the North Western Frontier Province Preemption Act. Balaram Vs. Shyamcharan, 24 CWN 1057, a similar question arose for determination by the Calcutta High Court and it was held that the possession of land, under common title, of one co-owner would not be presumed to be adverse to other co-sharers but ordinarily, it could be held for the benefit of all. It was observed : 

 "The law will never construe a possession tortious, unless from necessity : on the other hand its gill consider every possession lawful the commencement and continuance of which is not proved to be wrongful and this, upon the principle that every man shall be presumed to act in obedience to his duty, until the contrary appears. In other words, the only difference between the possess slots of a co-owner and other cases is, that acts, which, if done, by a stranger, would perse be a disseisin, are, in the case of tenancies in common,  susceptible of explanation consistently with the real title acts of ownership are not, in tenancies in common, acts of disseisin; it depends upon the intent with winch they are done and their notoriety; the law will not presume that cue tenant in common intends to oust another; the facts must be notorious and the intent must be established in proof." 

 Facts in this case are that the property belonged to three brothers two of whom had left their ancestral home in the village and settled in another village and were not in possession for 50 years; during this period their brother who stayed back possessed the hind paying rent alone in his name, and dealt with the entire properly as his own and then transferred it to the defendant, a stronger. Plaintiffs purchased 2/3rd share from these two absentee brothers and filed a suit for partition on declaration of title. The defendant pleaded adverse possession as a stranger purchaser, but the contention was rejected on the ground that he became a co-sharer in the land and his possession was on behalf of other two co-sharers and that his possession did not exclude them. 

 41. The next case relied upon by Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed is Izat Baksh Sarkar v. Abdul Quadir Bhuiyan, 21 DLR (SC) 444. In that case a brother sold certain property to a stranger claiming the property as his own, whereas it belonged to him and his two minor brothers. The purchaser possessed the property openly, exclusively and in assertion of his own title or mutation of his name and by payment of rent. The minors took no step to assert their title for long 21 years even, after they attained majority. In that case the general rule that a co-sharers possession is possession on behalf of other co-sharers was applied and the plea of adverse possession was rejected, The Court, however, observed that this does not mean that a co-sharer can never possess adversely to the other co-sharers and acquire title by adverse possession. To enable one of the co-sharers to acquire title by adverse possession as against the other co-sharers, his possession must be of such an actual, open, notorious, exclusive and hostile character as to amount to an ouster or exclusion of the other co-sharers. Moreover, such possession must be for a continuous period of at least 12 years in assertion of a hostile title to the knowledge of the co-sharers against whom title by adverse possession is claimed. Such knowledge may be proved directly or inferentially," It may be noted that in both these cases original title of the contending co-sharers was not in dispute and that they got the property by inheritance; whereas in the instant case the original title of the plaintiffs predecessor, Hedayet, is in dispute. Kh. Mahbubuddin has also relied upon the following cases where the same principle as to a co sharer's possession has been re-stated and applied. Maroon Mia v. Majiduddin, 4 DLR 114; Bindhu Bala v. Rabati Mohan, 4 DLR 293, Maharaja Bhupendra Singh v. Sudhindra Chandra Singh, 5 DLR 251; Abdul Jalil Shikder  v. Khurshed Ali, 27 DLR AD 143, and & Mohar Ali v. Zafar Ali, 27 DLR 451. 

 "Adverse possession must be within the knowledge of the co-sharer; mere possession by mortgagee from the co-owner does not amount to ouster. A co-owner has no duty cast upon him to watch the conduct of another co-owner and be on lookout to find out the extent of the share purported to be transferred by him and to intervene if more than the real shave has been transferred. He is entitled to assume that the permissive nature of Vie possession has passed on to his co-owner's transferee who has now become the co-owner in place of the original co-owner. Of course if the assertion of title to the whole is brought to his knowledge and it is accompanied by his ouster and exclusion, adverse possession would then commence as against him". The minority view was, however, that "a mortgage of the entire property by one of the proprietors is a clear assertion of adverse title and the possession of the mortgagee is surely adverse to the co-owners of the mortgagors." 

 42. Now coming back to the instant case, the position of Alfazuddin as I find was that of a trespasser from 1935 if Hedayet had acquired title to the extent of 6 ½  pakhis under the kabuliyat. This was so because Alfazuddin entered into possession of the whole of land on claim of 16-annas title under his title deeds which were invalid to the extent of the plaintiffs share. But whether Alfazuddin entered into possession as a trespasser or as plaintiffs co-sharer, his exclusive possession exercised openly on claim of 16 annas title constituted complete ouster of the plaintiffs; and this possession is certainly adverse and has over the period of 33 years extinguished whatever title the plaintiffs had in the land. This adverse possession was very much within the knowledge of the plaintiffs from the time of this entry into the land. from 1935. This knowledge is clearly established from paragraph 3 of their plaint and also from their total unconcern about the land. As to the knowledge of their co-sharer Rabat Baksh about the transfer, since his interest in the land was common with theirs, there was no season why he would not disclose the matter to them. By the Sale deeds he attested his own interest also was transferred, if he had any. Possession on Alfazadnin was open, in total exclusion of the plaintiffs, on claim of title and without any attempt at concealment over this long period during which plaintiffs had no participation in profits of the land or payment of rent; their names were not recorded in any document nor did they ever claim any benefit from or partition of this land. In fact they had no connection with the land from 1935, and nothing was known about them till they filed the suit, according to the defendants, just to take a chance to establish title. The suit is hopelessly barred under Article 144 of the Limitation Act. Views taken by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division tend to show that once a co-sharer always a co-sharer and that against a co-sharer there can be no extinguishment of title by adverse possession. Plaintiff and before them, their predecessor were completely out of scene from the date of the kabuliyat. In these circumstances, the suit was rightly dismissed by the trial Court.
