parties:
Mokarram Ali & others
Vs.
Abdul Samad & others
full_judgment:
2. The appeal raises an important question of law, in that whether the doctrine of res judicata as provided in section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure has got any application in the case where two suits, one title suit instituted by the appellants and the other partition suit instituted by the respondents making the plaintiffs of the title suit as defendants in respect of the selfsame property, having been disposed of by one judgment, dismissing the title suits and decreeing the partition suit, and the plaintiffs in the title suit preferring appeal against the decree in the partition suit, the decree in the title suit operates as res judicata in the appeal. 

 3. Facts, in short, necessary for disposal of the appeal may be stated thus : two suits being Title Suit No. 55 of 1961/ 80 of 1962 and Partition Suit No. 25 of 1961/79 of 1962 between the same parties were heard analogously and disposed of by one judgment and separate decrees. The appellants instituted Title Suit No. 55 of 1961 on February 17, 1961 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Third Court, Comilla which on transfer to the court of Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Comilla was renumbered as Title Suit No. 80 of 1962, for confirmation of their possession and for a declaration of their title that the property described in schedule (1) to the plaint were the self-acquired property of Kala Gazi and not of the father of Kala Gazi as claimed by the plaintiffs of the portion suit. Respondents 1 to 23 instituted Partition Suit No. 25 of 1961 on February 29, 1961 in the 3rd Court of the Subordinate Judge which on transfer to the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Comilla was renumbered as Partition Suit No. 79 of 1962. The case of the said plaintiffs, inter alia, is that all the lands described in the schedules 1 to 4 to the plaint belonged to two brothers, Ashok Gazi and Kala Gazi in equal shares. Ashok Gazi died leaving behind two sons Jinnat Ali and Ashraf Ali who inherited 4 annas share each in the case land. Thereafter Jinnat Ali died leaving behind the plaintiffs 1 to 17 and Ashraf Ali died leaving behind the plaintiffs 18 to 23. Thus the plaintiffs 1 to 23 collectively inherited 8 annas share in the entire case land. On the other hand Kala Gazi died leaving behind two sons Fazle Ali, predecessor of defendants 1 to 3, and Tamizuddin predecessor of defendants 4 to 8. Thus the defendants 1 to 8 collectively inherited 8 annas share in the entire suit property. The partition suit was contested by the defendants 1, 4, 5 and 6 by filing a joint written statement. There was no dispute with regard to the lands described in schedules 2, 3 and 4. The dispute was in respect of the property described in schedule 1 only. The defendants claimed that the property described in schedule were the self-acquired property of their predecessor Kala Gazi who acquired the same by a patta dated 4th Flagon, 1293 B.S. Both the suits were disposed of by one judgment dismissing the title suit and decreeing the partition suit on the finding that the schedule property in the partition suit was not the self-acquired property of Kala Gazi but belonged to the father of Kala Gazi. The appellants who were the defendants in the partition suit filed an appeal against the decree passed in the partition suit but they did not file any appeal against the decree dismissing their title suit. At the hearing of the appeal the learned Judges of the High Court accepted the contention of the respondents that the question regarding the appellants claim to schedule 1 property on the ground that the properties were the self-acquired property of Kala Gazi, could not be agitated in the appeal, because, the appellants were estopped from raising this question, inasmuch as, the issue was decided in the title suit itself, wherein it was held by the trial court that the properties of schedule 1 to the plaint in the title suit were not the self-acquired property of Kala Gazi but were the properties belonged to the common ancestor of the parties, namely, father of Kala Gazi. On this finding the appeal was dismissed. 

 4. In this back ground leave was granted to examine the question whether doctrine of res judicata as provided in section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure has any application to such a case, that is, the judgment in the title suit in the absence of any appeal therefrom, being a decision in the former suit within the meaning of section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, operates as res judicata in the appeal from the decree in the partition suit. 

 5. Mr. Shaukat Ali Khan, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellants submitted that the learned Judges of the High Court on clear misconception about the provision of res judicata as contained in section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure wrongly held that the appellants were not entitled to agitate the question of title to schedule property in the appeal from the decree in the partition suit. In support of this contention he argued that both the title suit and the partition suit involving substantially the same disputed question as to whether schedule property was the self-acquired property of the appellants' predecessor and both the suits having been heard together and disposed of by one judgment, the learned Judges committed an error of procedure in not allowing the appellants to agitate the said question, which being practically the common question in both the suits, was sought to be raised in appeal from the partition decree. According to the learned Counsel the decision in the title suit cannot be taken to be the decision in the "former suit" as contemplated in section 11. 

 6. Mr. Saukat Ali Khan relied upon a decision of a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court in the case of Pramatha Nath Chaudhury etc. v. Rai Dwarka Nath Chakraborti Chaudhury Bahadur etc. (1). Relying on the authority of this decision the learned Counsel submitted that the test of res judicata in such cases tried analogously is whether the Judge did apply his mind to the issue involved in the suits separately or whether there has been in fact one trial, one finding and one decision. According to him in the instant case the issues were framed separately but issue No. 4 in the title suit relating to the question whether the suit land was the self-acquired property of Kala Gazi, was considered along with issue Nos. 1 and 2 of the partition suit, that is, whether the plaintiffs have any right, title and interest in the suit land. The learned Counsel referred to relevant portion of the judgment to show how the issues have been considered and disposed of. The Trial Court concluded as follows: 

 Let me examine whether the test applied in Pramatha Nath Chaudhury's case and also in the Lahore Full Bench case is applicable to the facts of the instant case. It has been already noted above that two suits were instituted in the same Court being Title Suit No. 55 of 1961 and Partition Suit No. 25 of 1961; and on transfer to the court of Subordinate Judge, Second Court; Comilla, the suits were renumbered as Title Suit No. 55 of 1961/80 of 1962 and Partition Suit No. 79 of 196/25 of 19612. The plaintiffs in the former suit were defendants in the later suit and the plaintiffs in the later suit were defendants in the former suit; and that both the suits were heard analogously and disposed of by one judgment; title suit was dismissed and the partition suit was decreed. Partition suit was filed by the descendants of Ashok Gazi. One of the issues framed in Title Suit filed by defendants 1 to 8 of the Partition Suit is— 

 Issue No. 5 Have the plaintiffs any right, title and interest in the suit land? 

 Issue No. 6 Are the plaintiffs entitled to get any decree for partition, if so, what is the share of the plaintiffs? 

 9. Contest in both the suits was with regard to the first schedule lands and there was no controversy with regard to the lands of other 3 schedules. Defendants in the partition suit who were the plaintiffs in the title suit claimed the entire first schedule property with the exception of plots 578 and 579 measuring 93 decimals as belonging exclusively to them. With regard to the first schedule property their case is that the lands comprising of five plots measuring 4.97 acres was acquired by a patta dated 4th Falgoon, 1293 B.S. by Kala Gazi alone and it was his exclusive property; and that Kala Gazi out of sympathy allowed his brother Ashok Gazi to possess 93 decimals of plots 578 and 579. The plaintiffs in the partition suit who were the defendants in the title suit claimed that all the lands of "Ka", "Kha" and "Ga" schedules of the title suit were the ejmali properties of their predecessors Jinnat Ali, Ashraf Ali, Fazle Ali and Tamizuddin in equal shares. The trial Court accepted the case of the plaintiffs in the partition suit that the first schedule property was acquired by Ashok Gazi and Kala Gazi together while they were joint but the document was taken in the name of Kala Gazi, and arrived at the following conclusion:- 

 "So following from the above conclusions the 4th issue of the title suit is answered in the negative and on the fifth issue of the partition suit it is found that the plaintiffs have their half share in the lands of all the four schedules." 

 On the above finding the partition suit was decreed in preliminary form on contest with necessary directions, and the title suit was dismissed. The appeal preferred against the decree passed in partition suit was dismissed on the ground that the appeal was barred by operation of the decision in the title suit as no appeal from that decree was preferred. 

 10. The main object of the doctrine of res judicata is to prevent multiplicity of suits and interminable disputes between litigants. There is some controversy on the question of application of the principle of res judicata to a case arising out of similar situation. This question was elaborately examined by Sir Ashutosh Mookerjee in the case of Isup Ali v. Gour Chandra Deb, (1). Facts in that case are as follows: A, B and C brought a suit against D for recovery of possession of certain land. A few days later, D and his brothers instituted against A, B and C a suit for establishment of their title to the home-stead portion of the property involved in the suit. The suits were jointly tried together and disposed of by one judgment. The former suit was dismissed but the latter suit was decreed. The plaintiffs in the first suit preferred an appeal annexing both the decrees with the memorandum of appeal, which, however, set out the name of D alone as the respondent. Objection was raised on the maintainability of the appeal on the ground that the appeal was barred by the decision in the subsequent suit between the same parties and others. The contention was accepted on the ground that the decision could not be collaterally attacked or implicitly ignored in appeal. 

 13. So far available, the leading case on the point is the case of Mt. Lachhmi v. Mt. Bhulli, (5) In this case a Full Bench of the Lahore High Court discussed extensively the principles governing the doctrine of res judicata. Two widows A and B were jointly in possession of certain laid. Each sued the other for declaration that she (plaintiff) was the exclusive owner of that land, and that the other (defendant) had no right in it of any kind. Both the suits were disposed of by a single judgment which decided that A was the owner, but that B was entitled to hold possession of half of the land in lieu of maintenance. A separate decree was drawn up in each suit declaring the rights of the respective plaintiff according to that decision. B appealed against one of these decree only, namely, the decree given in the suit in which she was the plaintiff. It was held (by the majority judgment) that the decree in the other suit cannot bar B's appeal. With regard to the question of analogous hearing of suits Tek Chand, J. dealt with the question at length. The learned Judge, inter alia, observed: 

 “The essence of the rule seems to me to be that the two proceedings should be so independent of each other that the trial of one cannot be confused with the trial of the other. (Where two suits, having a common issue are, by consent of parties or by order of the court, tried together the evidence being written in one record, and both suits disposed of by a single judgment, can it be said that there have been two distinct and independent trials? There being but one finding and one judgment on what principle can the hearing of the appeal in which this finding and this judgment are under consideration be barred, merely because no appeal has been filed in the connected suit which was disposed of by that very judgment ? There has been in substance, as well as in form but one verdict and I venture to think, it will be a travesty of justice to stifle the hearing of the appeal against such a judgment on the ground that the findings contained in it operate as res judicata. In such case there can be no question of the successful party being vexed twice over the same matter, nor does the hearing of the appeal in any way, militate against any rule of public policy which required that there must be an end of litigation. There is not only nothing here to attract the principles underlying the rule of res judicata, but, on the other hand it seems to me that the acceptance of such a plea in such circumstances would strike at the very root of the basic conception of the doctrine, which requires that a pasty must have at least one fair trial of the issue resulting in a decision by the court of ultimate appeal as allowed by the law for the time being in force". 

 The Supreme Court of India in the case of Narahari v. Shankar, (1) has noted the above noted decision of the Lahore Full Bench in Mt. Lachhmi v. Mt. Bhulli and it has been approved. Naik, J. observed as follows: 

 15. Mr. Shaukat Ali Khan on the authority of this decision vigorously argued that the first appeal preferred by the appellants was not barred by the-decision in the title suit not appealed from. According to him the principles of res judicata have no application in such a case. 

 "11. Res judicata.—No Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a court competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such court". 

 The meaning and scope of the expression "former suit" has been clarified by introducing Explanation I to section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure of 1908. The expression "former suit" contemplates a suit which has been decided earlier than the suit in question, irrespective of the fact of the suit being instituted prior or after the institution of the suit in question. If two suits are filed one after another and the same question is in controversy, the decision in the later suit if given earlier operates as res judicata. For instance, the defendant in a suit for ejectment takes the plea that the plaintiff has no title. Pending disposal of the suit a third person claiming title to the suit property by instituting a suit gets his title established. The decision operates as res judicata to the suit for ejectment. The principle however is not applicable in a case where several suits involving common issues between the same parties are disposed of by one judgment, decrees being passed in each, but one decree is appealed from, the matter decided in the decrees not appealed from does not operate as res judicata to the appeal. Application of the doctrine of res judicata to a suit or appeal preferred therefrom is dependent on the nature of the suit and the common issues framed in the suits. If the suits are connected and the issue framed therein is also common so as to constitute virtually a single suit on the issue, in such a case the decree not appealed from will not operate as res judicata. 

 17. In the instant case the position is different. Title Suit No. 80 of 1962 was instituted by the present appellants on 17-2-61 and the defendants of the suit instituted Partition Suit No. 25 of 1961 on 29-2-61 for Partition of lands which of course includes amongst others the suit lands of the title suit. The question as to whether the properties in dispute were the exclusive properties of Kala Gazi was the principal issue for adjudication in the title suit, which issue might have been incidentally considered in the partition suit, but there was no scope for deciding the question of title in the partition suit. In disposing of the partition suit, the issue on the question of title might have been examined incidentally, but from this it cannot be said that the issue relating to title has been decided by the judgment so far it relates to the partition suit. 

 18. In the title suit the decision was that the suit property did not belong to Kala Gazi alone and the suit was dismissed. In that view of the matter although in the title suit and the partition suit some common issues were framed, and both the suits were disposed of by one judgment, the decision of the court on the question of title cannot be said to have been given in the partition suit also, because, the issue was not directly and substantially in issue therein. Obviously the property was partitioned treating the property of 'Ka' schedule as the property jointly acquired by Ashok Gazi and Kala Gazi. So, the decree passed in the title suit not appealed from operates as res judicata to the appeal from the decree in the partition suit. The decision on the question of title to the Schedule 1 property given in the title suit could not be collaterally attacked in the appeal from the decree in the Partition Suit. 

 19. The doctrine of res judicata, so far as it relates to prohibiting retrial of an issue refers not to the date of commencement of the suit but to the time when the Judge is called upon to decide the issue. The rule is not limited to the court of first instance, but it also applies to the proceedings of the first and second Appellate Courts. The main object of the doctrine of res judicata is to prevent multiplicity of suits and interminable dispute between litigants. The question of title cannot be said to be substantially in issue in the partition suit, but it was so in the title suit. So, the question of title cannot be said to be common in the two suits. From the judgment of the trial Court it appears that the trial court dealt with 4th issue of title suit separately and answered in the negative. And the 5th issue of the partition was answered separately. It has been found that the plaintiffs have their half share in the lands of all the four schedules. The decision on the question of title given in the title suit became final in the absence of any appeal therefrom. It could not be reopened in the appeal from the decree in the partition suit. The High Court has taken the correct view in the matter. In the result, the appeal is dismissed with costs.

parties:
Zakir Hossain and another
Vs.
Md. Yousuf Kabir and others
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J: This first appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 31.03.2004 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 59 of 1994 decreeing the suit. 

 2. Respondent Nos.1 and 2 as plaintiffs filed the said title suit in the Court of Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka for declaration of title to the suit land on the averments, inter-alia, that the land of C.S. khatian No. 241 being plot No. 390/3940 measuring an area of 0568 ajutangsha originally belonged to Khiroda Shundari Daishya which was put to auction for arrear of rent in certificate Case No. 660 of 1952-53 and was purchased by Ali Ahmed @ Dr. Monjurul Hoque, son of late Munshi Nowab Ali of 74, Mirpur, Dhaka on 20.06.1953. The sale was confirmed on 24.08.1953 and sale certificate was issued in favour of said Ali Ahmed on 19.11.1953. The auction purchaser (Ali Ahmed) got possession of the auction purchased land on 20.01.1954 through court. Ali Ahmed being in possession of the auction purchased land (hereinafter referred to as the suit property) for more than 12 years mutated his name in the Government record and paid rents accordingly; S.A. Khatian being No.197 and R.S. Khatian being No.1248 were prepared in his name. Ali Ahmed while had been in possession of the suit property died issueless on 18.06.1975 leaving behind a widow, named, Khatibunnassa who inherited the entire suit property as her 4 annas share as his wife and the remaining 12 annas share because of the 'Doctrine of Return'. Khatibunnesa being the 16 annas owner of the suit property died on 10.02.78 leaving behind her only full brother Abdul Mannan who inherited the entire property of his deceased sister. While Abdul Mannan had been in possession of the suit property as the 16 annas owner, by a registered heba-bil-ewaj dated 29.11.79 being No. 45060 transferred the suit property in favour of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs being minors their father Abdul Majid as their natural guardian took over the possession of the transferred land. Thus the plaintiffs being the 16 annas owners of the suit property have been in peaceful possession thereof. Defendants having no right, title, interest and possession in the suit property by resorting to various tactics created forged papers and tried to take possession of the suit property forcibly, but due to the intervention of the respectable people of the mahalla failed. On 06.07.80 the defendants along with the process server of the Court and the police attacked (in the plaint in Bengali it has been written as “হামলা চালায়” in the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs by showing a decree. The bailiff of the Court having seen the valid title documents of the plaintiffs failed to execute the decree in Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980. However, after making inquiry from the bailiff of the Court the father of the plaintiffs Abdul Mazid came to know that the defendants obtained a fraudulent decree on 15.11.79 in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka. On further query the plaintiffs came to know that a so-called bainapatra to sell the suit property allegedly entered into by one Rasheda Begum, wife of Salimuddin of 321, Lalbag Road, Dhaka on 12.08.92 with the defendants was the basis of the said decree. Rasheda Begum went to Pakistan Via Nepal after liberation of Bangladesh, so the alleged bainapatra was fraudulent and was not legally enforceable in respect of the suit property. Rasheda Begum had no right, title, interest and possession in the suit property. Therefore, the defendants did not acquire any title to the suit property either on the basis of the bainapatra or their alleged purchase. The plaintiffs themselves and through their predecessor have been in possession of the suit property for more than 12 years since the purchase of the same in auction. The defendants got a kabala executed and registered in their names through court in execution of the ex-parte decree passed in the said suit, but by the said kabala they did not acquire right, tide and interest in the suit property. As neither the plaintiffs nor their predecessor were made parties in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979, the decree passed therein suit was not binding upon them. A reading of the judgments passed in Title Appeal No. 196 of 1984, Civil Revision 76 of 1987 and Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal No. 297 of 1992 it is primafacie clear that the plaintiffs suit was dismissed as complicated questions of title were involved, but all the courts found their possession in the suit property. It is also a well settled legal proposition that in a suit for permanent injunction regarding an immovable property the court shall see whether the plaintiffs are in exclusive possession of the suit property and it can see title of the plaintiffs incidentally, so all the courts rightly refrained from giving any finding as to the title of the parties to the suit property as well as the auction purchase by Ali Ahmed on 20.06.1953. When all the 3 (three) courts dismissed Title Suit No. 329 of 1980 on the categorical finding that complicated questions of title being involved the suit was not maintainable then how the stray observations even if any made regarding the auction purchase by plaintiffs vendor's predecessor Ali Ahmed can be said to be a constructive res-judicata to nonsuit the plaintiffs, the instant suit being one for title along with the consequential reliefs. We are of the view that in order to non suit the plaintiffs from maintaining a suit of the instant nature on the plea of constructive res-judicata as conceived of in explanation IV to section 11 of the Code the defendants were obliged to prove that in the earlier suit the plaintiffs did not at all plead their title on the basis of the auction purchase by their vendor's processor Ali Ahmed or that there was a conclusive decision in the previous suit on the title of the plaintiffs or the auction purchase but the plaintiffs could prove none. At the risk of repetition we hold that since no issue as to the title of the parties to the suit property and the auction purchase by Ali Ahmed was raised and decided in neither of the suits fought by the parties and the plaintiffs vendors vendor having pleaded in the very first suit his own right title to the suit property it cannot be said that the plaintiffs claim was barred by the principle of constructive res-judicata. So, we find no substance in the submission Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, on the first point and hold that the instant was quite maintainable in law. 

 21. Now let us see whether the plaintiffs proved their title to the suit property. The whole basis of the plaintiffs title to the suit property was the auction purchase by Ali Ahmed on 20.06.1953. Further case of the plaintiffs was that the sale was confirmed on 24.08.1953, the sale certificate was issued on 19.11.1953 and Ali Ahmed got possession of the suit property through court 20.01.1954 and since then he had been in possession thereof. After the death of Ali Ahmed his wife Khatibunnesa inherited his entire property and on her death Abdul Mannan, her full brother inherited the same. In support of the said case of the plaintiffs they filed the sale certificate (exhibit 2) and the writ of delivery of possession (exhibit 2 (ka). In the written statement exhibit 2 and 2 (ka) were not challenged as spurious or forged. In the deposition of D.W. 1 only a general denial was given to the effect: 

 22. From exhibit 2 it is clear that the sale was confirmed on 24.08.1953. From exhibit 2 it is further clear that the entire suit land measuring .568 ajutangsha was sold in auction and not 7 (seven) annas share out of the suit plot. From exhibit 2 it further appears that the said 568 ajutangsha was the 7th annas share of the "হিস্যে" of the touzi being No. 61/1 of Dhaka Collectorate. `Touzi' refers to a page of the register of the tenant. When a property is sold in auction giving specific description thereof and mentioning the area how can it be said that 7 (seven) annas share out of the plot mentioned in the schedule of the sale certificate was sold. Mr. A. J. Mohammad vehemently argued that since in the compromise applications dated 16.11.59 filed in Title Suit No. 50 of 1959 and House Rent Case No. 598 of 1959 and in the two registered agreements of the same date Ali Ahmed claimed to have purchased 7 (seven) annas share out of the suit land, in no case the plaintiffs could claim more than said 7 (seven) annas share of the suit property. But we do not find any substance in the said submission of Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, our reason being that when the alleged agreements and the compromise applications were cancelled at the instance of the defendant's predecessor Rasheda Begum in Title Suit No. 221 of 1964 how reliance could be put on the said agreements and the compromise applications. Further as those were not filed in the instant suit neither the trial court had any chance to see the recitals therein nor this court has any chance to go through the same to verify the submission of Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali. In the plaint the plaintiffs claimed the entire suit property which is clearly mentioned in the sale certificate as well as in the writ of delivery of possession, but the defendants never challenged the identify of the suit property or the area of the suit property. 

 23. The submission of Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali that auction purchase by Ali Ahmed being after the transfer of the suit property to Salimunnesa by the admitted rightful owners, namely, Khiroda Sundari Shaha and Lalit Mohan Das Shaha no title accrued to him appeared to us absolutely fallacious. Because, though the auction sale took place on 20.06.53, yet the number of the certificate case shows that it was started in 1952 being No. 60 of 1952-53. It is also very pertinent to keep in mind that before auction sale notice under section 7 of the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 (the Act) must have been served after observing the other requirements as mandated in sections 4, 5 and 6 of the Act. The said provisions of the Act deal with filing of certificate for public demand payable to the Collector, requisition for certificate in other cases and the filing of certificate on requisition. Rules framed under section 38 of the Act have provided the details as to how the notice under section 7 of the Act shall be served. Section 8 of the Act has clearly stipulated that from and after the service of notice of any certificate under section 7 of the Act upon a certificate debtor any private transfer or delivery of any of his immovable property situated in the district in which the certificate is filed, or of any interest in any such property, shall be void against any claim enforceable in execution of the certificate and the amount due from time to time in respect of the certificate shall be a charge upon the immovable property of the certificate-debtor, wherever situated, to which every other charge created subsequently to the service of the said notice shall be postponed. Section 9 of the Act has clearly provided for filing petition denying the liability and section 10 thereof has spelt out about the hearing and determination of such petition. The defendants in their written statement did not specifically challenge the auction sale, what they pleaded was that Ali Ahmed having earlier claimed that he purchased 7 (seven) annas share of the suit plot the plaintiffs could not claim the entire suit property. Whether the certificate of demand and certificate of requisition were filed before the certificate officer prior to the alleged sale by Khiroda Sundari Daishya and Lalit Mohan Shaha to Salimunnessa are questions of fact and as the defendants did not challenge the certificate proceedings in which Ali Ahmed auction purchased the suit property the plaintiffs were not required to prove all those facts. In support of the plaintiffs claim of title through auction purchase by Ali Ahmed they having filed the sale certificate and the writ of delivery of possession their onus was discharged. Further, as per the own admission of the defendants that Ali Ahmed disclosed the fact of auction purchase as far back as in 1959 when he allegedly created two deeds of agreements and two applications for compromise filed in Money Suit No. 50 of 1959 and in House Rent Case No. 598 of 1959 which were ultimately cancelled in Title Suit No. 221 of 1964, but Rasheda Begum never took any attempt to set aside the said auction purchase by Ali Ahmed. In this regard we like to observe that in a revenue matter proceeding follows the land not the person, so even if Khiroda Sundari Daishaya and Lalit Mohan Shaha sold the suit property prior to the auction sale but that shall not automatically make the auction sale a nullity. It was obligatory upon Rasheda Begum to take step to set aside the sale. In this regard we like point out that rule 39 of the Rules as detailed in schedule 11 to the Act which have binding effect in view of the provision of section 38 of the Act (hereinafter refereed to as the Rules) has clearly provided that if any claim is preferred to or any objection is made to the attachment or sale of, any property in execution of a certificate, on the ground that such property is not liable to such attachment or sale, the certificate officer shall proceed to investigate the claim or objection. Rule 40 has provided that the claimant or the objector must adduce evidence to show that (in case of immovable property) at the date of service of the notice under section 7 of the Act he had some interest in, or was possessed of, the property attached. Rule 41 has given power to the certificate officer to release the property from attachment or sale. Rule 43 has provided that the party against whom an order is made may instant a suit in a civil court to establish the right which he claims to the property in dispute, but subject to the result of such suit (if any) the order shall be conclusive. But Salimunnessa or Rasheda Begum did not take shelter under the said provisions of law to set aside the sale. In the Act or in the rules nothing has been provided for as to when an auction sale shall take its effect, but we can easily take the aid of section 65 of the Code which reads as under: 

 24. It is true that the auction sale in question was not held in execution of a decree of a civil court, but we do not see any wrong in borrowing the concept from the Code it being a civil proceeding and appeared to us quite akin to an auction sale held under the Code in execution of a decree. Mr. Mohammad Ali like a drowning man who catches a straw tried to challenge the auction sale by submitting that the sale certificate does not tally with Form 28 and Rule 74 of the Rules, so on such defective sale certificate the plaintiffs could not claim their title to the suit property. On such submission of Mr. Mohammad Ali we have examined the sale certificate along with the said form and the rule but we have not found any major deviation or noncompliance with the said form and the rule to make the sale certificate void or voidable. We are of the view that the moment the auction sale was confirmed it took its effect from the date of its sale on 20.06.1953 and it was also acted upon with the delivery of possession of the auction sold property. After all these years the defendants cannot be allowed to challenge the same and that too by way of oral submission through their learned Advocate and thus to deny plaintiffs title to the suit property. 

 25. Admittedly the plaintiffs had been in possession of the suit property which was clearly found by all the courts in connection with the proceedings which arose out of Title Suit No. 329 of 1980 of the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka. The plaintiffs by amending the plaint prayed for recovery of khas possession of the suit property and also for mesne profit stating categorically that the defendants dispossessed them and their tenants therefrom forcibly on 16.09.1997. All along plaintiff's case was that their predecessor's predecessor Ali Ahmed got possession of the suit property through court on the basis of his auction purchase and in support of their said case they filed the writ of delivery of possession, exhibit 2 (ka). From exhibit 1 (ka) and 1 (kha) it appears that the S.A. and R.S. khatians were prepared in the name of Ali Ahmed. Exhibit 5 shows that plaintiffs names were mutated and a new khatian being No. 197 was opened in their names. Exhibit 6-6 (Na) series show that Ali Ahmed paid rents to the government and then the plaintiffs paid rents to the government after mutation of their names. Exhibit 7-7 (Nia) series show that the holding in respect of the suit property was recorded with the Dhaka City Corporation in the name of the plaintiffs and they paid City Corporation tax. Exhibits 8. 9 and 10 series show that it is the plaintiffs who paid the utility bills such as Dhaka Was a, gas and electricity in respect of the suit property. Exhibits 11 and 12 series show that the plaintiffs inducted tenants in the suit property who paid rents to them. And those documents primafacie proved that it was Ali Ahmed and the plaintiffs who exercised their right of ownership in the suit property and had been in possession thereof uninterruptedly since the delivery of possession on 20.01.54 by virtue of the auction purchase. On the other hand, the contesting defendants failed to file a single scrape of paper to show that their so-called vendor Rasheda Begum and before that Salimunnesa ever exercised their right of ownership and possession in the suit property or that Ali Ahmed or his wife had ever attorned Salimunnessa as land lord after purchase from Khiroda Sundari Daishya and Lalit Mohan Shaha or they ever paid any rent to Rasheda Begum attorning as their land lord. Not only that the defendants also failed to file/produce any original deed of their alleged vendor Rasheda Begum. It is a well settled legal proposition that though the khatians and rent receipts are not the documents of title, yet they can very much be used for collateral purpose to prove title. The very fact that S.A. and R.S. khatians were prepared in the name of Ali Ahmed and he paid rents to the government and after his death the plaintiffs paid rents and they also paid other utility bills proved their title to the suit property. It is also a salutory legal proposition that possession follows title, so even if it is presumed for argument's sake that the plaintiff's vendor's vendor Ali Ahmed purchased the 7th share of the suit plot as argued by Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, yet due to the long and continuous uninterrupted possession in the suit property since 20.01.1954, the plaintiffs acquired absolute title to the suit property. 

 26. From the judgment passed in Title Suit No. 221 of 1964 it is apparent that Rasheda Begum filed Money Suit No. 50 of 1959 in the Court of the then Munsif 3rd Court, Dhaka for realization of arrear rent and also House Rent Case No. 598 of 1959 in the same court for eviction of her tenant and although Ali Ahmed allegedly took attempt to nullify the result of the said suit and the house rent case by filing two compromise petitions and eventually the said two compromise petitions were declared cancelled in Title Suit No. 221 of 1964, yet thereafter no step was taken by her either to realize arrear rents from Ali Ahmed and his wife Khatibunnesa or to evict them from the suit property. From exhibit 13 it appeared that Rasheda Begum filed Title Suit No. 106 of 1970 on 13.04.70 in the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka against Khatibunnesa and others for declaration of title and injunction. Exhibit 13 further shows that the said suit was dismissed for default on 28.06.72. The said fact was asserted in the plaint as well as in the deposition of p. w. 1. Rasheda Begum did not take any step to set aside the said order of dismissal by filing an application under Order 9, rule 9 of the Code. Exhibit 14, the application filed by the plaintiffs for the certified copy of the plaint of said Title Suit No. 106 of 1970 also shows that the said order of dismissal was passed on 28.06.72; the certified copy of the plaint could not be supplied as the record was destroyed. Rule 9 of Order 9 of the Code has clearly spelt out that where a suit is dismissed wholly or partly under rule 8 of Order 9 of the Code the plaintiff shall be precluded from bringing a fresh suit on the same cause of action. Section 12 of the Code has clearly debarred a plaintiff from instituting a further suit in respect of any particular cause of action where he is precluded by rules from instituting a further suit. In this regard we may also refer to the provision of sub rule (3) of Rule 1 of Order XXIII of the Code which is as under: 

 27. Thus, it appeared to us that in fact, Rasheda Begum defendant's so-called vendor abandoned her claim to the suit property by not taking any step to set aside the order of dismissal of Title Suit No. 106 of 1970. It is true that it is not the defendants who have come for title, but when they set up a specific case of their title to the suit property through Rasheda Begum by obtaining an ex-parte decree for specific performance of contract and tried to justify their possession in the suit property we can very much see whether their vendor had any right and title to the suit property. From the above, it is clear that Rasheda Begum failed to establish her title to the suit property, so how the defendants could claim title to the suit property through Rasheda Begum in their defence to deny the plaintiffs title when they proved their story of acquisition of title and possession in the suit property by filing documents without any gape right from the auction purchase of the suit property by, Ali Ahmed. In this regard it is also very pertinent to state that the plaintiffs in theft plaint categorically stated that after a few days of the liberation of Bangladesh Resheda Begum left Bangladesh for Pakistan Via Nepal and did not enter into any contract with the defendants to sell the suit property, but they created a forged bainapatra. P.W.1 also deposed in court to the said effect. But the defendants failed to produce any evidence whatsoever to show that at the time of bainapatra which was allegedly executed on 12.08.72 or thereafter Rasheda Begum was in Bangladesh. Rather, the evidence of D.W.1 in his cross-examination to the effect: 

 corroborates the plaintiff's case that at the relevant time of execution of the alleged bainapatra by Rasheda Begum and during the period of filing of Title Suit No. 62 of 1979, at the time of passing of the decree as well as up to the execution and registration of the kabala in favour of the defendants she was not in Bangladesh. Our view is further strengthen from the further fact that Title Suit No. 106 of 1970 brought by Rasheda Begum was dismissed for default on 28.06.72, had she remained present in Bangladesh after liberation then she would not have allowed the suit to be dismissed for default. Further though the defendants filed the bainapatra, yet none proved the same and none deposed as to the fact of passing of consideration to Rasheda Begum as part performance of the contract. Since the plaintiffs were not party in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979 filed by the defendants and they were claiming title to the suit property on the basis of a decree passed therein the plaintiffs had every right to challenge the propriety of the decree passed in the suit, particularly when they prayed for a declaration to the effect that they were not bound by the judgment and decree passed therein. As the plaintiffs challenged the bainapatra allegedly entered into by Rasheda Begum and the ex-parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979 as fraudulent the onus was upon the defendants to prove that the bainapatra was genuine and the decree in the said suit was obtained in a regular course on due service of summons of the suit upon Rasheda Begum in Bangladesh but they failed to discharge the said onus. It is also very significant to state that the defendants could not file any original title deed of their alleged vendor Rasheda Begum which also creates primafacie doubt about their case of bainapatra entered into by Rasheda Begum. 

 28. We conclude by holding that the plaintiffs proved their 16 (sixteen) annas title to the suit property. 

 30. So, the plaintiffs could not be evicted from the suit property other that due process of law. The defendants levied Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka for execution of the decree. The defendants admitted in the written statement that though the bailiff went to the suit property yet he could not deliver possession thereof to them because of the resistance put by the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs specific case was that the defendants dispossessed them and their tenants forcibly on 16.09.97 and looted away the goods for which they amended the plaint and prayed for recovery of khas possession along with other reliefs including mesne profit. Whereas the defendant's case was that the plaintiffs of their own delivered vacant possession of the suit property to them on 05.10.97 on receipt of, a sum of taka 16,60,000/00 on 30.09.97 on the basis of a salish/mediation done by Hajee Md. Selim, the local member of the parliament and the other respectable people of the locality. Defendant's further case was that Abdul Majid, father of the plaintiffs acknowledged the receipt of the said amount of money in writing in a paper by putting his signature which was subsequently signed by plaintiff No. 2 on 05.10.97. P.W.1 categorically denied the said assertion of the defendants. In support of the forcible dispossession by the defendants from the suit property the plaintiffs besides examining plaintiff No. 2 as p.w.1 also examined 3 (three) other witnesses and filed documentary evidence. P.W.1 in his examination-in-chief categorically stated that while the suit was pending the defendants entered into the suit property along with 20/30 terrorists and dispossessed them and looted away the goods which included gold ornaments. The defendants also looted away the goods of their tenants. P.W.1 further stated that over the said incident their father lodged a complaint with Lalbag Police Station which gave rise to Case No. 32 (9) 97. On behalf of the 'bharatias' Wazir Ahmed also lodged a general dairy with Lalbag Police Station being No. 940 dated 16.09.97. The certified copy of the First Information Report (FIR) was filed and marked as exhibit 16 and the copy of the general diary was filed and marked as exhibit 17. The p. w. further stated that the news of their illegal eviction from the suit property and the looting away of goods therefrom were published in the daily Inquilab and the Bhorer Kagaj on 18.09.97 and 20.09.97 respectively. The copies of the said news papers were filed and marked as exhibits 18 series. P.W.1 further deposed that on 30.09.97 the defendants by force obtained a writing from his father in a white paper to the effect that he received taka 16,60,000/00 and then on 05.10.75 also obtained a similar writing from him in the same paper though they did not receive any money. In cross-examination p.w.1 further asserted that no salish took place on 30.09.97 at the house of the ex-member of the parliament. Hajee Selim at the presence of the plaintiffs and the Ward Commissioner and they did not put their signature on receipt of a sum of taka 16,60,000/00 (sixteen lacs sixty thousand). P.W.1 further asserted that his signature was obtained in the receipt on 05.10.97 by force. P.W.2, Abdul Majid, the father of the plaintiffs categorically stated in his examination-in-chief that Rasheda Begum was never the owner of the suit property and she never possessed the same and Title Suit No. 106 of 1970 filed by her for declaration of title was dismissed for default. This P.W. further stated that on 16.09.97 the defendants being accompanied by 20/25 goondas dispossessed the plaintiffs and their bharatias by force and looted away the goods. After eviction the defendants took him to court forcibly and got the suit withdrawn on the threat that if he did not withdraw the suit they would kill his sons (the plaintiffs). On 30.09.97 the defendants took him to their office and then got a paper written by him to the effect that he received taka sixteen lacs and sixty thousand. At first it was written as 16,000/00. He further stated that he did not receive any money from the defendants. P.W.2 denied the defendant's case that he, on 30.09.97 in presence of the former member of the parliament Hajee Selim and others demanded taka 20,00,000/00 (twenty lacs) from the defendants as compensation and on receipt of taka 16,60,000/00 delivered possession of the suit property and withdrew the civil and criminal cases. This p. w. corroborated P.W.1 on all other points. By cross-examining these two P.W. s the defendants could not at all shake the credibility of their testimony in examination-in-chief. 

 33. The defendants examined 9 (nine) witnesses, of them D.W.1 is defendant No. 2. D.W.1 admitted that the plaintiffs had been in possession of the suit property but asserted that the plaintiffs were not the owners of the suit property. D.W.1 asserted in his examination-in-chief that on 30.09.1997 at the mediation (ম��্যস্থতায়) of the former local member of the parliament Hajee Md. Selim, Ward Commissioner of Ward No. 61, Hajee Md. Masum, ex-ward Commissioner of Ward No. 60 Mosharaf Hossain and the others, namely, Janab Lal, Janab Md. Uzir (p.w.3), Md. Yousup, Md. Aziz, Md. Shawkat, Md. Mesbahuddin including the plaintiffs, their mother, their maternal uncle Abdul Gani, the plaintiffs father admitted that it was the defendants who were entitled to get the suit property and on demand of compensation to leave the suit property as well as to settle somewhere else Hajee Selim settled the amount of compensation at taka 16,60,000/00 on the further condition that the plaintiff's father would withdraw the cases both civil and criminal and that in the very salish they paid the said amount which was received by the plaintiffs, their father and maternal uncle. D.W.1 further asserted that Abdul Majid in his own hand wrote in a paper to the effect that he received the said amount and put his own signature which was also signed by the plaintiffs maternal uncle Abdul Gani on 30.09.97 and thereafter plaintiff No. 2 wrote similar thing on 05.10.73 in the said paper and then he put his signature. D.W.1 further asserted that after receiving the money on 30.09.97 the plaintiffs shifted their goods from the suit property to the house of their maternal uncle from 01.10.97 to 04.10.97 and then on 05.10.1997 delivered possession of the suit property to them. D.W.2 is one Md. Islam. He did not say a ward about the salish/settlement and payment of money on 30.09.97 at the mediation of Hajee Selim and others. He stated that the plaintiffs and their father delivered possession of the suit property to the defendants on 05.10.1997 and he was present at the said time. After 7/8 months therefrom the process server from the court went to the suit property and having found the defendants in possession gave the report which he signed. In cross-examination he stated that Din Mohammad father of defendant No. 2 was his tenant. In the suit land there were shops and the plaintiffs also used to live there. He further stated to the effect: 

 42. The evidence of the D.W.S does not inspire confidence in our mind to believe defendant's case that the plaintiffs voluntarily handed over possession of the suit property to them on 05.10.1997 on receipt of a sum of taka 16,60,000/00 (sixteen lacs sixty thousand), on 30.09.97, as it sounded absurd to us that when the plaintiffs fought upto the Appellate Division to maintain their possession in the suit property by filing Title Suit No. 329 of 1980 in the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka against the defendants and then filed application in Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980 so that they could not be evicted through the execution of the said case and fought upto this Division they would leave the same on receipt of a sum of taka 16,60,000/00 the suit being ready for peremptory hearing. Defendant's story of delivery of possession by the plaintiffs also appear to us against the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business in relation to the facts of the case as articulated in section 114 of the Evidence Act. If the plaintiffs handed over the vacant possession of the suit property to the defendants voluntarily then why there should be “ভাংচুর” as deposed by P.W.3 and evident from exhibits 16, 17 and 18 series. Had such a huge amount been paid as a. prize for the compromise then it would have been written in a form of document signed by both the parties and duly witnessed by the witnesses stating in detail the terms of compromise and the fact of voluntary delivery of possession. And what prevented the defendants to take step to file a compromise application in the suit to dispose of the same as per terms of the compromise. We have seen the alleged writing of Mr. Abdul Majid as to the receipt of taka 16,60,000/00 allegedly paid to him by the defendants as a settlement to leave the suit property as incorporated in the additional paper book. It is to be noted that original money receipt was not filed but from the evidence of D.W.1 it appeared that the same was written on the pad of Hajee Selim local member of the parliament. Though a photostat copy of the same was allegedly filed when D.W.1 was examined, we could not find out the same from the record. However, the said writing is as under: 

 43. The very writing as relied upon by the defendants as a proof of their payment of taka 16,60,000/00 to the plaintiffs appeared to us shocking and repulsive. It is unbelievable that when the bailiff from the Court failed to deliver possession of the suit property due to the resistance put by the plaintiffs they would hand over vacant possession of the same to the defendants on the basis of a mere money receipt written on a pad of a local member of the parliament; and that to in four lines having no reference to the suit property and the names of the parties. None of the persons who were allegedly present in the salish including the local member of the parliament Hajee Selim and the local Ward Commissioner was examined in court. What business the local member of the parliament had to meddle in the matter when both the suit and the execution case were pending in Court. Further, from the evidence of the D.W.S it is apparent that the alleged salish was held only on one date, that is, on 30.09.97, if that be so, how is that on the same sitting such a huge amount could be arranged and given by the defendants. How did they know that there would be a settlement on that very date and they would be required to pay the said amount. How is that in the alleged money receipt Abdul Majid put his signature on 30.09.97, whereas defendant No. 2 put his signature on 05.10.97. Moreno, if possession of the suit property was delivered voluntarily as claimed by the defendants then there must be a paper showing delivery of possession by the plaintiffs or their father executed in favour of the defendants. In this regard it is very pertinent to state that after the plaintiffs failed to resist the proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980 by filing an application under Order XXI, rule 99 of the Code they filed an application in the suit on 28.11.94 for temporary injunction praying for restraining the defendants from evicting them from the suit property till disposal of the suit. On the said application a notice was issued upon the defendants asking them to show cause within 10 (ten) days as to why an order of temporary injunction as prayed for shall not be granted. As the said application for temporary injunction could not be heard and the defendants were taking desperate attempt to dispossess them the plain-tiffs on 14.09.97 filed an application under section 151 of the Code praying for an order of temporary injunction with a prayer for ad-interim injunction so that they could not be evicted through the proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980. Copy of the said application was duly served upon the learned Advocate of the defendants. The court below fixed the said application for hearing on the next date, that is, on 07.10.97. In the meantime the plaintiffs were evicted on 16.09.97 and the reason for such action by the defendants is obvious. P.W.1, categorically asserted the said facts in his deposition but he was not cross-examined on the said facts. The fact of forcible dispossession is also borne out from the photographs taken from the suit property after the eviction and exhibit 18 series which show that the structures on the suit property were damaged by resorting to vandalism. D.W.1 also admitted that he did not protest the news item published in the two dailies, namely, the Bhorer Kagaz and the Inquilab in that respect. From the evidence as discussed hereinbefore, it appeared to us that the defendants by taking law in their own hands dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit property forcibly just to frustrate the result of the suit which is very much deplorable and shocking and if such action of the defendants is countenanced to that would bring the whole legal system of dispensation of justice through court into jeopardy. 

 44. The fact that there was a one storied building, 10 (ten) family rooms and 13 (thirteen) shops in the suit property and after taking possession of the suit land those were demolished are also admitted by the D.W.S apart from the evidence of the p. w. s particularly,P.W.3, an independent and disinterested witness as already discussed hereinbefore. Therefore, we find no reason to disbelieve plaintiffs case that because of their forcible dispossession from the suit property by the defendants on 16.09.97 and then demolition of the 10 (ten) family quarters and 13 (thirteen) shop rooms they were deprived of monthly rent from the tenants and so they were entitled to get the mesne profit as decreed by the court below.

full_judgment:
10. Mr Ahmed then submits that Taka 1,06,48,600 which was alleged to have been recovered from his house was shown in his wealth statement. The father-in-law of the appellant sworn an affidavit before the notary public at New York declaring that he gave approximately Taka 1,61,14,000 and gold ornaments to the appellant and his wife to purchase land, for construction of building etc. 125 bhoris of gold ornaments was also mentioned in the statement and shown in the tax return of 1990-91, out of which 25 bhoris were of his own. He received the rest from his mother-in-law, sister-in-law and brother-in-law. Taka 47,586 in the savings account and Taka 6,44,114 in account of fixed deposit in Janata Bank, Barisal Corporate Branch was duly shown in the return. Taka 20,321.88 in account No. 512 maintained with United Commercial Bank, Barisal Branch was also shown in the statement which was admitted by PW 46. Taka (5+5.10) 10 lac in another account of fixed deposit maintained with Standard Charter Bank has been proved by PW 43. Savings Certificate of Taka 1,11,500 in Patuakhali post office, furniture of his residence worth Taka 2,21,000 and electronic goods of Taka 7,05,600 was mentioned in his wealth statement. 7.5 kathas of land belongs to the appellant at Purbachal, Sector- 2, as stated in the statement has also been admitted by PW 50; 5 kathas of land of sector- 10, Uttara is yet to be partitioned; 1762 square feet of land in the name of Mohsenara and her mother; a six storied building at 96/4/B Moneswar Road, Jigatola, were yet to be partitioned, also mentioned and shown in his tax return. The Commission did not issue any notice upon his wife, father-in-law and brother-in-law. The Investigating Officer did not investigate into the original ownership of the ornaments. PW 8 admitted in the cross-examination that he had no warrant with him at the time of raiding the appellant's houses. Them was no provision to inquire the cases of ACC by the police, but the Investigating Officer made inquiry by the police and the police within a day inquired the 50 addresses of the relatives of his wife, which was absurd and not believable. The appellant in the wealth statement gave the approximate value of his properties, but the 10 treated the same as untrue. It was impossible for him to write the correct figure in his statement of wealth from inside the Jail. The income tax returns were not submitted as evidence during trial. The informant admitted in his evidence that the appellant told him that he obtained the property from his father-in-law. His wife failed to show any documents as the law enforcing agency took all the documents at the time of raiding his house. The Investigating Officer did not visit all the places where the convict served. Some materials were seized from his house on the basis of a GD entry and subsequently the case was filed by the ACC, and, as such, the alamots and seized articles cannot be taken into consideration as prosecution materials according to the provisions of law. Relying on the cases of Anti-Corruption Commission vs Shamima Begum, 60 DLR (AD) 277; Anti-Corruption Commission vs Nargis Begum, 62 DLR (AD) 279 and the Anti-Corruption Commission vs Mohiuddin Khan Alomgir, 62 DLR (AD) 290, Mr Ahmed further submits that a notice must allow a reasonable time to check-up the details of the assets of a person, if necessary, on examination of his records and after consultation with his lawyers and others concerned persons. Section 26 certainly does not envisage a notice upon a person who is in detention. The person concerned most be afforded a fair and reasonable opportunity to respond to the notice, otherwise, it is no notice in the eye of law. A notice under section 26 of the Ain, 2004 to a detenu away from his hearth and home, cannot be said to be fair and bonafide exercise of power. By pointing out the evidence of some prosecution witnesses, the learned Advocate submits that the prosecution by adducing the oral and documentary evidence failed to prove the charge against the appellant beyond all reasonable doubt, and, as such, he is entitled to be acquitted.

PW 48 Bidip Ranjan Saha, a Sub-Divisional Engineer, deposed that in presence of a Magistrate 1st class and the Assistant Director of ACC and others he determined the value of electrical and electronic goods In different items and ascertained value at Taka 7,05,600. He proved the statement Exhibit-29, his signatures-29/5 and 29 /5(Ka)-5 (Ga). In the cross-examination he replied that he did not know when the goods were purchased, but he saw the brand name of those. The procedure for determining the value has been mentioned in the statement. He did not call for any one from adjacent houses, but the forest guards were present. 

 62. PW 49 Md. Abdul Mannan, a Sub-Assistant Engineer of Public Works, deposed that on 2-10-2007 the high officials of their Department and the ACC officials determined the value of goods of accused's house and submitted a report. He proved the report Exhibit-29, his signatures- 29/5 (Kha)-(Cha). In the cross-examination he replied that he did not know when the goods were purchased. The statement was prepared according to the standard rate of 2002. 

 65. PW 52 Rafiqul Islam, a public witness and a tenant of a house near to the house of the accused, deposed that on 2-10-2007 the lock of the house was broken in presence of a Magistrate and the ACC personnel . He proved the statement Exhibit-28, his signature-28/8. In the cross-examination he replied that he was a tenant beside that house. The house was of 2 units and the flat was of Shaleha Begum whose husband resided abroad. 

 66. PW 53 Alamgir Hossain, a public witness, deposed that on 2-10-2007 a Magistrate, police and officials of ACC broke the lock of the house at Moneswar road and prepared the statement. He proved the statement Exhibit-41. In the cross-examination he replied that his brother used to reside at the 4th floor of the house. He did not know the person to whom his brother paid rent. 

 (I) Magistrate and Polices:  PW 2 Rina Saha, a Sub-Inspector of police recorded the FIR. PW 3 Md Golam Haider was the Jail Super, forwarded the statement of wealth to the ACC. PW 7 Md Kamruzzaman was a Sub-Inspector who verified the addresses of 50 persons and submitted the report. PW 8 Md Mijanur Rahman, a Sub-Inspector of police, recovered the money and dollar from the government staff quarter allotted to the appellant. PW 9 Md. Masudur Rahman, another Sub-Inspector of police recovered the cash money, gold ornaments and foreign currency from his quarter. PW 10 Md. Anwar Hossein, a Sub-Inspector, who searched the house of the appellant proved the materials recovered from the quarter. PW 31 Md. Ehteshamul Haque, was the Magistrate of 1st Class. In his presence the electronic goods and furniture were seized from the houses of the accused. 

 77. Appellant Osman Goni did not show Taka 6,44,114 kept against fixed deposit No. 419533/2036 in Janata Bank, Corporate Branch, Barisal in his wealth statement and the said deposit has been proved by PWs 18 and 19, two officers of the said bank. Seizure list of the same has been proved as Exhibit-17 and documents as Material Exhibit-VII. The said amount was not denied by the appellant in the cross-examination of those PWs. The appellant in the wealth statement did also not show the amount of Taka 3,05,766.02 kept against Savings Account No. 181571648/01 in Standard Chartered Bank, Khulna Branch, which was substantiated by the evidence of PW 54, the investigating officer vide seizure list, Exhibit-21 and Material Exhibit-XI The amount was subsequently transferred from the account of Osman Goni to the joint account in their name. PW 27 proved the said joint account. The same was also not denied by the appellant in the cross-examination. The other materials recovered from the house of the appellant worth Taka 7,05,600 was proved by PW 38 AKM Ruhul Amin a 1st Class Magistrate, PW 45 Sree Gopal Chandra Roy, PW 54 the investigating officer, PW 48 Bidip Ranjan Saha Roy, PW 49 Md. Abdul Mannan and PW 47 Md. Shakhawat Hossain and by Exhibit-29. But no specific suggestion was put to those witnesses that he was not the owner of those articles. The appellant also did not mention the value of those goods in his wealth statement and thus suppressed it. The value of the furniture of his houses was ascertained at Taka 2,21,000 and has been proved by PW 35 Md. Ahsan Aziz and PW 36 Kazi Mahbubul Hoque and they were not challenged to that effect by the defense. Thus the appellant also suppressed the value of the furniture. Although he mentioned in his wealth statement that he had Taka 1 (one) crore in his home but it has been proved by the evidence of PW 8 Md. Mijanur Rahaman a sub-Inspector, PW 11 Md. Ashrafuzzaman, PW 9 Md. Masudur Rahman and Exhibit-14 and Material Exhibit-IV that they recovered cash Taka 1,06,84,600 in total from his house and thus he suppressed Taka 6,84,600 in his statement. In addition he suppressed some other Bank statements regarding his wealth maintained in different banks in Dhaka, Barisal and Khulna. In view of the above, the prosecution has been able to prove that the appellant suppressed wealth of Taka 1,02,53,584.87 in his statement for which he is liable to be convicted under section 26(2) of the Ain, 2004. 

 78. Let us see whether the prosecution has been able to prove that the appellant acquired wealth beyond his legal source of income. It is already found that Taka 1,06,84,600 was seized and recovered from the house of the appellant. He failed to show any reasonable and acceptable explanation about the source of such huge money. Although he disclosed that the money so recovered was his own money, but no such declaration was made in his income tax return. The appellant in his statement of wealth disclosed that the house on 5 kathas of land at Moneswar Road was purchased in the name of his wife and mother-in-law at the cost of Taka 12 lac and the estimated value of the building was at Taka 50 lac, but the prosecution by the evidence of PW 13 proved the seized docu Ment Exhibit-40 and found the value of it at Taka 1,50,000 purchased by his mother-in-law and gifted it to accused Mohsenara Goni. In the income tax return the total value of it was shown as Taka 62,00,000 but the concerned engineers, i.e., PWs 41 and 42 ascertained the value of it at Taka 1,01,17,793 out of which 50% was gifted to Mohsenara was valid, but remaining 50% of the same was not donated to her as evident from Exhibit-40 and Material Exhibit-XVIII which has been proved by the evidence of PW 13 and the some was not denied by the appellant by cross-examination, and, as such, the gift of 50% from his mother-in-law was false. According to the income tax file of accused Mohsenara Goni Exhibit-10, proved by PW 25 Shahjahan Ali, Additional Assistant Commissioner of Taxes, she received gift from 50 persons, Taka 1,85,000 from each, i.e., totally of Taka 92,50,000 and US $ 19000, but in the enquiry the story of gift was found false. PW 7 SI Kamruuaman verified the addresses and found no existence of the persons and submitted the report vide Exhibit-10. The value ascertained by the engineers of the concerned department was at the scheduled rate applicable for the relevant time, which cannot be disbelieved without any contrary evidence and, as such, the cost of construction and the value of land amounting to Taka 1,03,17,793 is also beyond his legal source of income. The investigating officer also recovered 155 bhoris of gold from the locker of Standard Chartered Bank, out of which the appellant showed in his income tax return Taka 40,000, which is equivalent to the value of 20 bhoris, but failed to show the source of the ornaments of remaining 270 bhoris, and, as such, those are also beyond his legal source of income. The prosecution by the evidence of PWs 8,12 and 13 proved the value of the gold as ascertained. The prosecution also proved that the value of 5 khthas of land in the name of Mohsenara Goni at Sector-10, Uttara although was shown at Taka 25,00,000, but PW 33 Nurul Islam Howlader by the oral evidence proved that he paid Taka 30,00,000 for the said land and thus he suppressed Taka 5 lac in the 'wealth statement, which was also beyond his legal source of income. The prosecution also proved keeping of Taka 15,000 in the savings account of United Commercial Bank, Barisal and Taka 25 lac in their joint names in Agrani Bank, Ray Shaheb Bazar Branch by the oral evidence PW 46 Md Abdul Hai, OW 54 SM Akhtar Hamid Bhuyan and PW 29 Md Abdus Samad and also by Exhibit-23 and Material Exhibit-XII. Taka 22,62,778.88 kept in the Standard Chartered Bank, Dhanmondi branch in their joint names was proved by the evidence of PW 43 and PW 54 and also by Material Exhibits-XIV and XV . The amount of Taka 20 lac in the name of accused Mohsenara Goni in Royer Bazar Branch of Agrani Bank was proved by the evidence PW 20 and by Material Exhibit-VIII Fixed deposit of Taka 20 lac in the name of Mohsenara Goni was proved by PW 22 and PW 23 and vide Material Exhibit-IX series. The appellant although in the wealth statement stated that they had fixed deposit of Taka 30,00,000 in their joint names, but during investigation Taka 41,11,500 was found in those accounts which has been proved by Material Exhibit-XIII and Exhibit-25. 

 79. It further appears that the appellant was a Government servant and his wife was a simple housewife. The appellant joined the service in 1979 and during his tenure till 2007 he totally withdrew Taka 28,48,650.92 and paid tax by submitting returns. In the tax return submitted in 2006 (Material Exhibit-VI) he showed his total wealth of Taka 16,93,037/-. His wife Mohsenara Goni (absconding) was a housewife and she had shown her wealth in her tax file on account of ornaments, furniture, 50% of the land measuring 1762 sq. feet at Moneswar Road, 0.24 acres of land at Dakshin Khan and 3 kathas of land at Uttara from her father. But on consideration of the evidence it appears that the appellant had wealth of immovable property of Taka 13,12,500 and movable property of Taka 1,34,34,704, i.e., in total Taka 1,47,47,204+130 bhoris gold ornaments. On the other hand the movable and immovable property belonged to his wife was of Taka (1,36,52,729 + 1,05,64,448.41) = 2,42,17, 241.41 and in their joint names of taka 76,29,139.06+150 bhoris of gold. Totally they hold wealth of Taka 4,65,93,584.47+290 bhoris of gold, i.e., totally take 5,16,11,991.31 including gold. The appellant thus excluding his legal income illegally acquired wealth of Taka (5,16,11,991.31-19,30,527) = 4,96,81,464.31 which was beyond his legal source of income and his wife also abetted in acquiring and keeping the wealth in her name and possession. The appellant failed to make out a believable case by the evident of 2 DWs that the wealth in the name of his wife, was obtained from her father and other relatives. The above defense has been proved false by the evidence of prosecution witnesses. The appellant being a Government servant who withdrew fixed salary and had no paternal property of his own, as per income tax return, cannot be the owner and possessor of such huge wealth as found. The explanation given in the statement and the suggestions offered to the prosecution witnesses during cross-examination do not show that it was proportionate to his legal source of income, and, as such, the appellant committed the offence under section 27(1) of the Ain, 2004. In the above premises we hold that the prosecution witnesses by oral and documentary evidence successfully proved that the wealth acquired by the appellant was quite disproportionate to his legal and known source of income. 

 80. Let us see whether the property beyond the legal source of income should be confiscated. Most of the property of the appellant Osman Goni and in his wife's name found by the investigating officer and proved by the prosecution witnesses to be the property acquired by the appellant by illegal means beyond his known and legal sources of income. Convict Mohsenara Goni being a house wife cannot be the owner of the wealth as described and as found and proved by the witnesses, and, as such, the huge wealth which is beyond the legal source of income must be confiscated in favour of the state. So, the properties as described in the ordering portion of the impugned judgment, has rightly been confiscated by the Special Judge keeping out the properties from the list which proved to be acquired by his legal income. The trial Court confiscated the property relying on the evidence and materials on record, and, as such, we do not find any illegality in confiscation of the property.
