 746. The Third learned Judge disbelieved PW 60 who proved Exhibits 10/5, 35, 10/5/A about the absorption and deployment of the accused persons in the Foreign Embassies on the reasonings that this absorption could not be taken as reward of their involvement in the carnage of 15th August and that no adverse presumption could be drawn against the accused by reason of such employment. The Third learned Judge erred in law in failing to consider that there is uncontroverted evidence on record that after Ziaur Rahman assuming power from Khandaker Mustaque Ahmed absorbed their services in the Foreign Ministry and posted most of the accused persons at different Embassies of Bangladesh and that unless they were not involved in the occurrence, there was no reason for their being absorbed in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, some of them were removed officers. PWs 44 and 47 proved that they were absorbed by General Ziaur Rahman after he came to power on 7th March 1975 and that they left the country on the evening of 3rd March when Khondker Mustaque Ahmed was dethroned by Khaled Mosharraf. The accused did not deny those facts. There is nexus between the accused persons' fleeing away from the country on 3rd November and their absorption in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs after Ziaur Rahman assumed power on 7th November, and in the intervening period Khaled Mosharraf was in power. The Third learned Judge without properly appreciating the evidence of PWs 44, 45 and 47 disbelieved PW 60. If the evidence of those witnesses are read together no inference could be drawn other than that the killers of Bangabandhu were rewarded by General Ziaur Rahman after he assumed power on 7th November, 1975. 

 747. The evidence of these witnesses proved that the appellants and other co-accused, as part of their premeditated plan arranged night parade and then came out from the cantonment with their troops armed with tanks, cannons and other arms, to the house of Bangabandhu situated at Road No. 32, and killed Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and family members, and after the killing they compelled the Chiefs of Army, Navy and Air Force to express their allegiance of the killing and to accept Khondker Mustaque Ahmed as the President of the country. Thereafter they stayed at Bangabhaban, guarded Khondker Mustaque Ahmed and the Radio Station so that anybody could topple him. They attended the oath taking ceremonies of the President and the Cabinet although they were not supposed to be present at such national ceremonies. Lieutenant Colonel Shahriar Rashid Khan was a removed officer but he was seen at the night parade and then at the Radio Station in the early hours of 15th August. He was also found present at Bangabhaban with other accused at the state ceremony after the carnage. Some of the accused arranged for burying the dead bodies. All these circumstances sufficiently proved that they were involved in the killing of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and other members of his family. These conducts of the accused persons are relevant under section 8 of the Evidence Act and may be taken as corroborative evidence for furnishing further proof of their guilt. These previous and subsequent conducts of the accused appellants played an important part in the determination of their guilt and could be taken as circumstantial evidence. All these evidence sufficiently proved beyond doubt that these appellants and other convicts were involved in the carnage of 15th August 1975, and the learned Judges of the High Court Division were perfectly justified in finding them guilty of the charges and accepting the death reference. 

 753. Let us now apply these principles to the facts of the present case. As observed above, these appellants attended in the night parade, and it was organised to fulfil and implement their object. They deployed jawans under the command of the officers at different key points such as, Rakhibahani headquarter, BDR headquarter, Radio Station, Minto Road. and Road No. 32. This deployment of army at Rakhibahini headquarter gate and BDR gate was a part of their preconcerted plan to prevent these paramilitary forces if they came forward for protecting the President on getting any information for help. The deployment at the Radio Station was for preventing any person on behalf of the then Government to seek any help from the army, navy, air force, paramilitary forces, political activists or from other sources. The deployment at Minto Road was also to prevent the Ministers to mobilise the public or any other force for the protection of the President. The existence of the conspiracy and its objects have to be inferred from the circumstances and the conduct of the accused. The principles governing circumstances so proved must form a chain of events from which the only irresistible conclusion about the guilt of the accused can safely be drawn and on the hypothesis against the guilt is possible [1977 SCC (Cri) 1004]. The circumstances before, during and after the occurrence can be proved to decide about the complicity of  the. accused .In Nalini case [(1999)5 SCC 253] Wadha, J pointed out the criminal responsibility for a conspiracy requires more or less passive attitude towards an existing conspiracy. Learned Judge set out the legal position as under: 

 754. They proved that Lieutenant Colonel Mohiuddin (artillery) was deputed with cannons at Kalabagan play ground near road No. 32, Lieutenant Colonel Sultan Shahriar Rashid Khan was deputed at the Radio Station, Lieutenant Colonel Faruque Rahman took the overall responsibility for checking Rakhibahani and the Bangabandhu's house, Major Mohiuddin (lancer), Major Bazlul Huda, Major Noor with some troops were given the task of implementing the main object the killing of the President and other members of his family, 

 759. These views have been approved in Ramaswami Ayyangar s case (AIR 1976 SC 2027) as under: 

 762.The learned second Judge also considered the case of Rasool Bux vs State 22 DLR (SC) 297, in which case the views taken in Barendra Ghosh have been approved. In that case accused Lal Bux and Rasul Bux abducted Mst Roshna from the house of her father, if necessary, by the use of force. They were both armed with deadly weapons. When their presence was discovered in the Courtyard they abandoned their original plan but were nevertheless determined to escape, if necessary by use of weapons carried by them'. 

 "Criminal conspiracy postulates an agreement between two or more persons to do, or cause to be done, an illegal act or an act which is not illegal, by illegal means. It differs from other offences in that mere agreement is made an offence even if no step is taken to carry out that agreement. Though there is close association of conspiracy with incitement and abetment the substantive offence of criminal conspiracy is somewhat wider in amplitude than abetment by conspiracy as contemplated its very nature is generally hatched in secret. It is, therefore, extremely rare that direct evidence in proof of conspiracy can be forthcoming from wholly disinterested quarters or from utter strangers. But, like other offences criminal conspiracy can be proved by circumstantial evidence. Indeed, in most cases proof of conspiracy is largely inferential though the inference must be founded on solid facts. Surrounding circumstances and antecedent and subsequent conduct, among other factors, constitute relevant material. In fact, because of the difficulties in having direct evidence of criminal conspiracy, once reasonable ground is shown for believing that two or more persons have conspired to commit an offence then anything, done by any- one of them in reference to their common intention after the same is entertained becomes according to the law of Evidence, relevant for proving both conspiracy and the offences comitted pursuant thereto. 

 778. In a later case in Suresh Chandra Bahri vs Gurbachan Singh AIR 1994 S.C 2420, Suresh Bahri Bachan and Raj Pal Sharma were convicted under section 302 of the Penal Code-they were also convicted under sections 302/120B for committing murder of three persons in pursuance of the offence of criminal conspiracy. Two of them were also convicted under section 201 for causing disappearance of evidence. The Patna High Court maintained the sentence of death. In the Supreme Court it was argued that there is no direct and legal evidence against Gurbachan and Raj Pal for their involvement in the conspiracy and that there is no evidence against Gurbachan about his participation in the crime. In the context of the matter, the Supreme Court while maintaining the conviction under sections 302/120B of the accused on the basis of circumstantial evidence considered whether such conviction can be given in pursuance of criminal conspiracy. It is said that the provisions of section 120A of the Penal Code defines criminal conspiracy. It provides that when two or more persons agree to do, or cause to be done (1) an illegal act, or (2) an act which is not illegal by illegal means, such agreement is designated a criminal conspiracy; provided that no agreement except an agreement to commit an offence shall amount to criminal conspiracy unless some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties to such agreement in pursuance thereof. Thus a cursory look to the provisions contained in section 120A reveal that a criminal conspiracy envisages an agreement between two or more persons to commit an illegal act or an act which by itself may not be illegal but the same is done or executed by illegal means. The essential ingredient of the offence of criminal conspiracy is the agreement to commit an offence. In a case where the agreement is for accomplishment of an act which by itself constitutes an offence, then in that event no overt act is necessary to be proved by the prosecution because in such a fact situation criminal conspiracy is established by proving such an agreement. In other words, where the conspiracy alleged is with regard to commission of a serious crime of the nature as contemplated in section 120B read with the proviso to sub- section (2) of section 120A, Penal Code, then in that event mere proof of an agreement between the accused for commission of such a crime alone is enough to bring about a conviction under section 120B and the proof of any overt act by the accused or by anyone of them would not be necessary. Faizan Uddin, J on consideration of almost all earlier decisions on the point argued as under: 

 779. Therefore, in order to constitute the offence of conspiracy, there must first be a combining together of two or more persons in the conspiracy; secondly, an act or illegal omission must take place in pursuance of that conspiracy in order to the doing of that thing. It is not necessary that the abettor should concert the offence with the person who commits it. It is sufficient if he engages in the conspiracy in pursuance of which the offence is committed. Therefore, I find that each conspirator plays his separate part in one integrated and united effort to achieve the common purpose. The cumulative effect of the proved circumstances should be taken into account in determining the guilt of the accused rather than adopting an isolated approach to each of the circumstances. Each one is aware that he has a part to play in a general conspiracy though he may not know all its secrets or the means by which the common purpose is to be accomplished. The common intention of the conspirators then is to work for the furtherance of the common design. Mr Abdur Razaque Khan finally argues that the act of Lieu ten-ant Colonel Sultan Shahriar Rashid Khan's attracts an offence of abetment of murder punishable under section 109 of the Penal Code. In support of his contention, the learned Counsel has referred the cases of Md Shamsul Hoque vs State 20 DLR 540, Amor Kumar Takur vs State 40 DLR (AD) 147, Hazrat Ali vs State 44 DLR (AD)51 and Dharan Pal vs State of Haryana (1978) 4 SCC 440. Md Shamsul Hoque s case was decided following the case in AIR 1938 Mad 130, which was also followed in 8 DLR 48. It was observed in the Madras case that where an offence is alleged to have been committed by two or more persons, the person responsiblefor commission of the offence should be charged with the substantive offence, while the persons alleged to have abetted it by conspiracy should be charged with the offence of abetment under section 109. The views in AIR 1938 Mad 130 have been overruled in Kandimalla Subbaiah s case (AIR 1961 SC 1241 paras 7 and 8). The facts and the principles of law applicable in Amar Kumar Thakur s case are quite distinguishable. In that case the accused were charged for an offence punishable under sections 302/34, and this Court on sifting evidence-came to the conclusion that "the appellant Nos.2-4 had no intention of their own to cause the death of Nand alaI particularly when he was proceeding at their request to hold the mediation at that unearthly hour of the night." In Hazrat Ali's case, the Appellate Division on assessment of the evidence came to the conclusion that Hazrat Ali abetted the offence of the murder of Zahura Khatun and converted his conviction to 'one under sections 30211 09 from an 'offence of sections 302/34 In Dharam Pals case, it was observed that the existence or otherwise of the common intention depends upon the' facts and circumstances of each case, and in the absence of materials, "the companion or companions cannot justifiably be held guilty for every offence committed by the principal offender." These cases are quite distinguishable and' not applicable in this case. On an overall consideration of the evidence and the principles of law discussed above, I fully agree with the conclusion arrived by the High Court Division that the appellants and other convicts hatched up conspiracy to kill Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and the members of his family and accomplished their object by killing them and three other security personnel. In a case where the agreement is for accomplishment of an act which constitutes an offence, then if the prosecution fails to prove the overt act committed by each of the conspirators, the criminal conspiracy is established by proving such agreement and the proof of overt act by all the accused would not be necessary. In other words, in such situation it is not required that each and every accused who is a party to the conspiracy must do some overt act towards the fulfilment of the object of conspiracy. In this case, although an offence of murder has been committed in pursuance of conspiracy; the liability of the conspirators for the conspiracy cannot disappear. When specific act done by each of the accused have been established showing their common intention, they are admissible against each and every other accused. In the case of Nalini [(1999) 5 SCC 253] the accused persons were arraigned as members of the conspiracy to extirpate former Prime Minister of India Rajiv Gandhi. The accused persons were convicted under sections 302/120B of the Indian Penal Code. Their conviction was maintained by the Supreme Court. Similarly, in Kehar Singh s case, (AIR 1988 SC 1883), Kehar Singh, Balbir Singh and Sat want Singh were charged under section 302 read with section 120B and other offences for the assassination of Smt. Indira Gandhi, the Prime Minister of India by her security guards. The conviction of the two accused was maintained by the Supreme Court. In Suresh Chandra Bahris case (AIR 1994 SC 2420) the Supreme Court of India maintained the conviction of three accused under sections 302/ 120B of the Penal Code. On consideration of the evidence on record and the principles of law discussed above, I am of the view that the proper conviction of the appellants Lieutenant Coloriel Syed Faruque Rahman, Lieutenant Colonel. Mohiuddin Ahmed (Artillery), Major AKM Mohiuddin Ahmed and Major Bazlul Huda would have been under section 302 read with section 120B and section 34 of the Penal Code instead of sections 302/34 and section 120B of the Penal Code, and that of Lieutenant Colonel Sultan Shahriar Rashid Khan under sections 302/120B of the Penal Code. Their conviction is modified accordingly.Confirmation of sentence. 

 794. In Machhi Singh vs State of Punjab, AIR J 983 SC 957, after considering Jagmohan's case and some other cases on the point of sentence, the Supreme Court of India classified the cases in which death penalty may be imposed as follows: "When the victim of murder is (a) an innocent child who could not have or has not proved even an excuse, much less a provocation, for murder, (b) a helpless woman or a person rendered helpless by old age or infirmity, (c) when the victim is a person vis-a-vis whom the murderer is in a position of domination or trust, (d) when the victim is a public figure generally loved and respected by the community for the services rendered by him and the murder is commit- ted for political or similar reasons other than personal reasons." 

 799. There is no denial of the 'fact the appellants and other accused persons not only killed the sitting President of the country, they killed the entire family. The victim, the then President, who had sacrificed his life for the cause of the people his struggle for the just and the democratic rights of the people of the country was marked by extraordinary patriotism. The liberation struggle of Bangladesh from the treacherous occupation of the marauding military ruler of Pakistan, was a rare example of a patriot was fought by the people from inside and outside under order of Bangabandhu which was clearly proclaimed in a historic public meeting on 7th March 1971. This historic speech not only proclaimed guidelines for action but also inspired the deep determination of the people to fight for the independence. He was determined on the creation of independent Bangladesh and advanced strategically through the Six-Point chatter of demands. The six points were later on led to one point-the independence from which Bangabandhu did not retract. Consequently we had achieved our independence. The accused persons brutally killed such a leader who is none but the Father of the Nation. They even did not spare a child, son of the President who was below 10 years age. They killed him in such a brutal manner the nation was shocked and dumbfounded. There was no explanation why they also killed three women. They committed the crime against humanity by killing a child and three innocent women who were unarmed. They eliminated almost the entire family who were found in the house. There is no explanation on the side of the accused as to why they killed these innocent persons. The acts of the accused was so barbarous which could only be compared with orgies. The accused persons by their barbarous act proved that the object of the conspiracy was not to oust the President from power, but their object was to eliminate the entire family and it was an act of exceptional depravity on the part of the accused persons, an unparalleled act in the annals of crime committed in the country. Although there is no evidence against all the accused persons of directly participating in the carnage but it should be borne in mind that for the killing of the sitting President, all the accused persons with a view to attainment of the object played different roles. Without jointly operating in concert the criminal object could not have been executed. It was not possible to bring about the result of the criminal object without support of all. In view of the matter, all the conspirators who actually participated, acted in the crime do not deserve any leniency in the matter of sentence. On consideration of the brutality in the commission of the offence, the appellants and other co-accused do not deserve any leniency in the matter of sentence. The appellants failed to make out a case of mitigating circumstance to commute their sentence.

parties:
Raqib Sheikh (Md) ------ Convict-Appellant 
vs 
State ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
2. Short prosecution case is that on 12-8-1928 appellant Raqib without the consent of his wife, deceased Anowara with intent to cause her miscarriage got a piece of root of plant placed in her vagina by absconding convict Ful Banu resulting in profuse bleeding from her private parts and miscarriage. Then on 13-8-1998 he got his wife admitted into Terakhada Upazila Health Complex where she died on 14-8-1997 at 5-10 AM due to haemorrhage. 

 7. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant, having taken us through the impugned judgment and order, the First Information Report, the charge, the, depositions of the prosecution and defence witnesses and other materials on record makes his submission supporting the appeal and assailing the impugned judgment and order. He submits that the prosecution failed to prove the charge against the appellant beyond all reasonable doubt. There is no convincing evidence that at the instance of the appellant miscarriage of his deceased wife was done which resulted in her death. None of the prosecution witnesses had direct knowledge that the appellant with intent to cause miscarriage of his deceased wife got a root of plant placed in her uterus by absconding convict Ful Banu. The evidence of PW 5 shows that the deceased had consent in causing her miscarriage. The Court below wrongly convicted and sentenced the appellant under section 314 of Penal Code, who is entitled to get acquittal. 

 8. Mr Md Faisal Hossain Khan, the learned Deputy Attorney-General with Mrs Parvin Hannan, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent, opposes the appeal supporting the impugned judgment and order. He submits that by the uncontroverted evidence of PW 9, the father of the deceased, it is well proved that the appellant without the consent of his deceased wife with intent to cause her miscarriage got herb placed in the uterus of the deceased by absconding convict Ful Banu and thereby caused abortion, which resulted in her death. The defence taken is after thought and got up and also not proved. Such defence case had not been suggested in cross- examination to the PWs. At last stage of the trial a new story was advanced through the mouths of the DWs. Even the appellant at the time of examination under: section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not disclose such defence case. Such belated defence case is doubtful. The Court below rightly and legally convicted the appellant. Therefore, there is no ground for interference with the impugned judgment and order. 

 10. PW 1 and PW 8 SI Mosharraf  Hossain, the informant and the investigating officer of the present case and also the investigating officer of the unnatural death case, deposed that on 14-8-1997, while he was attached to Terakhada Police Station as sr of Police he received a report from Dr Muniruzzaman, medical officer of Terakhada Upazila Health Complex, to the effect that a woman named Anowara Begum died in the hospital due to hemorrhage. On the basis of that information he recorded Terakhada Police Station UD Case No. 14 of 1997 dated 14-8-1997 and himself took up investigation of the case. He rushed to Terakhada Upazila Health Complex taking constable Faruque Hossain with him, where in presence of the witnesses and the nurse on duty made inquest of the dead-body of the deceased as identified by PW 9, the father of the deceased. At that time the nurse recovered a piece of root of plant from the uterus of the dead body and gave the same to him, which he seized under a seizure list. Then for ascertaining cause of death he sent the dead body of the deceased to the morgue for post mortem examination through constable Faruque Hossain. He came to know from the post mortem examination report .that the deceased died due to haemorrhage resulting from abortion. Then he ending the UD Case lodged First Information Report against the appellant and absconding convict Ful Banu accusing them for causing her miscarriage, which resulted in her death. He proved the First Information Report written by him which was marked as Exhibit 1. Sayed Ahmed, the officer-in-charge of the police station, on receipt of his written First Information Report recorded the case filling up prescribed First Information Report form. He arrested the appellant from his house under section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in connection with the UD case. When he (PW 1) went to the hospital the appellant was not present there. On investigation he found that miscarriage was done against the will of the deceased. He further stated that he visited the place of occurrence, prepared sketch map, Exhibit 8 with separate index, Exhibit 9, recorded the statements of the witnesses under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and then after completion of investigation submitted charge-sheet against the appellant and absconding convict Ful Banu. 

 11. PW 2 Dr FM Muniruzzaman deposed that while he was medical officer of Terakhada Upazila Health Complex on 14-8-1997 at 5-10. AM a patient named Anowara Begum, aged nineteen years, wife of Sheikh Raqib, suffering from septicemia resulting from critical abortion, died in the hospital. He informed such fact to the officer-in-charge of Terakhada Police Station in writing. He proved his report, which was marked as Exhibit 3. In cross- examination he stated that septicemia is an infectious disease. It might be caused due to external or internal infection. So far he could remember the deceased was admitted "in the hospital by her parents and mother-in-law, but that fact he did not mention in his report given to the police station. Haemorrhage might be caused due to receipt of any injury. He knew nothing about abortion of the deceased. At the relevant time he was not present. 

 14. PW 5 Taslima Khatun deposed that on 13- 8-1997 she was on duty at Terakhada Upazila Health Complex as a nurse. On that date deceased her husband accused Raqib. Doctor Muniruzzaman (PW 2) asked her to see the patient. Accordingly, she went to the patient, who on her query disclosed that she was suffering on severe bleeding with pain. She reported it to the doctor, who instructed her to give treatment to the patient. On her query the deceased told her that there was a piece of root of a plant in her uterus. Then she removed that root of plant therefrom. Thereafter, the deceased due to profuse bleeding died. She identified that piece of root of plant in the Court, which was marked as Material Exhibit 1. She further said that the piece of root of plant was seized by the police under a seizure list, wherein she put her signature as a witness. She gave the piece of root of plant to the Daroga at about 4-00 PM. The seizure list was. marked as Exhibit 5. In cross-examination, she stated that she gave treatment to deceased Anowara Begum as instructed by the doctor. The deceased was in full sense, when she was brought to the hospital. She enquired to the deceased who placed the root of plant in her uterus. The deceased replied that she did not want a child at that time. She (deceased) suppressed the name of the man who penetrated the root of plant in her uterus. This witness (PW 5) again said that the deceased told her that she was not willing to carry the child. She (PW 5) did not enquire to the deceased whether her husband penetrated the root of plant in her vagina. This witness volunteered that it was not possible on the part of the deceased herself to penetrate the root in her vagina. 

 17. PW 9 Mohammad Ali, the father of the deceased, identifying his signature in the inquest report said that inquest of the dead body of the deceased was made in his presence in the hospital by the Daroga on 14-8-1997 at 3-00/4-00 PM. Anowara told him that her husband accused Raqib taking her to the house of accused Ful Banu got a herb placed in her uterus. He further said that a piece of root of plant, measuring 8/9 fingers in length, was recovered from the uterus of Anowara in his presence. Then Anowara died. Accused Raqib put pressure on Anowara, who was not willing to miscarriage her first conception. The appellant forcibly caused the miscarriage. In cross- examination he stated that before marriage there was affair between accused Raqib and the deceased. Raqib, his parents and he (PW 9) got the deceased admitted in the hospital. He volunteered that he deposed the truth. He never told lie. Accused Raqib compelled the deceased to use the herb. 

 18. PW 10 Kawsar Chowdhury deposed that while he was sitting beside the nurse in the hospital, a Daroga seized a piece of root of plant from nurse Taslima on 14-8-1997 at 4-00 PM. He put his signature in the seizure list, Exhibit 5. He identified his signature in the seizure list. He also identified a piece of root of the plant, Material Exhibit I, seized by the Daroga in his presence. Deceased Anowara was the wife of accused Raqib. 

 22. These are all of the material evidence adduced by both the parties, on consideration of which we find that undisputedly on 14-8-1997 at 5-10 AM deceased Anowara died at Terakhada Upazila Health Complex, where she was under treatment of profuse bleeding from her private parts. On that very days PW 2, a medical officer attached to that hospital, in writing informed Terakhada Police that Anowara, a patient, under treatment in the hospital suffering from septicemia due to critical abortion died at 5-10 AM. On the basis of that report Unnatural Death Case No. 14 dated 14-8-1997 of Terakhada Police Station was recorded. PWs 1 and 8 the investigating officer of the UD case, going to Terakhada Upazila Health Complex made inquest of the dead body of deceased Anowara as identified by her father PW 9 Mohammad Ali and sent the same to the morgue for post mortem examination through PW 3 constable Faruque Hossain. PW 3 testified that he escorted the dead body of deceased Anowara to the morgue for post mortem examination and identified the same to the doctor. PW 6 testified that he held autopsy of the dead body of the deceased, Anowara brought and identified by PW 3. He found presence of clotted blood inside the vagina, perforation at the fundal region of uterus and presence of product of conception and clotted blood inside the uterus. He opined that death was due to shock and haemorrhage resulting from abortion, which was ante-mortem. Such evidence of the doctor as to the cause of death of the deceased had gone unchallenged. Moreover, such medical evidence as to cause of death does not suffer from any infirmity or inherent defect. Thus, it is well proved that abortion was the cause of death of the deceased. Now the question is whether such abortion which resulted in her death was natural, that is, act of God, or caused by any human. 

 23. PW 5, the nurse of the hospital where the deceased was under treatment at the time of her death, testified that on 13-8-1997 with profuse bleeding from the vagina the deceased was brought to the hospital by her accused-husband. On her query the deceased told her that there was a piece of root of plant placed in her uterus. She PW 5 then recovered the root of plant from her uterus. She handed over that piece of root of plant to PW 1, who seized the same. She identified the piece of root, Material Exhibit I, in the trial Court. PWs 1, 7 and 9 also supported recovery of the piece of root Material Exhibit 1 from the uterus of the deceased by PW 5. Thus it is proved that placing Material Exhibit I (a piece of root of plant) in the uterus abortion was caused. It was a human act. Someone placed the root of plant in the vagina of the deceased with intent to cause her miscarriage. We also find support of it from PW 7 who said that the appellant- husband told him that his deceased wife asked him to bring herbal medicine for causing miscarriage and asked him to take away her to accused Ful Banu for causing miscarriage. On 12-8-1997 a piece of root of pant was penetrated in her vagina. PW 9, the father of the deceased, also supported causing of miscarriage penetrating root of plant in the uterus. Thus it is established that someone caused abortion of the deceased which resulted in her death and an offence punishable under section 314 of the Penal Code was committed. 

 24. On careful examination, scrutiny and critical analysis of the evidence on record we find that there is no ocular evidence. No one of the prosecution witnesses saw the appellant to get the root of plant, material Exhibit 1, placed in the uterus of his deceased wife by absconding convict Ful Banu against the will of the deceased resulting in her miscarriage and ultimately causing her death. 

 25. PW 5 deposed that the appellant brought the deceased to the hospital. The deceased complained of severe bleeding from her private part. She further said that the deceased was brought to the hospital with full sense. She (deceased) told her that she was unwilling to carry child for the moment. She did not want baby. She suppressed the name of the person who placed the root of plant in her uterus. This witness also said that penetration of the root in the private part by the deceased herself was not possible. 

 26. PW 7 said that on 13-8-1997 at 10-00/10-30 AM he came to know that there was bleeding from the private parts of the deceased. Thereafter, he along with the appellant and his parents shifted the deceased to the hospital and got her admitted there. On his query appellant Raqib told him that his wife asked her to bring herbal medicine for causing miscarriage and requested him to take her to the house of accused Ful Banu. The root of plant was penetrated in the private organ of the deceased by accused Ful Banu in her house on 12-8-1997. The deceased admitted causing of abortion. 

 27. PW 9 gave evidence that on 13-8-1997 at 3-00/4-00 PM the deceased told him in the hospital that her husband accused Raqib taking her in the house of Ful Banu got a piece of root of plant applied in her private part by accused Ful Banu. She also told him (PW 9) that accused Raqib forcibly took away her to that house and that she was not willing to miscarriage her first conception. The above evidence of PW 9 had not been challenged in cross-examination. It was not said that deceased did not say so to him. Thus such evidence of PW 9 has gone unassailed. 

 29. PW 7 said that the accused Raqib told him (PW 7) that his wife Anowara asked him to bring herbal medicine for causing miscarriage and asked him to take her to the house of accused Ful Banu, where on 12-8-1997 Anowara through accused Ful Banu penetrated a root of tree of plant in her uterus. PW 9 said that Anwara told him that accused Raqib took her to the house of Ful Banu and got the piece of root of plant placed in her uterus by Ful Banu. By their above evidence it is well proved that at the instance of accused-husband Raqib miscarriage was caused. Involvement of the appellant in causing miscarriage has been well established. At his instance miscarriage was done. 

 30. But from the evidence of PW 5 we find that the deceased wife was a consenting party. PW 5 is a disinterested and independent witness. She said that the deceased told her that she was pot ready to carry the child at that time. She did not want a child. The evidence given by PW 7 that Anowara was not willing to cause miscarriage is incredible. He is not supposed to know whether miscarriage was done against her will or with her consent. He did not say that the deceased told him that she had no consent or against her will forcibly miscarriage was caused. PW 9 also did not say that his daughter Anowara told him that she was unwilling to cause miscarriage or she opposed causing miscarriage or forcibly miscarriage was done by her husband against her will. PW 9 is not supposed to know whether the deceased was a consenting party or not. If Anowara had no consent it would not have been possible for the appellant to take her to the house of Ful Banu and forcibly to place the root of plant in her uterus. Moreover, she did not disclose to anybody that she had no consent. So, evidence given by PWs 7 and 9 that the deceased was unwilling to miscarriage and the appellant forcibly caused miscarriage suffers from infirmity and is unworthy of credit. 

 31. Having regard to the above finding we are of the view that the prosecution has been able to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant with intent to cause miscarriage of the deceased got a piece of root of plant, Material Exhibit 1, placed in the uterus of the deceased by accused Ful Banu, which resulted in her death. The deceased wife had consent in such act of the accused husband. Therefore, we find that the appellant committed an offence punishable under section 314 Part 1 of the Penal Code. His act does not attract Part II of the same section. Maximum punishment under section 314 Part I of the Penal Code is imprisonment of either description for a term up to ten years with fine. The Court below wrongly sentenced the appellant to suffer imprisonment for life under section 314 of the Penal Code. Ends of justice will be met if the appellant is sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for five years under section 314 Part 1 of the Penal Code.

Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court (Mahbubey Alam, Advocate, Supreme Court, with him), instructed by Syed Sakhawat Ali, Advocate on Record -----For the Appellant,

parties:
S.M. Basiruddin ----- Appellant
Vs. 
Zahurul Islam Chowdhury and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam J.—This appeal by special leave arises from an application under section 14 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 filed by respondent No. l in respect of certain land with the Dacca City. The sale under pre-emption was effected by Ayesha Khatun respondent No. 2 in favour of the appellant by a kabala dated 10-9-73 which was registered on 5-4-76. The case land appertained to a permanent tenure recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 214 under Mouza Shahar Dacca, owned by Akshoy Kumar SahaBanik, and Rangubala Choudhurani. Akshoy Kumar SahaBanik instituted Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca for partition and by the decree passed in the suit Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik got 1/3rd share and Ran-gubala got the remaining rd share. One Nafisa Khatun by purchasing the interest of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik by a registered deed of sale dated 19-7-52 became co-sharer of Rangubala. Rangubala created a lease in respect of her 2/3rd share for 99 years by a registered deed of lease dated 23-12-53 in favour of Ayesha Khatun, respondent No. 2 Nafisa Khatun sold her interest to respondent No. 1 by a registered sale deed dated 18-4-72. Ayesha Khatun also sold her interest to the appellant by a registered sale deed dated 10-9-73. Against this sale respondent No. 1 filed the application for pre-emption. The appellant contested the case by filing written objection contending, inter alia, that the respondent No. 2 was not a co-sharer in the tenancy, because the land of the tenure was partitioned by the decree in Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 between Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Choudhurani ; and that a separate tenancy was created in favour of Ayesha Khatun by Rangubala by granting permanent lease for 99 years, reserving for herself annual rent of Tk. 1/-; and that Ayesha Khatun paid rent of Tk. 1/- to the lessor Rangubala till the rent receiving interest was acquired by the Government; and that S.A. Khatian was not correctly prepared because neither respondent No. 1 nor his vendor was co-sharer of Ayesha Khatun. He further claimed that after his purchase he applied for mutation of his name and accordingly his name was mutated in the S A. Khatian and jama was separated. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed pre-emption case against the appellant and the appeal was dismissed. Thereafter the appellant moved the High Court Division in revision under section 115(1)1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and being unsuccessful moved this Court and obtained leave from this Court to appeal from the judgment of the High Court Division. 

 2. Leave was granted to consider whether the learned Judge of the High Court Division was correct in making no distinction between the expression 'holding' as occurring in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the expression 'non-agricultural land' as occurring in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. At the hearing of the appeal the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant made two points out of the leave order. Firstly, he argued that upgradation of an under tenant to the status of a tenant under the Government on the acquisition of the rent-receiving interest over the tenant by the notification in April, 1956 did not have the effect of merging the two distinct interests, that is, of Akshoy and Rangubala on one side and that of Ayesha Khatun on the other hand; and, according to the learned Advocate, Ayesha Khatun attained the status of full tenant on up gradation and ceased to be a co-sharer-tenant of successor-in-interest of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik. In this context, he alternatively argued that the shares of Akshoy Kumar and Rangubala having been partitioned by the decree of the civil court in partition suit, resulting in the creation of two separate holdings under the Municipality. Akshoy Kumar and Rangubala ceased to be co-sharer in the tenancy. Secondly he argued that the expression 'non-agricultural land' as occurring in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act not being expression 'holding' as occurring in section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the learned Judge of the High Court Division fell into an error in treating the successors-in interest of Akshoy Kumar Saba Banik as co-sharer of Ayesha Khatun, and allowing the pre-emption case. In this connection the learned Advocate submitted that the decision relied upon by the High Court Division in the case of Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury v. Mosammat Rezia Begum, (l964) 16 DLR 77 has not laid down the law on correct interpretation of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

 3. Now let me examine the first point argued by Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant The learned Advocate strenuously argued in support of the proposition that on the elimination of the rent-receiving interest the under raiyati interest of Ayesha Khatun by operation of law became upgraded and attained the independent status of raiyat under the Government. On careful consideration of the argument of the learned Advocate I find it difficult to accept his proposition. Chapter IV of Part IV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 provides for "preparation of record-of-rights." This chapter contains the provision of preparation of record of rights with a view to assessment of compensation regarding interests of all rent-receivers which are liable to be acquired and which have already been acquired under Chapter II of the Act. Section 17 empowers the Government to make an order for preparation of record-of-rights. Section 18 provides that the Revenue-officers are to record certain particulars in the record of rights. Section 19 provides that they are to prepare the draft as well as final publication of such records. Section 20 prescribed the quantum of land 'which can be retained' by a person in his possession. Sections 21 and 22 provide that all lands are subject to payment of fair and equitable rent, as determined by the Revenue-officer in accordance with the provisions of Chapter IV and the rent so determined shall be entered in the record-of-rights. Sections 23 to 28 require the Revenue-officers to assess fair and equitable rents for different classes of tenants. Section 29 provides that the rents entered in the record-of-rights shall be deemed to have been correctly determined and to be fair and equitable. Preparation of record-of-rights in a district, part of a district or local area as provided in section 17 was intended to- 

 (k) the special conditions and incidents, if any, of the tenancy; 

 4. According to section 18 the Revenue-officer is required to prepare or revise the record-of-rights in pursuance of the order passed under section 17, and in preparing or revising the record-of-eights the Revenue- officer has been directed to record such particulars as may be prescribed under the Rules. Rule 18 quoted above shows that the nature of the particulars to be recorded as provided in clause (b) of rule 18 the Revenue officer is required to record the class or the classes to which each tenant or occupant belongs, whether the tenant is a proprietor, tenure holder, raiyat holding at fixed rates, settled raiyar, occupancy raiyat, non-occupancy raiyat, under raiyat, with or without a right of occupancy, or a non-agricultural tenant, and if he is a tenure-holder, whether be is a permanent tenure-bolder or not, and whether his rent is liable to enhancement during the continuance of his tenure, Clause (f) requires that rent payable at the time the record-of-rights is being prepared as well as the rents determined as fair and equitable according to rules 28 to 30 to be mentioned. Rule 24 provides for preparation of preliminary record-of-rights which is also known as draft record-or-rights. According to this rule, the draft record shall consist of statements of rights which are styled as the khatians. This rule further directs that ordinarily there shall be a separate khatian for each person interested, or each group of persons jointly interested, in the land, whether as proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyar, under-raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant and each khatian shall show the rights and liabilities of each person or group of persons. Statutory provisions clearly show sections 18 and 19 and the rules 18, 19 and 24 do not support the proposition canvassed by the learned Advocate on the elimination of the rent receiving interests all under-raiyats became raiyats under the Government and their status having thus been upgraded, the Revenue-officer while preparing the record-ofrights was required to record the under-raiyat as a raiyat in separate khatian, fixing fair and equitable rent for such upgraded tenant. It has already been stated above that the preparation of record of rights as provided in section 17 was with a view to assessment of compensation payable for all such interests liable to be acquired under the Act. Rule 24 provides for preparation of statements of rights which is styled as the khatian. According to this rule ordinarily there shall be a separate khatian for each person interested or each group of persons jointly interested in the land whether as proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyat, under-raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant and each khatian shall show the rights and liabilities of each person or group of persons, according to particulars mentioned in rule 18. The rules neither authorize nor require the Revenue-officer to prepare separate khatians for the individual raiyats and under-raysts, but, on the other hand, it provides that each group of person jointly interested in the land, whether as proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyat, under raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant ordinarily are to be shown in separate khatian, and it further provides that each khatian shall show the rights and liabilities of each person or group of persons, recording the particulars as indicated in rule 18. In support of the proposition that the under raiyat was upgraded to the status of raiyat, on the elimination of rent receiving interest, support was sought from the doctrine of merger as provide in section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act which provides that when the raiyati disappears the under-raiyat cannot any longer remain as such. Section 22 as it stands after amendment of 1907 merely provides that 08 the transfer of the occupancy right to a person jointly interested in the land as proprietor or permanent tenure-holder, such person shall have no right to hold the land as the raiyat but shall hold it as a proprietor or permanent tenure-holder as the case may be. By the amendment of 1907 the principle of merger as contemplated in section 22 was altered. The most important incident of merger under sub-section (1) of section 22 is that the landlord does not hold the land upon merger as a raiyat but holds it only as a proprietor or a permanent tenure-holder. It necessarily follows that the under-raiyats are automatically promoted to the status of raiyats. This view received judicial recognition in Ram Charan Sutradhar Vs. SM. Makhan, 38 CWN 1976, and it was followed by a Division Bench in the case of Pramatha Nath Shikder Vs. Jitendra Nath Roy. 43 CWN 1102. Upon acquisition of the rent receiving interests all under-raiyats by operation of law became raiyats under the Government is not in controversy, but the doctrine of merger as provided in section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act has no application to the conversion of all tenants holding land as proprietor, tenure holder raiyat, under-raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant, as raiyats or maliks under the Government. 

 5. The khatian was rightly prepared in accordance with rule 18, recording the under-raiyat of Ayesha Khatun without changing its status. Rule 18 provides that while preparing the record-of-right the Revenue-officer concerned shall record the class or classes to which each tenant or occupant belongs, that is, occupancy raiyat, non-occupancy-raiyat, under raiyat, etc. There is nothing in rule 18, which requires the Revenue-officer to record the under-raiyat as the upgraded raiyat in the khatian. It is in evidence that the S. A. Khatian was prepared by the Revenue-officer under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act recording Akshoy Kumar Saba Banik and Rangubala Cboudhurani as raiyats and Ayesha Khatun as under raiyat, and Jama of Tk. 10/- fixed under the Bengal Tenancy Act remaining the same. According to Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, in the S. A.  6. It appears from the decision that the argument made on behalf of the pre-emptee did not make any impression on the learned Judges. The learned Judges following the doctrine of merger as contained in sec. 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act expressed the opinion that in that case the raiyati interest in view of creation of under-raiyati under it, was a rent receiving interest within the meaning of the Act; and once raiyati interest (rent receiving interest) vested in the Government which became the proprietos, and consequently there being a merger of the former in the latter the under raiyati automatically stood upgraded to a raiyati. The learned Judges further observed that if an under raiyat become a tenant direct under the Proprietor, be becomes a raiyat as his landlord who was araiyat disappeared from the scene. 

 7. On carefully examining the different sections of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder, I am of the opinion that it is not correct to say that on the publication of the Notifications under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act existing classification and gradation of tenants as provided under the Bengal Tenancy Act disappeared and there was only one class of tenants with effect from April 14, 1956. It is correct that with from that date all tenants irrespective of their status under the Bengal Tenancy Act became liable to pay rent direct to the Government end for that purpose alone they were treated as raiyats under the Government, but for all other purposes the tenancies continued to be regulated by the Bengal Tenancy Act, that is why the Bengal Tenancy Act was kept in force till Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into operation on the publication of the Notification under section 79 of the Act and Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed by operation of section 80 of the Act. In the case of Mobasher Ali V. Md. Makbul Hossain, the conclusions arrived at by learned Judges are not based on correct appreciation of the different provisions of the statute. The learned Judges applied the doctrine of merger as provided is section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act which in my opinion is not applicable in the case of acquisition of rent receiving interests under section 3 of the Act. And on this wrong premise the learned Judges held that on the elimination of rent receiving interests an under-raiyat stood upgraded to the status of raiyat. It is by operation of section 3(4)(e) all tenants became tenant. directly under the Government, and as such all tenants became tenants under the Government not by a process of up gradation in consequence of merger as provided under section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Government by several Notifications acquired the interests of some of the rent- receivers as shown in the Notifications; and then by a general Notification dated the 2nd April, 1956 under section 3, acquired all the interests of the remaining rent-receivers with effect from 14th April, 1956. According to clause (e) of sub-section (4) of section 3 all tenants holding lands in such estatestaluks tenures, holdings or tenancies directly under the rent-receiver specified in Notification under sub-section (1) shall become tenants directly under the Government and shall pay rent at the existing rate, in respect of the rent-paying lands so held by them to the Government and not to anybody else provided that in cases where no notification was issued under sub-section (2) of section 43 before commencement of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance 1957, declaring that Compensation Assessment-roll in respect of the interest of any such rent-receiver in any such estate, taluk, tenure, holding or tenancy directly under such rent-receiver, shall as the tenants under the Government, be liable to pay rents in respect of lands so held by them except rent-free lands, at the rates determined in the record of rights finally published under sub-section (3) of section 19 subject to modification under section 53. Sub-section (4), clause e) of section 3 clearly shows that purpose of this provision is to ensure collection of rent by the Government from all the tenants who were liable to pay rent to the rent- receivers before the Notification. So the mandate is that on the vesting of the receiving interests in the Government, all tenants under the rent- receivers shall be liable to pay rent direct to the Government and not to anybody else. The statutory provisions sufficiently indicate that only for the purpose of collection of rent the existing tenants became one class, that is, 'raiyats' under the Government. However, the classification and gradation of different tenancies, for all other purposes, such as, identification and determinant of their status and their rights and other liabilities, continued till the notification under sub- section (21 of section 43 was issued. Section 33 provides for preparation of Compensation Assessment roll after the publication of the record-of-rights. Section 40 provides for preliminary publication of Compensation Assessment-roll after the amount of compensation has been determined in accordance with the provisions of sections 37, 38-39. Section 42 speaks about final publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll after all objections and appeals under section 40 have been disposed of. Sub-section (2) of section 43 provides that after the final publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll under section 42 in respect of any village or villages or local area, the Government shall by notification declare that a Compensation Assessment-rolls have been finally published. Section 44 provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in Chapter II of this Act or in any contract, but subject to the provisions of clauses (a), (b), (c) and (d) of sub-section (4) of section 3 and Sub-section (3) of section 46E on the publication of the notification in the Official Gazette under sub-section (2) of section 43 declaring that the Compensation Assessment-roll has been finally published, the following amongst other consequences shall ensue, namely- 

 (2) each proprietor,  tenure-holder and other rent-receiver, whose interests in any estate, tenure Of holding or tenancy or in any part of any estate, tenure or holding or tenancy, as the case may be, within the area to which  such roll relates, are acquired under this Act, shall with effect from the first day of the agricultural year next following the date of publication of such notification in the Official Gazette, be entitled to retain possession of and hold, subject to the provisions of this Act, as a tenant directly under the Government, all lands of which he is entitled to retain possession under Chapter IV and be liable to pay rent for such lands to the Provincial Government: 

 9. The scheme of the Act as shown from the different chapters does not provide that on the publication of the Notification under section 3 all rent-receivers were eliminated and all raiyats, under raiyats non-agricultural tenants, etc. existing in the estates acquired stood upgraded and along with it classification of tenants as provided under the Bengal Tenancy Act disappeared. What as a matter of fact happened is that with the publication of the Notification under section 3 all the rent receiving interests no doubts stood acquired, and the raiyats, under raiyats, non- agricultural tenants, for the purpose of payment of rent to the Government, became 'raiyats' under the Government, but the existing classification of tenants as contemplated under the Bengal Tenancy Act, and record-of-rights prepared under the Bengal Tenancy Act continued until publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll under section 43; and the consequences as provided under section 44 ensued, namely, acquisition and vesting of the interests of proprietors, tenure-holders and other rent-receivers, absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances subject to the rights of such proprietors tenure-holders and other relit receivers specified in clause (2) of section 44. This view also gets support from the fact that Bengal Tenancy Act continued to be operative side by side with the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and this state continued till commencement of Part V of the Act and the consequent repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act. 1885. Until repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act the classification of tenants, for the purpose of determination of the tenant rights and liabilities continued to be governed by the Bengal Tenancy Act otherwise there was no necessity of keeping the Bengal Tenancy Act operative along with the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In view of the position in law is obtaining due to both the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the Bengal Tenancy Act bolding the same field, an under ralyat, no doubt, on the elimination of the rent-receiver (raiyat who created the under raiyat) attained the status of raiyat directly under the Government, as the Government by operation of law became the owner, and the under raiyat became liable to pay rent direct to the Government and to no other agency unless specifically authorized by the Government in this behalf. In my opinion in Mobasher Ali Vs. Md. Makbul Hossain, the learned Judges were not correct in taking the view that once the raiyati interest vested in the Government by virtue of acquisition of the superior interests, by the process of merger the under-raiyati automatically stood upgraded to a raiyat for all purposes. Correct analysis or the different provisions of the Act keeping in view the whole scheme of acquisition by the State of the interests of rent-receivers and certain other interests in" land in Bangladesh, does not warrant the following conclusion- 

 Rule 61 which speaks about the stage after the final publication of Compensation Assessment-rolls and the above noted provisions of the Act and other rules clearly show that the different classes of tenancies did not cease to exist immediately on the publication of the notification under section 3 of the Act; and the entire chain of rent-receivers would be eliminated only after the publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll. Chapter XII of Part V provides about application of this part and class of agricultural tenants. Section 79 of Chapter XII speaks about commencement of Part V. It provides that Part V or any portion thereof shall come into force in such areas on such-dates and to such extent as the Government may, by notification, direct and when any portion of this Part comes into force in any area, the provisions of such portion shall have effect in such area notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. As section 79 provides Part V came into force in such areas, on such dates and to such extent as the Government by notification directed this notification of necessity was after publication of the notification under sub-section (2) of section 43 of the Act. Part V came into force in different areas on different dates by different notifications, Section 80 deals with repeal of the enactments specified in the schedule to the Act. Section 81 deals with agricultural tenants and regulation of their rights and liabilities. This section provides that on and from the date of coming into force of the whole of this Part in any area there shall, within that area, be only one class of holders of agricultural land, namely. 'Malik’s," and the rights and liabilities of every such land-holder shall be regulated by the provisions of this Part. Section 81 A deals with rights and liabilities of non-agricultural tenants. Sub-section (1) of section 81 A provides that except as otherwise provided in this Part the rights and liabilities of a holder of non-agricultural land who has become a tenant under the Government in respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior right in such land under the provisions of this Act, shall, where the provisions of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 applied to such land at the time of such acquisition, be regulated by the provisions of that Act, Section 82 provides the relevant interpretations. 

 11. Mr. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, in support of the proposition that the under-raiyati of Ayesha Khatun became upgraded and formed a separate independent bolding, relied upon a decision of this Court in the case of Anwara Begum v. Nurjahan, 27 DLR(AD) 109. From the reported decision it appears that similar question was under consideration on almost similar facts. Two applications under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act were filed in the Court of the Munsif at North Rauzan, Chittagong for pre-emption of transfer of certain land to the preemptee, claiming to be co-sharers in the occupancy raiyati holding to which the said land appertained. The pre-emption cases were contested by the pre-emptee contending, inter alia, that the land sought to be pre-empted appertained to korfa (under-raiyati) holding and as such right of pre-emption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act was not available to a co-sharer in the raiyati holding. The trial Court on evidence found that the holding was an occupancy raiyati holding and accordingly the pre-emption cases were allowed.  12. On the prayer of the pre-emptee leave was granted to consider (1) whether prior to coming into operation of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (hereinafter referred to as the Act), the Korfa (under raiyati) tenancy became upgraded to a raiyati tenancy on and from 14-4-56 simply because by the general Notification under- section 3 of the Act the rent-receiving interests stood acquired with effect from 14-4-56; and (2) whether, in case of upgrading of under-raiyati to a raiyati in the above circumstances, pre-emption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act was available in the instant case. 

 "Having considered the contention of the learned Counsel with reference to the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as well as the relevant provisions of the B.T. Act, we are inclined to hold that the view expressed in the case of Mubasher Ali that after the Notification issued under section 3 of the Act, the status of the under-raiyat became upgraded to that of raiyat, was correct and the impugned judgment of the learned Single Judge of the High Court, being passed upon that view, calls for no interference.'' 

 (a) Whether before Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into operation the under-raiyati, 'although his liability to pay rent direct to the Government commenced from. 14.4.56, became a raiyat or Malik under the Government as contemplated in section 81 of the Act; and 

 (b) whether section 3 (4) (e) read with section 81 support the contention that on the publication of Notification under section 3 the classification of the tenants made under the Bengal Tenancy Act disappeared •and all tenants attained the status of raiyats. 

 Chapter XII of Part V contains the heading "Application of this Part and class of agricultural tenants." Section 79 provides that Part V or any portion thereon shall come into force only by a notification published in the Official Gazette. Section 80 provides that with the notification the enactments specified in the schedule shall be repealed. According to this section Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed when Part V of the Act came into operation on the publication of the statutory notification in the Official Gazette, and this was done by separate notifications for separate are is of districts on different dates. The expression "there shall be only one class of holders of agricultural land, namely, Malik’s", as occurring in section 81 clearly implies that the existing classification of tenants will continue as such till Part V of the Act comes into force. Sections 79, 80 and 81 clearly show that from the date mentioned in the notification there shall be only one class of holders of agricultural land, namely, 'mans', and the rights and liabilities of every such holder shall be regulated by Part V. It also impliedly shows that till V came into operation some of the rights and liabilities of holders of agricultural land were being governed by the Bengal Tenancy Act. 

 15. (c) In the case reported in 27 DLR (AD) 109 another relevant question was raised; namely, whether an under-raiyat becoming a tenant direct under the Government on the publication of the Notification under section 3, acquired the status of an occupancy raiyat as contemplated under the Bengal Tenancy Act, which was necessary for determination of the claim of pre-emption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act. An application for pre-emption under section 26F by such a tenant or against such a tenant cannot be decided without a finding regarding the status of the pre-emptor and the pre-emptee. Section 26F provides that in all cases of transfer of occupancy holding in raiyat land, whether by private sale or by sale in execution of a decree, or by foreclosure, a co-sharer in the holding shall have the right of pre-emption. In an application under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act one of the statutory requirements is that transfer sought to be pre-empted must to an occupancy holding. For successfully maintaining a case of pre-emption under section 26F it must be shown that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the holding with occupancy right ; and that transfer sought to be pre-empted is in respect of a part of an occupancy holding. The judgment does not show that this vital aspect of the case was examined. 

 16. All that sub-section (4)(e) of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides is that all tenants holding lands in such estates (rent-receiving) shall become tenants directly under the Government and shall pay rent at the existing rate to the Government and not to anybody else. This speaks about the tenant's liability to pay rent the tenant is directed to pay rent to the Government directly and to nobody else. There is nothing in the statute that with the elimination of the rent-receiving interests a non-occupancy holding shall automatically stand raised to the class of occupancy holding. Chapter XIII deals with the incidents of holdings raiyats. Section 83 provides that a raiyat shall have the right to occupy and use the land comprised in his holding in any manner he likes. This Chapter makes it clear that before the publication of notification under section 80 an under-raiyat although treated as a raiyat under the Government for the purpose of realization of rent, such holding did not acquire the status of occupancy holding. With due respect to the learned Judges I must say that the conclusions arrived at in that case are not based on correct interpretation of the different provisions of the Act and the rules framed thereunder; and it does not provide the necessary guidance. 

 17. In my opinion after the Notification under section 3 and until Part V of the Act was brought into, operation, the classification of tenants as contemplated under section 4of the Bengal Tenancy Act continued; and with the publication of notification under section 80 the classifications and gradation of tenants disappeared and then all tenants became 'raiyats' or' Malik’s' under the Government; and further, only after such notification their rights and liabilities were to be governed under Part V. 

 19. Now let me examine the question whether the expression 'holding' as occurring in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the expression 'non-agriculturaland' in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act are synonymous and without any distinction. The learned Judge of the High Court Division in taking the view that the two expressions are synonymous and without any distinction, followed a decision of East Pakistan High Court in the case of Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury v. Mosammat Rezia Begum16 DLR 77. In this decision it has been held that the word 'non-agricultural land' in section 24 of the Non- Agricultural Tenancy Act has been used in the same sense as the expression 'holding' has been used in section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act. In this case arising out of a proceeding under section 24 ofthe East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, one of the points for consideration was whether the pre-emptors were co-sharer tenants in the 'non-agricultural land' within the meaning of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and were entitled to pre-empt the land. Relying on a decision of Sekandar Ali, J. in the case of Manindra Chandra Ghose Vs. Mujibul Islam, 12-DLR 785, it was argued that the words 'non-agricultural land' used in section 24 is equivalent to 'holding' as defined in sub-section (5) of section 3 of the Bengal Tenancy Act In a subsequent case a Division Bench consisting of K.M. Hassan and Sekandar Ali J.J. differed on this question. According to Hasan, J. the words non-agricultural land means a 'piece' of land in joint possession and enjoyment without partition which may form a tenancy or a portion of a tenancy. The learned Judge explained that this interpretation will not throw the land open to unlimited number of persons but 'to persons who are co-sharer tenants under the same landlord in respect of the undivided land though such co-sharer tenants may be co-sharer-tenants of the tenancy. On taking this view Hasan, J. dismissed the appeal of the pre-emptors and affirmed the decision of the lower appellate C9Prt, dismissing the pre-emption case as not maintainable Ali, J. however took the view that the word land in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act has been used in the sense as 'holding" has been used in section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The reason given by the learned Judge for taking this view is that under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act in the case of transfer by one or more or a group of tenants in exclusive possession of a separate parcel on the basis of, a partition or division among themselves of some land appertaining to that parcel to a co-sharer tenant holding some other parcel but having no interest in the parcel to which the land transferred appertains, the other co-sharers interested in, or in exclusive possession of, the first mentioned parcel shall not be entitled to pre-empt. In other words, the transfer in favour of the said co-sharer though detached from the parcel concerned by partition or division shall stand good and absolute. The learned Judge further observed that the crux of the question whether a tenant is entitled to pre-empt is the undivided character of the tenancy and the word 'land' in section 24 has been used in the sense as 'holding' has been used in section 26A of the Bengal Tenancy Act. As the learned Judges differed the matter was referred to a third Judge for hearing and disposal of the appeal. Murshed J. as the third Judge agreed with the view taken by Sekander Ali J. Murshed J. proceeded on the assumption that the original tenancy was never divided or split up although there was separate possession of the land as a matter of mutual convenience. Murshed J. agreeing with the reasoning’s of Sekandar Ali J held that in spite of amicable partition and exclusive possession of the land by the co-sharers, the tenancy continued as a single unit. The learned Judge 'further observed that the tenancy being one the land possessed by the pre-emptor- appellants and that possessed by the respondents formed one unit under the same tenancy and each of them was liable for the payment of the rental to the landlord. 

 21. Murshed J. it appears, did not find any material difference in the two expressions—co-sharer-tenants of the holding occurring in section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and the expression co-sharer tenant of such land occurring in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. While considering why the word 'holding' has not been used in section 24, he found a good deal of force in the argument advanced by the alnico clear, namely, by the omission of the word 'holding' only a confusion of idea was sought to be avoided. The learned Judge agreeing with the view taken by Sekandar Ali J. allowed the appeals of the pre-emptors. 

 22. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed strenuously argued that the expression 'co- sharer-tenants of the non-agricultural land occurring in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and the expression a co-sharer in the tenancy' occurring in section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act connote different meaning, and the two expressions used in different context are not synonymous. With reference to different sub-sections of section 24 he pointed out that the Legislature while using the expressions 'co-sharer tenants of land' and 'co-sharer in the tenancy' in different sub-sections used the two expressions in different context for different purpose. 

 23. In the instant case it is in evidence that the shares of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Choudhurani 1/3rd and 2/3rd respectively were partitioned by a decree made in Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 of the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca. The preemptor being a successor-in-interest by purchasing the 1/3rd share of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik claimed pre-emption when Ayesha Khatun sold her under-raiyati interest, which comprises the entire land in the 2/3rd share of Rangubala Choudhurani. After partition the co-sharers started exclusive possession by separating their shares by metes and bound. On these facts the question has been raised whether the purchaser of the 1/3rd share of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik could lawfully maintain his application for pre-emption of the land transferred by Ayesha Khatun, that is the 2/3rd share of Rangubala Choudhurani acquired by her in under-raiyati right. I find sufficient force in, the submission of the learned advocate that the expression 'non-Agricultural land' occurring in section 24 of the Non-agricultural Tenancy Act does not convey the same meaning as conveyed by the expression "one or more co-sharer tenants of the holding" occurring in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The word 'holding' has been defined in section 2(13) of the Act. According to this definition 'hole ding' means a parcel or parcels of land or an undivided share thereof held by a raiyat or an under-raiyat and forming the subject of a separate tenancy. The expression 'non-agricultural-tenant' has been defined in section 2(17) means a tenants who holds land for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture, but does not include a person holding together with any building standing thereon and necessary adjuncts thereto under a lease other than a lease in perpetuity. The word 'land' has been defined in section 2(16). According to this definition "land' means land which is cultivated, uncultivated or covered with water at any time of the year and includes (arise out of the land) houses or buildings and also things attached to the earth, or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth. The expression 'non- agricultural land' has been defined in section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. It means land which is used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture and includes any land which is held on lease for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture irrespective of whether it is used for any such purposes or not, but does not include,- 

 (a) a homestead to which the provisions of section 182 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 apply, 

 Provided that where an order has been made under section 72 converting a parcel of land which is 'not non-agricultural land into a tenancy.to which the provisions of this Act apply such land shall be deemed to be non-agricultural land. 

 24. The word 'holding' means a parcel or parcels of land or an undivided share thereof, held by a raiyat or an under-raiyat and forming the subject of a separate tenancy. 'Non-agricultural land has not been used in the context of 'holding' as defined in section 2(13) of the Act. According to this definition 'holding' means a parcel or parcels of land or, an undivided share thereof. Different sub-sections of section 24 sufficiently indicate that the Legislature did not use the expression 'non-agricultural land' carrying the same meaning as the expression 'holding' defined in the Bengal Tenancy Act and State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The expression 'non-agricultural land' may represent the entire land comprised in a tenancy or it may form a part as owned and possessed by a tenant or tenants on partition. 

 25. According to Mr. M.H. Khondker, the learned Counsel appearing for the pre-emptor respondent the expression 'non-agricultural land' is equivalent to the word 'holding' as defined " in sub-section (5) of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act; and in support of his argument reliance was placed on the decisions in the case of Manindra Chandra chose Vs. M. Mujibul Islam, 12 DLR 785; and Brindaban Chandra Choudhury Vs.  26. On careful examination of the different sub-sections of section 24 I feel inclined to accept the argument of Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed that expression 'non-agricultural land' used in section 24 of the Act is not synonymous with the word 'holding' as used in the Bengal Tenancy Act or State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Sekandar Ali, J. sitting singly in the case reported in 12 DLR 785 took the view that the expression 'non-agricultural land' is equivalent to the word 'holding' as used in the Bengal Tenancy Act.  27. In Brindaban Chandra Choudhury v. Mosammat Rezia Begum this question was exathined.
